IBNKATHIR:1:1/r34.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r34.claim: Abu Saʿid ibn al-Muʿalla reports that the Prophet promised to teach him the Qur'an's greatest surah and identified it as al-Hamd, the seven oft-repeated and the great Qur'an.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r34.anchor: الحمد لله رب العالمين هي : السبع المثاني والقرآن العظيم الذي أوتيته

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r35.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r35.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r35.claim: Ibn Kathir distinguishes the Muwatta's Abu Saʿid, a Successor and client of Khuzāʿa, from the Companion Abu Saʿid ibn al-Muʿalla; the former report appears disconnected unless he heard it from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r35.anchor: فأبو سعيد هذا ليس بأبي سعيد بن المعلى ، كما اعتقده ابن الأثير

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r36.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r36.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r36.claim: A report through Abu Hurayra from Ubayy repeats that the Fatiha has no equal in the Torah, Gospel, Psalms, or Qur'an; al-Tirmidhi calls it hasan sahih.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r36.anchor: إني لأرجو ألا أخرج من هذا الباب حتى تعلمها

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r37.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r37.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r37.claim: Another report from Ubayy calls Umm al-Qur'an the seven oft-repeated, divided between God and His servant; al-Tirmidhi grades it hasan gharib.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r37.anchor: ما أنزل الله في التوراة ولا في الإنجيل مثل أم القرآن ، وهي السبع المثاني ، وهي مقسومة بيني وبين عبدي

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r38.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r38.speaker: عبد الله بن جابر
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r38.claim: The report that the Prophet called the Fatiha the best surah has a good chain according to Ibn Kathir; the Companion's identity is uncertain between al-ʿAbdi and al-Ansari al-Bayyadi.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r38.anchor: هذا إسناد جيد ،   وابن عقيل تحتج{[60]} به الأئمة الكبار ،   وعبد الله بن جابر هذا هو الصحابي

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r39.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r39.speaker: إسحاق بن راهويه وأبو بكر بن العربي وابن الحصار
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r39.claim: These scholars infer that some verses and surahs are superior to others from the superiority reports.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r39.anchor: واستدلوا بهذا الحديث وأمثاله على تفاضل بعض الآيات والسور

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r40.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r40.speaker: الأشعري وأبو بكر الباقلاني وابن حبان ويحيى بن يحيى
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r40.claim: Another group denies ranking Qur'anic passages, since all are God's speech and ranking could imply deficiency in what is less preferred; a report from Malik agrees.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r40.anchor: وذهبت طائفة أخرى إلى أنه لا تفاضل في ذلك ؛ لأن الجميع كلام الله ، ولئلا يوهم التفضيل نقص المفضل عليه

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r41.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r41.speaker: أبو سعيد الخدري
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r41.claim: In a report judged by the Prophet, a companion recited the Fatiha as ruqya over a stung man who recovered; the Prophet approved the reward of thirty sheep and asked how he knew it was ruqya.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r41.anchor: فبرأ ، فأمر له بثلاثين شاة ، وسقانا لبنا

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r42.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r42.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r42.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas reports that Gabriel announced two lights given to Muhammad alone: the Fatiha and the closing verses of al-Baqara; each letter brings a response.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r42.anchor: أبشر بنورين قد أوتيتهما لم يؤتهما نبي قبلك : فاتحة الكتاب ، وخواتيم سورة البقرة

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r43.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r43.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r43.claim: The Prophet says prayer without Umm al-Qur'an is deficient, and the divine hadith answers the servant's praise verse by verse as the Fatiha is divided between God and servant.

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r46.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r46.speaker: أبو حنيفة وأصحابه
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r46.claim: Abu Hanifa and his followers hold that Fatiha is not specifically required in prayer; any Qur'an passage suffices, citing 73:20 and “recite what is easy.”
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r46.anchor: فعند أبي حنيفة ومن وافقه من أصحابه وغيرهم أنها لا تتعين

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r47.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r47.speaker: مالك والشافعي وأحمد والجمهور
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r47.claim: The other major view requires the Fatiha in prayer, using the deficient-prayer hadith and reports that prayer does not count without it.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r47.anchor: والقول الثاني : أنه تتعين قراءة الفاتحة في الصلاة ، ولا تجزئ الصلاة بدونها

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r48.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r48.speaker: الشافعي وجماعة من أهل العلم
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r48.claim: Al-Shafiʿi and a group require the Fatiha in every prayer unit; others require it in most units, while Hasan and most Basrans require it in one unit.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r48.anchor: أنه تجب قراءتها في كل ركعة

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r49.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r49.speaker: الحسن وأكثر البصريين
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r49.claim: Hasan and most Basrans require the Fatiha in only one unit, relying on the unrestricted wording, “There is no prayer without Fatiha.”
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r49.anchor: وقال الحسن وأكثر البصريين : إنما تجب قراءتها في ركعة واحدة من الصلوات

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r50.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r50.speaker: أبو حنيفة والثوري والأوزاعي
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r50.claim: Abu Hanifa, al-Thawri, and al-Awzaʿi again hold that another Qur'anic passage can replace the Fatiha, citing 73:20.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r50.anchor: وقال أبو حنيفة وأصحابه والثوري والأوزاعي : لا تتعين

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r51.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r51.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r51.claim: A report that each prayer unit needs al-Hamd and another surah is questionable in authenticity.

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r52.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r52.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r52.claim: Scholars have three views on whether a follower must recite: that the follower must recite the Fatiha just like the imam.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r52.anchor: أحدها : أنه تجب عليه قراءتها ، كما تجب على إمامه

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r53.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r53.speaker: مالك
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r53.claim: A second view says a follower recites nothing, whether prayer is audible or silent, based on “one with an imam has the imam's recitation”; the marfuʿ routes are weak, and Malik transmits it as Jabir's own statement.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r53.anchor: من كان له إمام فقراءة الإمام له قراءة » ولكن في إسناده ضعف

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r54.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r54.speaker: الشافعي في قوله القديم وأحمد في رواية
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r54.claim: A third view requires the follower's recitation in silent prayer but not audible prayer, combining the general requirement with the command to listen when the imam recites.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r54.anchor: أنه تجب القراءة على المأموم في السرية

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r55.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r55.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r55.claim: Al-Bazzar reports that reciting the Fatiha and Surat al-Ikhlas before sleep protects from everything except death.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r55.anchor: فقد أمنت من كل شيء إلا الموت

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r104.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r104.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r104.claim: The Companions opened God's Book with the basmala; scholars agree it is part of the verse in Surat al-Naml, while disputing its status at surah openings.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r104.anchor: افتتح بها الصحابة كتاب الله ، واتفق العلماء على أنها بعض آية من سورة النمل

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r105.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r105.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r105.claim: A sound Abu Dawud report from Ibn ʿAbbas says the Prophet recognized a surah's division when the basmala was revealed; it is also reported mursal from Saʿid ibn Jubayr.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r105.anchor: كان لا يعرف فصل السورة حتى ينزل عليه

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r106.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r106.speaker: أم سلمة
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r106.claim: A report from Umm Salama says the Prophet recited and counted the basmala as a verse at the start of the Fatiha; Ibn Kathir notes the chain is weak because of ʿUmar ibn Harun.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r106.anchor: عن أم سلمة : أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم قرأ البسملة في أول الفاتحة في الصلاة وعدّها آية

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r107.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r107.speaker: ابن عباس وابن عمر وابن الزبير وأبو هريرة وعلي
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r107.claim: These Companions are cited as holding that the basmala is a verse at the start of every surah except al-Tawba; several Successors and a group of later authorities agree.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r107.anchor: وممن حكي عنه أنها آية من كل سورة إلا براءة : ابن عباس ، وابن عمر ، وابن الزبير

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r108.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r108.speaker: مالك وأبو حنيفة وأصحابهما
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r108.claim: Malik, Abu Hanifa, and their followers say the basmala is not a verse of the Fatiha or any other surah.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r108.anchor: وقال مالك وأبو حنيفة وأصحابهما : ليست آية من الفاتحة ولا من غيرها من السور

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r109.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r109.speaker: الشافعي
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r109.claim: One Shafiʿi position makes the basmala a verse of the Fatiha alone; another makes it part of the first verse of every surah, and Ibn Kathir calls both views unusual.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r109.anchor: وقال الشافعي في قول ، في بعض طرق مذهبه : هي آية من الفاتحة وليست من غيرها

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r110.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r110.speaker: داود وأحمد
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r110.claim: Dawud and one narration from Ahmad treat the basmala as an independent opening verse of each surah, not part of the surahs.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r110.anchor: وقال داود : هي آية مستقلة في أول كل سورة لا منها

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r111.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r111.speaker: الشافعي
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r111.claim: Al-Shafiʿi recites the basmala aloud with both Fatiha and the following surah when opening prayer; many early and later authorities also did so.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r111.anchor: فذهب الشافعي ، رحمه الله ، إلى أنه يجهر بها مع الفاتحة والسورة

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r112.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r112.speaker: أبو هريرة
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r112.claim: Abu Hurayra recited the basmala aloud and said his prayer most resembled the Prophet's; Ibn Kathir cites several scholars who authenticated the report.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r112.anchor: أنه صلى فجهر في قراءته بالبسملة ، وقال بعد أن فرغ : إني لأشبهكم صلاة برسول الله

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r113.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r113.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r113.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas reports that the Prophet opened prayer with the basmala; al-Tirmidhi says its chain is not strong.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r113.anchor: أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم كان يفتتح الصلاة ببسم الله الرحمن الرحيم

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r114.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r114.speaker: أنس بن مالك
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r114.claim: Anas describes the Prophet's recitation as prolonged, with lengthening on each word of the basmala.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r114.anchor: كانت قراءته مدا ، ثم قرأ بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم ، يمد بسم الله

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r115.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r115.speaker: أم سلمة
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r115.claim: Umm Salama says the Prophet paused phrase by phrase in recitation, and al-Daraqutni calls the report's chain sound.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r115.anchor: عن أم سلمة ، قالت{[812]} : كان رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم يقطع قراءته

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r116.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r116.speaker: أنس بن مالك
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r116.claim: When Muʿawiya omitted the basmala in Medina, the Muhajirun present objected; on his next prayer he recited it.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r116.anchor: فترك البسملة ، فأنكر عليه من حضره من المهاجرين ذلك

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r117.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r117.speaker: أبو حنيفة والثوري وأحمد
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r117.claim: Another group does not recite the basmala aloud; Ibn Kathir says this is established from the four caliphs, Ibn Mughaffal, and other early authorities.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r117.anchor: وذهب آخرون إلى أنه لا يجهر بالبسملة في الصلاة ، وهذا هو الثابت عن الخلفاء الأربعة

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r118.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r118.speaker: مالك
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r118.claim: Malik does not recite the basmala in prayer either aloud or quietly, relying on reports that the Prophet and first caliphs began with al-Hamd and did not mention it.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r118.anchor: وعند الإمام مالك : أنه لا يقرأ البسملة بالكلية ، لا جهرًا ولا سرًّا

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r119.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r119.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r119.claim: The legal disagreement is narrow: scholars agree a prayer is valid whether the basmala is recited aloud or quietly.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r119.anchor: لأنهم أجمعوا على صحة صلاة من جهر بالبسملة ومن أسر

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r120.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r120.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r120.claim: A report says the basmala is one of God's names, extremely close to the Greatest Name, like the closeness between the black and white of the eye.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r120.anchor: هو اسم من أسماء الله ، وما بينه وبين اسم الله الأكبر ، إلا كما بين سواد العينين وبياضهما

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r121.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r121.speaker: عيسى ابن مريم
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r121.claim: A report explains the letters as bāʾ for God's splendor, sīn for His glory, and mīm for His dominion; Rahman is merciful in both worlds and Rahim in the next. Ibn Kathir calls the report very strange and possibly Israelite rather than Prophetic.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r121.anchor: الباء بهاء الله ، والسين سناؤه ، والميم مملكته

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r122.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r122.speaker: الضحاك
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r122.claim: Al-Dahhak is said to have transmitted a similar explanation of the basmala.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r122.anchor: وقد روى جُوَيبر{[824]} ، عن الضحَّاك ،   نحوه من قبله

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r123.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r123.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r123.claim: A report from Burayda says the basmala was revealed to Muhammad and Solomon alone.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r123.anchor: أنزلت علي آية لم تنزل على نبي غير سليمان بن داود وغيري ، وهي بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r124.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r124.speaker: جابر بن عبد الله
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r124.claim: Jabir's report describes clouds fleeing, winds and sea becoming still, animals listening, devils pelted, and God's promise of blessing when His name is said over something.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r124.anchor: عن جابر بن عبد الله ،   قال : لما نزل

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r125.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r125.speaker: ابن مسعود
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r125.claim: Ibn Masʿud reportedly says reciting the basmala shields a person from each of the nineteen keepers of Hell; Ibn ʿAtiyya supports this with a report of more than thirty angels hastening to record praise.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r125.anchor: من أراد أن ينجيه الله من الزبانية التسعة عشر فليقرأ : بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r126.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r126.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r126.claim: A report says not to curse Satan after a fall because that makes him swell with pride; saying “in God's name” makes him shrink like a fly (another version says like a house).
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r126.anchor: لا تقل تعس الشيطان . فإنك إذا قلت : تعس الشيطان تعاظم

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r127.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r127.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r127.claim: Because the basmala humbles Satan, it is recommended at the beginning of actions and speech.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r127.anchor: فهذا من تأثير بركة بسم الله ؛ ولهذا تستحب في أوّل كل عمل وقول

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r128.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r128.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r128.claim: A report recommends beginning a sermon with the basmala and calls an affair begun without it defective.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r128.anchor: لا يبدأ فيه ببسم الله الرحمن الرحيم ،   فهو أجذم

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r129.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r129.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r129.claim: The basmala is recommended on entering the toilet, based on reports transmitted on that practice.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r129.anchor: وتستحب البسملة عند دخول الخلاء ولما ورد من الحديث في ذلك

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r130.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r130.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r130.claim: A hadith judged hasan says there is no ablution for one who does not mention God's name; scholars differ over whether it is obligatory when remembered or absolutely.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r130.anchor: من رواية أبي هريرة ،   وسعيد بن زيد ،   وأبي سعيد مرفوعًا

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r131.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r131.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r131.claim: The basmala is recommended before slaughter according to al-Shafiʿi and a group; others require it if remembered, and some require it absolutely.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r131.anchor: وكذا تستحب عند الذبيحة في مذهب الشافعي وجماعة ، وأوجبها آخرون عند الذكر

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r132.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r132.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r132.claim: The Prophet instructed his stepson ʿUmar ibn Abi Salama to say God's name, eat with his right hand, and eat from what is nearest; some scholars make the basmala obligatory at meals.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r132.anchor: قل : باسم الله ، وكل بيمينك ، وكل مما يليك

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r133.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r133.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r133.claim: The Prophet taught spouses to say God's name and ask protection from Satan before intercourse; if a child is conceived, Satan will not harm it.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r133.anchor: لو أن أحدكم إذا أتى أهله قال : باسم الله ، اللهم جنبنا الشيطان

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r134.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r134.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r134.claim: The preposition bi in the basmala may attach to an implied noun, “my beginning,” or verb, “I begin”; Qur'anic usage supports both.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r134.anchor: هل هو اسم أو فعل متقاربان وكل قد ورد به القرآن

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r135.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r135.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r135.claim: The implied action varies with the activity begun—standing, sitting, eating, drinking, reciting, ablution, or prayer—and the basmala seeks blessing, aid to completion, and acceptance.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r135.anchor: وذلك بحسب الفعل الذي سميت قبله ، إن كان قيامًا أو قعودًا أو أكلا أو شربًا

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r136.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r136.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r136.claim: In a report on the first revelation, Gabriel tells Muhammad to say the basmala and explains it as beginning, standing, and sitting in remembrance of God; Ibn Kathir elsewhere calls the report weak and disconnected.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r136.anchor: قال له جبريل : قل : باسم الله يا محمد ، يقول : اقرأ بذكر الله ربك

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r137.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r137.speaker: أبو عبيدة وسيبويه
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r137.claim: One position identifies a name with the named object; Abu ʿUbayda and Sibawayh hold this view, as do al-Baqillani and Ibn Furak.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r137.anchor: أن الاسم هو المسمى ، وهو قول أبي عبيدة وسيبويه

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r138.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r138.speaker: فخر الدين الرازي
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r138.claim: Al-Razi reports that the Hashwiyya, Karramiyya, and Ashʿariyya identify name and named but distinguish both from naming, while the Muʿtazila distinguish name from named and equate it with naming; he chooses a third view.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r138.anchor: قالت الحشوية والكرامية والأشعرية : الاسم نفس المسمى وغير التسمية ، وقالت المعتزلة : الاسم غير المسمى ونفس التسمية

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r139.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r139.speaker: فخر الدين الرازي
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r139.claim: Al-Razi's preferred view is that the name differs from both the named thing and the act of naming.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r139.anchor: والمختار عندنا : أن الاسم غير المسمى وغير التسمية

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r140.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r140.speaker: فخر الدين الرازي
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r140.claim: Al-Razi argues that names can exist without their referents, one thing can have many names, one name can refer to many things, and a word is an accident while its referent may be an entity.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r140.anchor: قد يكون الاسم موجودًا والمسمى مفقودًا كلفظة المعدوم

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r141.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r141.speaker: فخر الدين الرازي
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r141.claim: Al-Razi says God's many names refer to one God and that calling God by those names indicates their distinction from Him.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r141.anchor: فهذه أسماء كثيرة والمسمى واحد وهو الله تعالى

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r142.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r142.speaker: فخر الدين الرازي
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r142.claim: Those who equate name and named cite “blessed is the name of your Lord”; al-Razi answers that honoring the name honors the sacred essence, and a divorce utterance refers to the person bearing that name.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r142.anchor: والجواب : أن الاسم معظم لتعظيم الذات المقدسة

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r143.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r143.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r143.claim: Allah is the proper name of the Lord and is called the Greatest Name because all the other attributes are predicated of Him.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r143.anchor: على الرب تبارك وتعالى ، يقال : إنه الاسم الأعظم

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r144.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r144.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r144.claim: A sound hadith says God has ninety-nine names; whoever comprehends them enters Paradise, though the enumerated lists in al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah differ.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r144.anchor: إن لله تسعة وتسعين اسما ، مائة إلا واحدًا من أحصاها دخل الجنة

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r145.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r145.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r145.claim: Allah is a name not used for anyone else, and Arabic does not clearly derive it from an ordinary verb.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r145.anchor: وهو اسم لم يسم به غيره تبارك وتعالى ؛ ولهذا لا يعرف في كلام العرب له اشتقاق من فعل ويفعل

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r146.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r146.speaker: الشافعي والخطابي وإمام الحرمين والغزالي والخليل وسيبويه
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r146.claim: These scholars regard Allah as an underived, fixed proper name; al-Khattabi argues that the vocative “ya Allah” works, whereas “ya al-Rahman” does not.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r146.anchor: فذهب من ذهب من النحاة إلى أنه اسم جامد لا اشتقاق له

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r147.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r147.speaker: رؤبة بن العجاج
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r147.claim: Ruʾba's line uses taʾalluh, worship, as evidence that Allah is derived from the root for worship.

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r148.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r148.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r148.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas's reading “wa-yadharuka wa-ilahatak” is explained as “your worship”; Mujahid gives the same gloss.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r148.anchor: كما روي أن ابن عباس قرأ

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r149.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r149.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r149.claim: Those who derive Allah from divinity cite that God is worshipped in heaven and earth and is a god in both realms.

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r150.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r150.speaker: الخليل وسيبويه
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r150.claim: Al-Khalil and Sibawayh derive the word from ilah, with the article replacing an initial hamza, by analogy with al-nas from unas; another proposal takes it from lah for exalted.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r150.anchor: أن أصله : إلاه ، مثل فعال ، فأدخلت الألف واللام بدلا من الهمزة

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r151.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r151.speaker: الكسائي والفراء
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r151.claim: Al-Kisaʾi and al-Farraʾ derive it from al-ilah, with the hamza dropped and the two lams assimilated, like lakinna from lakin ana.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r151.anchor: أصله : الإله حذفوا الهمزة وأدغموا اللام الأولى في الثانية

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r152.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r152.speaker: فخر الدين الرازي
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r152.claim: Al-Razi lists proposed derivations from bewilderment, repose in God, concealment, a calf's attachment to its mother, and seeking refuge in God.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r152.anchor: ثم قيل : هو مشتق من وله : إذا تحير

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r153.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r153.speaker: فخر الدين الرازي
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r153.claim: Al-Razi says God alone is the refuge and provider, citing that He protects and cannot be protected against, gives every blessing, feeds without being fed, and all things come from Him.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r153.anchor: فالمجير لجميع الخلائق من كل المضار هو الله سبحانه

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r154.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r154.speaker: فخر الدين الرازي
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r154.claim: Al-Razi chooses Allah as an underived proper name; he argues that if it were derived, others could share its meaning, while the other names function as attributes.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r154.anchor: وقد اختار فخر الدين أنه اسم علم غير مشتق البتة

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r155.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r155.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r155.claim: Al-Razi also cites 19:65, “Do you know anyone like Him?” as evidence for an un-derived name, but Ibn Kathir finds that argument debatable.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r155.anchor: وفي الاستدلال بهذه على كون هذا الاسم جامدًا غير مشتق نظر

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r156.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r156.speaker: فخر الدين الرازي
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r156.claim: Al-Razi rejects the claim that the name Allah is Hebrew rather than Arabic.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r156.anchor: وحكى فخر الدين عن بعضهم أنه ذهب إلى أن اسم الله تعالى عبراني لا عربي ، ثم ضعفه

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r157.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r157.speaker: الخليل بن أحمد
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r157.claim: Al-Khalil explains that all creation is captivated by God, using a form of the root “to worship.”
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r157.anchor: لأن الخلق يألهون إليه بنصب اللام وجرها لغتان

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r158.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r158.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r158.claim: A further proposal derives Allah from elevation: Arabs called something high lahan and said lahat when the sun rose.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r158.anchor: وقيل : إنه مشتق من الارتفاع ، فكانت العرب تقول لكل شيء مرتفع : لاها

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r159.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r159.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r159.claim: The proposed form begins as al-ilah; deleting the hamza brings two lams together, which assimilate and are pronounced as one emphatic doubled lam.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r159.anchor: وأصل ذلك الإله ، فحذفت الهمزة التي هي فاء الكلمة

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r160.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r160.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r160.claim: Al-Rahman and al-Rahim are intensive forms derived from mercy, with al-Rahman more emphatic; Ibn Jarir's discussion suggests agreement.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r160.anchor: اسمان مشتقان من الرحمة على وجه المبالغة

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r161.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r161.speaker: عيسى ابن مريم
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r161.claim: A report attributed to Jesus distinguishes Rahman as merciful in this life and the next, and Rahim as merciful in the next life.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r161.anchor: والرحمن رحمن الدنيا والآخرة ، والرحيم رحيم الآخرة

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r162.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r162.speaker: المبرد وأحمد بن يحيى
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r162.claim: Some grammarians claim Rahman is not derived or is Hebrew while Rahim is Arabic; al-Zajjaj rejects this as an objectionable view.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r162.anchor: وقال أحمد بن يحيى : الرحيم عربي ، والرحمن عبراني ، فلهذا جمع بينهما

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r163.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r163.speaker: القرطبي
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r163.claim: Al-Qurtubi cites the hadith, graded sound by al-Tirmidhi, in which God says He is Rahman and derived the womb's name from His own; he treats it as explicit evidence of derivation.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r163.anchor: أنا الرحمن خلقت الرحم وشققت لها اسمًا من اسمي

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r164.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r164.speaker: القرطبي
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r164.claim: Al-Qurtubi says Arabs denied the name Rahman through ignorance of God and what is due to Him.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r164.anchor: وإنكار العرب لاسم الرحمن لجهلهم بالله وبما وجب له

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r165.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r165.speaker: أبو عبيد
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r165.claim: Abu ʿUbayd treats Rahman and Rahim as synonymous, like two parallel forms; others distinguish the intensive faʿlan form from faʿil.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r165.anchor: هما بمعنى واحد كندمان ونديم قاله أبو عبيد

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r166.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r166.speaker: أبو علي الفارسي
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r166.claim: Abu ʿAli al-Farisi says Rahman encompasses every kind of mercy and is exclusive to God, while Rahim describes His mercy toward believers.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r166.anchor: الرحمن : اسم عام في جميع أنواع الرحمة يختص به الله تعالى ، والرحيم إنما هو من جهة المؤمنين

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r167.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r167.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r167.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas calls the two names tender and says one is more tender—that is, more merciful—than the other.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r167.anchor: وقال ابن عباس : هما اسمان رقيقان ، أحدهما أرق من الآخر

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r168.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r168.speaker: ابن المبارك
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r168.claim: Ibn al-Mubarak says Rahman gives when asked, while Rahim becomes angry if not asked, linking the distinction to the hadith that God is angered by one who does not supplicate.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r168.anchor: الرحمن إذا سئل أعطى ، والرحيم إذا لم يسأل يغضب

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r169.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r169.speaker: العرزمي
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r169.claim: Al-ʿArzami says Rahman covers all creation, while Rahim specifically describes mercy to believers.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r169.anchor: الرحمن لجميع الخلق ، الرحيم ، قال : بالمؤمنين

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r170.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r170.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r170.claim: This distinction is supported by verses that name Rahman at God's establishing the Throne and Rahim for believers, although a traditional supplication calls Him Rahman and Rahim of both worlds.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r170.anchor: فدل على أن الرحمن أشد مبالغة في الرحمة لعمومها في الدارين لجميع خلقه

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r171.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r171.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r171.claim: Rahman is a name specific to God; Musaylima's self-title Rahman of Yamama became a byword for lying.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r171.anchor: واسمه تعالى الرحمن خاص به لم يسم به غيره

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r172.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r172.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r172.claim: The claim that Rahim must intensify Rahman because it follows it is mistaken: the second word is another adjective, not emphatic repetition.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r172.anchor: وإنما هو من باب النعت [ بعد النعت ]

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r173.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r173.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r173.claim: The naming sequence moves from the unique name Allah, to the exclusive Rahman, to Rahim, which also describes the Prophet and human beings; naming starts with the most honored and specific names.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r173.anchor: فلهذا بدأ باسم الله ، ووصفه بالرحمن ؛ لأنه أخص وأعرف من الرحيم

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r174.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r174.speaker: عطاء الخراساني
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r174.claim: ʿAta al-Khurasani explains that Rahim follows Rahman to prevent anyone claiming the exclusive title Rahman, since only God is described as both.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r174.anchor: جيء بلفظ الرحيم ليقطع التوهم بذلك ، فإنه لا يوصف بالرحمن الرحيم إلا الله تعالى

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r175.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r175.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r175.claim: Quraysh's denial of Rahman at Hudaybiyya and in 25:60 was stubbornness: pre-Islamic poems already used Rahman for God.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r175.anchor: والظاهر أن إنكارهم هذا إنما هو جحود وعناد وتعنت في كفرهم

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r176.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r176.speaker: سلامة بن جندب
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r176.claim: Salama ibn Jundub's pre-Islamic verse calls God Rahman, showing the name was already known among Arabs.

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r177.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r177.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r177.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas calls Rahman an intensive Arabic form of mercy and glosses the two names as gentle to whom God wills mercy and severe toward whom He wills to chastise.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r177.anchor: عن الضحاك ،   عن عبد الله بن عباس ،   قال : الرحمن : الفعلان من الرحمة

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r178.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r178.speaker: الحسن
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r178.claim: Hasan says Rahman is a protected name that people cannot assume for themselves.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r178.anchor: عن الحسن ، قال : الرحمن اسم ممنوع

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r179.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r179.speaker: author
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r179.claim: Umm Salama's report says the Prophet paused between the basmala, al-Hamd, Rahman al-Rahim, and Malik yawm al-din; some Kufans pause at the basmala while most connect it to al-Hamd.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r179.anchor: حديث أم سلمة أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم كان يقطع قرآنه حرفًا حرفًا

IBNKATHIR:1:1/r180.author: Ibn Kathīr
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r180.speaker: الكسائي
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r180.claim: Al-Kisaʾi says some Arabs connect the basmala to al-Hamd by transferring the vowel of the connecting hamza to the mīm; Ibn ʿAtiyya says he knew of no transmitted canonical reading for it.
IBNKATHIR:1:1/r180.anchor: وحكى الكسائي عن بعض العرب أنها تقرأ بفتح الميم وصلة الهمزة

FARRA:v1p1#2/r1.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v1p1#2/r1.speaker: القراء
FARRA:v1p1#2/r1.claim: Reciters and codex scribes omit the alif in the familiar basmala because its meaning is obvious and Arabic usage favors brevity in repeated, familiar expressions.
FARRA:v1p1#2/r1.anchor: اجتماع القراء وكتاب المصاحف على حذف الألف من «بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم»

FARRA:v1p1#2/r2.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v1p1#2/r2.speaker: author
FARRA:v1p1#2/r2.claim: They retain the alif in “fa-sabbih bi-ismi rabbika” because this name is not used with the preposition as frequently as Allah’s name.
FARRA:v1p1#2/r2.anchor: قوله: «فسبح باسم ربك» لأنها لا تلزم هذا الاسم، ولا تكثر معه ككثرتها مع الله

FARRA:v1p1#2/r3.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v1p1#2/r3.speaker: author
FARRA:v1p1#2/r3.claim: Do not omit the alif of ism with a name other than Allah or with a preposition other than bi; lām and kāf do not follow this spelling convention.
FARRA:v1p1#2/r3.anchor: إلى علم ذلك. فلا تحذفن ألف «اسم» إذا أضفته إلى غير الله

FARRA:v1p1#2/r4.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v1p1#2/r4.speaker: author
FARRA:v1p1#2/r4.claim: Arabic speakers shorten frequent expressions even more, as in “aysh ʿindak” and the altered form of shayʾ.
FARRA:v1p1#2/r4.anchor: قولهم: أيش عندك فحذفوا إعراب «أي» وإحدى ياءيه، وحذفت الهمزة من «شيء»

FARRA:v1p1#2/r5.author: al-Farrāʾ
FARRA:v1p1#2/r5.speaker: author
FARRA:v1p1#2/r5.claim: The claim that alif was dropped because bāʾ cannot be paused on is disproved by other non-pauseable letters that Arabs still write in similar forms.
FARRA:v1p1#2/r5.anchor: فقد كتبت العرب في المصاحف واضرب لهم مثلا بالألف والواو لا يسكت عليها في كثير من أشباهه.

IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p38/r1.author: Ibn Qutayba
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p38/r1.speaker: author
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p38/r1.claim: The basmala is an ellipsis meaning “I begin in the name of God” or “I began in the name of God.”
IBNQUTAYBA-GHARIB:v1p38/r1.anchor: {بسم الله} اختصار كأنه قال: أبدأ باسم الله. أو بدأت باسم الله.

JISHUMI:v1p200/r1.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v1p200/r1.speaker: قيل
JISHUMI:v1p200/r1.claim: The name al-mathānī is explained by the Fātiḥa having been revealed twice.

JISHUMI:v1p200/r2.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v1p200/r2.speaker: أبى بن كعب
JISHUMI:v1p200/r2.claim: Ubayy reports that the Prophet called the Fātiḥa the unmatched Mother of the Qur’an and seven oft-repeated verses, divided between God and servant, with the servant receiving what he asks.
JISHUMI:v1p200/r2.anchor: وعن أبى بن كعب، قال: قرأت على رسول الله - صلى الله عليه وسلم - فاتحة الكتاب

JISHUMI:v1p200/r3.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v1p200/r3.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v1p200/r3.claim: Ism derives from sumu, elevation, rather than simah, mark: its plural is asmāʾ, its diminutive sumayy, and words losing an initial radical do not take hamzat al-waṣl in this way.
JISHUMI:v1p200/r3.anchor: الأول أصح؛ لأنهم جمعوه على أسماء، وقالوا في تصغيره سمي

JISHUMI:v1p200/r4.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v1p200/r4.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v1p200/r4.claim: The proposed root of ism is elevation (also linked with samāʾ), a mark, or the verb meaning to rise and become manifest as a sign of the underlying meaning.

JISHUMI:v1p200/r5.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v1p200/r5.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v1p200/r5.claim: Ism can weigh fiʿl with either ḍamma or kasra, but not faʿl with fatḥa, since its regular plural would be afʿul rather than afʿāl.
JISHUMI:v1p200/r5.anchor: يجوز فعل، وفعل بضم الفاء وكسرها، ولا يجوز فعل بفتح الفاء

JISHUMI:v1p200/r6.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v1p200/r6.speaker: سيبويه
JISHUMI:v1p200/r6.claim: One derivation takes Allah from ilāh, dropping the hamza and making the alif-lām an obligatory substitute so the name becomes a proper name.
JISHUMI:v1p200/r6.anchor: هذا مذهب سيبويه، وقيل: أصله لاه، ألحقت بها الألف واللام

JISHUMI:v1p200/r7.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v1p200/r7.speaker: الخليل وأبي علي
JISHUMI:v1p200/r7.claim: Al-Khalīl and Abū ʿAlī regard Allah as an un-derived name; not every word must be derived, or derivation would regress without end.
JISHUMI:v1p200/r7.anchor: هذا مذهب الخليل وأبي علي. وقيل: إنه مشتق

JISHUMI:v1p200/r8.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v1p200/r8.speaker: النضر بن شميل
JISHUMI:v1p200/r8.claim: A group including al-Naḍr b. Shumayl derives Allah from taʾalluh, worship; Ibn ʿAbbās read ilāhatak as your worship, and a poetic line uses taʾalluh for devotion.
JISHUMI:v1p200/r8.anchor: وقرأ ابن عباس: وإلهتك، أي عبادتك، قال الشاعر: سبحن واسترجعن من تأله

JISHUMI:v1p200/r9.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v1p200/r9.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v1p200/r9.claim: Other derivations connect Allah with seeking refuge in someone, bewilderment (Abū ʿAmr), finding repose with someone (al-Mubarrad), or concealment from lāha.
JISHUMI:v1p200/r9.anchor: وقيل: هو مشتق من الوله، وهو التحير، يقال: أله يأله، إذا تحير عن أبي عمرو

JISHUMI:v1p200/r10.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v1p200/r10.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v1p200/r10.claim: Al-Raḥmān and al-Raḥīm derive from mercy, whose basis is benefaction to the needy; both are intensive forms, with faʿlān more emphatic than faʿīl because it departs further from the base pattern.
JISHUMI:v1p200/r10.anchor: والرحمن الرحيم: اسمان مشتقان من الرحمة، وأصل الرحمة: النعمة

JISHUMI:v1p203/r1.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v1p203/r1.speaker: أبي عمرو بن العلاء
JISHUMI:v1p203/r1.claim: Abū ʿAmr explains Allah as the one whose essential greatness leaves minds bewildered.
JISHUMI:v1p203/r1.anchor: معناه: أنه تتحير العقول في كنه عظمته، كما يقال للمكتوب: كتاب، عن أبي عمرو بن العلاء

JISHUMI:v1p203/r2.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v1p203/r2.speaker: المبرد
JISHUMI:v1p203/r2.claim: Al-Mubarrad explains Allah as the one whose remembrance creatures find repose in.
JISHUMI:v1p203/r2.anchor: معناه: أن الخلق يسكنون إلى ذكره، عن المبرد

JISHUMI:v1p203/r3.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v1p203/r3.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v1p203/r3.claim: Another reported explanation is that God is seen but does not see.
JISHUMI:v1p203/r3.anchor: وقيل: معناه: أنه يرى ولا يرى

JISHUMI:v1p203/r4.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v1p203/r4.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v1p203/r4.claim: The gloss “the worshipped one” is wrong because others besides God are worshipped and are not gods.
JISHUMI:v1p203/r4.anchor: فأما من قال: معناه: المعبود فقد أخطأ؛ لأن غيره عبد، وليس بإله

JISHUMI:v1p203/r5.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v1p203/r5.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v1p203/r5.claim: Defining Allah as “the one entitled to worship” wrongly implies that He was not God in eternity.
JISHUMI:v1p203/r5.anchor: ومن قال: إنه المستحق للعبادة يلزمه ألا يكون إلها في الأزل، وهذا خطأ

JISHUMI:v1p203/r6.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v1p203/r6.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v1p203/r6.claim: One view treats al-Raḥmān and al-Raḥīm as synonymous names for the merciful, like nadmān and nadīm.
JISHUMI:v1p203/r6.anchor: قيل: معناهما واحد، وهو ذو الرحمة، كندمان ونديم

JISHUMI:v1p203/r7.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v1p203/r7.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v1p203/r7.claim: Another view distinguishes the names because other beings may be called raḥīm but not raḥmān.
JISHUMI:v1p203/r7.anchor: وقيل: بينهما فرق، ولذلك يسمى غيره رحيما، ولا يسمى رحمانا

JISHUMI:v1p203/r8.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v1p203/r8.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v1p203/r8.claim: One distinction makes al-Raḥmān the provider for all creatures and al-Raḥīm the forgiver of all believers.
JISHUMI:v1p203/r8.anchor: قيل: الرحمن: الرازق لجميع خلقه، والرحيم: الغافر لجميع المؤمنين

JISHUMI:v1p203/r9.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v1p203/r9.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v1p203/r9.claim: Another makes al-Raḥmān the giver of foundational blessings only God can create, while al-Raḥīm denotes one possessing mercy.
JISHUMI:v1p203/r9.anchor: الرازق لجميع خلقه، والرحيم: الغافر لجميع المؤمنين، وقيل: الرحمن: فاعل أصول النعم

JISHUMI:v1p203/r10.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v1p203/r10.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v1p203/r10.claim: A further distinction assigns al-Raḥmān to creation and al-Raḥīm to provision.

JISHUMI:v1p203/r11.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v1p203/r11.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v1p203/r11.claim: The pairing intensifies the attribution of mercy and teaches that all blessings come from God.
JISHUMI:v1p203/r11.anchor: للمبالغة بصفته بالرحمة؛ ليعلم أن النعم كلها منه

JISHUMI:v1p203/r12.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v1p203/r12.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v1p203/r12.claim: Because Arabs commonly knew Allah but not al-Raḥmān, the names are paired to show that Allah, al-Raḥmān, and al-Raḥīm all name and describe Him.
JISHUMI:v1p203/r12.anchor: لأن العرب كثير في لغتهم لفظ، (الله)، ولم يعرفوا الرحمن، فجمع بينهما

JISHUMI:v1p203/r13.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v1p203/r13.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v1p203/r13.claim: Another explanation says al-Raḥmān is more frequent in the Torah, al-Raḥīm in the Gospel, and Allah in the Qur’an, so the pairing shows all refer to God.
JISHUMI:v1p203/r13.anchor: لأن في التوراة ذكر الرحمن أكثر، وفي الإنجيل ذكر الرحيم أكثر، وفي القرآن ذكر الله أكثر

JISHUMI:v1p203/r14.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v1p203/r14.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v1p203/r14.claim: Al-Raḥmān precedes al-Raḥīm because its stronger intensity and exclusive use make it like a proper name, and the more definite name comes first.
JISHUMI:v1p203/r14.anchor: لأنه لما كان أشد مبالغة، ولا يوصف به غيره صار كالعلم

JISHUMI:v1p203/r15.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v1p203/r15.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v1p203/r15.claim: The three names in the basmala serve seeking aid: God can bestow every blessing and has ample mercy and beneficence.
JISHUMI:v1p203/r15.anchor: لأن الغرض الاستعانة، ولكل واحد منها تأثير في ذلك

JISHUMI:v1p203/r16.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v1p203/r16.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v1p203/r16.claim: Beginning an important undertaking by naming God is recommended because it seeks His aid, acknowledges divinity, and admits His blessing; a report says an important matter begun without it is cut off.
JISHUMI:v1p203/r16.anchor: الآية تدل على أن ذكر اسم الله في ابتداء الأمر مسنون؛ لأن في ذلك استعانة به

JISHUMI:v1p205/r1.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v1p205/r1.speaker: أبو حنيفة
JISHUMI:v1p205/r1.claim: Abū Ḥanīfa holds that the basmala is recited once, in the first rakʿa.
JISHUMI:v1p205/r1.anchor: فقيل: يقرأ مرة في الركعة الأولى، عن أبي حنيفة

JISHUMI:v1p205/r2.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v1p205/r2.speaker: أبو يوسف
JISHUMI:v1p205/r2.claim: Abū Yūsuf holds that the basmala is recited in every rakʿa.
JISHUMI:v1p205/r2.anchor: وقيل: في كل ركعة، عن أبي يوسف

JISHUMI:v1p205/r3.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v1p205/r3.speaker: محمد
JISHUMI:v1p205/r3.claim: Muḥammad holds that the basmala is recited before each sūra.
JISHUMI:v1p205/r3.anchor: وقيل: عند كل سورة، عن محمد

JISHUMI:v1p205/r4.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v1p205/r4.speaker: أبو حنيفة
JISHUMI:v1p205/r4.claim: Abū Ḥanīfa holds that the basmala should not be recited aloud.
JISHUMI:v1p205/r4.anchor: واختلفوا فقيل: لا يجهر، عن أبي حنيفة

JISHUMI:v1p205/r5.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v1p205/r5.speaker: الشافعي
JISHUMI:v1p205/r5.claim: Al-Shāfiʿī holds that it should be recited aloud.

JISHUMI:v1p205/r6.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v1p205/r6.speaker: أنس
JISHUMI:v1p205/r6.claim: Anas says he heard neither the Prophet nor Abū Bakr nor ʿUmar recite the basmala aloud in prayer.
JISHUMI:v1p205/r6.anchor: وعن أنس (صليت خلف رسول الله - صلى الله عليه وسلم - وخلف أبي بكر وعمر فلم أسمع

JISHUMI:v1p206/r8.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v1p206/r8.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v1p206/r8.claim: Explanations for repeating al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm: the first occurrence is outside the sūra, it first seeks aid and the second assigns praise to God, or the repetition emphasizes mercy.
JISHUMI:v1p206/r8.anchor: قيل: لأن الأول ليس من السورة

JISHUMI:v1p206/r9.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v1p206/r9.speaker: علي بن عيسى
JISHUMI:v1p206/r9.claim: ʿAlī b. ʿĪsā denies mere repetition: the first occurrence links servitude to blessings warranting worship, the second links praise to blessings warranting praise.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p45#2/r1.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p45#2/r1.speaker: قراء المدينة والبصرة والشام وفقهاؤها
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p45#2/r1.claim: They hold that the basmala is not a Qur'anic verse, but was written to separate surahs and for blessing; they therefore do not recite it aloud in prayer.
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p45#2/r1.anchor: قراء المدينة والبصرة والشام وفقهاؤها على ان التسمية ليست بآية من الفاتحة ولا من غيرها من السور وإنما كتبت للفصل والتبرك

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p45#2/r2.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p45#2/r2.speaker: أبو حنيفة رحمه الله ومن تابعه
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p45#2/r2.claim: Abu Hanifa shares the view that the basmala is not a verse, and his followers accordingly do not recite it aloud in prayer.
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p45#2/r2.anchor: وهو مذهب أبي حنيفة رحمه الله ومن تابعه ولذلك لا يجهر بها عندهم في الصلاة

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p45#2/r3.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p45#2/r3.speaker: قراء مكة والكوفة وفقهاؤهما
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p45#2/r3.claim: They hold that the basmala is a verse of al-Fatiha and every surah; al-Shafi'i and his companions agree and recite it aloud.
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p45#2/r3.anchor: وقراء مكة والكوفة وفقهاؤهما على انها آية من الفاتحة ومن كل سورة وعليه الشافعي وأصحابه

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p45#2/r4.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p45#2/r4.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p45#2/r4.claim: The opposing jurists argue that the early community included the basmala in the codex while excluding Amin, so it must be Qur'an.
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p45#2/r4.anchor: وقالوا قد أثبتها السلف في المصحف مع توصيتهم بتجريد القرآن ولذلك لم يثبتوا

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p45#2/r5.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p45#2/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p45#2/r5.claim: Ibn Abbas says that whoever omits the basmala has omitted 114 verses from God's Book.
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p45#2/r5.anchor: وعن ابن عباس من تركها فقد ترك مائة وأربع عشرة آية من كتاب الله تعالى

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p45#2/r6.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p45#2/r6.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p45#2/r6.claim: The preposition bi is attached to an omitted verb such as I read or recite in God's name; the reciter supplies the action begun by the basmala.
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p45#2/r6.anchor: بمحذوف تقديره بسم الله اقرأ أو أتلو لأن الذي يتلو التسمية مقروء

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p46/r1.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p46/r1.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p46/r1.claim: The omitted governing verb is placed after the basmala because God's name, the more important element, should come first and signal exclusive invocation of God.
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p46/r1.anchor: لأن الأهم من الفعل والمتعلق به هو المتعلق به لأنهم كانوا يبدءون بأسماء آلهتهم

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p46/r2.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p46/r2.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p46/r2.claim: The preposed divine name conveys exclusivity, as in the explicit object-first wording of You alone we worship.
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p46/r2.anchor: فوجب ان يقصد الموحد معنى اختصاص اسم الله عز وجل بالابتداء وذلك بتقديمه وتأخير الفعل

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p46/r3.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p46/r3.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p46/r3.claim: The basmala's omitted verb is illustrated by Arabic prayers for a newly married couple and by a poet's account of being called to a meal.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p46/r4.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p46/r4.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p46/r4.claim: The construction is supported by Noah's words about embarking and landing in God's name.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p46#2/r1.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p46#2/r1.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p46#2/r1.claim: In the first-revealed surah, placing the command to read before the basmala is more fitting because the reading command is paramount.
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p46#2/r1.anchor: هناك تقديم الفعل اوقع لأنها اول سورة نزلت فكان الامر بالقراءة أهم

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p46#2/r2.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p46#2/r2.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p46#2/r2.claim: One analysis makes the name relate to reciting as a pen relates to writing: the believer makes the act God's by beginning with His name, as a prophetic report says.
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p46#2/r2.anchor: كل أمر ذي بال لم يبدأ فيه باسم الله فهو أبتر

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p46#2/r3.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p46#2/r3.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p46#2/r3.claim: A report from the Prophet says that an important matter begun without God's name is cut off.
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p46#2/r3.anchor: كل أمر ذي بال لم يبدأ فيه باسم الله فهو أبتر

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p46#2/r4.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p46#2/r4.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p46#2/r4.claim: The other analysis treats reciting as occurring in the blessing of God's name; al-Zamakhshari calls this account more idiomatic and better.
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p46#2/r4.anchor: على معنى متبركا بسم الله أقرأ وكذلك قول الداعي للمعرس بالرفاه والبنين معناه أعرست ملتبسا بالرفاه والبنين وهذا الوجه أعرب وأحسن

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p48/r1.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p48/r1.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p48/r1.claim: The divine basmala and praise on worshippers' tongues teach them how to invoke, praise, glorify, and magnify God.
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p48/r1.anchor: ومعناه تعليم عباده كيف يتبركون باسمه وكيف يحمدونه ويمجدونه ويعظمونه

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p48/r2.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p48/r2.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p48/r2.claim: One-letter particles usually take fatḥa; lām takes kasra to distinguish it from the introductory lām, while bi takes kasra because it is inherently a preposition.
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p48/r2.anchor: اما اللام فللفصل بينها وبين لام الابتداء واما الباء فلكونها لازمة للحرفية والجر

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p48/r3.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p48/r3.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p48/r3.claim: The noun ism begins with a consonant cluster, so speakers add a connecting hamza at utterance onset; some instead pronounce sim or sum by moving the initial consonant.
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p48/r3.anchor: فإذا نطقوا بها مبتدئين زادوا همزة لئلا يقع ابتداؤهم بالساكن

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p48/r4.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p48/r4.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p48/r4.claim: Ism is a noun with a deleted ending, originally sumw, derived from elevation because naming raises and publicizes the named one.
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p48/r4.anchor: وهو من الأسماء المحذوفة الأعجاز كيد ودم وأصله سمو بدليل تصريفه كأسماء وسمي وسميت واشتقاقه من السمو لأن التسمية تنويه بالمسمى وإشادة بذكره

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p48/r5.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p48/r5.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p48/r5.claim: The word nabz for a nickname is related to nabr, raising the voice; nabz also names the outer peel of a palm tree.
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p48/r5.anchor: ومنه قيل للقب النبز من النبز بمعنى النبر وهو رفع الصوت والنبز قشر النخلة الأعلى

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p48/r6.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p48/r6.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p48/r6.claim: The alif in bism is omitted in writing because connected use is frequent; the lengthened bā compensates for it, and Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz told his scribe to lengthen the bā.
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p48/r6.anchor: قد اتبعوا في حذفها حكم الدرج دون الابتداء الذي عليه وضع الخط لكثرة الاستعمال وقالوا طولت الباء تعويضا من طرح الألف وعن عمر بن عبد العزيز أنه قال لكاتبه طول الباء

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p48/r7.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p48/r7.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p48/r7.claim: Allah derives from al-ilah; the generic word for a deity became specific to the true God, just as al-najm came to denote the Pleiades.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p49/r1.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p49/r1.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p49/r1.claim: Allah, with its hamza deleted, is uniquely the name of the true God and is not used for another being; verbs meaning to deify derive from it.
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p49/r1.anchor: وأما ( الله ) بحذف الهمزة فمختص بالمعبود بالحق لم يطلق على غيره

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p49/r2.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p49/r2.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p49/r2.claim: Allah is a noun, not an adjective: it can be qualified but does not itself qualify an unspecified thing, and divine attributes require a named subject.
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p49/r2.anchor: بل اسم غير صفة ألا تراك تصفه ولا تصف به

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p49/r3.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p49/r3.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p49/r3.claim: He also links Allah to aliha, to be bewildered: minds are dazed by trying to comprehend God, and lack of sound reflection lets error spread.
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p49/r3.anchor: وصيغة هذا الاسم وصيغة قولهم أله إذا تحير

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p49/r4.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p49/r4.speaker: الزجاج
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p49/r4.claim: Al-Zajjaj says pronouncing Allah's lām emphatically is a sunnah; universal Arab practice shows it was inherited generation after generation.
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p49/r4.anchor: قد ذكر الزجاج ان تفخيمها سنة وعلى ذلك العرب كلهم وإطباقهم عليه دليل أنهم ورثوه كابرا عن كابر

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p49/r5.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p49/r5.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p49/r5.claim: Rahman is the emphatic fa'lan form of mercy, while Rahim is fa'il; the former is more intensive, and added form signals added meaning.
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p49/r5.anchor: وفي ( الرحمن ) من المبالغة ما ليس في ( الرحيم )

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p49/r6.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p49/r6.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p49/r6.claim: Rahman functions as an exclusive, established epithet for God, like Allah, and is not ordinarily used of anyone else.
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p49/r6.anchor: وهو من الصفات الغالبة كالدبران والعيوق والصعق لم يستعمل في غير الله عز وجل

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p50/r1.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p50/r1.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p50/r1.claim: Calling Musaylima Rahman of Yamama, including in his poet's praise, is presented as a facet of the Banu Hanifa's unbelieving perversity.

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p50/r2.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p50/r2.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p50/r2.claim: Rahman should be indeclinable by analogy with fa'lan adjectives such as عطشان and سكران, even though its divine specialization prevents a feminine form.
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p50/r2.anchor: أقيسه على أخواته من بابه أعني نحو عطشان وغرثان وسكران فلا أصرفه

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p50/r3.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p50/r3.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p50/r3.claim: God's mercy is figurative language for His beneficence: a kindly ruler does good to subjects, whereas harshness withholds favor.
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p50/r3.anchor: هو مجاز عن انعامه على عباده لأن الملك اذا عطف على رعيته ورق لهم أصابهم بمعروفه وإنعامه

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p50/r4.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p50/r4.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p50/r4.claim: He raises the question why the more emphatic attribute precedes the lesser when normal usage would progress from the lesser to the greater.
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p50/r4.anchor: فإن قلت فلم قدم ما هو أبلغ من الوصفين

KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p51/r1.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p51/r1.speaker: author
KASHSHAF-FULL:v1p51/r1.claim: The ordering is complementary: Rahman covers great and foundational blessings, and Rahim completes it by covering blessings that are delicate and subtle.

MAJAZ:v1p20#2/r1.author: Abū ʿUbayda Maʿmar b. al-Muthannā
MAJAZ:v1p20#2/r1.speaker: author
MAJAZ:v1p20#2/r1.claim: Al-Fātiḥa is Umm al-Kitāb because it is written first in codices and recited before every other surah in prayer.
MAJAZ:v1p20#2/r1.anchor: وهى «أم الكتاب» لأنه يبدأ بكتابتها فى المصاحف قبل سائر القرآن،

MAJAZ:v1p20#2/r2.author: Abū ʿUbayda Maʿmar b. al-Muthannā
MAJAZ:v1p20#2/r2.speaker: author
MAJAZ:v1p20#2/r2.claim: Unhamzated sūra derives from the tiers of a building, one level after another.
MAJAZ:v1p20#2/r2.anchor: وإنما سميت سورة لا تهمز، لأن مجازها من سورة البناء أي منزلة ثم منزلة،

MAJAZ:v1p20#2/r3.author: Abū ʿUbayda Maʿmar b. al-Muthannā
MAJAZ:v1p20#2/r3.speaker: author
MAJAZ:v1p20#2/r3.claim: Those who hamza sūra take it as a piece of the Qur’an; a surah is cut off from another, and joined surahs make the Qur’an.
MAJAZ:v1p20#2/r3.anchor: ومن همزها جعلها قطعة من القرآن، وسميت السورة لأنها مقطوعة من الأخرى، فلما قرن بعضها إلى بعض سمى قرآنا.

MAJAZ:v1p20#2/r4.author: Abū ʿUbayda Maʿmar b. al-Muthannā
MAJAZ:v1p20#2/r4.speaker: author
MAJAZ:v1p20#2/r4.claim: Al-Nābigha’s verse uses sūra to mean rank or status.
MAJAZ:v1p20#2/r4.anchor: قال النابغة: ألم تر أن الله أعطاك سورة ... ترى كل ملك دونها يتذبذب (2) أي منزلة،

MAJAZ:v1p20#2/r5.author: Abū ʿUbayda Maʿmar b. al-Muthannā
MAJAZ:v1p20#2/r5.speaker: author
MAJAZ:v1p20#2/r5.claim: Some Arabs hamza sūra and associate it with asʾartu, while the source distinguishes that form from this word.
MAJAZ:v1p20#2/r5.anchor: وبعض العرب يهمز سورة، ويذهب إلى «أسأرت» . نقول: هذه ليست من تلك.

MAJAZ:v1p20#2/r6.author: Abū ʿUbayda Maʿmar b. al-Muthannā
MAJAZ:v1p20#2/r6.speaker: author
MAJAZ:v1p20#2/r6.claim: The verb before bi-smi Allāh is elliptical: the sense is to begin in God’s name before everything and as the first thing.
MAJAZ:v1p20#2/r6.anchor: فمجاز تفسير قوله «بسم الله» مضمر، مجازه كأنك قلت: بسم الله قبل كل شىء وأول شىء ونحو ذلك،

MAJAZ:v1p20#2/r7.author: Abū ʿUbayda Maʿmar b. al-Muthannā
MAJAZ:v1p20#2/r7.speaker: author
MAJAZ:v1p20#2/r7.claim: Ibn Rawāḥa’s verse witnesses بدينا as a form of بدأنا; بدأنا and بديت are both used, with بدينا noted as a dialect form.
MAJAZ:v1p20#2/r7.anchor: قال عبد الله بن رواحة: بسم الإله وبه بدينا ... ولو عبدنا غيره شقينا يقال: بدأت وبديت، وبعضهم يقول: بدينا لغة.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p47/r1.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p47/r1.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p47/r1.claim: The basmala is agreed to be Qur'an in 27:30, but scholars dispute its status at the start of al-Fatiha and each sura; al-Shafi'i's group affirms it and Abu Hanifa's group does not.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p47/r2.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p47/r2.speaker: أبو عبيدة
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p47/r2.claim: He and others treat bi-sm as an extra connective, so the intended wording is Allah, the Merciful, the Compassionate.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p47/r3.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p47/r3.speaker: لبيد
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p47/r3.claim: His verse uses ism as an extra word, evidence for treating bi-sm as connective rather than essential.
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p47/r3.anchor: ثم اسم السلام عليكما … ومن يبك

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p47/r4.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p47/r4.speaker: قطرب
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p47/r4.claim: On the extra-word reading, ism magnifies and honors God's mention, distinguishing it from mention of creatures.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p47/r5.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p47/r5.speaker: الأخفش
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p47/r5.claim: On the extra-word reading, ism shifts the phrase away from an oath and toward seeking blessing.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p47/r6.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p47/r6.speaker: الجمهور
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p47/r6.claim: Most scholars hold that bi-sm is an essential, intended part of the phrase.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p47/r7.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p47/r7.speaker: الفراء
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p47/r7.claim: The prefixed bāʾ has imperative force: begin in the name of God.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p47/r8.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p47/r8.speaker: الزجاج
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p47/r8.claim: The prefixed bāʾ has declarative force: I began in the name of God.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p47/r9.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p47/r9.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p47/r9.claim: The alif of connection is omitted in speech and writing through frequent use, as in al-Rahman; it remains written in 96:1 because that form is less frequent.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p47/r10.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p47/r10.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p47/r10.claim: A name points to its referent, whereas an attribute conveys information about the one described; an attribute used as a name does both.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p47/r11.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p47/r11.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p47/r11.claim: The claim that a name is identical with its referent and the spoken form is merely naming is unsound: it would make names of actions identical to the actions.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p47/r12.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p47/r12.speaker: الفراء
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p47/r12.claim: He derives ism from sima, a mark, because a name distinguishes its referent.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p47/r13.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p47/r13.speaker: الخليل والزجاج
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p47/r13.claim: They derive ism from elevation, because a name raises the person named above others.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p49/r1.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p49/r1.speaker: عمرو بن معدي كرب
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p49/r1.claim: The cited verse witnesses the derivation of ism from elevation through the wording سما لك or سموت له.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p49/r2.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p49/r2.speaker: الكلبي
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p49/r2.claim: He assigns symbolic meanings to the letters: bāʾ signifies beauty, blessing, goodness, and insight; sīn splendor, eminence, and mastery; mīm glory, dominion, and beneficence.
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p49/r2.anchor: والميم مجده ومملكته ومنه , وهذا قول الكلبي

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p49/r3.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p49/r3.speaker: سليمان بن يسار
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p49/r3.claim: His letter symbolism says bāʾ means free of offspring, sīn hears voices, and mīm answers prayers.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p49/r4.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p49/r4.speaker: أبو روق
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p49/r4.claim: His letter symbolism says bāʾ means creator, sīn concealer of faults, and mīm benefactor.
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p49/r4.anchor: السين ساتر العيوب , والميم المنان , وهذا قول أبي روق

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p49/r5.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p49/r5.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p49/r5.claim: The letter-symbol speculation is remote and exceeds what is proper for God's names, but he records it because an influential authority said it and the book collects reported views.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p49/r6.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p49/r6.speaker: عمر بن أبي ربيعة
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p49/r6.claim: The poem uses basmala as a verb, evidence for the colloquial derived term basmala.
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p49/r6.anchor: قال عمر بن أبي ربيعة : لقد بسملت ليلى

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p49/r7.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p49/r7.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p49/r7.claim: Allah is God's most particular name because no one besides Him has borne it.
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p49/r7.anchor: فهو أخص أسمائه به , لأنه لم يتسم

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p49/r8.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p49/r8.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p49/r8.claim: A second interpretation asks whether anyone comparable to Him is known; this is broader because it applies to both name and act.
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p49/r8.anchor: هل تعلم له شبيها , وهذا أعم التأويلين

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p49/r9.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p49/r9.speaker: أبو حنيفة
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p49/r9.claim: He identifies Allah as the Greatest Name because no one shares this name.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p49/r10.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p49/r10.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p49/r10.claim: One view treats Allah as a proper name for the divine essence, not derived from an attribute, since attribute names depend on an essence name.
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p49/r10.anchor: غير مشتق من صفاته , لأن أسماء الصفات

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p49/r11.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p49/r11.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p49/r11.claim: A second view derives Allah from ilāh: the hamza is dropped and the pronunciation intensified.
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p49/r11.anchor: من أله , صار باشتقاقه عند حذف همزه

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p49/r12.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p49/r12.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p49/r12.claim: One etymology derives ilāh from yearning: creatures flee to Him in their affairs, as followers turn to an imam.
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p49/r12.anchor: من الوله , لأن العباد يألهون إليه

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p49/r13.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p49/r13.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p49/r13.claim: Another etymology derives ilāh from ulūhiyya, worship, as in the verb meaning to worship.
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p49/r13.anchor: من الألوهية , وهي العبادة , من قولهم

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p51/r1.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p51/r1.speaker: رؤبة بن العجاج
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p51/r1.claim: His poetic use of taʾalluh means worship and supports deriving ilāh from worship.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p51/r2.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p51/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p51/r2.claim: He reportedly read 5:117 as wa-yadharuka wa-ālihataka, meaning your worship.
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p51/r2.anchor: عن ابن عباس أنه قرأ : { ويذرك وءالهتك } أي

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p51/r3.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p51/r3.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p51/r3.claim: One view derives ilāh from the act of worship, making divinity an attribute of action that began when creatures were created; on this view God was not always worshiped as ilāh.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p51/r4.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p51/r4.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p51/r4.claim: The other view derives ilāh from deserving worship, making it an eternal essential attribute because God has always deserved worship.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p51/r5.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p51/r5.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p51/r5.claim: He prefers derivation from deserving worship: deriving it from the act would wrongly make Jesus and idols gods because people worshiped them.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p51/r6.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p51/r6.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p51/r6.claim: On the first derivation ilāh is an attribute of action; on the preferred derivation it is an attribute of the divine essence.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p51/r7.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p51/r7.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p51/r7.claim: Al-Rahim is a divine name derived from His attribute of mercy.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p51/r8.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p51/r8.speaker: ثعلب
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p51/r8.claim: He regards al-Rahman as a foreignized Hebrew word, not Arabic, since eloquent Quraysh did not know it until it was explained to them in 25:60.
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p51/r8.anchor: وهذا قول ثعلب واستشهد بقول جرير

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p51/r9.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p51/r9.speaker: جرير
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p51/r9.claim: His verse is cited as linguistic evidence for al-Rahman as an established name.

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p51/r10.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p51/r10.speaker: ثعلب
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p51/r10.claim: Pairing al-Rahman with al-Rahim removes ambiguity; on his theory the Arabic al-Rahim would originally come first, but al-Rahman is placed first for greater intensity.
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p51/r10.anchor: ليزول الالتباس , فعلى هذا يكون الأصل

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p51/r11.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p51/r11.speaker: الشنفرى
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p51/r11.claim: His poem is cited as evidence that al-Rahman is used in Arabic speech and poetry.
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p51/r11.anchor: وقد ظهر ذلك في كلام العرب , وجاءت به أشعارهم , قال الشنفري

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p52/r1.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p52/r1.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p52/r1.claim: If both names are Arabic, they derive from mercy; mercy is a benefit to someone in need, and a benefit is called mercy because it arises from compassion.
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p52/r1.anchor: الرحمة , والرحمة هي النعمة على المحتاج

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p52/r2.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p52/r2.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p52/r2.claim: The phrase mercy to the worlds in 21:107 means a benefit to them, linking the verse's usage to this definition.
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p52/r2.anchor: يعني نعمة عليهم , وإنما سميت النعمة رحمة

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p52/r3.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p52/r3.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p52/r3.claim: Al-Rahman is more emphatic than al-Rahim: its form and meaning extend mercy, whereas al-Rahim extends only in meaning; people may be named Rahim but not Rahman.
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p52/r3.anchor: لأن الرحمن يتعدى لفظه ومعناه , والرحيم

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p52/r4.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p52/r4.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p52/r4.claim: Pre-Islamic Arabs called God al-Rahman, and Musaylima later appropriated that divine name for himself.
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p52/r4.anchor: الله تعالى به وعليه بيت الشنفرى , ثم إن مسيلمة

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p52/r5.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p52/r5.speaker: عطاء
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p52/r5.claim: He says al-Rahman was paired with al-Rahim to distinguish God's name through its intensity, since no one else called himself both names.
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p52/r5.anchor: قال عطاء : فلذلك قرنه الله تعالى بالرحيم

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p52/r6.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p52/r6.speaker: أبو عبيدة
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p52/r6.claim: He distinguishes the names by saying al-Rahman is the possessor of mercy and al-Rahim is the merciful one.
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p52/r6.anchor: وفرق أبو عبيدة بينهما , فقال بأن الرحمن ذو

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p52/r7.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p52/r7.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p52/r7.claim: One view derives al-Rahman and al-Rahim from the same mercy, with al-Rahman simply more emphatic.
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p52/r7.anchor: من رحمة واحدة , جعل لفظ الرحمن أشد

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p52/r8.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p52/r8.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p52/r8.claim: Another view derives the names from two distinct mercies to distinguish the names and attributes.
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p52/r8.anchor: والرحمة التي اشتق منها الرحمن , غير الرحمة

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p52/r9.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p52/r9.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p52/r9.claim: One account of the two mercies assigns al-Rahman to mercy toward all creatures and al-Rahim to mercy toward the obedient.
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p52/r9.anchor: رحمة الله لجميع خلقه , والرحيم مشتق

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p52/r10.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p52/r10.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p52/r10.claim: A second account assigns al-Rahman to mercy for people of this world and the next, and al-Rahim to mercy for people of this world only.
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p52/r10.anchor: رحمة الله تعالى لأهل الدنيا والآخرة , والرحيم

MAWARDI-FULL:v1p52/r11.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p52/r11.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p52/r11.claim: A third account assigns al-Rahman to mercy exclusive to God and al-Rahim to mercy that creatures can share.
MAWARDI-FULL:v1p52/r11.anchor: يختص الله تعالى بها دون عباده , والرحيم

NASAFI-FULL:v1p4#2/r1.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p4#2/r1.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p4#2/r1.claim: Medina, Basra, and Syria's readers and jurists, with Abu Hanifa, hold that the basmala is not a verse of al-Fatiha or other surahs; it separates surahs and is blessed at the opening, so they do not recite it aloud.
NASAFI-FULL:v1p4#2/r1.anchor: هو مذهب أبي حنيفة ومن تابعه رحمهم الله ولذا لا يجهر بها عندهم في الصلاة

NASAFI-FULL:v1p4#2/r2.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p4#2/r2.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p4#2/r2.claim: Meccan and Kufan readers, with al-Shafi'i and his companions, count it as a verse of al-Fatiha and every surah and recite it aloud; they cite its inclusion in the early codices despite the instruction to exclude non-Qur'anic material.
NASAFI-FULL:v1p4#2/r2.anchor: وقراء مكة والكوفة على أنها آية من الفاتحة ومن كل سورة وعليه الشافعى وأصحابه

NASAFI-FULL:v1p4#2/r3.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p4#2/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
NASAFI-FULL:v1p4#2/r3.claim: Ibn Abbas says that whoever omits the basmala has omitted 114 verses from God's Book.
NASAFI-FULL:v1p4#2/r3.anchor: وعن ابن عباس رضى الله عنهما من تركها فقد ترك مائة وأربع عشرة آية من كتاب الله

NASAFI-FULL:v1p4#2/r4.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p4#2/r4.speaker: أبو هريرة
NASAFI-FULL:v1p4#2/r4.claim: A Prophetic report presents al-Fatiha as divided between God and His servant: God answers the praise, glorification, and magnification, shares the response to worship and aid, and grants the servant's request in the closing supplication.
NASAFI-FULL:v1p4#2/r4.anchor: حديث أبي هريرة قال سمعت النبي عليه السلام يقول قال الله تعالى قسمت الصلاة أي الفاتحة بينى وبين عبدى نصفين

NASAFI-FULL:v1p4#2/r5.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p4#2/r5.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p4#2/r5.claim: The report begins God's response when the servant says “Praise belongs to God,” which indicates the basmala is not part of al-Fatiha; if it is outside al-Fatiha, consensus excludes it from other surahs too.
NASAFI-FULL:v1p4#2/r5.anchor: فالابتداء بقوله الحمد لله دليل على أن التسمية ليست من الفاتحة

NASAFI-FULL:v1p4#2/r6.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p4#2/r6.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p4#2/r6.claim: In the Hanafi account the basmala remains a Qur'anic verse revealed to separate surahs; this does not contradict its exclusion from the surahs themselves.
NASAFI-FULL:v1p4#2/r6.anchor: التسمية آية من القرآن انزلت للفصل بين السور عندنا ذكره فخر الإسلام في المبسوط

NASAFI-FULL:v1p4#2/r7.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p4#2/r7.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p4#2/r7.claim: The initial ba attaches to an omitted verb such as “I read” or “I recite”; the act named is understood from the basmala that precedes it, as in a traveler saying it on departure or arrival.
NASAFI-FULL:v1p4#2/r7.anchor: وتعلقت الباء بمحذوف تقديره بسم الله اقرأ أو أتلو لأن الذى يتلو التسمية مقروء

NASAFI-FULL:v1p4#2/r8.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p4#2/r8.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p4#2/r8.claim: The omitted verb follows the basmala because the act and its object matter most; placing the divine name first gives it exclusive priority over the polytheists' invocations of al-Lat and al-Uzza.
NASAFI-FULL:v1p4#2/r8.anchor: وكانوا يبدءون بأسماء آلهتم فيقولون باسم اللات وباسم العزى

NASAFI-FULL:v1p4#2/r9.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p4#2/r9.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p4#2/r9.claim: In “Read in the name of your Lord,” the verb is brought forward because reading was the central command of the first-revealed surah; “read” may also mean perform reading absolutely, or take the following phrase as its object.
NASAFI-FULL:v1p4#2/r9.anchor: وكان الأمر بالقراءة اهم فكان تقديم الفعل اوقع ويجوز أن يحمل اقرأ على معنى افعل القراءة

NASAFI-FULL:v1p4#2/r10.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p4#2/r10.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p4#2/r10.claim: The ba is kasra-marked because it is invariably a preposition governing genitive; the noun's initial hamza is added only when it begins speech, while medial pronunciation drops it.
NASAFI-FULL:v1p4#2/r10.anchor: وبنيت الباء على الكسر لأنها تلازم الحرفية والجر فكسرت لتشابه حركتها عملها

NASAFI-FULL:v1p4#2/r11.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p4#2/r11.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p4#2/r11.claim: The noun ism has a prosthetic hamza for initial pronunciation, can be shortened to sim, and derives from deleted-final form samw, “elevation”: naming raises and publicizes the named one's mention.
NASAFI-FULL:v1p4#2/r11.anchor: واشتقاقه من السمو وهو الرفعة لأن التسمية تنويه بالمسمى وإشادة بذكره

NASAFI-FULL:v1p4#2/r12.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p4#2/r12.speaker: عمر بن عبد العزيز
NASAFI-FULL:v1p4#2/r12.claim: Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz instructed his scribe to lengthen the ba, make the sin strokes clear, and round the mim; the written alif is omitted here through frequent use.
NASAFI-FULL:v1p4#2/r12.anchor: وقال عمر بن عبد العزيز لكاتبه طول الباء واظهر السينات ودور الميم

NASAFI-FULL:v1p4#2/r13.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p4#2/r13.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p4#2/r13.claim: Allah is uniquely the name of the true God, not an attribute; the source derives it from al-ilah with hamza loss, while Khalil, al-Zajjaj, Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, and al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl deny derivation and other accounts link it to bewilderment or worship.
NASAFI-FULL:v1p4#2/r13.anchor: والله أصله الإله ونظيره الناس أصله الأناس حذفت الهمزة وعوض منها حرف التعريف

NASAFI-FULL:v1p6/r1.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p6/r1.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p6/r1.claim: The lām of Allah is generally emphatic after fatḥa or ḍamma and light after kasra; some readers lighten it in every position, others always emphasize it, while the first pattern is the majority practice.
NASAFI-FULL:v1p6/r1.anchor: وتفخم لامه إذا كان قبلها فتحة أو ضمة وترقق إذا كان قبلها كسرة ومنهم من يرققها بكل حال

NASAFI-FULL:v1p6/r2.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p6/r2.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p6/r2.claim: Rahman and Rahim are both derived from mercy, but Rahman is more emphatic because it has two augmentative patterns versus one in Rahim; added form signals added meaning.
NASAFI-FULL:v1p6/r2.anchor: وفي الرحمن من المبالغة ما ليس في الرحيم لأن في الرحيم زيادة واحدة وفى الرحمن زيادتين وزيادة اللفظ تدل على زيادة المعنى

NASAFI-FULL:v1p6/r3.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p6/r3.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p6/r3.claim: Rahman describes mercy encompassing all creation, believer and unbeliever, especially in this world; Rahim describes mercy particular to believers in the hereafter, explaining the supplicatory usage and the order of the names.
NASAFI-FULL:v1p6/r3.anchor: ولذا جاء في الدعاء يارحمن الدنيا لأنه يعم المؤمن والكافر ورحيم الآخرة لأنه يخص المؤمن

NASAFI-FULL:v1p6/r4.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p6/r4.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p6/r4.claim: Rahman is restricted as a name to God but universal in meaning, while Rahim can describe others and is particular in its referent; Rahman is nevertheless placed first despite its greater force.
NASAFI-FULL:v1p6/r4.anchor: وقالوا الرحمن خاص تسمية لأنه لا يوصف به غيره

NASAFI-FULL:v1p6/r5.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p6/r5.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p6/r5.claim: A hostile poet applied “Rahman” to Musaylima as a taunt in unbelief, not as a genuine divine description.
NASAFI-FULL:v1p6/r5.anchor: وأما قول الشاعر في مسيلمة وأنت غيث الورى لا زلت رحمانا فباب من تعنتهم في كفرهم

NASAFI-FULL:v1p6/r6.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v1p6/r6.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v1p6/r6.claim: Grammarians differ on whether Rahman declines: those requiring the absence of a faʿlān feminine form leave it indeclinable, while those requiring a faʿlā feminine form decline it; the first analysis is preferable.
NASAFI-FULL:v1p6/r6.anchor: ورحمن غير منصرف عند من زعم أن الشرط انتفاء فعلانه إذ ليس له فعلانة

QUTB-ZILAL:1:1/r1.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:1:1/r1.speaker: author
QUTB-ZILAL:1:1/r1.claim: Al-Fatiha is Meccan and has seven verses; Muslims recite it at least seventeen times daily, more with voluntary prayers, and may repeat it without limit.

QUTB-ZILAL:1:1/r2.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:1:1/r2.speaker: رسول الله [ ص ]
QUTB-ZILAL:1:1/r2.claim: The Prophet says prayer is invalid without reciting the Opening of the Book; the report is in both Sahih collections.
QUTB-ZILAL:1:1/r2.anchor: لا صلاة لمن لم يقرأ بفاتحة الكتاب

QUTB-ZILAL:1:1/r3.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:1:1/r3.speaker: author
QUTB-ZILAL:1:1/r3.claim: The short surah gathers core Islamic creed, worldview, feelings, and guidance, explaining its repetition in every rakʿa and why prayer without it is invalid.
QUTB-ZILAL:1:1/r3.anchor: ما يشير إلى طرف من حكمة اختيارها للتكرار

QUTB-ZILAL:1:1/r4.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:1:1/r4.speaker: author
QUTB-ZILAL:1:1/r4.claim: Against disagreement over the basmala's status, Quṭb prefers counting it as a verse of al-Fatiha, making the surah seven verses.
QUTB-ZILAL:1:1/r4.anchor: فإن الأرجح أنها آية من سورة الفاتحة

QUTB-ZILAL:1:1/r5.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:1:1/r5.speaker: author
QUTB-ZILAL:1:1/r5.claim: An unnamed view takes the seven oft-repeated verses in 15:87 to be al-Fatiha, seven verses repeated in prayer.
QUTB-ZILAL:1:1/r5.anchor: وهناك قول بأن المقصود بقوله تعالى

QUTB-ZILAL:1:1/r6.author: Sayyid Quṭb
QUTB-ZILAL:1:1/r6.speaker: author
QUTB-ZILAL:1:1/r6.claim: Beginning in God's name is the etiquette revealed to the Prophet at the first revelation and accords with God as First, Last, Manifest, and Hidden.
