RAZI-FULL:v1p173/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p173/r5.claim: Although a non-Arab may understand meaning more readily in translation, prayer seeks remembrance and reflection; treating translation as valid would perversely make Arabic recitation prohibited.
RAZI-FULL:v1p173/r5.anchor: المقصد الأقصى من إقامة الصلوات حصول هذه المعاني

RAZI-FULL:v1p173/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p173/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p173/r6.claim: Prayer preserves both meaning and Arabic wording: the wording carries the inimitable eloquence, and its required recitation safeguards memorization and fulfills God’s promise to preserve the Reminder.
RAZI-FULL:v1p173/r6.anchor: الإعجاز في فصاحته ؛ وفصاحته في لفظه

RAZI-FULL:v1p174/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p174/r1.speaker: عبد الله بن مسعود
RAZI-FULL:v1p174/r1.claim: Opponents cite Ibn Mas‘ud teaching an Ajami to replace al-athim with al-yatim, then saying Quranic error is replacing a mercy verse with a punishment verse rather than using a synonym.
RAZI-FULL:v1p174/r1.anchor: وكان الرجل عجميا فكان يقول : طعام اليتيم

RAZI-FULL:v1p174/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p174/r2.speaker: المخالف
RAZI-FULL:v1p174/r2.claim: Opponents argue that the Qur’an was in earlier scriptures, whose wording was Hebrew or Syriac rather than the Arabic wording, so meaning can be Qur’an in another language.
RAZI-FULL:v1p174/r2.anchor: فأخبر أن القرآن في زبر الأولين وقال تعالى

RAZI-FULL:v1p174/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p174/r3.speaker: المخالف
RAZI-FULL:v1p174/r3.claim: Opponents cite God’s statement that this Qur’an was revealed to warn people who do not understand Arabic, arguing that communicated meaning in their language is still Qur’an.
RAZI-FULL:v1p174/r3.anchor: وأوحي إلي هذا القرآن لأنذركم به

RAZI-FULL:v1p174/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p174/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p174/r4.claim: Razi objects that Hanafis selectively invoke Ibn Mas‘ud: they reject his reported uncertainty about faith, though they rely on him here; reports that he omitted al-Fatiha and the protective suras likely reflect views he later abandoned.
RAZI-FULL:v1p174/r4.anchor: فإن كان قول ابن مسعود حجة فلم لم يقبلوا قوله في تلك المسألة

RAZI-FULL:v1p174/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p174/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p174/r5.claim: Being in earlier scriptures means the Qur’an’s stories are found there, while warning people means warning them of its meaning; this limited figurative reading is warranted by decisive proofs.
RAZI-FULL:v1p174/r5.anchor: هذه القصص موجودة في زبر الأولين

RAZI-FULL:v1p174/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p174/r6.speaker: الشافعي
RAZI-FULL:v1p174/r6.claim: Al-Shafi‘i’s newer view requires the follower to recite; his earlier view requires it only when the imam recites quietly, as also held by Malik and Ibn al-Mubarak, while Abu Hanifa discourages recitation behind the imam.
RAZI-FULL:v1p174/r6.anchor: في القول الجديد تجب القراءة على المقتدي

RAZI-FULL:v1p174/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p174/r7.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p174/r7.claim: Qur’an 73:20 commands recitation for both a solitary worshipper and a follower behind an imam.

RAZI-FULL:v1p175/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p175/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p175/r1.claim: The Prophet recited in prayer, so believers follow him; saying that congregational following blocks recitation merely introduces a counterargument.
RAZI-FULL:v1p175/r1.anchor: كان يقرأ في الصلاة فيجب علينا ذلك لقوله تعالى

RAZI-FULL:v1p175/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p175/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p175/r2.claim: The command to establish prayer includes all the Prophet’s prayer actions, including reciting al-Fatiha.
RAZI-FULL:v1p175/r2.anchor: أمر بمجموع الأفعال التي كان رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم يفعلها

RAZI-FULL:v1p175/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p175/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p175/r3.claim: The hadith no prayer without the Opening is general; Razi says the opposing report exempting those behind an imam has been criticized.
RAZI-FULL:v1p175/r3.anchor: لا صلاة إلا بفاتحة الكتاب وقد ثبت تقرير وجه الدليل

RAZI-FULL:v1p175/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p175/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p175/r4.claim: The Prophet’s instruction to a Bedouin to read whatever Qur’an is easy applies equally to the follower and the solitary worshipper.

RAZI-FULL:v1p175/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p175/r5.speaker: عبادة بن الصامت
RAZI-FULL:v1p175/r5.claim: A Tirmidhi report says that after worshippers admitted reading behind the imam, the Prophet told them to read Umm al-Qur’an, since prayer is invalid without it; al-Tirmidhi grades the report hasan.
RAZI-FULL:v1p175/r5.anchor: قال أبو عيسى الترمذي : هذا حديث حسن

RAZI-FULL:v1p175/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p175/r6.speaker: أبو هريرة
RAZI-FULL:v1p175/r6.claim: Abu Hurayra tells a Persian worshipper to recite al-Fatiha silently even when behind an imam; Razi says this contradicts treating that prayer as deficient and supports the questioner’s understanding that recitation is required.

RAZI-FULL:v1p176/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p176/r1.speaker: أبو هريرة
RAZI-FULL:v1p176/r1.claim: The divided-prayer report makes al-Fatiha’s recitation integral to both solitary and congregational prayer because the division occurs through recitation.
RAZI-FULL:v1p176/r1.anchor: بين أن التنصيف إنما يحصل بسبب القراءة

RAZI-FULL:v1p176/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p176/r2.speaker: عبادة بن الصامت
RAZI-FULL:v1p176/r2.claim: Al-Daraqutni transmits the Prophet telling followers not to recite when he reads aloud except Umm al-Qur’an, because prayer is invalid without it.
RAZI-FULL:v1p176/r2.anchor: لا تقرؤا شيئا من القرآن إذا جهرت بقراءتي إلا أم القرآن

RAZI-FULL:v1p176/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p176/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p176/r3.claim: Many reports promise great reward for Qur’an recitation and apply to followers, so reciting behind the imam earns reward; Razi says those accepting that reward must accept obligation.
RAZI-FULL:v1p176/r3.anchor: الأحاديث الكثيرة دالة على أن قراءة القرآن توجب الثواب العظيم

RAZI-FULL:v1p176/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p176/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p176/r4.claim: Because Abu Hanifa agrees recitation behind the imam does not invalidate prayer while Shafi‘i holds omission invalidates it, reciting is the safer course.
RAZI-FULL:v1p176/r4.anchor: القراءة خلف الإمام لا تبطل الصلاة وأما عدم قراءتها

RAZI-FULL:v1p176/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p176/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p176/r5.claim: A follower unable to hear the imam would otherwise remain idle; since Qur’an recitation is the best deed, the reciter’s state is superior and therefore obligatory.
RAZI-FULL:v1p176/r5.anchor: أفضل الأعمال قراءة القرآن وإذا ثبت أن القراءة أفضل من السكوت

RAZI-FULL:v1p176/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p176/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p176/r6.claim: If congregational following prevented recitation, following would unlawfully block a great act of worship; since following is permitted, it cannot prevent reading.
RAZI-FULL:v1p176/r6.anchor: لو كان الاقتداء مانعا من القراءة لكان الاقتداء حراما

RAZI-FULL:v1p176/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p176/r7.speaker: أبو حنيفة
RAZI-FULL:v1p176/r7.claim: Abu Hanifa argues from the command to listen and be quiet when Qur’an is recited; Razi says his exegesis of that verse defeats the argument, and al-Bayhaqi weakened the cited reports.
RAZI-FULL:v1p176/r7.anchor: في تفسير هذه الآية أنها لا تدل على قولهم

RAZI-FULL:v1p176/r8.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p176/r8.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p176/r8.claim: Even assuming the opposing reports sound, Razi prefers recitation because it occupies prayer with worship, is safer, and avoids leaving time empty of remembrance.
RAZI-FULL:v1p176/r8.anchor: يوجب الاشتغال بقراءة القرآن وهو من أعظم الطاعات

RAZI-FULL:v1p176#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p176#2/r1.speaker: الأصم
RAZI-FULL:v1p176#2/r1.claim: The first of six positions denies that recitation is obligatory at all; this is attributed to al-Asamm and Ibn Ulayya.
RAZI-FULL:v1p176#2/r1.anchor: قول الأصم وابن علية وهو أن القراءة غير واجبة أصلا

RAZI-FULL:v1p176#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p176#2/r2.speaker: الحسن البصري
RAZI-FULL:v1p176#2/r2.claim: Al-Hasan al-Basri and al-Hasan ibn Salih require al-Fatiha only once, reasoning that the exception in no prayer without it is fulfilled by one recitation.
RAZI-FULL:v1p176#2/r2.anchor: أن القراءة إنما تجب في ركعة واحدة لقوله عليه الصلاة والسلام

RAZI-FULL:v1p176#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p176#2/r3.speaker: أبو حنيفة
RAZI-FULL:v1p176#2/r3.claim: Abu Hanifa requires reading in the first two rak‘as; in later ones the worshipper may read, glorify God, or remain silent, with another report requiring any two rak‘as without specifying which.
RAZI-FULL:v1p176#2/r3.anchor: القراءة في الركعتين الأولتين واجبة وهو في الأخيرتين بالخيار

RAZI-FULL:v1p176#2/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p176#2/r4.speaker: سفيان
RAZI-FULL:v1p176#2/r4.claim: Sufyan’s position requires reading in the first two rak‘as and regards reading in the final two as disliked.
RAZI-FULL:v1p176#2/r4.anchor: تجب القراءة في الركعتين الأوليين وتكره في الأخريين

RAZI-FULL:v1p176#2/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p176#2/r5.speaker: مالك
RAZI-FULL:v1p176#2/r5.claim: Malik requires recitation in most rak‘as: three in a four-rak‘a prayer, two in Maghrib, and both in Fajr.
RAZI-FULL:v1p176#2/r5.anchor: قول مالك أن القراءة واجبة في أكثر الركعات

RAZI-FULL:v1p176#2/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p176#2/r6.speaker: الشافعي
RAZI-FULL:v1p176#2/r6.claim: Al-Shafi‘i requires recitation in every rak‘a, which Razi supports by the Prophet’s consistent practice and the command to follow him.

RAZI-FULL:v1p176#2/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p176#2/r7.speaker: الشافعي
RAZI-FULL:v1p176#2/r7.claim: The Prophet told the Bedouin to read Umm al-Qur’an and then to do likewise in every rak‘a; the command includes verbal recitation because speech is an action of the tongue.
RAZI-FULL:v1p176#2/r7.anchor: وكذلك فافعل في كل ركعة والأمر للوجوب

RAZI-FULL:v1p176#2/r8.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p176#2/r8.speaker: أبو سعيد الخدري
RAZI-FULL:v1p176#2/r8.claim: Ibn al-Sabbagh introduces Abu Sa‘id al-Khudri’s report as evidence for reciting al-Fatiha in every rak‘a; the report’s wording continues in the next segment.
RAZI-FULL:v1p176#2/r8.anchor: عن أبي سعيد الخدري أنه قال

RAZI-FULL:v1p176#2/r9.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p176#2/r9.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p176#2/r9.claim: Al-Shafi‘i’s position is said to be agreed upon by Companions including Abu Bakr, Umar, Ali, and Ibn Mas‘ud.
RAZI-FULL:v1p176#2/r9.anchor: وهذا القول مجمع عليه بين الصحابة قال به أبو بكر وعمر وعلي وابن مسعود

RAZI-FULL:v1p177/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p177/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p177/r1.claim: Reading al-Fatiha in every rak‘a is the safer view; the standing duty remains until reciting in all units completes it fully.
RAZI-FULL:v1p177/r1.anchor: القراءة في الركعات أحوط فوجب القول بوجوبها

RAZI-FULL:v1p177/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p177/r2.speaker: عائشة
RAZI-FULL:v1p177/r2.claim: Aisha reports prayer was originally two rak‘as, retained while traveling and expanded at home; opponents infer that only the first two rak‘as are original and later ones allow lighter requirements.
RAZI-FULL:v1p177/r2.anchor: فرضت الصلاة في الأصل ركعتين فأقرت في السفر وزيدت في الحضر

RAZI-FULL:v1p177/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p177/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p177/r3.claim: Razi answers that his proofs are more numerous and stronger, and his position is more cautious.
RAZI-FULL:v1p177/r3.anchor: دلائلنا أكثر وأقوى ومذهبنا أحوط فكان أرجح

RAZI-FULL:v1p177/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p177/r4.speaker: الشافعي
RAZI-FULL:v1p177/r4.claim: Al-Shafi‘i’s earlier view excuses a forgotten recitation, citing Umar’s Maghrib prayer; his newer view invalidates it because the general proofs cover both deliberate and inadvertent omission.
RAZI-FULL:v1p177/r4.anchor: قال الشافعي في القديم لا تفسد صلاته

RAZI-FULL:v1p177/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p177/r5.speaker: عمر
RAZI-FULL:v1p177/r5.claim: A report says Umar omitted recitation in Maghrib and considered the prayer sound after the congregation confirmed his bowing and prostration were proper.
RAZI-FULL:v1p177/r5.anchor: صلى بنا عمر بن الخطاب رضي الله عنه المغرب فترك القراءة

RAZI-FULL:v1p177/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p177/r6.speaker: الشعبي
RAZI-FULL:v1p177/r6.claim: Al-Shafi‘i later answers the Umar report by citing al-Sha‘bi that Umar repeated the prayer, or by suggesting he omitted aloud recitation rather than recitation itself.
RAZI-FULL:v1p177/r6.anchor: الشعبي روى أن عمر رضي الله عنه أعاد الصلاة

RAZI-FULL:v1p177/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p177/r7.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p177/r7.claim: Recitation must follow sura order; if the latter half is read first and the first half afterward, only the first half counts.
RAZI-FULL:v1p177/r7.anchor: لو قرأ النصف الأخير ثم النصف الأول يحسب له الأول دون الأخير

RAZI-FULL:v1p177/r8.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p177/r8.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p177/r8.claim: Someone who knows part of al-Fatiha reads that portion plus six other verses; one who knows no part must read whatever Qur’an they know, or glorify and praise God if they know none.
RAZI-FULL:v1p177/r8.anchor: إن حفظ شيئا من القرآن لزمه قراءة ذلك المحفوظ

RAZI-FULL:v1p177/r9.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p177/r9.speaker: أبو سعيد الخدري
RAZI-FULL:v1p177/r9.claim: Abu Sa‘id reports that the Messenger commanded recitation of al-Fatiha in every rak‘a, obligatory or voluntary.
RAZI-FULL:v1p177/r9.anchor: أمرنا رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم أن نقرأ فاتحة الكتاب

RAZI-FULL:v1p178/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p178/r1.speaker: رفاعة بن مالك
RAZI-FULL:v1p178/r1.claim: Rifa‘a ibn Malik reports the Prophet instructing an uninformed worshipper to praise and magnify God if he has memorized no Qur’an; for one unable to recite even Arabic remembrance, Razi recommends invoking God in any language one can manage.
RAZI-FULL:v1p178/r1.anchor: وإن لم يكن معه شيء من القرآن فليحمد الله وليكبر

RAZI-FULL:v1p178/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p178/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p178/r2.claim: For the remaining case of knowing no al-Fatiha, Qur’an, or Arabic remembrance, Razi requires whatever remembrance of God is possible in any language, following the command to do as much as one can.
RAZI-FULL:v1p178/r2.anchor: بأي لسان قدر عليه تمسكا بقوله عليه الصلاة والسلام

RAZI-FULL:v1p178/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p178/r3.speaker: ابن مسعود
RAZI-FULL:v1p178/r3.claim: Reports say Ibn Mas‘ud denied that al-Fatiha and the two protective suras belonged to the Qur’an, creating a dilemma for the status of transmission and his own knowledge.
RAZI-FULL:v1p178/r3.anchor: كان ينكر كون سورة الفاتحة من القرآن وكان ينكر كون المعوذتين من القرآن

RAZI-FULL:v1p178/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p178/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p178/r4.claim: If transmission was mass-transmitted in the Companions’ time, Ibn Mas‘ud’s denial would imply disbelief or deficient reason; if not, Qur’an’s transmission would lack certain proof, so Razi judges the attribution false.
RAZI-FULL:v1p178/r4.anchor: نقل هذا المذهب عن ابن مسعود نقل كاذب باطل

SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r1.claim: The verb basmala means to say bismillah, like hawqala, haylala, and hamdala for saying their respective formulas.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r1.anchor: مصدر بسمل، أي قال: بسم الله، نحو: حوقل وهيلل وحمدل

SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r2.claim: These clipped verbs resemble nisba coinages that combine names, as in hadrami, abqasi, and abshami from tribal names; a poem uses abshamiyya.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r2.anchor: وهذا شبيه بباب النحت في النسب، أي إنهم يأخذون اسمين فينحتون

SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r3.claim: Because basmala and haylala are non-analogical, some classify them as later colloquial coinages.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r3.anchor: وهو غير مقيس، فلا جرم أن بعضهم قال في: بسمل وهيلل إنها لغة مولدة

SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r4.speaker: الماوردي
SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r4.claim: Al-Mawardi calls the person who says bismillah mubasmil and labels that usage a later coinage.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r4.anchor: قال الماوردي: يقال لمن قال: بسم الله: مبسمل وهي] لغة مولدة

SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r5.speaker: عمر بن أبي ربيعة
SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r5.claim: Ibn Abi Rabi'a's verse attests basmala as established poetic usage, while Tha'lab and al-Mutarriz transmit it without calling it a late coinage.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r5.anchor:
قال عمر بن أبي ربيعة:
7 لقد بسملت ليلى غداة لقيتها

SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r6.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r6.claim: The preposition ba here expresses seeking aid: the implied sense is that I recite while relying on God.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r6.anchor: والباء هنا للاستعانة كعملت وبالقدوم، لأن المعنى: أقرأ مستعينا بالله

SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r7.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r7.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r7.claim: Ba can mark real or figurative attachment, illustrated by wiping the head and passing by Zayd.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r7.anchor: وهي: الإلصاق حقيقة أو مجازا، نحو: مسحت برأسي، مررت بزيد

SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r8.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r8.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r8.claim: Ba can mean cause, as in God forbidding things because of the wrongdoing of the Jews.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r8.anchor:
والسببية: [نحو]
فبظلم من الذين هادوا حرمنا عليهم

SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r9.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r9.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r9.claim: Ba can mark accompaniment, as in Zayd going out with his clothes.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r9.anchor: والمصاحبة نحو: خرج زيد بثيابه، أي مصاحبا لها

SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r10.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r10.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r10.claim: Ba can mean exchange or substitution, as in the prophetic saying about red camels and in a poem wishing for replacement companions.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r10.anchor:
والبدل كقوله عليه السلام:
" ما يسرني بها حمر النعم

SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r11.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r11.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r11.claim: Ba also marks an oath and location, as in swearing by God and saying Zayd is in Mecca.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r11.anchor: والقسم: أحلف بالله لأفعلن، والظرفية نحو: زيد بمكة أي فيها

SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r12.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r12.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r12.claim: Ba can make a verb transitive, as in God taking away their light.

SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r13.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r13.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r13.claim: A poet's ba in drinking from seawater means from it, showing the partitive use.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r13.anchor:
والتبعيض كقول الشاعر:
9 شربن بماء البحر ثم ترفعت

SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r14.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r14.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r14.claim: Ba can mark price or equivalence in buying something for a thousand.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r14.anchor: والمقابلة: " اشتريته بألف " أي: قابلته بهذا الثمن

SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r15.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r15.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r15.claim: Ba can mean away from, as in the sky splitting away from clouds; some restrict this sense to contexts of asking, as in ask an expert about it.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r15.anchor:
والمجاوزة مثل قوله تعالى:
ويوم تشقق السمآء بالغمام

SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r16.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r16.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r16.claim: Alqama's line uses ba with asking women to mean asking about them, illustrating the restricted sense of departure.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1/r16.anchor:
وقول علقمة:
10 فإن تسألوني بالنساء فإنني
خبير بأدواء النساء طبيب

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#2/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#2/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#2/r1.claim: Most grammarians allow ba only for attachment or transitivity, reducing the other examples to those two senses.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#2/r1.anchor: والجمهور يأبون جعلها إلا للإلصاق أو التعدية، ويردون جميع المواضع المذكورة إليهما

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#2/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#2/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#2/r2.claim: Ba may mark superposition, as in entrusting someone with a qintar.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#2/r2.anchor:
والاستعلاء كقوله تعالى:
من إن تأمنه بقنطار

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#2/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#2/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#2/r3.claim: Ba is regularly added to the subject of kafa, as in God sufficing his servant; a poem shows the preposition omitted with the same construction.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#2/r3.anchor: أي: كفى الله، بدليل سقوطها في قول الشاعر

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#2/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#2/r4.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#2/r4.claim: Ba is regularly added to predicates of laysa and its negative sister ma, and in the expression bisabika Zayd.

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#2/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#2/r5.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#2/r5.claim: Ba is irregularly added to the object of kafa; the quoted poem means the Prophet's love suffices us.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#2/r5.anchor:
وفي: بحسبك زيد. وغير مطردة في مفعول " كفى " ، كقوله:
12 فكفى بنا فضلا على من غيرنا

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#2/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#2/r6.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#2/r6.claim: One analysis treats ba in the subject phrase of Qalam 6 as extra; another takes al-maftun as a verbal noun, making ba non-extra.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#2/r6.anchor:
ومنه في أحد القولين:
بأييكم المفتون
[القلم: 6] وقيل: المفتون مصدر كالمعقول والميسور

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#2/r7.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#2/r7.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#2/r7.claim: Ba may be irregularly added to the predicate of la, the negative counterpart of laysa; the verse means no intercessor can avail anything.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#2/r7.anchor:
وفي خبر " لا " أخت ليس، كقوله:
13 فكن لي شفيعا يوم لا ذو شفاعة
بمغن فتيلا

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#2/r8.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#2/r8.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#2/r8.claim: Ba can be added to a predicate after negated kana; the poet means I was not the quickest to the food.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#2/r8.anchor:
وإن مدت الأيدي إلى الزاد لم أكن
بأعجلهم

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#2/r9.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#2/r9.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#2/r9.claim: Ba may also be added in a negated circumstantial phrase or second object of ظن; the cited poems mean the caravan returned unsuccessful and he was not a coward.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#2/r9.anchor:
وفي الحال وثاني مفعولي ظن منفيين أيضا كقوله:
15 فما رجعت بخائبة ركاب

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#2/r10.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#2/r10.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#2/r10.claim: A poet uses ba in the predicate of inna, meaning you are the experienced one.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#2/r10.anchor:
وفي خبر " إن " كقول امرئ القيس:
17 فإن تنأ عنها حقبة لا تلاقها
فإنك مما أحدثت بالمجرب

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#2/r11.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#2/r11.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#2/r11.claim: Ba is also discussed as extra in the construction beginning a-wa-lam yaraw anna Allah and similar expressions.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#2/r11.anchor:
وفي:
أولم يروا أن الله
[الأحقاف: 33] وشبهه

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#2/r12.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#2/r12.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#2/r12.claim: A noun, technically, signifies a meaning in itself without time or meaningful parts; linguistically it identifies its referent, and naming makes a word signify that meaning.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#2/r12.anchor: والاسم لغة: ما أبان عن مسمى، واصطلاحا: ما دل على معنى في نفسه فقط

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#3/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#3/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#3/r1.claim: Scholars dispute whether a name is identical with its named referent; this creates an apparent problem of a thing being annexed to itself.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#3/r1.anchor: واختلف الناس: هل الاسم عين المسمى أو غيره؟ وهي مسألة طويلة

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#3/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#3/r2.speaker: أبو البقاء
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#3/r2.claim: Abu al-Baqa's best answer is that name here means naming, which differs from the name itself and its referent.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#3/r2.anchor: وأجاب أبو البقاء عن ذلك بثلاثة أجوبة، أجودها: أن الاسم هنا بمعنى التسمية

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#3/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#3/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#3/r3.claim: The author reports Abu al-Baqa's second answer: supply an omitted annex, yielding in the name of the named God.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#3/r3.anchor: الثاني: أن في الكلام حذف مضاف تقديره: باسم مسمى الله

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#3/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#3/r4.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#3/r4.claim: The author reports Abu al-Baqa's third solution, treating ism as superfluous, like the poetic phrase meaning peace be upon you.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#3/r4.anchor:
الثالث: أن لفظ " اسم " زائد كقوله:
18 إلى الحول ثم اسم السلام عليكما

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#3/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#3/r5.speaker: أبو عبيدة والأخفش وقطرب
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#3/r5.claim: Abu Ubayda, al-Akhfash, and Qutrub also adopt the analysis that ism is superfluous; poems by the cited poets illustrate it.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#3/r5.anchor: وإليه ذهب أبو عبيدة والأخفش وقطرب

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#3/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#3/r6.speaker: الأخفش
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#3/r6.claim: Al-Akhfash says the alleged extra word shifts the phrase from an oath to an invocation of blessing.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#3/r6.anchor: فقال الأخفش: ليخرج من حكم القسم إلى قصد التبرك

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#3/r7.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#3/r7.speaker: قطرب
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#3/r7.claim: Qutrub says the added word serves honor and exaltation.

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#3/r8.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#3/r8.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#3/r8.claim: The author calls both addition and deletion explanations weak because neither is adopted without necessity.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#3/r8.anchor: وهذان الجوابان ضعيفان لأن الزيادة والحذف لا يصار إليهما إلا إذا اضطر إليهما

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#3/r9.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#3/r9.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#3/r9.claim: Apparent self-annexation also occurs in name-plus-title and noun-plus-description phrases; grammarians explain these by meaning-name shifts or omitted annexes.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#3/r9.anchor: ومن هذا القبيل - أعني ما يوهم إضافة الشيء إلى نفسه - إضافة الاسم إلى اللقب

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#3/r10.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#3/r10.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#3/r10.claim: Basrans derive ism from sumu, elevation, because the name raises and reveals its referent; Kufans derive it from wasm, a mark, semantically plausible but morphologically unsound.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#3/r10.anchor: فذهب أهل البصرة إلى أنه مشتق من السمو وهو الارتفاع، لأنه يدل على مسماه فيرفعه ويظهره، وذهب الكوفيون إلى أنه مشتق من الوسم

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#4/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#4/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#4/r1.claim: Basrans cite the plural asma, diminutive sumayy, and related Arabic forms as evidence for derivation from sumu; a wasm derivation would predict awsam and wasim, which are not used.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#4/r1.anchor: استدل البصريون على مذهبهم بتكسيرهم له على " أسماء " وتصغيرهم له على سمي

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#4/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#4/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#4/r2.claim: The Basran analysis also fits common deletion of a word-final weak radical and treats initial hamzat al-wasl as its replacement; deleting an initial radical is less common.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#4/r2.anchor: وأيضا فجعله من السمو مدخل له في الباب الأكثر، وجعله من الوسم مدخل له في الباب الأقل؛ وذلك أن حذف اللام كثير

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#4/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#4/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#4/r3.claim: A proposed reordered form underlying asma and sumayy is an irregular metathesis and is rejected absent necessity.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#4/r3.anchor: فالجواب أن ادعاء ذلك لا يفيد، لأن القلب على خلاف القياس فلا يصار إليه

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#4/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#4/r4.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#4/r4.claim: The etymology has theological consequences: Basrans say God always had names and attributes, the Sunni position; Kufans say creatures assigned them after creation, the Mu'tazilite position, which the author condemns as worse than created-Qur'an doctrine.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#4/r4.anchor: وهي أن من قال باشتقاقه من العلو يقول: إنه لم يزل موصوفا قبل وجود الخلق

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#4/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#4/r5.speaker: أحمد بن يحيى
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#4/r5.claim: Ahmad ibn Yahya traces sam with damma to samawtu and with kasra to sammaytu; the two cited lines illustrate the forms, though the second line is specifically on kasra.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#4/r5.anchor: وقال أحمد بن يحيى: " سم بضم السين أخذه من سموت أسمو، ومن قاله بالكسر

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#4/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#4/r6.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#4/r6.claim: Ism has five reported forms, including ism, sim in either vowel, and suma like huda; the cited poetry illustrates these variants.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#4/r6.anchor: وفي الاسم خمس لغات: " اسم " بضم الهمزة وكسرها

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#5/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#5/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#5/r1.claim: The poem with samāka suman does not prove a nominative form, since it may reflect the shortened form with damma in the accusative; nominative or genitive would be decisive.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#5/r1.anchor: ولا دليل في ذلك لجواز أن يكون من لغة من يجعله منقوصا مضموم السين

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#5/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#5/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#5/r2.claim: The initial hamza is hamzat al-wasl, usually omitted in connected speech but retained by poetic necessity; ism is one of ten words beginning with it.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#5/r2.anchor: وهمزته همزة وصل أي تثبت ابتداء وتحذف درجا، وقد تثبت ضرورة

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#5/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#5/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#5/r3.claim: The spelling alif was normally retained, but was omitted specifically before Allah because the phrase is frequent; another explanation says spelling follows pronunciation.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#5/r3.anchor: والأصل في هذه الهمزة أن تثبت خطا كغيرها من همزات الوصل، وإنما حذفوها حين يضاف الاسم إلى الجلالة

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#5/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#5/r4.speaker: النحاس
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#5/r4.claim: Al-Nahhas explains there is no true deletion: the original short form loses a vowel after ba for ease, producing the written form; the author calls this a good account.

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#5/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#5/r5.speaker: الكسائي والأخفش
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#5/r5.claim: Al-Kisa'i and al-Akhfash reportedly allow dropping the hamza when ism is annexed to another divine name, as in bism rabbika or bism al-khaliq.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#5/r5.anchor: وحكي عن الكسائي والأخفش جواز حذفها إذا أضيفت إلى غير الجلالة من أسماء الباري

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#5/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#5/r6.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#5/r6.claim: Every genitive prepositional phrase needs a governor, except with an extra preposition and certain analyses of lalla and lawla; Ibn Asfur adds the simile kaf, which the author says is governed.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#5/r6.anchor: واعلم أن كل جار ومجرور لا بد له من شيء يتعلق به، فعل أو ما في معناه

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#5/r7.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#5/r7.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#5/r7.claim: Basrans take the omitted governor of bismillah to be a noun, while Kufans take it to be a verb.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#5/r7.anchor: واختلف النحويون في ذلك، فذهب أهل البصرة إلى أن المتعلق به اسم، وذهب أهل الكوفة إلى أنه فعل

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#5/r8.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#5/r8.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#5/r8.claim: Some Basrans omit a nominal subject and predicate, such as my beginning or recitation is established by God's name; Makkī objects that this deletes a verbal noun while retaining its complement.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#5/r8.anchor: فذهب بعض البصريين إلى أن ذلك المحذوف مبتدأ حذف هو وخبره

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#5/r9.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#5/r9.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#5/r9.claim: Other Basrans omit a predicate and its subject, leaving the prepositional phrase as predicate, either nominative or accusative according to its role.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#5/r9.anchor: وذهب بعضهم إلى أنه خبر حذف هو ومبتدؤه أيضا وبقي معموله قائما مقامه

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#5/r10.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#5/r10.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#5/r10.claim: Some Kufans place an implicit verb before the phrase; others, including al-Zamakhshari, place it after to mark exclusive dedication against pagan formulas naming al-Lat or al-Uzza.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#5/r10.anchor: ومنهم من قدر بعده: والتقدير: باسم الله أقرأ أو أبتدئ أو أتلو

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#6/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#6/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#6/r1.claim: The overt iqra bism rabbik is explained either by the priority of reading in the first-revealed sura or by attaching the phrase to a later iqra; the latter creates a long interruption and makes the second iqra redundant.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#6/r1.anchor:
اقرأ باسم ربك
[القلم: 1]، حيث صرح بهذا العامل مقدما على معموله

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#6/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#6/r2.speaker: الفراء
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#6/r2.claim: Al-Farra' takes the omitted governing verb as an imperative: you read in God's name.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#6/r2.anchor: فذهب الفراء أنه أمر تقديره: اقرأ أنت باسم الله

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#6/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#6/r3.speaker: الزجاج
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#6/r3.claim: Al-Zajjaj instead takes it as a declarative, I read or begin in God's name.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#6/r3.anchor: وذهب الزجاج أنه خبر تقديره: اقرأ أنا أو أبتدئ ونحوه

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#6/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#6/r4.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#6/r4.claim: The genitive Allah may be governed by the annexed noun, the implicit preposition, or the annexation relation; the author prefers the preposition.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#6/r4.anchor: وهل العامل في المضاف إليه المضاف أو حرف الجر المقدر أو معنى الإضافة؟ ثلاثة أقوال خيرها أوسطها

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#6/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#6/r5.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#6/r5.claim: Allah is a proper name exclusively for the true deity; ilah before contraction also has this exclusive sense, while bare ilah can name false gods too.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#6/r5.anchor: وهو علم على المعبود بحق، لا يطلق على غيره

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#6/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#6/r6.speaker: الزمخشري
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#6/r6.claim: Al-Zamakhshari says Allah became a proper name through common usage prevailing over other uses.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#6/r6.anchor: قال الزمخشري: " كأنه صار علما بالغلبة

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#6/r7.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#6/r7.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#6/r7.claim: The author prefers that Allah is primitive rather than derived and says it is the most definite of nouns; a dream story has Sibawayh praise God for making its name the most definite.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#6/r7.anchor: واختلف الناس هل هو مرتجل أو مشتق؟، والصواب الأول، وهو أعرف المعارف

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#6/r8.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#6/r8.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#6/r8.claim: One derivation links the name to lāha, to rise, and the sun-name ilāha; an elaborate explanation of lahanaka from lillahi innaka is condemned as contrived.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#6/r8.anchor: من قال: هو مشتق من لاه يليه أي ارتفع

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#7/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#7/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#7/r1.claim: The author calls the derivation of lahanaka in the cited verse by deleting the preposition, article, alif, and shifting a vowel an ugly analysis.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#7/r1.anchor: وهذا سماجة من قائله. وفي البيت قولان أيسر من هذا

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#7/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#7/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#7/r2.claim: Another derivation is from lāha yalūhu, to be hidden; on both analyses the original form is lāh and later article assimilation yields Allah.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#7/r2.anchor: ومنهم من قال: " هو مشتق من لاه يلوه لياها. أي احتجب

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#7/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#7/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#7/r3.claim: A third derivation is alaha, with senses worship, find repose, be bewildered, and fear; the name describes creatures worshipping, seeking refuge, wondering, and fearing God.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#7/r3.anchor: ومنهم من جعله مشتقا من أله، وأله لفظ مشترك بين معان وهي: العبادة والسكون والتحير والفزع

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#7/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#7/r4.speaker: رؤبة
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#7/r4.claim: Ru'ba's word ta'alluh witnesses the worship sense; the verse phrase wa-yadharuka wa-ālihataka is also read as your worship.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#7/r4.anchor:
ومنه قول رؤبة:
25 لله در الغانيات المده
سبحن واسترجعن من تألهي

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#7/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#7/r5.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#7/r5.claim: A report urging thought about God's blessings, not God Himself, and Ali's saying that reflection on divine attributes ends in bewilderment support the bewilderment sense.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#7/r5.anchor: معنى التحير أشار أمير المؤمنين بقوله: " كل دون صفاته تحبير الصفات

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#7/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#7/r6.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#7/r6.claim: On the al-ilah derivation, hamza is dropped through frequent use, like anās becoming nās; an alternative account transfers its vowel before deletion.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#7/r6.anchor: ثم حذفت الهمزة لكثرة الاستعمال كما حذفت في ناس

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#8/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#8/r1.speaker: الخليل
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#8/r1.claim: Al-Khalil derives Allah from walah, because all creatures long for God; philosophers say all things love God, supported by the verse that everything glorifies Him.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#8/r1.anchor: ويعزى هذا القول للخليل، فعلى هذين القولين وزن إلاه: فعال، وهو بمعنى مفعول أي: معبود أو متحير فيه كالكتاب بمعنى مكتوب

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#8/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#8/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#8/r2.claim: This derivation changes initial waw to hamza, like ishaah and i'aah from wishah and wi'aah; the name then has the pattern fa'al meaning worshipped or wondered at.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#8/r2.anchor: فأصله: ولاه ثم أبدلت الواو همزة كما أبدلت في إشاح وإعاء

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#8/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#8/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#8/r3.claim: The author rebuts al-Khalil: if hamza replaced waw, the original forms should remain pronounceable, and the word should pluralize as awliha; neither occurs.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#8/r3.anchor: ورد قول الخليل بوجهين، أحدهما: أنه لو كانت الهمزة بدلا من واو لجاز النطق بالأصل

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#8/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#8/r4.speaker: الخليل
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#8/r4.claim: Al-Khalil can answer that the replacement became obligatory because this name has unique grammatical properties and its plural preserves that replacement.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#8/r4.anchor: وللخليل أن ينفصل عن هذين الاعتراضين بأن البدل لزم في هذا الاسم لأنه اختص بأحكام لم يشركه فيها غيره

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#8/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#8/r5.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#8/r5.claim: Whether the article in Allah is original depends on whether the name is derived; if derived it is original, otherwise added.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#8/r5.anchor: وأما الألف واللام فيترتب الكلام فيها على كونه مشتقا أو غير مشتق

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#8/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#8/r6.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#8/r6.claim: The alif was omitted in writing to distinguish Allah from the idol al-Lat; another explanation invokes the word al-lāh, while a third calls the spelling a rare form fixed by frequent use.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#8/r6.anchor: قالوا: وحذفت الألف التي قبل الهاء خطا لئلا يشبه بخط " اللات

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#8/r7.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#8/r7.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#8/r7.claim: The lām of Allah is emphatic except after kasra; al-Zamakhshari's unqualified statement should be understood this way, while Abu al-Baqa's report of always-light pronunciation is rejected.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#8/r7.anchor: وحكم لامه التفخيم تعظيما ما لم يتقدمه كسر فترقق

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#8/r8.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#8/r8.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#8/r8.claim: Readers disagree about the lām after an imāla-like open vowel; al-Susi has one reading with a light lām in hatta nara Allah jahratan.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#8/r8.anchor: ونقل أهل القراءة خلافا فيما إذا تقدمه فتحة ممالة

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#9/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#9/r1.speaker: السهيلي وابن العربي
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#9/r1.claim: Al-Suhayli and Ibn al-Arabi unusually say the article is original; the author objects that this would make the pattern fa'al regularly take tanwin, which Allah does not.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#9/r1.anchor: ونقل السهيلي وابن العربي فيه قولا غريبا وهو أن الألف واللام فيه أصلية غير زائدة

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#9/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#9/r2.speaker: أبو زيد البلخي
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#9/r2.claim: Abu Zayd al-Balkhi reports that Allah is a Syriac loan from laha; a poem preserves the supposed original form lahi.

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#9/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#9/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#9/r3.claim: A strange proposal derives the name from the pronoun hu plus a possessive lām and article; the author says it resembles mysticism, not linguistic scholarship.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#9/r3.anchor: ومن غريب ما نقل فيه أيضا أن الأصل فيه الهاء التي هي كناية عن الغائب

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#9/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#9/r4.speaker: الزمخشري
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#9/r4.claim: Al-Zamakhshari rejects treating Allah as an adjective: it is used as a noun, while adjectives require a noun they describe and cannot all remain without one.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#9/r4.anchor: وقد رد الزمخشري هذا القول بما معناه أنك تصفه ولا تصف به

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#10/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#10/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#10/r1.claim: Al-Rahman and al-Rahim are derived adjectives from mercy, though some say al-Rahman is not derived because Arabs asked what al-Rahman is.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#10/r1.anchor: الرحمن الرحيم: صفتان مشتقتان من الرحمة، وقيل: الرحمن ليس مشتقا

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#10/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#10/r2.speaker: ابن العربي
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#10/r2.claim: Ibn al-Arabi answers that Arabs knew the referent but not the attribute, asking what al-Rahman is rather than who it is.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#10/r2.anchor: وأجاب ابن العربي عنه بأنهم جهلوا الصفة دون الموصوف

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#10/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#10/r3.speaker: الأعلم الشنتمري
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#10/r3.claim: Al-A'lam al-Shantamari treats al-Rahman as an appositive proper name, citing its independent use in two verses.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#10/r3.anchor: وذهب الأعلم الشنتمري إلى أن " الرحمن " بدل من اسم الله لا نعت له

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#10/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#10/r4.speaker: السهيلي
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#10/r4.claim: Al-Suhayli rejects the appositive analysis because Allah needs no clarification; Arabs ask what al-Rahman is but never what Allah is.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#10/r4.anchor: وقد رد عليه السهيلي بأنه لو كان بدلا لكان مبينا لما قبله

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#10/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#10/r5.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#10/r5.claim: An adjective may stand after its understood noun is omitted, so al-Rahman occurring without Allah does not prove it is an appositive; the verse and a simile poem illustrate this.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#10/r5.anchor: أما قوله: " جاء غير تابع " فذلك لا يمنع كونه صفة، لأنه إذا علم الموصوف جاز حذفه

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#10/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#10/r6.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#10/r6.claim: Mercy can mean tenderness, making divine mercy figuratively God's beneficence and an attribute of action; the author prefers the view that it is God's willing good, a real attribute of essence.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#10/r6.anchor: وقيل: الرحمة إرادة الخير لمن أراد الله به ذلك، ووصفه بها على هذا القول حقيقة

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#10/r7.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#10/r7.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#10/r7.claim: Another account says mercy is tenderness that prompts kindness; for God it means kindness alone, as a report contrasts divine beneficence with human tenderness.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#10/r7.anchor: وعلى هذا روي: " الرحمة من الله إنعام وإفضال، ومن الآدميين رقة وتعطف

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#11/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#11/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#11/r1.claim: Ibn Abbas calls the two names tender, one more tender than the other, meaning more merciful; al-Khattabi says tenderness does not belong among divine attributes.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#11/r1.anchor: وقال ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما: " وهما اسمان رقيقان أحدهما أرق من الآخر

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#11/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#11/r2.speaker: الحسين بن الفضل
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#11/r2.claim: Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl says the narrator erred: the names are rafīqān, one gentler than the other, a quality supported by a prophetic saying that God loves gentleness.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#11/r2.anchor: وقال الحسين بن الفضل: " هذا وهم من الراوي، وإنما هما اسمان رفيقان

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#11/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#11/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#11/r3.claim: Al-Rahim describes God as especially gentle toward believers.

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#11/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#11/r4.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#11/r4.claim: Some treat Rahman and Rahim as synonyms like nadman and nadim, with one view saying the pair is emphatic; another says Rahman is paired with Rahim because Musaylima claimed the former title.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#11/r4.anchor: فذهب بعضهم إلى أنهما بمعنى واحد كندمان ونديم، ثم اختلف هؤلاء على قولين

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#11/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#11/r5.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#11/r5.claim: The Musaylima explanation is very weak because his claim is irrelevant and the basmala predates his rise.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#11/r5.anchor: وهذا ضعيف جدا، فإن تسميته بذلك غير معتد بها البتة

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#11/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#11/r6.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#11/r6.claim: Others assign each name a distinct object: mercy is universal to believers and unbelievers in this world but reserved for believers in the next; a reversed report also circulates, and the author doubts this distinction alone.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#11/r6.anchor: ومنهم من قال: لكل واحد فائدة غير فائدة الآخر، وجعل ذلك بالنسبة إلى تغاير متعلقهما

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#11/r7.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#11/r7.speaker: الزمخشري
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#11/r7.claim: Al-Zamakhshari and the author hold Rahman to be more intensive and exclusive to God; despite normal progression from weaker to stronger, Rahim follows to cover subtler blessings after Rahman covers great ones.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#11/r7.anchor: من قال: الرحمن أبلغ، ولذلك لا يطلق على غير الباري تعالى، واختاره الزمخشري

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#12/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#12/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#12/r1.claim: Some make Rahim more intensive and cite a report of worldly Rahim and afterlife Rahman, but the author says it instead confirms Rahman is stronger because afterlife mercy is greater.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#12/r1.anchor: ومنهم من عكس فجعل الرحيم أبلغ، ويؤيده رواية من قال: " رحيم الدنيا

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#12/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#12/r2.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#12/r2.claim: The author invokes the report that God has stored ninety-nine mercies for the Day of Resurrection to support Rahman's stronger intensity.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#12/r2.anchor: على ما يروى أنه خبأ لعباده تسعا وتسعين رحمة ليوم القيامة

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#12/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#12/r3.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#12/r3.claim: The patterns intensify differently: fa'lan conveys fullness and dominance, while fa'il conveys repeated occurrence at sites of mercy.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#12/r3.anchor: والظاهر أن جهة المبالغة فيهما مختلفة، فمبالغة " فعلان " من حيث الامتلاء والغلبة

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#12/r4.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#12/r4.speaker: أبو عبيدة
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#12/r4.claim: Abu Ubayda says fa'lan marks an intensified act, while fa'il can mean either agent or patient; his poem calls someone in war compassionate.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#12/r4.anchor: وقال أبو عبيدة: " وبناء فعلان ليس كبناء فعيل، فإن بناء فعلان لا يقع إلا على مبالغة الفعل

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#12/r5.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#12/r5.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#12/r5.claim: Rahman is restricted in name but broad in action, whereas Rahim is broad in name but restricted in action; hence fa'lan is not transitive while fa'il is.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#12/r5.anchor: فالرحمن خاص الاسم عام الفعل. والرحيم عام الاسم خاص الفعل، ولذلك لا يتعدى فعلان ويتعدى فعيل

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#12/r6.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#12/r6.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#12/r6.claim: The article in al-Rahman marks dominance; most scholars restrict it to God, unlike Rahim, which also describes the Prophet toward believers.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#12/r6.anchor: والألف واللام في " الرحمن " للغلبة كهي في " الصعق " ، ولا يطلق على غير الباري تعالى

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#12/r7.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#12/r7.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#12/r7.claim: The poet's use of Rahman for Musaylima is dismissed as obstinate excess; the name normally occurs with the article or in annexation.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#12/r7.anchor:
وأما قول الشاعر في مسيلمة الكذاب -لعنه الله تعالى-:
32...................................
وأنت غيث الورى لا زلت رحمانا
فلا يلتفت إلى قوله لفرط تعنتهم

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#12/r8.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#12/r8.speaker: ثعلب والمبرد
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#12/r8.claim: Tha'lab and al-Mubarrad transmit an unusual claim that the word is non-Arabic and pronounced with khā', citing a poem with rakhman.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#12/r8.anchor:
قاله ثعلب [والمبرد وأنشد]:
33 لن تدركوا المجد أو تشروا عباءكم

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#13/r1.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#13/r1.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#13/r1.claim: Most connect al-Rahim to al-hamd with kasra on mīm, normally as an inflectional ending; a second explanation treats it as a pause form restored with kasra before a consonant.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#13/r1.anchor: وفي وصل الرحيم بالحمد ثلاثة أوجه، الذي عليه الجمهور: الرحيم بكسر الميم موصولة بالحمد

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#13/r2.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#13/r2.speaker: أم سلمة
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#13/r2.claim: Umm Salama transmits stopping after al-Rahim and beginning al-hamd with a cut hamza.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#13/r2.anchor: والثاني من وجهي الوصل: سكون الميم والوقف عليها، والابتداء بقطع ألف " الحمد " ، روت ذلك أم سلمة

SAMIN-DURR:1:1#13/r3.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#13/r3.speaker: الكسائي
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#13/r3.claim: Al-Kisa'i reports a dialectal reading fathing mīm and connecting al-hamd by transferring the hamza's vowel; Ibn Atiyya says it is not established as a reading, and the author prefers parsing the fathah as an accusative cut-off construction.
SAMIN-DURR:1:1#13/r3.anchor: حكى الكسائي عن بعض العرب أنها تقرأ: الرحيم الحمد " بفتح الميم ووصل ألف الحمد

RAZI-FULL:v1p214#2/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p214#2/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p214#2/r5.claim: The seven Fatiha verses remove seven vices: praise dispels desire, Lord of the worlds greed, Judgment Day anger, worship and aid pride and vanity, guidance caprice, the favored path unbelief and doubt, and the final phrase innovation.
RAZI-FULL:v1p214#2/r5.anchor: فثبت أن هذه الآيات السبع دافعة لتلك الأخلاق القبيحة السبعة

RAZI-FULL:v1p215/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p215/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p215/r1.claim: Al-Fatiha gathers what people need to know about the origin, the middle of servitude, and the return; Razi begins its proof of the Creator from human creation, citing Abraham and Moses.
RAZI-FULL:v1p215/r1.anchor: في تقرير أن سورة الفاتحة جامعة لكل ما يحتاج الإنسان إليه في معرفة المبدأ والوسط والمعاد

RAZI-FULL:v1p215/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p215/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p215/r2.claim: The Qur'an repeatedly establishes the Creator by reflecting on human creation: Abraham says his Lord gives life and death and created him, and Moses says his Lord gave each thing its form and guided it.
RAZI-FULL:v1p215/r2.anchor: ألا ترى أن إبراهيم عليه السلام قال

RAZI-FULL:v1p215#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p215#2/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p215#2/r1.claim: The Qur'an uses human creation to prove the Creator, as in the command to worship the Lord who created people and the first revelation about creating humanity from a clot.
RAZI-FULL:v1p215#2/r1.anchor: استدل بخلق الإنسان على وجود الصانع تعالى

RAZI-FULL:v1p215#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p215#2/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p215#2/r2.claim: The proof from creation is also a blessing: it teaches the servant that God exists and gives a great benefit, so it is both evidence and grace.
RAZI-FULL:v1p215#2/r2.anchor: فهذه الحالة من حيث أنها تعرف العبد وجود الإله دليل ومن حيث أنها نفع عظيم وصل من الله إلى العبد إنعام

RAZI-FULL:v1p215#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p215#2/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p215#2/r3.claim: The varied organs formed from similar semen show that a knowing, powerful Creator deliberately shapes them for human interests through mercy, making Him worthy of praise.
RAZI-FULL:v1p215#2/r3.anchor: تولد الأعضاء المختلفة الطبائع والصور والأشكال من النطفة المتشابهة الأجزاء

RAZI-FULL:v1p215#2/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p215#2/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p215#2/r4.claim: “Praise belongs to God” indicates the Creator's existence, knowledge, power, mercy, perfect wisdom, and entitlement to praise and glorification.
RAZI-FULL:v1p215#2/r4.anchor: يدل على وجود الصانع وعلى علمه وقدرته ورحمته وكمال حكمته

RAZI-FULL:v1p217/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p217/r1.speaker: الله تعالى
RAZI-FULL:v1p217/r1.claim: In a divine report transmitted by the Prophet, God responds to each Fatiha phrase: the opening remembers Him, praise praises Him, the mercy names magnify Him, Judgment Day glorifies Him or is entrusted to Him, worship belongs to Him, aid relies on Him, and guidance is the servant's request.
RAZI-FULL:v1p217/r1.anchor: فإذا قال العبد : بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم يقول الله تعالى ذكرني عبدي

RAZI-FULL:v1p217/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p217/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p217/r2.claim: Calling the Fatiha “prayer” shows that religious law serves human interests: people most need knowledge of God's lordship and servitude, which the surah's two halves provide to fulfill the covenant.
RAZI-FULL:v1p217/r2.anchor: مدار الشرائع على رعاية مصالح الخلق

RAZI-FULL:v1p217/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p217/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p217/r3.claim: Since God names the Fatiha “prayer,” prayer without its recitation does not occur; Razi takes this to establish that reciting it is a pillar, as his school holds.
RAZI-FULL:v1p217/r3.anchor: أن عند عدم قراءة الفاتحة وجب أن لا تحصل الصلاة

RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r1.claim: Razi supports obligatory Fatiha recitation because the Prophet consistently recited it and commands require following him.

RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r2.claim: The rightly guided caliphs also consistently recited it, and the Prophet commanded Muslims to follow their sunna.
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r2.anchor: أن الخلفاء الراشدين واظبوا على قراءتها

RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r3.claim: Muslims everywhere recite it in prayer, and the Qur'an commands following the path of believers.
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r3.anchor: أن جميع المسلمين شرقا وغربا لا يصلون إلا بقراءة الفاتحة

RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r4.claim: The prophetic statement “no prayer without the Opening of the Book” directly supports the requirement.

RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r5.claim: The command to recite what is easy from the Qur'an is obligatory; because reciting other passages is not, the obligatory recitation must be the Fatiha.
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r5.anchor: وظاهره الوجوب فكانت قراءة ما تيسر من القرآن واجبة

RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r6.claim: Reciting the Fatiha is the safer course, following the prophetic instruction to leave what causes doubt for what does not.
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r6.anchor: أن قراءة الفاتحة أحوط فوجب المصير إليها

RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r7.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r7.claim: The Prophet's constant practice makes abandoning his command forbidden, and Muslims agree that the Fatiha is better and more complete than another recitation.
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r7.anchor: وسابعها : أن الرسول عليه السلام واظب على قراءتها فوجب أن يكون العدول عنه محرما

RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r8.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r8.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r8.claim: If the superior prayer with the Fatiha discharges the obligation, it does not follow that the inferior prayer with another passage does; the obligation remains due.
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r8.anchor: ولا يلزم من الخروج عن العهدة بالعمل الكامل الخروج عن العهدة بالعمل الناقص

RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r9.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r9.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r9.claim: Prayer seeks remembrance of the heart, and this concise surah gathers lordship and servitude and is equated with the mighty Qur'an; nothing else can replace it.
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r9.anchor: المقصود من الصلاة حصول ذكر القلب

RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r10.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r10.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r10.claim: The transmitted report itself says that prayer is not established without the Fatiha.
RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r10.anchor: أن هذا الخبر الذي رويناه يدل على أن عند فقدان الفاتحة لا تحصل الصلاة

RAZI-FULL:v1p218/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p218/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p218/r1.claim: When the servant remembers God through the opening, God remembers him in turn, as promised in the Qur'an.
RAZI-FULL:v1p218/r1.anchor: لما أقدم العبد على ذكر الله لا جرم ذكره تعالى

RAZI-FULL:v1p218/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p218/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p218/r2.claim: Remembrance is a high and honored form of worship: God repeatedly commands abundant remembrance and praises those who remember in every posture and when resisting Satan.
RAZI-FULL:v1p218/r2.anchor: أن مقام الذكر مقام عال شريف في العبودية

RAZI-FULL:v1p218/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p218/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p218/r3.claim: The report supports taking “Allah” as a proper name for God's unique essence, since a derived general noun could not identify that individual essence; “All-Merciful” and “Merciful” are universal terms.
RAZI-FULL:v1p218/r3.anchor: يدل على أن قولنا الله اسم علم لذاته المخصوصة

RAZI-FULL:v1p219/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p219/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p219/r4.claim: The seven Fatiha verses correspond to the seven bodily prayer acts—standing, bowing, rising, first prostration, rising between prostrations, second prostration, and sitting—as soul to body.
RAZI-FULL:v1p219/r4.anchor: أن آيات الفاتحة سبع والأعمال المحسوسة أيضا في الصلاة سبعة

RAZI-FULL:v1p220/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p220/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p220/r1.claim: The opening formula corresponds to standing: the connected letter bāʾ remains upright, and both the formula and standing begin the acts of prayer and other important matters.
RAZI-FULL:v1p220/r1.anchor: حصلت المناسبة بين التسمية وبين القيام من هذه الوجوه

RAZI-FULL:v1p220/r8.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p220/r8.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p220/r8.claim: The seven Fatiha verses are the soul of the seven prayer acts, themselves the soul of seven stages of human formation; God is the soul of souls and light of lights.
RAZI-FULL:v1p220/r8.anchor: روح الأرواح ونور الأنوار هو الله تعالى

RAZI-FULL:v1p221/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p221/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p221/r1.claim: Muhammad's ascent has a bodily journey from Mecca to Jerusalem and then the high kingdom, and a spiritual journey from the visible to the unseen and from the unseen to the unseen of the unseen.
RAZI-FULL:v1p221/r1.anchor: أما ما يتعلق بعالم الأرواح فله معراجان

RAZI-FULL:v1p221/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p221/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p221/r2.claim: The spiritual ascent rises through human spirits, the spirits of the heavens, angels, throne-bearers, and pure spirits detached from bodies, whose worship and love of God exceed human comprehension.
RAZI-FULL:v1p221/r2.anchor: ثم تترقى فتنتهي إلى الأرواح المقدسة عن التعلقات بالأجسام

RAZI-FULL:v1p221/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p221/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p221/r3.claim: The ascent continues through ever-higher spiritual ranks until God, the source of all good and mercy; thus the spirit-world is the unseen and God's presence the unseen of the unseen.
RAZI-FULL:v1p221/r3.anchor: فثبت أن عالم الأرواح هو عالم الغيب وحضرة جلال الربوبية هي غيب الغيب

RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r1.speaker: النبي
RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r1.claim: A prophetic report says God has seventy veils of light; if unveiled, the splendor of His face would burn everything perceived by sight, and only prophetic light reveals the number.
RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r1.anchor: إن لله سبعين حجابا من النور لو كشفها لأحرقت سبحات وجهه كل ما أدرك البصر

RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r2.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r2.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r2.claim: Prayer was given to Muhammad as a gift for his community because it joins bodily ascent through actions with spiritual ascent through remembrances.
RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r2.anchor: إن تحفة أمتك الصلاة وذلك لأنها جامعة بين المعراج الجسماني وبين المعراج الروحاني

RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r3.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r3.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r3.claim: Before beginning the ascent, the worshipper purifies body and clothing for the holy presence and chooses which of opposing companions—angel or devil, reason or desire, truth or falsehood, and so forth—to follow, since settled companionship is hard to break.
RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r3.anchor: فإنه إذا استحكمت المرافقة تعذرت المفارقة

RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r4.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r4.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r4.claim: Raising the hands signals leaving both worlds and directing all inner faculties toward God; “God is greatest” means He exceeds all beings, knowledge, comparison, and even the claim that He is simply greater.
RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r4.anchor: فاقطع نظرك عنهما بالكلية ووجه قلبك وروحك وسرك وعقلك وفهمك

RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r5.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r5.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r5.claim: The opening glorification reveals the lights of divine majesty and moves from declaring God's transcendence to praising Him.
RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r5.anchor: ثم قل : سبحانك اللهم وبحمدك وفي هذا المقام تجلى لك نور سبحات الجلال

RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r6.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r6.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r6.claim: “Blessed is Your name” unveils pre-eternity and eternity, since blessing here indicates abiding beyond extinction and nonexistence.
RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r6.anchor: لأن قوله تبارك إشارة إلى الدوام المنزه عن الإفناء والإعدام

RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r7.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r7.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r7.claim: “Exalted is Your majesty” signifies that God's knowledge and greatness exceed every stated measure.
RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r7.anchor: أعلم وأعظم من أن تكون صفات جلاله ونعوت كماله محصورة في القدر المذكور

RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r8.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r8.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r8.claim: “There is no god but You” means every attribute of majesty and perfection belongs only to God; ultimately reason, speech, understanding, and imagination fail before Him.
RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r8.anchor: كل صفات الجلال وسمات الكمال له لا لغيره

STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r1.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r1.claim: Most scholars place al-Fātiḥah among the earliest sūrahs revealed in Makkah.
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r1.anchor: to have been revealed in Makkah

STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r2.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r2.speaker: Mujāhid
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r2.claim: Mujāhid says al-Fātiḥah was revealed in Madinah.
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r2.anchor: According to Mujāhid (d. 104/722–23), one of the leading scholars among the second generation of Muslims, this sūrah was revealed in Madinah

STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r3.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r3.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r3.claim: Most scholars reject a Medinan origin because Muslims needed the sūrah to perform obligatory prayers.
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r3.anchor: Most scholars claim that this is impossible, however, as the Muslims would not have been able to perform their required prayers without it

STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r4.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r4.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r4.claim: Al-Fātiḥah means The Opening: it opens the Book, each prayer cycle, many everyday acts, and may open the breast to faith.
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r4.anchor: The primary meaning of al-Fātiḥah is “The Opening,” which indicates the sūrah’s function as “the opening of the Book”

STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r5.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r5.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r5.claim: The sūrah is seen as a synthesis and the Quran’s most important chapter, hence Umm al-kitāb; the title also refers to 3:7 and the celestial archetype of scripture.
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r5.anchor: has been given the title Umm al-kitāb, “Mother of the Book,” a

STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r6.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r6.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r6.claim: It is called the Mother of the Quran because it contains the meaning of the entire Quran.
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r6.anchor: It is also known as “The Mother of the Quran” (IK, Ṭ), a reference to its containing the meaning of the entire Quran

STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r7.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r7.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r7.claim: Another title, The Seven Oft-Repeated, is linked to 15:87.

STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r8.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r8.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r8.claim: The title The Cure reflects its reputed healing power for body and soul.
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r8.anchor: is said to have healing powers for both body and soul

STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r9.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r9.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r9.claim: The title The Foundation reflects the Fātiḥah’s role as a foundation for the whole Quran.
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r9.anchor: because it serves as a foundation

STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r10.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r10.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r10.claim: As Sūrat al-Ḥamd and Sūrat al-Ṣalāh, the Fātiḥah begins each prayer cycle for Sunnis and many Shiites.
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r10.anchor: the Fātiḥah is recited at the beginning of each

STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r11.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r11.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r11.claim: Shiite law permits reciting the Fātiḥah in the third and fourth cycles or an alternative formula praising God.
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r11.anchor: In Shiite law one is allowed to recite the Fātiḥah

STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r12.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r12.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r12.claim: Muslims recite the Fātiḥah at diverse life events; funeral services are called fātiḥah in some lands as an opening from one life to another.
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r12.anchor: It is also recited by Muslims on occasions as diverse as a funeral, a wedding, the birth of a child, the inauguration of an official event

STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r13.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r13.speaker: Prophet Muhammad
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r13.claim: The Prophet identifies the Fātiḥah as the greatest sūrah, calling it Praise be to God and the seven oft-repeated, and linking it to 15:87.
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r13.anchor: the Prophet told a man that he would teach him the greatest sūrah; when asked what it was, the Prophet responded

STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r14.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r14.speaker: God
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r14.claim: In a hadith qudsī, God responds to the servant’s praise, magnification, and glorification during the prayer, which is divided between them.
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r14.anchor: I have divided the prayer between Myself and My

STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r15.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r15.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r15.claim: The Fātiḥah is a prayer encapsulating metaphysical and eschatological realities and teaches the proper human disposition toward God.
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r15.anchor: the Fātiḥah is more than the confessional prayer of Muslims. It is a prayer that encapsulates all the metaphysical and eschatological realities

STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r16.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r16.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r16.claim: Its structure moves from God’s nature in the first three verses, through the God-human relationship, to human states in the final three.
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r16.anchor: The Fātiḥah thus has a threefold structure: the first three verses deal with the nature of God, the middle verse deals with the relationship between God and human beings

STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r17.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r17.speaker: Prophet Muhammad
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r17.claim: A report says nothing like the Fātiḥah was revealed in the Torah, Psalms, Gospel, or Quran.
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r17.anchor: In one the Prophet says, “By Him in Whose Hand lies my soul, in neither the Torah, the Psalms, the Gospel, nor the Quran was the like of it revealed”

STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r18.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r18.speaker: Mujāhid
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r18.claim: One attribution says Satan was frightened when the Fātiḥah was revealed, among four events; others attribute the saying to the Prophet.
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r18.anchor: attributed by some to Mujāhid (Q) and by

STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r19.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r19.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r19.claim: The Fātiḥah’s exalted status generated many independent commentaries, often showing how the Quran as a whole is contained in it.
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r19.anchor: The exalted status of the Fātiḥah has resulted in numerous independent commentaries upon it, some numbering hundreds of pages

STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r20.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r20.speaker: ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r20.claim: A saying attributed to ʿAlī compresses the Quran into the Fātiḥah, the basmalah, its opening bāʾ, and the diacritical point beneath it.
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r20.anchor: a famous saying attributed to ʿAlī ibn AbīṬālib

STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r21.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r21.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r21.claim: The point beneath bāʾ can symbolize the Divine Pen’s first drop of ink, which inscribed all archetypes on the Preserved Tablet before creation; thus basmalah marks both Quranic and cosmic beginnings.
STUDYQURAN:1:intro/r21.anchor:
This point can be understood to represent the first
drop of ink

STUDYQURAN:1:1/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:1/r1.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:1/r1.claim: Every sūrah except one opens with the basmalah, also found in 27:30.
STUDYQURAN:1:1/r1.anchor: known as the basmalah in Arabic

STUDYQURAN:1:1/r2.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:1/r2.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:1/r2.claim: Scholars disagree whether the basmalah is a verse of each sūrah or a marker beginning a new sūrah.
STUDYQURAN:1:1/r2.anchor: There is a debate as to whether the basmalah is a verse of each sūrah or an indication of the beginning of a new sūrah

STUDYQURAN:1:1/r3.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:1/r3.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:1/r3.claim: Except in Shāfiʿī and Jaʿfarī law, most schools do not recite the basmalah with sūrahs during daily prayers.
STUDYQURAN:1:1/r3.anchor: with the exception of the Shāfiʿī and Jaʿfarī schools

STUDYQURAN:1:1/r4.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:1/r4.speaker: Anas ibn Mālik
STUDYQURAN:1:1/r4.claim: Anas reports that the Prophet and first three caliphs began prayer recitation with Praise be to God, omitting the basmalah.
STUDYQURAN:1:1/r4.anchor: Anas ibn Mālik (d. 91/709), a close Companion of the Prophet, is reported to have said, “I have prayed behind the Prophet, Abū Bakr

STUDYQURAN:1:1/r5.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:1/r5.speaker: Abū Hurayrah
STUDYQURAN:1:1/r5.claim: Abū Hurayrah recited the basmalah while leading prayer and said his prayer most resembled the Messenger’s.
STUDYQURAN:1:1/r5.anchor: Abū Hurayrah (d. 61/681), another of the Prophet’s Companions, is reported to have recited the basmalah

STUDYQURAN:1:1/r6.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:1/r6.speaker: Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq
STUDYQURAN:1:1/r6.claim: Jaʿfar calls the basmalah the greatest Quranic verse; Shiite scholars consequently treat it as a verse of the Fātiḥah and every sūrah beginning with it.
STUDYQURAN:1:1/r6.anchor: Based upon a saying of Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq (d. 148/765), the sixth Shiite Imam

STUDYQURAN:1:1/r7.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:1/r7.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:1/r7.claim: Some scholars count the basmalah as a verse separate from the sūrahs that begin with it.
STUDYQURAN:1:1/r7.anchor: Others say that it is a verse, though separate from the

STUDYQURAN:1:1/r8.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:1/r8.speaker: Ibn ʿAbbās
STUDYQURAN:1:1/r8.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās reports that revelation of the basmalah taught the Prophet where one sūrah ends and the next begins.
STUDYQURAN:1:1/r8.anchor: Ibn ʿAbbās (d. 68/687), a cousin of the Prophet who was among the most important scholars of the Quran in the first generation of Muslims

STUDYQURAN:1:1/r9.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:1/r9.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:1/r9.claim: The basmalah, or its shortened form, consecrates licit actions because all things should be done for God’s sake and in His Name.
STUDYQURAN:1:1/r9.anchor: The basmalah, or its shortened form, In the Name of God, is employed by pious Muslims to consecrate all licit actions

STUDYQURAN:1:1/r10.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:1/r10.speaker: Prophet Muhammad
STUDYQURAN:1:1/r10.claim: The Prophet says an important matter not begun in God’s Name will be cut off.
STUDYQURAN:1:1/r10.anchor: the Prophet said, “Any important matter not begun with the Name of God shall be cut off”

STUDYQURAN:1:1/r11.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:1/r11.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:1/r11.claim: The preposition bi may govern an implied verb such as begin or seek help, or a noun, with the phrase either preceding or following it.
STUDYQURAN:1:1/r11.anchor: could imply a verb at the beginning of the sentence

STUDYQURAN:1:1/r12.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:1/r12.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:1/r12.claim: Another interpretation makes God’s opening in His Name an invitation for people to begin, unite, and commence through His Name as well.
STUDYQURAN:1:1/r12.anchor: so you too begin,” as if God were saying

STUDYQURAN:1:1/r13.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:1/r13.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:1/r13.claim: Some consider Allāh a unique word without a root; others derive it from al-Ilāh, meaning the Divine.
STUDYQURAN:1:1/r13.anchor: God renders Allāh, which according to some is a unique word with no root and according to others derives from the word al-Ilāh

STUDYQURAN:1:1/r14.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:1/r14.speaker: author
