STUDYQURAN:1:1/r14.claim: The Quran shows pre-Islamic Arabs knew the name Allāh as creator, although most idol worshippers denied His supreme sovereignty in the Age of Ignorance.
STUDYQURAN:1:1/r14.anchor: The Quranic usage of Allāh indicates that it was already known to the pre-Islamic Arabs, as in 43:87

STUDYQURAN:1:1/r15.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:1/r15.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:1/r15.claim: Allāh is the most universal and all-embracing Divine Name, yet uniquely applies only to God, unlike other Divine Names.
STUDYQURAN:1:1/r15.anchor: Allāh is not only the most universal and all-embracing Name, but also the most specific of the Divine Names

STUDYQURAN:1:1/r16.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:1/r16.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:1/r16.claim: Some call Allāh the All-Encompassing Name, comprising all divine Names and Attributes.
STUDYQURAN:1:1/r16.anchor: Some referto Allāh as the All-Encompassing Name

STUDYQURAN:1:1/r17.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:1:1/r17.speaker: author
STUDYQURAN:1:1/r17.claim: The order Allāh, al-Raḥmān, al-Raḥīm can symbolize Essence, unity of Attributes, and unity of divine acts, respectively.
STUDYQURAN:1:1/r17.anchor: The ordering of the three Divine Names in the basmalah can be seen as an allusion to the levels of Divinity in relation to the created order

TAB-FULL:v1p111#3/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p111#3/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v1p111#3/r1.claim: God taught Muhammad to put His beautiful names before every action, establishing a practice for people opening speech, letters, books, and requests.
TAB-FULL:v1p111#3/r1.anchor: أدب نبيه محمدا صلى الله عليه وسلم بتعليمه تقديم ذكر أسمائه الحسنى أمام جميع أفعاله

TAB-FULL:v1p111#3/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p111#3/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v1p111#3/r2.claim: The prefixed bāʾ requires a governing verb omitted from the wording; the listener recovers it from the immediately accompanying action or speech.
TAB-FULL:v1p111#3/r2.anchor: مقتضية فعلا يكون لها جالبا، ولا فعل معها ظاهر

TAB-FULL:v1p111#3/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p111#3/r3.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v1p111#3/r3.claim: At Qurʾān recitation the implicit verb is read, while in other acts it is rise, sit, or the relevant action, all begun with God’s name.
TAB-FULL:v1p111#3/r3.anchor: أراد بقيله {بسم الله} [الفاتحة: 1] : أقوم بسم الله

TAB-FULL:v1p113/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p113/r1.speaker: عبد الله بن عباس
TAB-FULL:v1p113/r1.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās reports Gabriel first taught seeking refuge and then instructed Muhammad to read, rise, and sit in remembrance of his Lord.
TAB-FULL:v1p113/r1.anchor: يا محمد يقول: اقرأ بذكر الله ربك، وقم واقعد بذكر الله

TAB-FULL:v1p113/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p113/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v1p113/r2.claim: The phrase means beginning by naming and remembering God, rather than claiming that the act itself is performed through God’s power.
TAB-FULL:v1p113/r2.anchor: أبدأ بتسمية الله وذكره قبل كل شيء، أو أقرأ بتسمية الله

TAB-FULL:v1p113/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p113/r3.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v1p113/r3.claim: Arabic can use a verbal noun in a form normally associated with a noun; thus bismillah can express beginning with the act of naming.
TAB-FULL:v1p113/r3.anchor: العرب قد تخرج المصادر مبهمة على أسماء مختلفة

TAB-FULL:v1p115/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p115/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v1p115/r1.claim: Poetic usage confirms verbal nouns can take other noun forms: ʿaṭāʾika means iʿṭāʾika, ṭūl means iṭāla, and muṣāb means iṣāba.
TAB-FULL:v1p115/r1.anchor: أكفرا بعد رد الموت عني … وبعد عطائك المائة الرتاعا يريد: إعطائك

TAB-FULL:v1p115/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p115/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v1p115/r2.claim: Accordingly, the name stands for naming: the phrase means that one begins an action or recitation by naming God.
TAB-FULL:v1p115/r2.anchor: فجعل الاسم مكان التسمية، كما جعل الكلام مكان التكليم، والعطاء مكان الإعطاء

TAB-FULL:v1p116/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p116/r1.speaker: عبد الله بن عباس
TAB-FULL:v1p116/r1.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās reports Gabriel’s instruction that Muhammad read and undertake actions in remembrance of God his Lord.
TAB-FULL:v1p116/r1.anchor: يا محمد اقرأ بذكر الله ربك، وقم واقعد بذكر الله

TAB-FULL:v1p116/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p116/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v1p116/r2.claim: Ṭabarī adopts the interpretation that recitation starts with God’s naming and remembrance, using His beautiful names and exalted attributes.
TAB-FULL:v1p116/r2.anchor: أقرأ بتسمية الله وذكره، وأفتتح القراءة بتسمية الله، بأسمائه الحسنى، وصفاته العلى

TAB-FULL:v1p116/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p116/r3.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v1p116/r3.claim: The wording does not mean simply “by God”; the consensus on slaughter treats saying bi-llāh without bismillah as omitting the prescribed invocation.
TAB-FULL:v1p116/r3.anchor: أن قائلا لو قال عند تذكيته بعض بهائم الأنعام: بالله

TAB-FULL:v1p116/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p116/r4.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v1p116/r4.claim: The present question concerns whether the attached “name” is a noun or a verbal noun meaning naming; the broader identity of name and named is outside this discussion.
TAB-FULL:v1p116/r4.anchor: وليس هذا الموضع من مواضع الإكثار في الإبانة عن الاسم، أهو المسمى أم غيره أم هو صفة له

TAB-FULL:v1p118/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p118/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v1p118/r1.claim: Ṭabarī rejects taking Labīd’s “name of peace” simply as “peace”; that reading would license impossible Arabic such as eating the name of honey.
TAB-FULL:v1p118/r1.anchor: وفي إجماع جميع العرب على إحالة ذلك ما ينبئ عن فساد تأويل من تأول قول لبيد

TAB-FULL:v1p118/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p118/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v1p118/r2.claim: One possible reading makes al-Salām a divine name: “adhere to God’s name” after a year, with the command for adherence delayed in the wording; Ṭabarī finds this likelier.
TAB-FULL:v1p118/r2.anchor: أن السلام اسم من أسماء الله؛ فجائز أن يكون لبيد عنى بقوله: ثم اسم السلام عليكما

TAB-FULL:v1p118/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p118/r3.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v1p118/r3.claim: A second possible reading is a protective invocation: may God’s name be upon the two addressed people against harm.
TAB-FULL:v1p118/r3.anchor: ثم تسميتي الله عليكما، كما يقول القائل للشيء يراه فيعجبه: واسم الله عليك

TAB-FULL:v1p118/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p118/r4.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v1p118/r4.claim: Of the two defensible readings of Labīd, the first—taking al-Salām as God’s name and an exhortation to keep His remembrance—is more apt.
TAB-FULL:v1p118/r4.anchor: وكأن الوجه الأول أشبه المعنيين بقول لبيد

TAB-FULL:v1p120/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p120/r1.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
TAB-FULL:v1p120/r1.claim: A report says Jesus explained the letters bāʾ, sīn, and mīm as God’s beauty, splendor, and dominion when a teacher asked about bism.
TAB-FULL:v1p120/r1.anchor: فقال عيسى: الباء: بهاء الله، والسين: سناؤه، والميم: مملكته

TAB-FULL:v1p120/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p120/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v1p120/r2.claim: Ṭabarī suspects a transmitter mistakenly joined the beginner’s alphabet letters b-s-m into bism; the explanation is impossible in ordinary Arabic when the whole basmala is recited.
TAB-FULL:v1p120/r2.anchor: فأخشى أن يكون غلطا من المحدث

TAB-FULL:v1p121/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p121/r1.speaker: عبد الله بن عباس
TAB-FULL:v1p121/r1.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās defines God as the one whom everything worships and every creature serves.
TAB-FULL:v1p121/r1.anchor: عن عبد الله بن عباس، قال: «الله ذو الألوهية والمعبودية على خلقه أجمعين»

TAB-FULL:v1p121/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p121/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v1p121/r2.claim: The proposed derivation of Allāh from ilāh is an inference rather than an attested form heard directly from Arab speech.
TAB-FULL:v1p121/r2.anchor: أما سماعا من العرب فلا، ولكن استدلالا

TAB-FULL:v1p121/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p121/r3.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v1p121/r3.claim: Arab usage of taʾallaha for worship and seeking God supports the root’s devotional sense; a line by Ruʾba uses taʾalluhī in that sense.
TAB-FULL:v1p121/r3.anchor: سبحن واسترجعن من تألهي يعني: من تعبدي وطلبي الله بعمل

TAB-FULL:v1p121/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p121/r4.speaker: عبد الله بن عباس
TAB-FULL:v1p121/r4.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās reads the Pharaoh passage’s ilāhataka as worship, explaining that Pharaoh worshipped rather than being worshipped.
TAB-FULL:v1p121/r4.anchor: عن ابن عباس أنه قرأ: (ويذرك وإلاهتك) قال: عبادتك

TAB-FULL:v1p121/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p121/r5.speaker: مجاهد
TAB-FULL:v1p121/r5.claim: Mujāhid likewise glosses ilāhataka in the Pharaoh passage as worship, a reading also attributed there to Ibn ʿAbbās.

TAB-FULL:v1p121/r6.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p121/r6.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v1p121/r6.claim: These explanations establish that alaha means worship and ilāha is its verbal noun, supporting the interpretation of God as the worshipped one.
TAB-FULL:v1p121/r6.anchor: أن أله: عبد، وأن الإلاهة مصدره

TAB-FULL:v1p124/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p124/r1.speaker: عيسى ابن مريم
TAB-FULL:v1p124/r1.claim: A prophetic report quotes Jesus telling his teacher that Allāh is the god of gods.
TAB-FULL:v1p124/r1.anchor: إن عيسى أسلمته أمه إلى الكتاب ليعلمه

TAB-FULL:v1p124/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p124/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v1p124/r2.claim: Ṭabarī proposes that Allāh derives from al-ilāh: the initial hamza is dropped and the adjacent lām sounds assimilate into one doubled lām.
TAB-FULL:v1p124/r2.anchor: فكذلك الله، أصله الإله، أسقطت الهمزة، التي هي فاء الاسم، فالتقت اللام

TAB-FULL:v1p124/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p124/r3.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v1p124/r3.claim: The contraction is comparable to the Qurʾānic form lakinnā from wa-lākin anā, illustrated by a poet’s similar elision and assimilation.
TAB-FULL:v1p124/r3.anchor: فكذلك الله، أصله الإله، أسقطت الهمزة

TAB-FULL:v1p124#2/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p124#2/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v1p124#2/r1.claim: Al-Raḥmān follows the faʿlān pattern from raḥima, while al-Raḥīm follows faʿīl, a praise form that can occur despite the root’s vowel pattern.
TAB-FULL:v1p124#2/r1.anchor: أما الرحمن، فهو فعلان، من رحم، والرحيم فعيل منه

TAB-FULL:v1p124#2/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p124#2/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v1p124#2/r2.claim: In Arabic, the more distant a praise name is from its ordinary verbal pattern, the stronger its commendation; thus al-Raḥmān adds intensity beyond al-Raḥīm.
TAB-FULL:v1p124#2/r2.anchor: أن قول القائل الرحمن عن أبنية الأسماء من فعل يفعل أشد عدولا من قوله الرحيم

TAB-FULL:v1p124#2/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p124#2/r3.speaker: العرزمي
TAB-FULL:v1p124#2/r3.claim: Al-ʿAzramī distinguishes al-Raḥmān as mercy extending to all creation and al-Raḥīm as mercy toward believers.
TAB-FULL:v1p124#2/r3.anchor: الرحمن بجميع الخلق. الرحيم قال: بالمؤمنين

TAB-FULL:v1p127/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p127/r1.speaker: عيسى ابن مريم
TAB-FULL:v1p127/r1.claim: A report from the Prophet quotes Jesus distinguishing al-Raḥmān as merciful in this world and the next, and al-Raḥīm as merciful in the next.
TAB-FULL:v1p127/r1.anchor: إن عيسى ابن مريم قال: الرحمن: رحمن الآخرة والدنيا

TAB-FULL:v1p127/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p127/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v1p127/r2.claim: Ṭabarī reconciles both transmitted distinctions: al-Raḥmān denotes universal mercy and al-Raḥīm particular mercy, whether in this life, the next, or both.
TAB-FULL:v1p127/r2.anchor: ربنا جل ثناؤه رحمن جميع خلقه في الدنيا والآخرة. ورحيم المؤمنين خاصة في الدنيا والآخرة

TAB-FULL:v1p127/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p127/r3.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v1p127/r3.claim: Universal worldly mercy includes provision, rain, crops, bodily and intellectual health, and other blessings shared by believers and unbelievers.
TAB-FULL:v1p127/r3.anchor: في البسط في الرزق، وتسخير السحاب بالغيث، وإخراج النبات من الأرض، وصحة الأجسام والعقول

TAB-FULL:v1p127/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p127/r4.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v1p127/r4.claim: In the afterlife God’s universal mercy includes just treatment of everyone without the slightest wrong, while special mercy reserves guidance and the promised Garden for believers.
TAB-FULL:v1p127/r4.anchor: تسويته بين جميعهم جل ذكره في عدله وقضائه، فلا يظلم أحدا منهم مثقال ذرة

TAB-FULL:v1p129/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p129/r1.speaker: عبد الله بن عباس
TAB-FULL:v1p129/r1.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās glosses al-Raḥmān as tender toward those God wills to show mercy and severe toward those He wills to chastise; al-Raḥīm is the gentle toward those shown mercy.
TAB-FULL:v1p129/r1.anchor: الرقيق الرفيق بمن أحب أن يرحمه

TAB-FULL:v1p129/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p129/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v1p129/r2.claim: Ṭabarī finds the prophetic report and al-ʿAzramī’s distinction more apt than Ibn ʿAbbās’s wording, while agreeing the names carry distinguishable meanings.
TAB-FULL:v1p129/r2.anchor: والقول الذي رويناه في تأويل ذلك عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم وذكرناه عن العرزمي، أشبه بتأويله

TAB-FULL:v1p129/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p129/r3.speaker: عطاء الخراساني
TAB-FULL:v1p129/r3.claim: ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī says al-Raḥmān was an exclusive divine name, then was separated from God’s name when Musaylima appropriated it.
TAB-FULL:v1p129/r3.anchor: فلما اختزل الرحمن من اسمه كان الرحمن الرحيم

TAB-FULL:v1p129/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p129/r4.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v1p129/r4.claim: Ṭabarī explains that adding al-Raḥīm distinguishes God from Musaylima: no one else has ever combined al-Raḥmān and al-Raḥīm as names.
TAB-FULL:v1p129/r4.anchor: فأما رحمن رحيم، فلم يجتمعا قط لأحد سواه، ولا يجمعان لأحد غيره

TAB-FULL:v1p129/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p129/r5.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v1p129/r5.claim: Ṭabarī rejects the claim that Arabs did not know al-Raḥmān: their question in the Qurʾān can be denial despite knowledge, as with people who recognized but rejected Muhammad.
TAB-FULL:v1p129/r5.anchor: كأنه كان محالا عنده أن ينكر أهل الشرك ما كانوا عالمين بصحته

TAB-FULL:v1p131/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p131/r1.speaker: سلامة بن جندل الطهوي
TAB-FULL:v1p131/r1.claim: A pre-Islamic poem invokes al-Raḥmān as Lord, further demonstrating the name was familiar in Arabic.
TAB-FULL:v1p131/r1.anchor: ألا ضربت تلك الفتاة هجينها … ألا قضب الرحمن ربي يمينها

TAB-FULL:v1p131/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p131/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v1p131/r2.claim: Ṭabarī rejects the gloss of al-Raḥmān as merely possessing mercy and al-Raḥīm as merciful: the latter need not assert that mercy is a settled attribute.
TAB-FULL:v1p131/r2.anchor: أن ذا الرحمة هو الذي ثبت أن له الرحمة وصح أنها له صفة

TAB-FULL:v1p131/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p131/r3.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v1p131/r3.claim: Arabic convention places a referent’s name before its attributes; Ṭabarī applies that order to the divine names.
TAB-FULL:v1p131/r3.anchor: أن يقدموا اسمه، ثم يتبعوه صفاته ونعوته

TAB-FULL:v1p131/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p131/r4.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v1p131/r4.claim: Ṭabarī rejects the gloss of al-Raḥmān as merely possessing mercy and al-Raḥīm as merciful: the latter need not assert that mercy is a settled attribute.
TAB-FULL:v1p131/r4.anchor: ولا شك أن ذا الرحمة هو الذي ثبت أن له الرحمة وصح أنها له صفة، وأن الراحم هو الموصوف

TAB-FULL:v1p131/r5.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p131/r5.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v1p131/r5.claim: Arabic convention places a referent’s name before its attributes; Ṭabarī applies that order to the divine names.
TAB-FULL:v1p131/r5.anchor: أن يقدموا اسمه، ثم يتبعوه صفاته ونعوته

TAB-FULL:v1p133/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p133/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v1p133/r1.claim: Ṭabarī explains that God’s unique name remains exclusive even if people bear names such as Saʿīd while being its opposite.
TAB-FULL:v1p133/r1.anchor: وإن قصد المتسمي به ما يقصد المتسمي بسعيد وهو شقي

TAB-FULL:v1p133/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p133/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v1p133/r2.claim: Ṭabarī places Allāh first because no other being shares divine worship, then al-Raḥmān, which is also reserved for God, before the shared descriptor al-Raḥīm.
TAB-FULL:v1p133/r2.anchor: فبدأ الله جل ذكره باسمه الذي هو الله؛ لأن الألوهية ليست لغيره جل ثناؤه بوجه من الوجوه

TAB-FULL:v1p133/r3.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p133/r3.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v1p133/r3.claim: Allāh and al-Raḥmān are reserved for God, while al-Raḥīm may describe creatures; no one shares God’s divinity or deserves His exclusive names.
TAB-FULL:v1p133/r3.anchor: قد يجوز وصف كثير ممن هو دون الله من خلقه ببعض صفات الرحمة

TAB-FULL:v1p133/r4.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p133/r4.speaker: الحسن البصري
TAB-FULL:v1p133/r4.claim: Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī calls al-Raḥmān a forbidden name for others; Ṭabarī says the community’s consensus already establishes the prohibition.
TAB-FULL:v1p133/r4.anchor: حدثنا محمد بن بشار، قال: حدثنا حماد بن مسعدة، عن عوف، عن الحسن، قال: «الرحمن اسم ممنوع»

TAB-FULL:v1p147#2/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p147#2/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v1p147#2/r1.claim: Ṭabarī argues the basmala is not a verse of the Opening: otherwise al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm would repeat immediately, word for word and sense for sense, without an intervening divider.
TAB-FULL:v1p147#2/r1.anchor: لو كان ذلك كذلك لكان ذلك إعادة آية بمعنى واحد ولفظ واحد مرتين من غير فصل

TAB-FULL:v1p147#2/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p147#2/r2.speaker: جماعة من أهل التأويل
TAB-FULL:v1p147#2/r2.claim: Some interpreters treat al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm as advanced in meaning before rabb al-ʿālamīn, making the apparent repetition part of reordered description rather than adjacent verses.
TAB-FULL:v1p147#2/r2.anchor: أن ذلك من المؤخر الذي معناه التقديم، وإنما هو: الحمد لله الرحمن الرحيم رب العالمين

TAB-FULL:v1p149/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p149/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v1p149/r1.claim: Poetry by Jarīr and Qurʾān 18:2 illustrate fronting and delaying in Arabic; the apparent order can place the “upright” description before its intended antecedent.
TAB-FULL:v1p149/r1.anchor: الحمد لله الذي أنزل على عبده الكتاب قيما ولم يجعل له عوجا

TAB-FULL:v1p149/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p149/r2.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v1p149/r2.claim: These reorderings support the interpreters who deny that the basmala belongs to the Opening as a verse.
TAB-FULL:v1p149/r2.anchor: دليل شاهد على صحة قول من أنكر أن تكون {بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم} [الفاتحة: 1] من فاتحة الكتاب آية

TAB-FULL:v1p203/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p203/r2.speaker: أبو هريرة عن رسول الله
TAB-FULL:v1p203/r2.claim: The Prophet reports God praises the servant’s recitation of praise, mercy, and sovereignty, then says the invocation from You alone we worship through the end belongs to the servant.
TAB-FULL:v1p203/r2.anchor: عن أبي هريرة، قال: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: " إذا قال العبد: {الحمد لله رب العالمين}

TAB-FULL:v1p203#2/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v1p203#2/r1.speaker: جابر بن عبد الله الأنصاري عن رسول الله
TAB-FULL:v1p203#2/r1.claim: The Prophet says the prayer is divided between God and the servant: the opening praise, mercy, and judgment belong to God, and the remainder is the servant’s request.
TAB-FULL:v1p203#2/r1.anchor: عن جابر بن عبد الله الأنصاري، قال: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: " قال الله عز وجل: قسمت الصلاة بيني وبين عبدي نصفين

TABATABAI:1:1/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:1:1/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:1:1/r1.claim: People begin important acts or name new things after honored people to seek blessing, honor them, and keep their memory alive.
TABATABAI:1:1/r1.anchor: ليكون عملهم ذاك مباركا بذلك متشرفا، أو ليكون ذكرى يذكرهم به

TABATABAI:1:1/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:1:1/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:1:1/r2.claim: Beginning revelation with God's name ties its meaning to Him and teaches servants to begin their acts, words, and deeds in His name.
TABATABAI:1:1/r2.anchor: فيبتدؤوا باسمه ويعملوا به، فيكون ما يعملونه معلما باسمه

TABATABAI:1:1/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:1:1/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:1:1/r3.claim: Only acts done for God's face endure; other deeds are rendered scattered dust, so the basmala marks an act for Him as enduring.
TABATABAI:1:1/r3.anchor: فما عمل لوجهه الكريم وصنع باسمه هو الذي يبقى ولا يفنى

TABATABAI:1:1/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:1:1/r4.speaker: النبي
TABATABAI:1:1/r4.claim: A report transmitted by both communities from the Prophet says every significant matter begun without God's name is cut off at the end.
TABATABAI:1:1/r4.anchor: كل أمر ذي بال لم يبدأ فيه باسم الله فهو أبتر الحديث

TABATABAI:1:1/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:1:1/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:1:1/r5.claim: The preposition in the basmala means beginning in God's name, since speech is an act with one intended meaning and purpose.
TABATABAI:1:1/r5.anchor: فالأنسب أن متعلق الباء في البسملة ابتدئ بالمعنى الذي ذكرناه

TABATABAI:1:1-5/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:1:1-5/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:1:1-5/r1.claim: The Qur'an's purpose is to guide people; its opening names God as the return of servants, the giver of universal mercy, and the guide to believers' lasting mercy.
TABATABAI:1:1-5/r1.anchor: الغاية من كتابه وكلامه هداية العباد، فالهداية جملة هي المبتدئة باسم الله الرحمن الرحيم

TABATABAI:1:1-5/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:1:1-5/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:1:1-5/r2.claim: Gods mercy called Rahman reaches believers and disbelievers and supplies what they need for existence and life.
TABATABAI:1:1-5/r2.anchor: وهو الرحمن يبين لعباده سبيل رحمته العامة للمؤمن والكافر

TABATABAI:1:1-5/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:1:1-5/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:1:1-5/r3.claim: Rahim guides believers to Gods special mercy, their happiness in the afterlife and meeting their Lord.
TABATABAI:1:1-5/r3.anchor: وهو الرحيم يبين لهم سبيل رحمته الخاصة بالمؤمنين وهو سعادة آخرتهم ولقاء ربهم

TABATABAI:1:1-5/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:1:1-5/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:1:1-5/r4.claim: God says His mercy encompasses everything, then promises a special share to those who are mindful.
TABATABAI:1:1-5/r4.anchor: ورحمتي وسعت كل شيء فسأكتبها للذين يتقون

TABATABAI:1:1-5/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:1:1-5/r5.speaker: author
TABATABAI:1:1-5/r5.claim: The Quran repeatedly refers to revealed divisions as suras, citing several examples.
TABATABAI:1:1-5/r5.anchor: ثم إنه سبحانه كرر ذكر السورة في كلامه كثيرا

TABATABAI:1:5/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:1:5/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:1:5/r1.claim: The basmala in each sura is tied to that sura's distinct purpose; here the purpose is worshipful praise, so the basmala begins that act of servitude.
TABATABAI:1:5/r1.anchor: فالبسملة في مبتدأ كل سورة راجعة إلى الغرض الخاص من تلك السورة

TABATABAI:1:5/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:1:5/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:1:5/r2.claim: A name, linguistically, is an indicating word, from either the root for marking or the root for elevation.
TABATABAI:1:5/r2.anchor: فهو اللفظ الدال على المسمى مشتق من السمة بمعنى العلامة أو من السمو بمعنى الرفعة

TABATABAI:1:5/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:1:5/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:1:5/r3.claim: Theoretical analysis distinguishes a spoken name from an attribute that indicates an external essence, sometimes calling the former the name of the latter; this distinction should not be imposed on ordinary language.
TABATABAI:1:5/r3.anchor: ولكن هذا كله أمر أدى إليه التحليل النظري ولا ينبغي أن يحمل على اللغة

TABATABAI:1:1-5#2/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:1:1-5#2/r1.speaker: author
TABATABAI:1:1-5#2/r1.claim: Early theologians disputed whether a name is identical to what it names, but the author considers the issue now obvious and says it need not be rehearsed.
TABATABAI:1:1-5#2/r1.anchor: وقد شاع النزاع بين المتكلمين في الصدر الأول من الإسلام في أن الاسم عين المسمى أو غيره

TABATABAI:1:1-5#2/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:1:1-5#2/r2.speaker: author
TABATABAI:1:1-5#2/r2.claim: Allah derives from al-ilah, with the hamza dropped through frequent use; the root can mean worship or bewilderment, and the name was already familiar among pre-Islamic Arabs.
TABATABAI:1:1-5#2/r2.anchor: فالله أصله الإله، حذفت الهمزة لكثرة الاستعمال

TABATABAI:1:1-5#2/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:1:1-5#2/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:1:1-5#2/r3.claim: Allah functions as a proper name because it takes all beautiful names and their derived actions as predicates, while none of them predicates or derives from it.
TABATABAI:1:1-5#2/r3.anchor: ومما يدل على كونه علما أنه يوصف بجميع الأسماء الحسنى وسائر أفعاله المأخوذة من تلك الأسماء

TABATABAI:1:1-5#2/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:1:1-5#2/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:1:1-5#2/r4.claim: Because God is the deity of everything, the divine name implies every perfection; it names the necessary existent who possesses all perfections, while lexically it remains the established name derived from ilah.
TABATABAI:1:1-5#2/r4.anchor: اسم للذات الواجب الوجود المستجمع لجميع صفات الكمال

TABATABAI:1:1-5#5/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:1:1-5#5/r3.speaker: الإمام الرضا
TABATABAI:1:1-5#5/r3.claim: Al-Ridha explains bismillah as marking oneself with a mark of God, namely worship; the author sees it as a consequence of beginning worship in God's name.
TABATABAI:1:1-5#5/r3.anchor: يعني اسم نفسي بسمة من سمات الله وهي العبادة

TABATABAI:1:1-5#5/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:1:1-5#5/r4.speaker: الصادق
TABATABAI:1:1-5#5/r4.claim: Al-Sadiq, and separately al-Ridha in reports cited by al-Ayyashi and al-Uyun, say the basmala is nearer to God's greatest name than the eye's pupil is to its white; its explanation is deferred.
TABATABAI:1:1-5#5/r4.anchor: أنها أقرب إلى اسم الله الأعظم من ناظر العين إلى بياضها

TABATABAI:1:1-5#5/r5.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:1:1-5#5/r5.speaker: علي
TABATABAI:1:1-5#5/r5.claim: Ali reports that the basmala is part of al-Fatiha, which the Prophet recited and counted as one of its verses; similar Sunni reports exist.
TABATABAI:1:1-5#5/r5.anchor: أنها من الفاتحة وأن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم كان يقرؤها ويعدها آية منها

TABATABAI:1:1-5#6/r1.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:1:1-5#6/r1.speaker: النبي
TABATABAI:1:1-5#6/r1.claim: A report from Abu Hurayra says to recite the basmala with al-Fatiha, since it is the Mother of the Qur'an, the seven oft-repeated verses, and one of its verses.
TABATABAI:1:1-5#6/r1.anchor: فإنها أم القرآن والسبع المثاني، وبسم الله الرحمن الرحيم إحدى آياتها

TABATABAI:1:1-5#6/r2.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:1:1-5#6/r2.speaker: الصادق
TABATABAI:1:1-5#6/r2.claim: Al-Sadiq condemns those who called the greatest verse an innovation when recited aloud; al-Baqir says they stole the Qur'an's noblest verse and urges beginning every affair with it for blessing.
TABATABAI:1:1-5#6/r2.anchor: عمدوا إلى أعظم آية في كتاب الله فزعموا أنها بدعة إذا أظهروها

TABATABAI:1:1-5#6/r3.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:1:1-5#6/r3.speaker: author
TABATABAI:1:1-5#6/r3.claim: Numerous reports from the Imams of the Prophet's household and Sunni reports indicate that the basmala is part of every sura except al-Bara'a.
TABATABAI:1:1-5#6/r3.anchor: تدل على أن البسملة جزء من كل سورة إلا سورة البراءة

TABATABAI:1:1-5#6/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:1:1-5#6/r4.speaker: النبي
TABATABAI:1:1-5#6/r4.claim: Anas reports the Prophet reciting the basmala when a sura was newly revealed; Ibn Abbas reports that it marked the boundary between suras, and the author notes corroboration from al-Baqir.
TABATABAI:1:1-5#6/r4.anchor: ان رسول الله صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم كان لا يعرف فصل السورة

TABATABAI:1:6-7#11/r6.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:1:6-7#11/r6.speaker: النبي
TABATABAI:1:6-7#11/r6.claim: The Prophet transmits God's division of al-Fatiha between Himself and the servant: each phrase receives divine acknowledgement and a tailored promise of blessing, mercy, ease of judgment, reward, help, and fulfillment of the servant's requests.
TABATABAI:1:6-7#11/r6.anchor: قسمت فاتحة الكتاب بيني وبين عبدي فنصفها لي ونصفها لعبدي، ولعبدي ما سأل

TABRISI:1:1/r1.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:1:1/r1.speaker: أصحابنا
TABRISI:1:1/r1.claim: The author's companions hold that the basmala is a verse of al-Fatiha and every sura; omitting it invalidates obligatory and supererogatory prayer, and they favor audible recitation.
TABRISI:1:1/r1.anchor: اتفق أصحابنا أنها آية من سورة الحمد ومن كل سورة وأن من تركها في الصلاة بطلت صلاته سواء كانت الصلاة فرضا أو نفلا

TABRISI:1:1/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:1:1/r2.speaker: حمزة وخلف ويعقوب واليزيدي
TABRISI:1:1/r2.claim: These readers do not use the basmala to separate suras; the other readers do, except between al-Anfal and al-Tawba.
TABRISI:1:1/r2.anchor: حمزة وخلفا ويعقوب واليزيدي تركوا الفصل بين السور بالتسمية والباقون يفصلون بينها بالتسمية إلا بين الأنفال والتوبة

TABRISI:1:1/r3.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:1:1/r3.speaker: علي بن موسى الرضا
TABRISI:1:1/r3.claim: Al-Rida says the basmala is nearer to God's Greatest Name than the black of the eye is to its white.
TABRISI:1:1/r3.anchor: عن علي بن موسى الرضا ع أنه قال: بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم أقرب إلى اسم الله الأعظم من سواد العين إلى بياضها

TABRISI:1:1/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:1:1/r4.speaker: النبي
TABRISI:1:1/r4.claim: The Prophet promises absolution for a child, the child's parents, and the teacher when the child learns and recites the basmala.
TABRISI:1:1/r4.anchor:
عن ابن عباس عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم أنه قال:
" إذا قال المعلم للصبي قل بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم

TABRISI:1:1/r5.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:1:1/r5.speaker: ابن مسعود
TABRISI:1:1/r5.claim: Ibn Masud says reciting the basmala protects a person from the nineteen keepers of Hell, one letter serving as protection from each.
TABRISI:1:1/r5.anchor: وعن ابن مسعود قال: من أراد أن ينجيه الله من الزبانية التسعة عشر

TABRISI:1:1/r6.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:1:1/r6.speaker: الصادق
TABRISI:1:1/r6.claim: Al-Sadiq condemns those who call the basmala an innovation when they recite it aloud, calling it the greatest verse in God's Book.
TABRISI:1:1/r6.anchor: روي عن الصادق ع أنه قال: ما لهم قاتلهم الله عمدوا إلى أعظم آية

TABRISI:1:1/r7.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:1:1/r7.speaker: author
TABRISI:1:1/r7.claim: The author prefers deriving ism from sumu, elevation: its original waw is supported by its plural asma and diminutive sumayy.
TABRISI:1:1/r7.anchor: الاسم مشتق من السمو وهو الرفعة أصله سمو بالواو لأن جمعه أسماء مثل قنو وأقناء

TABRISI:1:1/r8.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:1:1/r8.speaker: author
TABRISI:1:1/r8.claim: Allah is an exclusive divine name and is not applied to anyone besides God.
TABRISI:1:1/r8.anchor: { الله } اسم لا يطلق إلا عليه سبحانه وتعالى

TABRISI:1:1/r9.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:1:1/r9.speaker: سيبويه
TABRISI:1:1/r9.claim: One analysis derives Allah from lah; the article marks glorification and exaltation, not definiteness, since God's names are already definite.
TABRISI:1:1/r9.anchor: وذكر سيبويه في أصله قولين أحدهما: إنه إلآه على وزن فعال فحذفت الفاء التي هي الهمزة وجعلت الألف واللام عوضا لازما عنها بدلالة

TABRISI:1:1/r10.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:1:1/r10.speaker: سيبويه
TABRISI:1:1/r10.claim: On this analysis the alif in lah comes from yā; Sibawayh explains a transposition of the letters and cites lahi as evidence.
TABRISI:1:1/r10.anchor: وذكر سيبويه في أصله قولين أحدهما: إنه إلآه على وزن فعال فحذفت الفاء التي هي الهمزة وجعلت الألف واللام عوضا لازما عنها بدلالة

TABRISI:1:1#2/r1.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:1:1#2/r1.speaker: author
TABRISI:1:1#2/r1.claim: The idiom lah abūk means lillah abūk; Dhū al-Isba's verse uses it for governing or managing someone.
TABRISI:1:1#2/r1.anchor:
قال ذو الإصبع العدواني:
لاه ابن عمك لا أفضلت في حسب

TABRISI:1:1#2/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:1:1#2/r2.speaker: سيبويه
TABRISI:1:1#2/r2.claim: Sibawayh allows the deleted prepositional lām to retain its grammatical effect and cites الله لأخرجن for والله لأخرجن.
TABRISI:1:1#2/r2.anchor: قال سيبويه: حذفوا لام الإضافة واللام الأخرى ولم ينكر بقاء عمل اللام بعد حذفها

TABRISI:1:1#2/r3.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:1:1#2/r3.speaker: الخليل
TABRISI:1:1#2/r3.claim: Al-Khalil treats Allah as an un-derived proper name, arguing that not every word must have a derivation or derivation would regress forever.
TABRISI:1:1#2/r3.anchor: هذا قول الخليل ومنهم من قال إنه مشتق ثم اختلفوا في اشتقاقه

TABRISI:1:1#2/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:1:1#2/r4.speaker: author
TABRISI:1:1#2/r4.claim: One reported derivation connects Allah with worship and servitude; on it God alone deserves worship, and a cited Ibn Abbas reading glosses the verb as worship.
TABRISI:1:1#2/r4.anchor:
مشتق من الألوهية التي هي العبادة والتأله التعبد قال رؤبة:
لله در الغانيات المده

TABRISI:1:1#2/r5.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:1:1#2/r5.speaker: أبو عمرو
TABRISI:1:1#2/r5.claim: Abu Amr derives the name from bewilderment: minds are bewildered by the essence of God's greatness.
TABRISI:1:1#2/r5.anchor: ومنها أنه مشتق من الوله وهو التحير يقال آله يأله إذا تحير - عن أبي عمرو -

TABRISI:1:1#2/r6.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:1:1#2/r6.speaker: author
TABRISI:1:1#2/r6.claim: Another derivation links the name with fleeing for refuge, because creatures turn to God for their needs.
TABRISI:1:1#2/r6.anchor: ومنها أنه مشتق من قولهم ألهت إلى فلان أي فزعت إليه لأن الخلق يألهون إليه أي يفزعون إليه

TABRISI:1:1#2/r7.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:1:1#2/r7.speaker: المبرد
TABRISI:1:1#2/r7.claim: Al-Mubarrad derives the name from finding repose with God, since creatures become at rest through remembering Him.
TABRISI:1:1#2/r7.anchor: ومنها أنه مشتق من ألهت إليه أي سكنت إليه عن المبرد ومعناه أن الخلق يسكنون إلى ذكره

TABRISI:1:1#2/r8.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:1:1#2/r8.speaker: author
TABRISI:1:1#2/r8.claim: A final derivation takes it from lah, meaning hidden: God is hidden in modality from minds but manifest through signs and proofs.
TABRISI:1:1#2/r8.anchor: ومنها أنه من لاه أي احتجب فمعناه أنه المحتجب بالكيفية عن الأوهام الظاهر بالدلائل والأعلام

TABRISI:1:1#2/r9.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:1:1#2/r9.speaker: author
TABRISI:1:1#2/r9.claim: Rahman and Rahim are intensive forms derived from mercy, and Rahman is more intensive; Abu Ubayda distinguishes the possessor of mercy from the merciful one.
TABRISI:1:1#2/r9.anchor: { الرحمن الرحيم } اسمان وضعا للمبالغة واشتقا من الرحمة وهي النعمة إلا أن فعلان أشد مبالغة من فعيل

TABRISI:1:1#2/r10.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:1:1#2/r10.speaker: ابن عباس
TABRISI:1:1#2/r10.claim: Ibn Abbas calls both names tender, with Rahim the more tender; the author interprets this as successive divine favor, not literal softness.
TABRISI:1:1#2/r10.anchor: ما روي عن ابن عباس أنهما اسمان رقيقان أحدهما أرق من الآخر فالرحمن الرقيق والرحيم العطاف على عباده بالرزق والنعم

TABRISI:1:1#2/r11.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:1:1#2/r11.speaker: تغلب
TABRISI:1:1#2/r11.claim: Thaʿlab claims Rahman is non-Arabic, citing the Quraysh denial of the name in the Qur'an as evidence.
TABRISI:1:1#2/r11.anchor: وما حكي عن تغلب أن لفظة الرحمن ليست بعربية وإنما هي ببعض اللغات مستدلا بقوله تعالى

TABRISI:1:1#3/r1.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:1:1#3/r1.speaker: author
TABRISI:1:1#3/r1.claim: The author rejects Thaʿlab's claim that Rahman is foreign because Arabic poetry attests the word.
TABRISI:1:1#3/r1.anchor: فليس بصحيح لأن هذه اللفظة مشهورة عند العرب موجودة في أشعارها قال الشنفرى

TABRISI:1:1#3/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:1:1#3/r2.speaker: author
TABRISI:1:1#3/r2.claim: The preposition bā originally marks attachment and brings an action onto its object; an implicit verb such as begin or say governs it.
TABRISI:1:1#3/r2.anchor: الباء حرف جر أصله الإلصاق والحروف الجارة موضوعة لمعنى المفعولية ألا ترى أنها توصل الأفعال إلى الأسماء

TABRISI:1:1#3/r3.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:1:1#3/r3.speaker: الأخفش وأبو علي الفارسي
TABRISI:1:1#3/r3.claim: They analyze the basmala as an implicit nominal clause, with the prepositional phrase filling the place of its omitted predicate.
TABRISI:1:1#3/r3.anchor: وقيل إن محل الباء رفع على تقدير مبتدأ محذوف وتقديره ابتدائي بسم الله فالباء على هذا متعلقة بالخبر المحذوف

TABRISI:1:1#3/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:1:1#3/r4.speaker: أبو علي الفارسي
TABRISI:1:1#3/r4.claim: Abu Ali rejects attaching bā to the hidden verbal noun ibtidaʾ because this would leave the implied subject without a predicate.
TABRISI:1:1#3/r4.anchor: ولا يجوز أن يتعلق الباء بابتدائي المضمر لأنه مصدر وإذا تعلقت به صارت من صلته وبقي المبتدأ بلا خبر

TABRISI:1:1#3/r5.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:1:1#3/r5.speaker: أبو عمرو الجرمي
TABRISI:1:1#3/r5.claim: The bā is kasra because it must be pronounceable at the start of speech; kasra was chosen as the appropriate connecting vowel.
TABRISI:1:1#3/r5.anchor: حرك للزوم الإبتداء به ولا يمكن الإبتداء بالساكن وإنما حرك بالكسر ليكون حركته من جنس ما يحدثه

TABRISI:1:1#3/r6.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:1:1#3/r6.speaker: أبو علي الحسن بن عبد الغفار الفارسي
TABRISI:1:1#3/r6.claim: Abu Ali al-Farsi says any vowel would have served for starting the word; some Arabs use fatḥa, though the author calls that dialect weak.
TABRISI:1:1#3/r6.anchor: فقال: إنهم لو فتحوا أو ضموا لجاز لأن الغرض التوصل إلى الإبتداء

TABRISI:1:1#3/r7.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:1:1#3/r7.speaker: author
TABRISI:1:1#3/r7.claim: The hamzat al-waṣl of ism drops in connected pronunciation and is omitted in writing here because the basmala is frequent and unambiguous, unlike the less frequent Qur'anic form in 96:1.
TABRISI:1:1#3/r7.anchor: وإنما حذفت الهمزة من بسم الله في اللفظ لأنها همزة الوصل تسقط في الدرج وحذفت هاهنا في الخط أيضا لكثرة الاستعمال

TABRISI:1:1#4/r1.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:1:1#4/r1.speaker: author
TABRISI:1:1#4/r1.claim: God's lām is pronounced emphatically after fatḥa or ḍamma to glorify Him and distinguish the name from al-Lāt.
TABRISI:1:1#4/r1.anchor: وإنما تغلظ لام الله إذا تقدمته الضمة أو الفتحة تفخيما لذكره وإجلالا لقدره وليكون فرقا بينه وبين ذكر اللات

TABRISI:1:1#4/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:1:1#4/r2.speaker: author
TABRISI:1:1#4/r2.claim: Allah is genitive by annexation, and Rahman and Rahim are genitive as adjectives of Allah.
TABRISI:1:1#4/r2.anchor: { الله } مجرور بالإضافة و { الرحمن الرحيم } مجروران لأنهما صفتان لله

TABRISI:1:1#4/r3.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:1:1#4/r3.speaker: author
TABRISI:1:1#4/r3.claim: One interpretation makes the basmala an appeal for aid through God's beautiful names and exalted attributes; another simply means seek help from God.
TABRISI:1:1#4/r3.anchor: قيل المراد به تضمين الاستعانة فتقديره استعينوا بأن تسموا الله بأسمائه الحسنى وتصفوه بصفاته العلى

TABRISI:1:1#4/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:1:1#4/r4.speaker: أبو عبيدة
TABRISI:1:1#4/r4.claim: Abu Ubayda treats the word ism as an extra connective and takes the basmala to mean Allah Himself, as in Labid's verse.
TABRISI:1:1#4/r4.anchor: ويلتفت إليه قول أبي عبيدة إن الاسم صلة والمراد هو الله كقول لبيد

TABRISI:1:1#4/r5.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:1:1#4/r5.speaker: author
TABRISI:1:1#4/r5.claim: A name can stand for its referent because speech or address attached to the name is in reality attached to the named thing.
TABRISI:1:1#4/r5.anchor: والاسم قد يوضع المسمى لما كان المعلق على الاسم ذكرا أو خطابا معلقا على المسمى

TABRISI:1:1#4/r6.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:1:1#4/r6.speaker: author
TABRISI:1:1#4/r6.claim: The preferred reading is begin by naming God: the command teaches opening actions with God's name, as in eating, drinking, and slaughter, rather than merely reporting His majesty.
TABRISI:1:1#4/r6.anchor: وهذا القول أولى بالصواب لأنا إنما أمرنا بأن نفتتح أمورنا بتسمية الله لا بالخبر عن كبريائه وعظمته

TABRISI:1:1#4/r7.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:1:1#4/r7.speaker: author
TABRISI:1:1#4/r7.claim: God alone merits worship because He can create bodies, give life, and bestow blessings; defining deity only by earned benefaction wrongly excludes God before creation.
TABRISI:1:1#4/r7.anchor: ومعنى الله والإله أنه الذي تحق له العبادة وإنما تحق له العبادة لأنه قادر على خلق الأجسام وإحيائها والإنعام عليها

TABRISI:1:1#4/r8.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:1:1#4/r8.speaker: author
TABRISI:1:1#4/r8.claim: Rahman precedes Rahim because Rahman functions like a proper name exclusive to God, while Rahim can describe others too.
TABRISI:1:1#4/r8.anchor: وإنما قدم الرحمن على الرحيم لأن الرحمن بمنزلة اسم العلم من حيث لا يوصف به إلا الله

TABRISI:1:1#5/r1.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:1:1#5/r1.speaker: عيسى ابن مريم
TABRISI:1:1#5/r1.claim: A prophetic report quotes Jesus as saying Rahman is merciful in this world and Rahim is merciful in the afterlife.
TABRISI:1:1#5/r1.anchor: إن عيسى ابن مريم قال الرحمن رحمن الدنيا والرحيم رحيم الآخرة

TABRISI:1:1#5/r2.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:1:1#5/r2.speaker: بعض التابعين
TABRISI:1:1#5/r2.claim: Some Successors say Rahman embraces all creation while Rahim is especially for believers; the author explains this by creation and provision for all and guidance, Paradise, honor, and forgiveness for believers.
TABRISI:1:1#5/r2.anchor: وعن بعض التابعين قال: " الرحمن بجميع الخلق والرحيم بالمؤمنين خاصة

TABRISI:1:1#5/r3.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:1:1#5/r3.speaker: الصادق
TABRISI:1:1#5/r3.claim: Al-Sadiq formulates the distinction as a special name with a general attribute for Rahman, and a general name with a special attribute for Rahim.
TABRISI:1:1#5/r3.anchor: ما روي عن الصادق ع أنه قال: الرحمن اسم خاص بصفة عامة والرحيم اسم عام بصفة خاصة

TABRISI:1:1#5/r4.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:1:1#5/r4.speaker: عكرمة
TABRISI:1:1#5/r4.claim: Ikrima says Rahman signifies one mercy and Rahim a hundred mercies.
TABRISI:1:1#5/r4.anchor: وعن عكرمة قال: الرحمن برحمة واحدة والرحيم بمائة رحمة

TABRISI:1:1#5/r5.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:1:1#5/r5.speaker: النبي
TABRISI:1:1#5/r5.claim: The Prophet says God has one hundred mercies, sent one to earth for mutual compassion and reserved ninety-nine to show mercy on Judgment Day.
TABRISI:1:1#5/r5.anchor: إن لله عز وجل مائة رحمة وإنه أنزل منها واحدة إلى الأرض فقسمها بين خلقه بها يتعاطفون ويتراحمون وأخر تسعا وتسعين

TABRISI:1:1#5/r6.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:1:1#5/r6.speaker: author
TABRISI:1:1#5/r6.claim: Another report says God will take the earthly mercy back and complete it to one hundred to show mercy to His servants on Judgment Day.
TABRISI:1:1#5/r6.anchor: وروي أن الله قابض هذه إلى تلك فيكملها مائة يرحم بها عباده يوم القيامة

THALABI:v1p92/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p92/r1.speaker: author
THALABI:v1p92/r1.claim: The prefixed bā is an extra particle of attachment or inclusion, as in writing with a pen, where the writing adheres to the pen.
THALABI:v1p92/r1.anchor: هذه الباء زائدة، وهي تسمى باء التضمين أو باء الإلصاق

THALABI:v1p92/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p92/r2.speaker: author
THALABI:v1p92/r2.claim: The bā is always kasra because it is an incomplete, inclined letter; imāla signals kasra.
THALABI:v1p92/r2.anchor: وهي مكسورة أبدا والعلة في ذلك أن الباء حرف ناقص ممال

THALABI:v1p92/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p92/r3.speaker: سيبويه
THALABI:v1p92/r3.claim: Sibawayh explains the kasra by saying that kasra is the bā’s only function.
THALABI:v1p92/r3.anchor: قال سيبويه: لما لم يكن للباء عمل إلا الكسر كسرت

THALABI:v1p92/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p92/r4.speaker: المبرد
THALABI:v1p92/r4.claim: Al-Mubarrad says its kasra restores it to its original form, comparing yāʾ with kasra as wāw with ḍamma and alif with fatḥa.
THALABI:v1p92/r4.anchor: وقال المبرد: العلة في كسرها ردها إلى الأصل

THALABI:v1p92/r5.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p92/r5.speaker: القيسي
THALABI:v1p92/r5.claim: Al-Qaysi says the opening bā was lengthened and likened to alif-lām so God’s Book would begin with an exalted, emphatic letter.
THALABI:v1p92/r5.anchor: وطولت هاهنا وشبهت بالألف واللام لأنهم لم يريدوا أن يفتتحوا كتاب الله إلا بحرف مفخم معظم. قاله القيسي

THALABI:v1p92/r6.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p92/r6.speaker: عمر بن عبد العزيز
THALABI:v1p92/r6.claim: ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz instructed scribes to lengthen the bā, show the sīn, separate them, and round the mīm in reverence for God’s speech.
THALABI:v1p92/r6.anchor: قال: وكان عمر بن عبد العزيز (رحمه الله) يقول لكتابه:

THALABI:v1p92/r7.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p92/r7.speaker: أبو خالد بن يزيد المرادي
THALABI:v1p92/r7.claim: Abu Khalid ibn Yazid al-Muradi says the alif of ism was dropped for frequent use and its length was transferred to the bā; where ism retains alif, the bā keeps its ordinary form.
THALABI:v1p92/r7.anchor: العلة فيها إسقاط الألف من الاسم، فلما أسقطوا الألف ردوا طول الألف الى الباء

THALABI:v1p92/r8.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p92/r8.speaker: author
THALABI:v1p92/r8.claim: The phrase has an omitted command, understood as “say” or “begin” in God’s name.
THALABI:v1p92/r8.anchor: وفي الكلام إضمار واختصار تقديره: قل، أو ابدأ بسم الله

THALABI:v1p92/r9.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p92/r9.speaker: آدم
THALABI:v1p92/r9.claim: Adam treats ism as an added word, glossing the phrase as “By God, the Merciful, the Compassionate, He is”; Labid’s verse uses ism for “peace.”
THALABI:v1p92/r9.anchor: وقال آدم: الاسم فيه صلة، مجازه: بالله الرحمن الرحيم هو

THALABI:v1p92/r10.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p92/r10.speaker: author
THALABI:v1p92/r10.claim: The basmala means that beings came into existence through God and creatures subsist through Him; ism distinguishes the one invoking blessing from its object.
THALABI:v1p92/r10.anchor: ومعناه: بالله تكونت الموجودات، وبه قامت المخلوقات

THALABI:v1p92/r11.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p92/r11.speaker: author
THALABI:v1p92/r11.claim: The author identifies name with the named, the existent thing, its essence, and itself, citing the announcement that a boy’s name is Yaḥyā and then addressing him as Yaḥyā.
THALABI:v1p92/r11.anchor: والدليل على أن الاسم عين المسمى قوله تعالى: إنا نبشرك بغلام اسمه يحيى

THALABI:v1p93/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p93/r1.speaker: author
THALABI:v1p93/r1.claim: The Qurʾānic phrase about people worshiping only names they assigned means the objects themselves, since they worshiped the named beings.
THALABI:v1p93/r1.anchor: وأراد الأشخاص المعبودة لأنهم كانوا يعبدون المسميات

THALABI:v1p93/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p93/r2.speaker: author
THALABI:v1p93/r2.claim: The commands to glorify or bless God’s name use “name” to mean God Himself; the report about Mudar likewise says no one would worship Him.

THALABI:v1p93/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p93/r3.speaker: author
THALABI:v1p93/r3.claim: Although ism is more commonly used for naming than for the named, its plural is asmāʾ; its derivation from samā means to rise, since existence rises above nonexistence, while naming is an expression or description.
THALABI:v1p93/r3.anchor: واشتقاقه من (سما) (يسمو) ، فكأن المخبر عنه بأنه معدوم

THALABI:v1p93/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p93/r4.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
THALABI:v1p93/r4.claim: In a report from Abu Saʿid al-Khudri, Jesus asks his teacher about bismillah; Jesus explains bā as God’s splendor, sīn as His radiance, and mīm as His kingdom.
THALABI:v1p93/r4.anchor: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: «إن عيسى بن مريم

THALABI:v1p93/r5.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p93/r5.speaker: أبو بكر محمد بن عمر الوراق
THALABI:v1p93/r5.claim: Abu Bakr al-Warraq describes bismillah as a garden of Paradise whose every letter has its own interpretation, expanded in the following segment.
THALABI:v1p93/r5.anchor: سمعت أبا بكر محمد بن عمر الوراق يقول في بسم الله: إنها روضة من رياض الجنة

THALABI:v1p94/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p94/r1.speaker: أبو بكر الوراق
THALABI:v1p94/r1.claim: Al-Warraq’s letter gloss gives six b-attributes: creator, seer, provider, everlasting, raiser of the dead, and benefactor; the commentary supplies Qurʾānic proofs for them.
THALABI:v1p94/r1.anchor: فالباء على ستة أوجه: بارئ خلقه من العرش الى الثرى

THALABI:v1p94/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p94/r2.speaker: أبو بكر الوراق
THALABI:v1p94/r2.claim: The sīn gloss gives five attributes: hearing, lordship, swift reckoning, safeguarding creatures from injustice, and forgiving sins, with Qurʾānic proofs.
THALABI:v1p94/r2.anchor: والسين على خمسة أوجه: سميع لأصوات خلقه من العرش إلى الثرى

THALABI:v1p94/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p94/r3.speaker: أبو بكر الوراق
THALABI:v1p94/r3.claim: The mīm gloss gives twelve attributes, including ruler, owner, benefactor, glorious, giver of security, overseer, powerful, sustainer, ennobler, bestower, and creator; each receives a Qurʾānic proof.
THALABI:v1p94/r3.anchor: والميم على اثني عشر وجها: ملك الخلق من العرش إلى الثرى

THALABI:v1p95/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p95/r1.speaker: أبو بكر الوراق
THALABI:v1p95/r1.claim: The final mīm glosses are that God grants favor to all creation and forms His creation, supported by verses on divine favor and creation.
THALABI:v1p95/r1.anchor: متفضل على خلقه من العرش إلى الثرى، بيانه: ولكن الله ذو فضل على العالمين

THALABI:v1p95/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p95/r2.speaker: أهل الحقائق
THALABI:v1p95/r2.claim: The people of spiritual realities say the basmala is for blessing and encourages beginning words and deeds with it, following the Qurʾān’s own opening.
THALABI:v1p95/r2.anchor: في بسم الله التيمن والتبرك وحث الناس على الابتداء في أقوالهم وأفعالهم

THALABI:v1p95/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p95/r3.speaker: أهل الكوفة
THALABI:v1p95/r3.claim: The Kufans derive Allah from ilāh: the definite article magnified the name, then the hamza dropped through frequent use and the two lām letters assimilated.
THALABI:v1p95/r3.anchor: أصل هذه الكلمة (إله) في قول أهل الكوفة، فأدخلت الألف واللام فيها

THALABI:v1p95/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p95/r4.speaker: أهل البصرة
THALABI:v1p95/r4.claim: The Basrans derive Allah from lāh with the definite article, citing a verse that preserves the alleged original form.
THALABI:v1p95/r4.anchor: وقال أهل البصرة: أصلها (لاه) ، فألحقت بها الألف واللام

THALABI:v1p95/r5.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p95/r5.speaker: بعضهم
THALABI:v1p95/r5.claim: Another account says the definite article replaced the deleted hamza and therefore remains inseparable; this explains why one cannot say “yā ayyuhā Allāh.”
THALABI:v1p95/r5.anchor: وقال بعضهم: أدخلت الألف واللام بدلا من الهمزة المحذوفة في (إله)

THALABI:v1p95/r6.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p95/r6.speaker: الخليل بن أحمد وجماعة
THALABI:v1p95/r6.claim: Al-Khalil and others say Allah is a proper name, not derived; the verse “Do you know any namesake for Him?” supports its unique reference.
THALABI:v1p95/r6.anchor: فقال الخليل بن أحمد وجماعة: (الله) اسم علم موضوع غير مشتق بوجه

THALABI:v1p95/r7.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p95/r7.speaker: الخليل بن أحمد وجماعة
THALABI:v1p95/r7.claim: They say Allah is exclusive to God because it contains lordship and encompasses all meanings; its successive deletions yield li-llāh, lah, and huwa.
THALABI:v1p95/r7.anchor: ألا ترى أنك إذا أسقطت منه الألف بقي لله، وإذا أسقطت من لله اللام الأولى بقي (له)

THALABI:v1p95/r8.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p95/r8.speaker: author
THALABI:v1p95/r8.claim: When applied to another being, the source says the form must be qualified or indefinite; Allah and al-ilāh are reserved for God, as in the Israelites’ request for a god.

THALABI:v1p96/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p96/r1.speaker: قوم
THALABI:v1p96/r1.claim: Some say the name came from Syriac lāhā, whose final long vowel was removed when the word entered Arabic.
THALABI:v1p96/r1.anchor: وقال قوم: أصله (لاها) بالسريانية، وذلك أن في آخر أسمائهم مدة

THALABI:v1p96/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p96/r2.speaker: النضر بن إسماعيل
THALABI:v1p96/r2.claim: Al-Naḍr derives Allah from taʾalluh, worship and devotion; Ibn ʿAbbas’s reading of “your worship” is offered as evidence.
THALABI:v1p96/r2.anchor: فقال النضر بن إسماعيل: هو من التأله، وهو التنسك والتعبد

THALABI:v1p96/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p96/r3.speaker: ابن عباس والضحاك
THALABI:v1p96/r3.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Daḥḥāk derive ilāh from seeking refuge and relying on someone: creatures turn to God in crises, and He protects them.
THALABI:v1p96/r3.anchor: وهذا معنى قول ابن عباس والضحاك

THALABI:v1p96/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p96/r4.speaker: أبو عمرو بن العلاء
THALABI:v1p96/r4.claim: Abu ʿAmr derives the name from bewilderment: minds are perplexed by God’s essence, greatness, and unknowable nature.
THALABI:v1p96/r4.anchor: وقال أبو عمرو بن العلاء: هو من (ألهت في الشيء) إذا تحيرت فيه

THALABI:v1p96/r5.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p96/r5.speaker: المبرد
THALABI:v1p96/r5.claim: Al-Mubarrad derives it from finding repose with someone; creatures become calm through remembrance of God.
THALABI:v1p96/r5.anchor: وقال المبرد: هو من قول العرب: (ألهت إلى فلان) أي سكنت إليه

THALABI:v1p96/r6.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p96/r6.speaker: علي بن عبد الرحيم القناد
THALABI:v1p96/r6.claim: Al-Qannād derives it from walāh, loss of reason at losing a beloved; the author says hearts long for God in love and tremble at His remembrance.
THALABI:v1p96/r6.anchor: أصله من (الوله) ، وهو ذهاب العقل لفقدان من يعز عليك

THALABI:v1p98/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p98/r1.speaker: علي بن عبد الرحيم القناد
THALABI:v1p98/r1.claim: The Kummayt verse illustrates hearts becoming lovesick for God and yearning at His remembrance.

THALABI:v1p98/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p98/r2.speaker: قوم
THALABI:v1p98/r2.claim: Some derive ilāh from concealment: God is manifest through signs of lordship yet hidden from minds in His modality.
THALABI:v1p98/r2.anchor: والله تعالى هو الظاهر بالربوبية [بالدلائل والأعلام] وهو المحتجب

THALABI:v1p98/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p98/r3.speaker: قوم
THALABI:v1p98/r3.claim: Another derivation is from elevation, since lāh means to rise.
THALABI:v1p98/r3.anchor: وقيل: معناه المتعالي، يقال: (لاه) أي ارتفع

THALABI:v1p98/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p98/r4.speaker: قوم
THALABI:v1p98/r4.claim: One proposed derivation links the name to alāhat, illustrated by a line about delaying the goddess’s return.
THALABI:v1p98/r4.anchor: وقد قيل: من [إلا هتك] ، فهو كما قال الشاعر:

THALABI:v1p98/r5.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p98/r5.speaker: قوم
THALABI:v1p98/r5.claim: A derivation from dwelling in a place gives the sense of the eternally abiding and enduring.

THALABI:v1p98/r6.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p98/r6.speaker: قوم
THALABI:v1p98/r6.claim: Another gloss describes God’s essence as His power to subdue.
THALABI:v1p98/r6.anchor: وقال قوم: [ان يقال] ذاته وهي قدرته على الإخضاع

THALABI:v1p98/r7.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p98/r7.speaker: الحارث بن أسد المجلسي
THALABI:v1p98/r7.claim: Al-Ḥārith says Allah comes from “made them needy”: servants need their Creator for benefits and harms like distressed, overpowered people.
THALABI:v1p98/r7.anchor: وقال الحارث بن أسد المجلسي، أبو عبد الله البغدادي: الله من (ألههم) أي أحوجهم

THALABI:v1p98/r8.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p98/r8.speaker: شهر بن حوشب
THALABI:v1p98/r8.claim: Shahr ibn Ḥawshab glosses Allah as the Creator of everything.
THALABI:v1p98/r8.anchor: وقال شهر بن حوشب: الله خالق كل شيء

THALABI:v1p98/r9.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p98/r9.speaker: أبو بكر الوراق
THALABI:v1p98/r9.claim: Abu Bakr al-Warrāq gives the terse gloss “He is.”

THALABI:v1p98/r10.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p98/r10.speaker: author
THALABI:v1p98/r10.claim: The source notes a heavy pronunciation of the lām in Allah, with the tongue pressed to the palate in reverence for the name.
THALABI:v1p98/r10.anchor: حتى طبقوا اللسان به الحنك لفخامة ذكره

THALABI:v1p98/r11.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p98/r11.speaker: قوم
THALABI:v1p98/r11.claim: Some say al-Raḥmān and al-Raḥīm are synonymous names for the merciful; mercy is either God’s will of good, an essential attribute, or withholding deserved punishment and doing good, an act-attribute.
THALABI:v1p98/r11.anchor: الرحمن الرحيم، قال قوم: هما بمعنى واحد مثل (ندمان، ونديم)

THALABI:v1p98/r12.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p98/r12.speaker: قوم
THALABI:v1p98/r12.claim: Those who distinguish the names say al-Raḥmān’s intensive pattern denotes one filled with mercy.
THALABI:v1p98/r12.anchor: فمعنى (الرحمن) : الذي وسعت رحمته كل شيء

THALABI:v1p99/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p99/r1.speaker: قوم
THALABI:v1p99/r1.claim: One view makes al-Raḥmān merciful to all creation through creation and provision, while al-Raḥīm specially guides believers in this life and grants them Paradise and vision in the next.
THALABI:v1p99/r1.anchor: وقال بعضهم: (الرحمن) العاطف على جميع خلقه كافرهم ومؤمنهم

THALABI:v1p99/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p99/r2.speaker: جعفر بن محمد الصادق
THALABI:v1p99/r2.claim: Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq summarizes the distinction as al-Raḥmān being a specific name with general scope and al-Raḥīm a general name with specific scope.
THALABI:v1p99/r2.anchor: وهذا قول جعفر بن محمد الصادق

THALABI:v1p99/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p99/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
THALABI:v1p99/r3.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās calls the two names subtle, with one more delicate than the other.
THALABI:v1p99/r3.anchor: وقول ابن عباس: هما اسمان رقيقان أحدهما أرق من الآخر

THALABI:v1p99/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p99/r4.speaker: مجاهد
THALABI:v1p99/r4.claim: Mujāhid says al-Raḥmān is for the people of this world and al-Raḥīm for the people of the afterlife.
THALABI:v1p99/r4.anchor: عن مجاهد قال: الرحمن بأهل الدنيا، والرحيم بأهل الآخرة

THALABI:v1p99/r5.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p99/r5.speaker: الضحاك
THALABI:v1p99/r5.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk assigns al-Raḥmān’s mercy to heaven’s inhabitants through their dwelling, obedience, and protection, and al-Raḥīm’s to earthly people through messengers, scriptures, counsel, and relief from calamities.
THALABI:v1p99/r5.anchor: وقال الضحاك: الرحمن بأهل السماء حين أسكنهم السماوات

THALABI:v1p99/r6.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p99/r6.speaker: عكرمة
THALABI:v1p99/r6.claim: ʿIkrima says al-Raḥmān is associated with one mercy and al-Raḥīm with one hundred; he derives this from the Prophetic report that one mercy was sent to earth and ninety-nine are reserved for Judgment Day.
THALABI:v1p99/r6.anchor: وقال عكرمة: الرحمن برحمة واحدة، والرحيم بمائة رحمة

THALABI:v1p99/r7.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p99/r7.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
THALABI:v1p99/r7.claim: The Prophet reports that God has one hundred mercies: one is shared among creation, while ninety-nine are reserved to show mercy to servants on the Resurrection Day.
THALABI:v1p99/r7.anchor: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: «إن لله تعالى مائة رحمة أنزل منها واحدة إلى الأرض

THALABI:v1p100/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p100/r1.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
THALABI:v1p100/r1.claim: A second report says God will join the one mercy to the other ninety-nine, completing one hundred for His servants on Judgment Day.
THALABI:v1p100/r1.anchor: إن الله تعالى قابض هذه إلى تلك فمكملها مائة يوم القيامة

THALABI:v1p100/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p100/r2.speaker: ابن المبارك
THALABI:v1p100/r2.claim: Ibn al-Mubārak says al-Raḥmān gives when asked, while al-Raḥīm is displeased when not asked.
THALABI:v1p100/r2.anchor: وقال ابن المبارك: (الرحمن: الذي إذا سئل أعطى، والرحيم إذا لم يسأل غضب

THALABI:v1p100/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p100/r3.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
THALABI:v1p100/r3.claim: The Prophet says whoever does not ask God makes Him angry; a poem contrasts God’s anger at unanswered supplication with people’s anger at being asked.
THALABI:v1p100/r3.anchor: عن أبي هريرة عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم أنه قال: من لم يسأل الله يغضب عليه

THALABI:v1p100/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p100/r4.speaker: أبو بكر الوراق
THALABI:v1p100/r4.claim: Al-Warrāq distinguishes al-Raḥmān as bestowed blessings and al-Raḥīm as benefits God has spared or withdrawn.
THALABI:v1p100/r4.anchor: الرحمن: بالنعماء وهي ما أعطي وحبا، والرحيم بالآلاء وهي ما صرف وزوى

THALABI:v1p100/r5.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p100/r5.speaker: محمد بن علي المزيدي
THALABI:v1p100/r5.claim: Al-Muzaydī says al-Raḥmān rescues people from the Fire and al-Raḥīm admits them to gardens.
THALABI:v1p100/r5.anchor: الرحمن بالانقاذ من النيران، وبيانه قوله تعالى: وكنتم على شفا حفرة من النار فأنقذكم منها

THALABI:v1p100/r6.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p100/r6.speaker: المحاسبي
THALABI:v1p100/r6.claim: Al-Muḥāsibī assigns al-Raḥmān mercy to souls and al-Raḥīm mercy to hearts.
THALABI:v1p100/r6.anchor: وقال المحاسبي: (الرحمن: برحمة النفوس، والرحيم برحمة القلوب)

THALABI:v1p100/r7.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p100/r7.speaker: السري بن مغلس
THALABI:v1p100/r7.claim: Al-Sarī ibn Mughlis says al-Raḥmān removes distress and al-Raḥīm forgives sins.
THALABI:v1p100/r7.anchor: وقال السري بن مغلس: (الرحمن بكشف الكروب، والرحيم بغفران الذنوب)

THALABI:v1p100/r8.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p100/r8.speaker: عبد الله بن الجراح
THALABI:v1p100/r8.claim: Ibn al-Jarrāḥ’s first gloss is damaged in the text; he says al-Raḥīm provides protection and divine success.

THALABI:v1p100/r9.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p100/r9.speaker: مطهر بن الوراق
THALABI:v1p100/r9.claim: Muṭahhar al-Warrāq says al-Raḥmān forgives even grave sins, while al-Raḥīm accepts even few acts of obedience.
THALABI:v1p100/r9.anchor: وقال مطهر بن الوراق: (الرحمن بغفران السيئات وإن كن عظيمات

THALABI:v1p100/r10.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p100/r10.speaker: يحيى بن معاذ الرازي
THALABI:v1p100/r10.claim: Yaḥyā ibn Muʿādh says al-Raḥmān provides for worldly livelihoods and al-Raḥīm for the afterlife.
THALABI:v1p100/r10.anchor: الرحمن بمصالح معاشهم، والرحيم بمصالح معادهم

THALABI:v1p100/r11.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p100/r11.speaker: الحسين بن الفضل
THALABI:v1p100/r11.claim: Al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Faḍl says al-Raḥmān removes harm and evil, while al-Raḥīm is compassionate but may be unable to remove them.
THALABI:v1p100/r11.anchor: الرحمن الذي يرحم العبد على كشف الضر ودفع الشر

THALABI:v1p100/r12.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p100/r12.speaker: أبو بكر الوراق
THALABI:v1p100/r12.claim: Al-Warrāq says al-Raḥmān is merciful to deniers and unbelievers, while al-Raḥīm is merciful to monotheists and the grateful.
THALABI:v1p100/r12.anchor: الرحمن بمن جحده والرحيم بمن وحده، والرحمن بمن كفر والرحيم بمن شكر

THALABI:v1p101/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p101/r1.speaker: قراء المدينة والبصرة والكوفة، مالك، الأوزاعي، أبو حنيفة
THALABI:v1p101/r1.claim: The Medinan, Basran, and Kufan reciters, with Mālik, al-Awzāʿī, and Abū Ḥanīfa, treat the basmala as an opening blessing, not a verse of this or other suras, and say it need not be recited; on this count “those You favored” is verse six.
THALABI:v1p101/r1.anchor: فقال قراء المدينة والبصرة وقراء الكوفة: إنها افتتاح التيمن والتبرك بذكره، وليست من الفاتحة

THALABI:v1p101/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p101/r2.speaker: سعيد بن المسيب
THALABI:v1p101/r2.claim: Another group, reporting from Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib and followed by Meccan and many Hijazi reciters, counts the basmala as a verse of the Fātiḥa and does not count “those You favored” separately.
THALABI:v1p101/r2.anchor: رووا ذلك عن سعيد بن المسيب، وبه قال قراء مكة والكوفة وأكثر قراء الحجاز

THALABI:v1p101/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p101/r3.speaker: الشافعي والشعبي وعبد الله
THALABI:v1p101/r3.claim: Al-Shāfiʿī, al-Shaʿbī, and a view attributed to ʿAbd Allāh say it was revealed as the first verse of al-Fātiḥa and is a verse in every sura except al-Tawba; written repetitions and the Naml occurrence are their evidence.
THALABI:v1p101/r3.anchor: وقال الشافعي والشعبي وهو رأي عبد الله أنها نزلت في الآية الأولى من فاتحة الكتاب

THALABI:v1p101/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p101/r4.speaker: author
THALABI:v1p101/r4.claim: A report traces the written opening from “In Your name, O God,” to bismillah, then bismillah al-Raḥmān, and finally the full basmala after the verse in Solomon’s letter was revealed.
THALABI:v1p101/r4.anchor: حتى نزلت: إنه من سليمان وإنه بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم ، فكتب مثلها

THALABI:v1p102/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p102/r1.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
THALABI:v1p102/r1.claim: The Prophet calls the basmala the unique verse revealed after Solomon; the author takes his recitation of the full formula to show it is a complete verse of al-Fātiḥa and the sura openings, whereas Naml contains it within a longer verse.
THALABI:v1p102/r1.anchor: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: «ألا أخبرك بآية لم تنزل على أحد بعد سليمان بن داود غيري؟»

THALABI:v1p102/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p102/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
THALABI:v1p102/r2.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says that when a basmala verse was revealed, the Prophet knew the previous sura had ended and another had begun.
THALABI:v1p102/r2.anchor: سمعت سعيد بن جبير يقول: سمعت ابن عباس يقول: كان رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم إذا نزلت آية بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم

THALABI:v1p102/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p102/r3.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
THALABI:v1p102/r3.claim: In a report from Jābir, the Prophet tells him to say the basmala when beginning prayer after Jābir says al-ḥamdu lillāh.
THALABI:v1p102/r3.anchor: عن جابر بن عبد الله أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم قال: «كيف تقول إذا قمت إلى الصلاة؟»

THALABI:v1p102/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p102/r4.speaker: مسلمة
THALABI:v1p102/r4.claim: The report says the Prophet recited the Fātiḥa verse by verse, counting seven, including the basmala.
THALABI:v1p102/r4.anchor: عن مسلمة أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم كان يقرأ: بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم الحمد لله رب العالمين

THALABI:v1p103/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p103/r1.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
THALABI:v1p103/r1.claim: ʿAlī recited the basmala when opening a sura in prayer, said omitting it diminishes the prayer, and called it the completion of the seven oft-repeated verses and the Great Qurʾān.
THALABI:v1p103/r1.anchor: علي بن أبي طالب (كرم الله وجهه) أنه كان إذا افتتح السورة في الصلاة

THALABI:v1p103/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p103/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
THALABI:v1p103/r2.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās identifies the seven oft-repeated verses as al-Fātiḥa and counts the basmala as its seventh verse.
THALABI:v1p103/r2.anchor: وقيل لابن عباس: أين السابعة؟ قال: بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم

THALABI:v1p103/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p103/r3.speaker: أبو هريرة
THALABI:v1p103/r3.claim: Abū Hurayra says readers of the Mother of the Qurʾān should not leave the basmala because it is one of its verses and part of the seven oft-repeated.
THALABI:v1p103/r3.anchor: عن أبي هريرة أنه قال: إذا قرأتم أم القرآن فلا تبرحوا بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم

THALABI:v1p103/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p103/r4.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
THALABI:v1p103/r4.claim: In the divine report dividing prayer between God and the servant, the basmala glorifies God, al-ḥamdu praises Him, al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm extols Him, Mālik delegates the matter, the worship-and-help verse is shared, and guidance is granted to the servant.
THALABI:v1p103/r4.anchor: عن أبي هريرة أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم قال: «يقول الله: قسمت الصلاة بيني وبين عبادي نصفين

THALABI:v1p104/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p104/r1.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
THALABI:v1p104/r1.claim: The Prophet tells a man who began reciting al-ḥamdu without the basmala that he cut off his prayer: leaving out this verse cuts off the Fātiḥa and invalidates the prayer.
THALABI:v1p104/r1.anchor: عن أبي هريرة قال: كنت مع النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم، والنبي صلى الله عليه وسلم يحدث أصحابه

THALABI:v1p104/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p104/r2.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
THALABI:v1p104/r2.claim: A report from Ṭalḥa ibn ʿUbayd Allāh says that whoever omits the basmala has omitted a verse from God’s Book.
THALABI:v1p104/r2.anchor: عن طلحة بن عبيد الله قال: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: «من ترك بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم فقد ترك آية من كتاب الله»

THALABI:v1p104/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p104/r3.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
THALABI:v1p104/r3.claim: The author notes that ʿAlī included the basmala among the verses he counted as the Mother of the Book.
THALABI:v1p104/r3.anchor: وقد عدها علي عليه السلام فيما عد من أم الكتاب

THALABI:v1p104/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p104/r4.speaker: المهاجرون والأنصار
THALABI:v1p104/r4.claim: When Muʿāwiya omitted the basmala while leading prayer in Medina, the Emigrants and Helpers called out that he had forgotten it, so he repeated the prayer with it.
THALABI:v1p104/r4.anchor: ناداه المهاجرون والأنصار من كل ناحية: أنسيت! أين بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم حين استفتحت القرآن

THALABI:v1p105/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p105/r1.speaker: المهاجرون
THALABI:v1p105/r1.claim: A separate report says Muʿāwiya recited the basmala for al-Fātiḥa but not the next sura; the Emigrants challenged him, and he repeated the prayer while reading that sura.
THALABI:v1p105/r1.anchor: فلما سلم ناداه المهاجرون من كل مكان: يا معاوية، أسرقت الصلاة أم نسيت

THALABI:v1p105/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p105/r2.speaker: author
THALABI:v1p105/r2.claim: The author argues from the arrangement of verse endings and the basmala’s placement that it was written where revealed, rather than inserted merely to divide suras.
THALABI:v1p105/r2.anchor: فلما أبطلت هذه الوجوه علمنا أنها كتبت حيث نزلت، وحيث لم تنزل لم تكتب

THALABI:v1p105/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p105/r3.speaker: author
THALABI:v1p105/r3.claim: The author adds that scribes used black ink for the basmala, unlike non-Qurʾānic marginal material, which supports its status as Qurʾān.
THALABI:v1p105/r3.anchor: وكتبوا التسمية بالسواد فعلمنا أنها قرآن

THALABI:v1p105#2/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p105#2/r1.speaker: author
THALABI:v1p105#2/r1.claim: The author says reciting the basmala aloud in prayer is sunnah, citing commands to read in the Lord’s name and to remember the Lord’s name when praying.
THALABI:v1p105#2/r1.anchor: ثم الجهر بها في الصلاة سنة لقول الله تعالى: اقرأ باسم ربك

THALABI:v1p105#2/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p105#2/r2.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
THALABI:v1p105#2/r2.claim: A report relayed by al-Mahdī from his father and grandfather, Ibn ʿAbbās, says the Prophet recited the basmala aloud.
THALABI:v1p105#2/r2.anchor: عن عبد الله بن عباس أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم جهر ب بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم

THALABI:v1p105#2/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p105#2/r3.speaker: عطاء وطاوس ومجاهد
THALABI:v1p105#2/r3.claim: Al-Layth reports that ʿAṭāʾ, Ṭāwūs, and Mujāhid recited the basmala aloud.
THALABI:v1p105#2/r3.anchor: قال: سمعت ليثا قال: كان عطاء وطاوس ومجاهد يجهرون ب بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم

THALABI:v1p105#2/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p105#2/r4.speaker: عبد الله بن عباس، عبد الله بن عمر، عبد الله بن الزبير، عبد الله بن صفوان
THALABI:v1p105#2/r4.claim: A report says the four ʿAbādila opened recitation with the basmala and voiced it.
THALABI:v1p105#2/r4.anchor: أن العبادلة كانوا يستفتحون القراءة ب بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم يجهرون بها

THALABI:v1p105#2/r5.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p105#2/r5.speaker: جعفر بن محمد
THALABI:v1p105#2/r5.claim: Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq says the Prophet’s family agreed on voicing the basmala, making up missed night prayer in daytime, and speaking well of Abū Bakr and ʿUmar and their companion.
THALABI:v1p105#2/r5.anchor: عن جعفر بن محمد أنه قال: «اجتمع آل محمد على الجهر ب بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم

THALABI:v1p105#2/r6.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p105#2/r6.speaker: جعفر بن محمد الصادق
THALABI:v1p105#2/r6.claim: Al-Ṣādiq calls audible recitation the truth and links it to the verse about people turning away when God alone is mentioned in the Qurʾān.
THALABI:v1p105#2/r6.anchor: سئل الصادق عن الجهر بالتسمية، فقال: «الحق الجهر به

THALABI:v1p106/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p106/r1.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
THALABI:v1p106/r1.claim: Abū Hurayra reports that Gabriel taught the Prophet prayer, after which the Prophet stood, said takbīr, and voiced the basmala.
THALABI:v1p106/r1.anchor: عن أبي هريرة قال: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم: «أتاني جبريل فعلمني الصلاة»

THALABI:v1p106/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p106/r2.speaker: الزهري
THALABI:v1p106/r2.claim: Al-Zuhrī calls reciting the basmala in the Fātiḥa part of prayer’s sunnah and says one who omits it has not recited the sura; he names ʿAmr ibn Saʿīd as the first to abandon it in Medina.
THALABI:v1p106/r2.anchor: عن الزهري قال: من سنة الصلاة أن تقرأ بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم في فاتحة الكتاب

THALABI:v1p106/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p106/r3.speaker: أنس بن مالك
THALABI:v1p106/r3.claim: Anas reports that he did not hear the Prophet, Abū Bakr, ʿUmar, or ʿUthmān recite the basmala aloud.
THALABI:v1p106/r3.anchor: عن أنس بن مالك قال: صليت مع رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم وأبي بكر وعمر وعثمان

THALABI:v1p106/r4.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p106/r4.speaker: author
THALABI:v1p106/r4.claim: The author says Anas’s report only denies raising the voice; it does not deny that the basmala is part of the sura, and “not aloud” need not mean whispering or omitting it.
THALABI:v1p106/r4.anchor: فعلم بهذا الحديث أنه لم ينف كون هذه الآية من جملة السورة، لكنه تعرض لترك الجهر فقط

THALABI:v1p107/r1.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p107/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
THALABI:v1p107/r1.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says the Prophet voiced the basmala in Mecca, prompting pagans to mock the mention of the “god of al-Yamāma,” meaning Musaylima; the author connects this to the command for moderate volume.
THALABI:v1p107/r1.anchor: عن ابن عباس، قال: كان رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم يجهر ب بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم

THALABI:v1p107/r2.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v1p107/r2.speaker: أنس بن مالك
THALABI:v1p107/r2.claim: Anas says the Prophet, Abū Bakr, and ʿUmar opened recitation with al-ḥamdu lillāh; the author interprets this as opening prayer with the sura called al-Ḥamd, not beginning at verse two.
THALABI:v1p107/r2.anchor: أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم وأبا بكر وعمر كانوا يستفتحون القراءة ب الحمد لله رب العالمين

THALABI:v10p244/r3.author: al-Thaʿlabī
THALABI:v10p244/r3.speaker: author
THALABI:v10p244/r3.claim: In this account, the voice tells the Prophet to recite the basmala and the opening of al-Fātiḥa through its final words, then affirm God’s oneness.
THALABI:v10p244/r3.anchor: فلما خلا ناداه يا محمد قل: بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم الحمد لله رب العالمين حتى بلغ ولا الضالين قل: لا إله إلا الله

ASAD-NOTES:1:1#n1/r1.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:1:1#n1/r1.speaker: author
ASAD-NOTES:1:1#n1/r1.claim: Most authorities count the opening invocation as verse 1 of Al-Fatihah; in other surahs it precedes the text without being counted.
ASAD-NOTES:1:1#n1/r1.anchor: According to most of the authorities, this invocation (which occurs at the beginning of every surah

ASAD-NOTES:1:1#n1/r2.author: Muhammad Asad
ASAD-NOTES:1:1#n1/r2.speaker: Ibn al-Qayyim
ASAD-NOTES:1:1#n1/r2.claim: Ibn al-Qayyim distinguishes rahman as God's inherent, inseparable abounding grace and rahim as that grace manifested in creation.
ASAD-NOTES:1:1#n1/r2.anchor: the one advanced by Ibn al-Qayyim (as quoted in Manar I,48)

WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p433#2/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p433#2/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p433#2/r1.claim: Grammarians give the bāʾ names such as attachment, instrumental aid, and addition; each describes a real use.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p433#2/r1.anchor: اختلفت عبارة النحويين في تسمية هذه الباء الجارة، فسموها مرة: حرف إلصاق، ومرة: حرف استعانة،

WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p433#2/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p433#2/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p433#2/r2.claim: Attachment means joining one's sphere of capacity to the person or thing expressed after bāʾ.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p433#2/r2.anchor: أما الإلصاق: فنحو قولك: تمسكت بزيد، وذلك أنك ألصقت محل قدرتك به،

WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p433#2/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p433#2/r3.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p433#2/r3.claim: Instrumental bāʾ marks a tool used to perform an action, as in striking with a sword or writing with a pen.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p433#2/r3.anchor: وأما الاستعانة: فقولك: ضربت بالسيف، وكتبت بالقلم، وبريت بالمدية، أي: استعنت بهذه الأدوات

WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p433#2/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p433#2/r4.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p433#2/r4.claim: Additive bāʾ associates the act of passing with the person passed, as in passing by Zayd.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p433#2/r4.anchor: وأما الإضافة: فقولك: مررت بزيد، أضفت مرورك إلى زيد بالباء

WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p433#2/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p433#2/r5.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p433#2/r5.claim: Some grammarians call bāʾ, kāf, and lām surplus because their one-letter forms are short and can blend with the following word.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p433#2/r5.anchor: وأما قول النحويين (¬5): (الباء والكاف واللام الزوائد) فإنما قالوا فيهن:

WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p433#2/r6.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p433#2/r6.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p433#2/r6.claim: Expert grammarians avoid calling them surplus: bāʾ and lām are additive particles, while kāf is a preposition.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p433#2/r6.anchor: وحذاق النحويين لا يسمونها زوائد، بل يقولون في الباء واللام: إنهما حرفا إضافة

WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p433#2/r7.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p433#2/r7.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p433#2/r7.claim: These are functioning particles that govern the genitive case of the nouns they precede, like min, ʿan, and fī.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p433#2/r7.anchor: وهذه حروف أدوات عاملة (¬5)، تجر ما تدخل عليه من الأسماء نحو: من وعن وفي

WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p433#2/r8.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p433#2/r8.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p433#2/r8.claim: Prepositions supply a link because verbs such as wonder, pass, and go are too weak in ordinary usage to reach these nouns directly.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p433#2/r8.anchor: وإنما جرت (¬1) الأسماء من قبل أن الأفعال التي قبلها ضعفت عن وصولها وإفضائها إلى الأسماء

WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p433#2/r9.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p433#2/r9.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p433#2/r9.claim: The added preposition makes those verbs reach their nouns; genitive distinguishes indirect connection from direct verbal accusative, while nominative is already occupied by the subject.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p433#2/r9.anchor: فلما قصرت هذه الأفعال عن الوصول إلى الأسماء رفدت بحرف الإضافة، فجعلت موصلة (¬4) لها إليها

WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p433#2/r10.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p433#2/r10.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p433#2/r10.claim: The prepositional phrase remains in an accusative syntactic position, as shown when a following conjunct is accusative and by Sibawayh's cited verse.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p433#2/r10.anchor: الجار والمجرور جميعا في موضع نصب (¬3)، ألا ترى أنهم عطفوا عليه بالنصب (¬4)

WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p436/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p436/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p436/r1.claim: Although bāʾ puts Zayd in the genitive, the phrase occupies the accusative position of a direct object, as Sibawayh's paraphrase and the accusative adjective show.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p436/r1.anchor: قال سيبويه: (إنك إذا قلت: مررت بزيد

WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p436/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p436/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p436/r2.claim: The standalone particles at the beginnings of words normally take fatḥa; bāʾ in bi-Zayd is kasra because it resembles genitive lām.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p436/r2.anchor: (وجميع (¬6) الحروف المفردة التي تقع في أوائل الكلم حكمها الفتح أبدا.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p436/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p436/r3.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p436/r3.claim: Bāʾ resembles lām because both are particles and both govern genitive nouns; the author defers the reason for lām's kasra to verse 2.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p436/r3.anchor: فأما (الباء) في (بزيد) فإنما كسرت لمضارعتها (اللام) الجارة (¬7) في قولك: (المال لزيد)

WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p436/r4.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p436/r4.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p436/r4.claim: The verb governed by bāʾ in the basmala is omitted because context supplies the sense: I began, or begin, in God's name.
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p436/r4.anchor: فأما المتعلق به (الباء) في قوله {بسم الله} فإنه محذوف، ويستغنى عن إظهارها

WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p436/r5.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p436/r5.speaker: author
