ALUSI-FULL:v1p53#2/r4.claim: Al-Alusi answers that seeking aid through a means differs from seeking aid directly, and that invoking a name can confer blessing; several explanations are offered for naming rather than saying by God.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p53#2/r4.anchor: وفيه أنه فرق بين الإستعانة المتعدية بنفسها والإستعانة المعتدية بالباء

ALUSI-FULL:v1p53#2/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p53#2/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p53#2/r5.claim: He treats the spelling of the basmala as Uthmanic and its precise rationale as obscure, then offers a mystical reading: joining the sin to the ba intensifies the connection and reception of grace.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p53#2/r5.anchor: وعندي أن هذا رسم عثماني وهو مما لا يكاد يعرف السر فيه أرباب الرسوم

ALUSI-FULL:v1p53#2/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p53#2/r6.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p53#2/r6.claim: The silent sin reached through an alif suggests the emergence of what was absent through God; depending on its symbolism, the basmala signals universal mercy or Muhammad’s universal mission.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p53#2/r6.anchor: فإن كان عبارة عن صفات الجمال ظهر عموم الرحمة ( ورحمتي وسعت كل شيء )

ALUSI-FULL:v1p53#2/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p53#2/r7.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p53#2/r7.claim: The elongated ba signifies complete manifestation or that humility before God raises a person; the two readings make the basmala’s calligraphic form symbolically meaningful.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p53#2/r7.anchor: وإنما طولت الباء للإشارة إلى أن الظهور تام

ALUSI-FULL:v1p54/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p54/r1.speaker: الرسميون
ALUSI-FULL:v1p54/r1.claim: Calligraphers say the ba is lengthened to represent the omitted alif, compensate for it, and begin scripture with a majestic letter; a report attributes penmanship instructions to the Prophet addressing Muʿawiya.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p54/r1.anchor: وقال الرسميون طولت لتدل على الألف المحذوفة ولتكون عوضا عنها

ALUSI-FULL:v1p54/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p54/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p54/r2.claim: Al-Alusi regards some further calligraphic explanations as opaque or fanciful rather than demonstrative.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p54/r2.anchor: ولبعضهم في التعليل ما أدعى أنه ليس من عمل الأفهام بل مبذولات الإلهام

ALUSI-FULL:v1p54/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p54/r3.speaker: الصحاح والكشاف
ALUSI-FULL:v1p54/r3.claim: The lexicons differ between deriving Allah from al-ilāh and ilāh; al-Alusi says the hamza was most likely dropped without a regular cause and replaced by the article.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p54/r3.anchor: أصله الأعلالي إله كما في الصحاح أو الإله كما في الكشاف

ALUSI-FULL:v1p54/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p54/r4.speaker: السيد السند
ALUSI-FULL:v1p54/r4.claim: Al-Sayyid al-Sanad treats both forms as names of the divine essence, with al-ilāh usable of another before deletion but Allah exclusive afterward.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p54/r4.anchor: هما علم لذاته إلا أنه قبل الحذف قد يطلق على غيره تعالى وبعده لا يطلق على غيره

ALUSI-FULL:v1p54/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p54/r5.speaker: السعد
ALUSI-FULL:v1p54/r5.claim: Al-Saʿd distinguishes al-ilāh as the general concept of the deity worshiped in truth from Allah as the proper name of God.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p54/r5.anchor: إن الإله اسم لمفهوم كلي هو المعبود بحق والله علم لذاته تعالى

ALUSI-FULL:v1p54/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p54/r6.speaker: الرضي
ALUSI-FULL:v1p54/r6.claim: Al-Raḍī says both forms are exclusive to God, though before assimilation the word is an established common proper name and afterward a fully specific proper name.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p54/r6.anchor: هما قبل الإدغام وبعده مختصان بذاته تعالى لا يطلقان على غيره أصلا

ALUSI-FULL:v1p54/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p54/r7.speaker: ابن مالك
ALUSI-FULL:v1p54/r7.claim: Ibn Malik argues Allah was formed with the article from the outset, not from al-ilāh, because the forms differ in both morphology and meaning.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p54/r7.anchor: أن الله من الأعلام التي قارن وضعها أل وليس أصله الإله

ALUSI-FULL:v1p55/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p55/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p55/r1.claim: Deriving Allah from al-ilāh by deleting or transferring the hamza requires several unmotivated irregularities, including moving a vowel across words and assimilating across a boundary.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p55/r1.anchor: نقل حركة همزة إلى مثل ما بعدها وهو يوجب إجتماع مثلين متحركين

ALUSI-FULL:v1p55/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p55/r2.speaker: ناظر الجيش
ALUSI-FULL:v1p55/r2.claim: Naẓir al-Jaysh praises the preceding derivation as unsurpassed; al-Alusi finds it acceptable except for claiming al-ilāh means any object of worship.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p55/r2.anchor: قال ناظر الجيش : إنه لا مزيد عليه في الحسن وأنا أقول لا بأس به

ALUSI-FULL:v1p55/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p55/r3.speaker: البلقيني
ALUSI-FULL:v1p55/r3.claim: Al-Balqini insists al-ilāh applies only to the true God and says applying it to another is unbelief; al-Alusi considers this objection open to reply.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p55/r3.anchor: فقد بالغ البلقيني في رده وأدعى أنه لا يقع إلا على المعبود بالحق

ALUSI-FULL:v1p55/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p55/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p55/r4.claim: Reported derivations connect ilāh with worship, bewilderment at God’s essence, refuge sought from God, or a young animal’s attachment to its mother; al-Alusi discusses problems with each.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p55/r4.anchor: واشتقاقه من أله كعبد إلاهة كعبادة وألوهة كعبودة وألوهية كعبودية

ALUSI-FULL:v1p55/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p55/r5.speaker: بعضهم
ALUSI-FULL:v1p55/r5.claim: Some derive the name from walah, bewilderment, by turning waw into hamza; al-Alusi objects that the plural and sound changes do not support this derivation.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p55/r5.anchor: وقيل هو من وله الواوي بمعنى تحير أيضا وأصله ولاه

ALUSI-FULL:v1p55/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p55/r6.speaker: ميمون بن قيس الأعشى
ALUSI-FULL:v1p55/r6.claim: A line attributed to Maymun ibn Qays al-Aʿsha, containing lāhahu al-kibār, is cited as evidence for deriving the divine name from lāh, to be elevated or hidden.

ALUSI-FULL:v1p56/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p56/r1.speaker: بعضهم
ALUSI-FULL:v1p56/r1.claim: A mystical derivation takes the name from the pronoun of the absent, then adds the lām of ownership and lengthens the sound; removal of letters is read as leaving li-llah, lahu, and huwa.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p56/r1.anchor: وقيل أصله الكناية لأنها للغائب وهو سبحانه الغائب عن أن تدركه الأبصار

ALUSI-FULL:v1p56/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p56/r2.speaker: الصوفية
ALUSI-FULL:v1p56/r2.claim: Many Sufis favor this mystical account, which al-Alusi says is close to their spiritual mode of interpretation.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p56/r2.anchor: ولهذا مال كثير من الصوفية إلى هذا القول وهو إلى المشرب قريب

ALUSI-FULL:v1p56/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p56/r3.speaker: البلخي
ALUSI-FULL:v1p56/r3.claim: Al-Balkhi calls Allah a loan from Hebrew or Syriac meaning powerful; al-Alusi rejects this as unsupported and inconsistent with Arabic usage and derivation.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p56/r3.anchor: وزعم البلخي أنه ليس بعربي بل هو عبراني أو سرياني معرب

ALUSI-FULL:v1p56/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p56/r4.speaker: أكابر المعتبرين
ALUSI-FULL:v1p56/r4.claim: Most major authorities, including al-Shafiʿi, Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, al-Ashʿari, al-Khalil, and Sibawayh, regard Allah as Arabic and originally a proper name for God’s unique essence.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p56/r4.anchor: والذي عليه أكابر المعتبرين كالشافعي ومحمد بن الحسن والأشعري

ALUSI-FULL:v1p56/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p56/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p56/r5.claim: One proof that Allah is a proper name is that it can be described but is not itself used as a description; an apparent counterexample is treated as apposition.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p56/r5.anchor: الأول أنه يوصف ولايوصف به وقراءة صراط العزيز الحميد الله بالجر محمولة على البيان

ALUSI-FULL:v1p56/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p56/r6.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p56/r6.claim: A second proof is that all realities needing expression have a name, so the creator must have a name that can bear divine attributes rather than only a generic title.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p56/r6.anchor: أنه لا بد له منأسم يجري عليه صفاته فإن كل شيء تتوجه إليه

ALUSI-FULL:v1p56/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p56/r7.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p56/r7.claim: A third proof is that if Allah were merely a descriptive title or common noun, the confession of divine oneness would not exclude partners as it does with a proper name.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p56/r7.anchor: لو كان وصفا لم تكن الكلمة توحيدا مثل لا إله إلا الرحمن

ALUSI-FULL:v1p57/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p57/r1.speaker: البيضاوي
ALUSI-FULL:v1p57/r1.claim: Al-Bayḍawi treats Allah as originally a descriptor that became a name through exclusive usage; he argues its essence cannot be directly conceived and cites usage and derivation.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p57/r1.anchor: فأختار أنه وصف في أصله لكنه لما غلب عليه بحيث لا يستعمل في غيره

ALUSI-FULL:v1p57/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p57/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p57/r2.claim: Al-Alusi disputes al-Bayḍawi’s objections: a proper name can refer to an essence conceived through an identifying aspect, and the cited verse permits other syntactic analyses.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p57/r2.anchor: والتحقيق أن تصوير الموضوع له بوجه ما كاف في وضع العلم

ALUSI-FULL:v1p57/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p57/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p57/r3.claim: Al-Alusi prefers Allah as an original proper name for the essence encompassing all attributes; a name acquired only through dominance has less force and dignity.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p57/r3.anchor: فالعدول عن الأشرف في هذا الاسم الأقدس مما لا أسوغ الإقدام عليه

ALUSI-FULL:v1p57/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p57/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p57/r4.claim: In the Naqshbandi practice of heart remembrance, the worshiper attends to the incomparable essence signified by Allah; al-Alusi says Ibn Arabi developed this view in several works.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p57/r4.anchor: هذا الاسم الأقدس ذاتا بلا مثل وحققه الشيخ الأكبر قدس سره في مواضع عديدة

ALUSI-FULL:v1p57/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p57/r5.speaker: القراء
ALUSI-FULL:v1p57/r5.claim: Readers generally velarize Allah’s lām after an a or u vowel, though an unrestricted form is reported; deleting the alif is less eloquent and, in one view, invalid in prayer or an oath.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p57/r5.anchor: وتفخيم اللام من هذا الاسم الكريم إذا انفتح ما قبله أو انضم طريقة معروفة عند القراء

ALUSI-FULL:v1p58/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p58/r1.speaker: ابن عربي
ALUSI-FULL:v1p58/r1.claim: Ibn Arabi reads the letters and patterns of Allah mystically, finding signs in the alif, lām, and changing vowels; al-Alusi directs readers to the esoteric writings.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p58/r1.anchor: وقد أطال الشيخ قدس سره الكلام في الفتوحات عن أسرار حروفه

ALUSI-FULL:v1p58/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p58/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p58/r2.claim: The familiar grammatical view is that al-Rahman and al-Rahim are intensive adjectives derived from rahima after a transitivity and vowel shift.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p58/r2.anchor: والرحمن الرحيم المشهور أنهما صفتان مشبهتان بنيتا لإفادة المبالغة

ALUSI-FULL:v1p58/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p58/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p58/r3.claim: Because human mercy can mean tenderness of heart, commentators explain divine mercy figuratively as its effect, by a comparison, or as a metaphor for beneficence or will.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p58/r3.anchor: ولكونها من الكيفيات التابعة للمزاج المستحيل عليه سبحانه تؤخذ باعتبار غايتها

ALUSI-FULL:v1p58/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p58/r4.speaker: القاضي أبو بكر والأشعري
ALUSI-FULL:v1p58/r4.claim: In one explicit-metaphor account, beneficence is the referent for mercy according to Qadi Abu Bakr, while al-Ashʿari takes the referent to be the will to show beneficence.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p58/r4.anchor: بأن يشبه الإحسان على ما اختاره القاضي أبو بكر أو إرادته على ما اختاره الأشعري

ALUSI-FULL:v1p59/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p59/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p59/r1.claim: A concealed metaphor pictures God as a king whose heart softens toward subjects; the word mercy then stands for one of its supposed concomitants.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p59/r1.anchor: بأن يشبه معنى الضمير فيهما العائد إليه تعالى بملك رق قلبه على رعيته

ALUSI-FULL:v1p59/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p59/r2.speaker: بعضهم
ALUSI-FULL:v1p59/r2.claim: Some say Rahman is more intensive by the number of recipients, covering believers and unbelievers in worldly life, while Rahim is reserved for believers in the afterlife.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p59/r2.anchor: فعلى الأول قيل يارحمن الدنيا لأنه يعم المؤمن والكافر ورحيم الآخرة لأنه يخص المؤمن

ALUSI-FULL:v1p59/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p59/r3.speaker: بعضهم
ALUSI-FULL:v1p59/r3.claim: Others distinguish by quality: Rahman covers both worlds’ great blessings, while Rahim covers lesser worldly blessings; other explanations cite divine exclusivity, foundational favors, or rhyme.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p59/r3.anchor: وعلى الثاني قيل يارحمن الدنيا والآخرة ورحيم الدنيا لأن النعم الأخروية كلها جسام

ALUSI-FULL:v1p59/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p59/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p59/r4.claim: Al-Alusi rejects these explanations as disputed and argues that the forms are more plausibly intensive active forms from transitive verbs, especially clear in Rahim.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p59/r4.anchor: فالأصح أنهما من أبنية المبالغة الملحقة بإسم الفاعل وأخذا من فعل متعد

ALUSI-FULL:v1p59/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p59/r5.speaker: التسهيل
ALUSI-FULL:v1p59/r5.claim: The Tasheel excludes Rabb, Malik, and Rahman from the intensive adjective pattern because their verbs are transitive or no intransitive derivation is established.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p59/r5.anchor: ولذا قال في التسهيل : إن ربا وملكا ورحمانا ليست منها لتعدى أفعالها

ALUSI-FULL:v1p59/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p59/r6.speaker: بعضهم
ALUSI-FULL:v1p59/r6.claim: Another account treats mercy in this context as a technical religious meaning rather than a figurative use.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p59/r6.anchor: وقيل الرحمة في ذلك حقيقة شرعية

ALUSI-FULL:v1p60/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p60/r1.speaker: الأعلم وابن مالك
ALUSI-FULL:v1p60/r1.claim: Al-Aʿlam and Ibn Malik say Rahman was originally a proper name, not an adjective or a name formed merely through prevailing usage.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p60/r1.anchor: قال الأعلم وإبن مالك : أنه علم في الأصل لا صفة ولا علم بالغلبة التقديرية

ALUSI-FULL:v1p60/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p60/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p60/r2.claim: Al-Alusi argues that the alleged vowel shift need not be preceded by making the verb intransitive, since the shift itself makes it so.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p60/r2.anchor: فلأن نقل فعل المكسور إلى فعل المضموم لا يتوقف على جعله لازما أولا

ALUSI-FULL:v1p60/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p60/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p60/r3.claim: Human mercy as tenderness does not force figurative interpretation when mercy is attributed to God; divine attributes are real in a manner befitting God, beyond creaturely comparison.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p60/r3.anchor: فلأن كون الرحمة في اللغة رقة القلب إنما هو فينا وذا لا يستلزم ارتكاب التجوز

ALUSI-FULL:v1p60/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p60/r4.speaker: السكوتي
ALUSI-FULL:v1p60/r4.claim: Al-Sukuti calls interpreting mercy as metaphor a Muʿtazilite tendency and says early Sunni authorities affirmed the revealed attribute without recasting it.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p60/r4.anchor: بأن جعل الرحمة مجازا نزغة اعتزالية قد حفظ الله تعالى منها سلف المسلمين

ALUSI-FULL:v1p60/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p60/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p60/r5.claim: Al-Alusi says one cannot treat mercy as metaphor while affirming life, knowledge, will, power, speech, hearing, and sight literally on no principled distinction.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p60/r5.anchor: فأما أن يقال بارتكاب المجاز فيها كلها إذا نسبت إليه عز شأنه أو بتركه كذلك

ALUSI-FULL:v1p60#2/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p60#2/r1.speaker: أهل السنة
ALUSI-FULL:v1p60#2/r1.claim: Sunni authorities affirm scriptural attributes as transmitted, without asking how or resorting to figurative reinterpretation; al-Alusi cites al-Ashʿari’s al-Ibana as his final position.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p60#2/r1.anchor: فقد قال في أول كتاب الإبانة الذي هو آخر مصنفاته

ALUSI-FULL:v1p60#2/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p60#2/r2.speaker: الأشعري
ALUSI-FULL:v1p60#2/r2.claim: Al-Ashʿari says his creed is to adhere to scripture, the Prophet’s Sunna, reports from early Muslims, and what Ahmad ibn Hanbal taught.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p60#2/r2.anchor: التمسك بكتاب الله وسنة نبيه صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم وما روى عن الصحابة والتابعين

ALUSI-FULL:v1p60#2/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p60#2/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p60#2/r3.claim: Al-Alusi says reports that al-Ashʿari interpreted mercy are unverified or later retracted; those claiming early Muslims endorsed such interpretation must provide clear proof.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p60#2/r3.anchor: فما نقل عنه من تأويل صفة الرحمة إما غير ثاتب أو مرجوع عنه

ALUSI-FULL:v1p60#2/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p60#2/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p60#2/r4.claim: He rejects the kingly-heart simile as an improper comparison about God, and says a softened heart does not itself benefit anyone; actual beneficence does.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p60#2/r4.anchor: إذ لا يقال أن لله تعالى هيئة شبيهة بهيئة الملك ولم يرد إطلاق الحال عليه

ALUSI-FULL:v1p60#2/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p60#2/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p60#2/r5.claim: Al-Alusi also rejects identifying divine mercy with will or beneficence: the proposed causal links are unproven for God, and analogy from visible causes is inappropriate.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p60#2/r5.anchor: ومجرد السببية والمسببية في هذه الحالة لا يوجب كون الرحمة المنسوبة إليه عز شأنه مجازا

ALUSI-FULL:v1p60#2/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p60#2/r6.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p60#2/r6.claim: He challenges the claim that Rahman is more intensive than Rahim, beginning a broader critique of deriving comparative force solely from word length.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p60#2/r6.anchor: وأما سادسا فلأن كون الرحمن أبلغ من الرحيم غير مسلم

ALUSI-FULL:v1p61/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p61/r1.speaker: الراغب
ALUSI-FULL:v1p61/r1.claim: Al-Raghib says faʿil marks frequent action while faʿlan marks action that is frequent and recurrent; some use this to call Rahman stronger.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p61/r1.anchor: قال الراغب أن فعيلا لمن كثر منه الفعل وفعلان لمن كثر منه وتكرر

ALUSI-FULL:v1p61/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p61/r2.speaker: ابن المبارك
ALUSI-FULL:v1p61/r2.claim: Ibn al-Mubarak explains Rahman as the giver when asked and Rahim as the one who becomes angry when not asked.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p61/r2.anchor: وقول إبن المبارك الرحمن إذا سئل أعطى والرحيم إذا لم يسئل غضب

ALUSI-FULL:v1p61/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p61/r3.speaker: الجويني
ALUSI-FULL:v1p61/r3.claim: Al-Juwayni treats Rahman and Rahim as equal in force, citing a report that God is the Merciful of this world and the next and their two mercies.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p61/r3.anchor: وقيل هما سواء لظاهر الحديث الذي أخرجه الحاكم في المستدرك مرفوعا

ALUSI-FULL:v1p61/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p61/r4.speaker: بعضهم
ALUSI-FULL:v1p61/r4.claim: Another distinction makes Rahman the attribute of mercy itself and Rahim the relation of that mercy to those who receive it.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p61/r4.anchor: وفرق بعضهم بينهما بأن الرحمن دال على الصفة القائمة به تعالى والرحيم دال على تعلقها بالمرحوم

ALUSI-FULL:v1p61/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p61/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p61/r5.claim: Al-Alusi says greater word length does not establish greater meaning in every case; the rule is general, and examples such as hadhir and hadhir show exceptions.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p61/r5.anchor: وما ذكر من قولهم لأن زيادة البناء تدل على زيادة المعنى قاعدة أغلبية

ALUSI-FULL:v1p61/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p61/r6.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p61/r6.claim: The puzzle about divine intensification concerns relations and recipients rather than an increase in God’s attribute; theologians answer differently depending on whether mercy is an essential or active attribute.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p61/r6.anchor: وأجيب بأن المراد الأكثرية في التعلقات والمتعلقات لا في الصفة نفسها

ALUSI-FULL:v1p61/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p61/r7.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p61/r7.claim: The view assigning worldly mercy to believers and unbelievers but afterlife mercy only to believers falters because afterlife blessings are vastly more numerous and unbelievers may receive some relief.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p61/r7.anchor: فهذا الوجه مخدوش على الحالين على أن في اختصاص رحمة الآخرة بالمؤمنين مقالا

ALUSI-FULL:v1p61/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p61/r8.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p61/r8.claim: Reports cited include the Prophet’s intercession for all people at the praised station and reduced punishment for some damned people in the afterlife.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p61/r8.anchor: إذ قد ورد في الصحيح شفاعته صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم لعامة الناس من هول الموقف

ALUSI-FULL:v1p61/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p61/r9.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p61/r9.claim: Al-Alusi argues that treating unbelievers’ worldly benefits as merely apparent would also defeat the claim that worldly mercy embraces both believers and unbelievers.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p61/r9.anchor: فيبطل حينئذ دعوى شمول الرحمة المؤمن والكافر في الدنيا

ALUSI-FULL:v1p62/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p62/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p62/r1.claim: Even a partial reduction of punishment counts as mercy in some respect, since people in Hell ask its keepers for relief and any lesser evil is easier than a greater one.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p62/r1.anchor: وقال الذين في انار لخزنة جهنم أدعوا ربكم يخفف عنا يوما من العذاب

ALUSI-FULL:v1p62/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p62/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p62/r2.claim: The claim that Rahman covers both worlds while Rahim covers lesser worldly blessings lacks support and conflicts with the transmitted wording naming both mercies in both worlds.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p62/r2.anchor: إلا أنه يرد عليه كسابقه أن الأثر لا يعرف والمعروف المرفوع رحمن الدنيا والآخرة ورحيمهما

ALUSI-FULL:v1p62/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p62/r3.speaker: ابن هشام
ALUSI-FULL:v1p62/r3.claim: Ibn Hisham says the ordering question is misplaced: Rahman is a substantivized appositive, not an adjective, and Rahim modifies it rather than Allah.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p62/r3.anchor: وذكر ابن هشام أنه غير متجه لأن هذا خارج عن كلام العرب

ALUSI-FULL:v1p62/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p62/r4.speaker: ابن خروف
ALUSI-FULL:v1p62/r4.claim: Ibn Khuruf calls Rahman a dominant adjective, but its rare use as an indefinite or annexed form makes it more noun-like.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p62/r4.anchor: وقال ابن خروف هو صفة غالبة ولم يقع تابعا إلا لله تعالى في البسملة

ALUSI-FULL:v1p62/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p62/r5.speaker: العلامة المدقق في الكشف
ALUSI-FULL:v1p62/r5.claim: The scholar of al-Kashf says the sequence follows a descending order: Allah names the essence, Rahman universal mercy and existence, and Rahim each being’s particular share and perfections.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p62/r5.anchor: أن الله اسم للذات الإلهية باعتبار أن الكل منه وإليه وجودا ورتبة وماهية

ALUSI-FULL:v1p62/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p62/r6.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p62/r6.claim: Al-Alusi objects that assigning general existence to Rahman and individualized existence to Rahim is arbitrary, since every existent thing is already a particular share.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p62/r6.anchor: وهل يوجد في الخارج من النوع إلا الحصص الأفرادية

ALUSI-FULL:v1p63/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p63/r1.speaker: الزمخشري وعبد القاهر
ALUSI-FULL:v1p63/r1.claim: Al-Zamakhshari and Abd al-Qahir say rhyme or verse endings should follow meanings and coherent ordering; sound alone cannot justify moving words, especially when the pattern is inconsistent.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p63/r1.anchor: فمجرد المحافظة على الرؤوس لا يصير نكتة للتقديم إلا بعد أن يثبت أن المعاني

ALUSI-FULL:v1p63/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p63/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p63/r2.claim: Al-Alusi offers a mystical reading of the order: Rahim points to Muhammad, whose completion of the basmala mirrors the completion of the created world.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p63/r2.anchor: وعندي من باب الإشارة أن تأخير الرحيم لأنه صفة محمد صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم

ALUSI-FULL:v1p63/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p63/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p63/r3.claim: In this symbolism Adam bears the names while Muhammad bears their meanings; Adam’s names are words, whereas Muhammad received comprehensive speech.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p63/r3.anchor: قال تعالى ( وعلم آدم الأسماء كلها )

ALUSI-FULL:v1p63/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p63/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p63/r4.claim: Al-Alusi contrasts Companions, who experienced the divine essence, with later believers who know the names, and cites a report promising the latter fiftyfold reward.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p63/r4.anchor: فإنهم حصلوا الذات وحصلنا الأسماء ولما راعينا الاسم مراعاتهم الذات ضوعف لنا الأجر

ALUSI-FULL:v1p63/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p63/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p63/r5.claim: He further says the Prophet longs for later believers who are his brothers and would rejoice to meet one of them.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p63/r5.anchor: فنحن الإخوان وهم الأصحاب وهو صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم إلينا بالأشواق

ALUSI-FULL:v1p64/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p64/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p64/r1.claim: The pairing of Allah and Rahman is especially close, supporting the appositive reading and symbolizing the divine essence; al-Alusi links it to the report that Adam was created in God’s image.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p64/r1.anchor: قل أدعوا الله أو أدعوا الرحمن أيا ما تدعوا فله الأسماء الحسنى

ALUSI-FULL:v1p64/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p64/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p64/r2.claim: A mystical letter reading assigns hidden and manifest alifs in Allah and Rahman to essence and knowledge, with other letters indicating divine attributes; life is their necessary condition.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p64/r2.anchor: في الله وفي الرحمن ألفين ألف الذات وألف العلم والأولى في كل خفية والثانية ظاهرة

ALUSI-FULL:v1p64/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p64/r3.speaker: بعض العارفين
ALUSI-FULL:v1p64/r3.claim: Some mystics see even Satan as sharing universal mercy because an alif appears fractionally in its name; Rahim differs by having only the alif of knowledge.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p64/r3.anchor: أن الألف الخفية هنا ظهرت من حيث الجزئية من هذا اللفظ في الشيطان

ALUSI-FULL:v1p64/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p64/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p64/r4.claim: Rahim symbolizes Muhammad in his rank as messenger to all people, with its alif representing knowledge and divine support for his universal mission.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p64/r4.anchor: ولما كان هذا الأسم مشيرا إلى سيدنا محمد صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم بإعتبار رتبته

ALUSI-FULL:v1p64/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p64/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p64/r5.claim: The question whether Rahman is Arabic is longstanding; al-Alusi begins to explain the Arabs’ response by their fear of multiple gods rather than foreign origin.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p64/r5.anchor: فقد طال النزاع في تحقيق لفظ الرحمن كما طال في تحقيق لفظ الله

ALUSI-FULL:v1p64#2/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p64#2/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p64#2/r1.claim: Al-Alusi says Arabs’ question about Rahman reflected fear that they were being directed to another deity like themselves, not evidence that the word was non-Arabic.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p64#2/r1.anchor: ولعل سبب ذلك توهمهم التعدد وأنهم خافوا أن يكون المعبود الذي يدلهم عليهم من جنسهم

ALUSI-FULL:v1p64#2/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p64#2/r2.speaker: ابن الحاجب
ALUSI-FULL:v1p64#2/r2.claim: Ibn al-Hajib gives competing conditions for declension of faʿlan forms used as names or adjectives, which leaves Rahman disputed while Sukran and Nadman are clearer.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p64#2/r2.anchor: النون والألف إذا كانا في اسم فشرطه العلمية وفي صفة فانتفاء فعلانة

ALUSI-FULL:v1p64#2/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p64#2/r3.speaker: الزمخشري والرضي وابن مالك والبيضاوي
ALUSI-FULL:v1p64#2/r3.claim: Al-Zamakhshari, al-Radi, Ibn Malik, and al-Bayḍawi prefer leaving Rahman indeclinable by analogy with the common faʿlan pattern whose feminine is faʿla.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p64#2/r3.anchor: وأختار الزمشخري والشيخ الرضي وإبن مالك وأستظهره البيضاوي عدم الصرف

ALUSI-FULL:v1p64#2/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p64#2/r4.speaker: السعد
ALUSI-FULL:v1p64#2/r4.claim: Because the rule’s original noun pattern and the more frequent adjective pattern conflict, al-Saʿd allows both declension and indeclinability rather than neglecting either principle.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p64#2/r4.anchor: ولما رأى السعد أن هذه المسألة مما تعارض فيها الأصل والغالب

ALUSI-FULL:v1p64#2/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p64#2/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p64#2/r5.claim: Since Rahman is heard only definite, annexed, or vocative, rare poetic evidence cannot settle its declension; Rahim does not share this ambiguity.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p64#2/r5.anchor: وحيث لم يسمع هذا الاسم إلا مضافا أو معرفا بأل أو منادى

ALUSI-FULL:v1p64#2/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p64#2/r6.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p64#2/r6.claim: The basmala begins God’s speech because it summarizes what follows and is a magnificent verse whose benefits are immense; investigating it requires a wide range of disciplines.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p64#2/r6.anchor: وإنما جعل الله البسملة مبدأ كلامه لوجهين أما الأول فلأنها إجمال ما بعدها وهي آية عظيمة

ALUSI-FULL:v1p64#2/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p64#2/r7.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p64#2/r7.claim: Al-Alusi illustrates the range of required learning, from grammar, morphology, rhetoric and language to theology, law, hadith, philosophy, letters, natural sciences, and ethics.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p64#2/r7.anchor: أحتاج إل ى علم النحو وإذا أراد أن يبحث عنأصول كلماتها كيف كانت وكيف آلت

ALUSI-FULL:v1p65/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p65/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p65/r1.claim: The basmala’s hidden indications are inexhaustible; it is the Qur’an’s title and a gateway to secrets beyond the formal scholars’ semantic discussions.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p65/r1.anchor: معرفة ما خفى على أرباب الرسوم من الإشارات فليضرع إلى ربه

ALUSI-FULL:v1p65/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p65/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p65/r2.claim: The opening and ending letters, alif forms, and nine groups of triads invite mystical reflection: articulation points, omitted letters, written/spoken forms, vowel states, word classes, genitives, divine names, agency, and connection patterns.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p65/r2.anchor: إن أردت أن تمتحن ذهنك في بعض أسرارها فتأمل سر إفتتاحها وإختتامها بحرفين

ALUSI-FULL:v1p65/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p65/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p65/r3.claim: He also asks about the four elements, nineteen letters, letter connections and spellings, and other graphic details, while saying formal scholars generally stop at meanings and possibilities.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p65/r3.anchor: وأنظر لم أشتملت حروفها على الطبائع الأربع وتقدم في الظهور الهواء

ALUSI-FULL:v1p65/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p65/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p65/r4.claim: Al-Sarmīnī enumerated 5,391,360 possible interpretations; al-Ālūsī says divine favor let him add roughly the square of that number, though only some possibilities occur.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p65/r4.anchor: وقد صرح السرميني بإبداء خمسة آلاف ألف وثلثمائة ألف

ALUSI-FULL:v1p65/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p65/r5.speaker: أبو هريرة
ALUSI-FULL:v1p65/r5.claim: The Prophet said that an important affair begun without the basmala is cut off; al-Ālūsī cites Abū Hurayra’s report as transmitted by ʿAbd al-Qādir al-Rahāwī and gives no grading.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p65/r5.anchor: كل أمر ذي بال لا يبدأ فيه ببسم الله فهو أبتر

ALUSI-FULL:v1p65/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p65/r6.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p65/r6.claim: Bal means a state or affair of consequence that occupies the heart; another explanation likens a great matter to something possessing a heart through implied metaphor.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p65/r6.anchor: والبال الحال والشأن فمعنى ذي بال شريف يحتفل به ويهتم

ALUSI-FULL:v1p65/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p65/r7.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p65/r7.claim: One explanation says the wording honors God by beginning significant affairs with His name while easing the obligation for trivial affairs; al-Ālūsī prefers applying it to all affairs, great or small.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p65/r7.anchor: وفي هذا الوصف فائدتان إحداهما رعاية تعظيم أسم الله تعالى

ALUSI-FULL:v1p66/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p66/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p66/r1.claim: Al-Ālūsī reads the hadith universally: every matter that comes to mind, important or trivial, should begin with the basmala, as the verse says every bird flies with its wings.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p66/r1.anchor: وعندي أن الأظهر جعل الوصف للتعميم كما في قوله تعالى : ( ولا طائر يطير بجناحيه )

ALUSI-FULL:v1p66/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p66/r2.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p66/r2.claim: The universal reading magnifies God and teaches disavowal of independent power: carrying a straw is like carrying a mountain unless God helps.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p66/r2.anchor: وحث على التبري عن الحول والقوة إلا بالله

ALUSI-FULL:v1p66/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p66/r3.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p66/r3.claim: God commands abundant remembrance, and the Prophet taught asking God for every need, down to a sandal strap; a report says God told Moses to ask even for cooking salt and sandal straps.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p66/r3.anchor: ليسأل أحدكم ربه حاجته كلها حتى شثع نعله

ALUSI-FULL:v1p66/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p66/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p66/r4.claim: Asking for small things does not violate reverence: the Qur’an finds no disparity in creation, and a discerning believer sees no created thing as insignificant.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p66/r4.anchor: ما ترى في خلق الرحمن من تفاوت فأرجع البصر هل ترى من فطور

ALUSI-FULL:v1p66/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p66/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p66/r5.claim: Invoking God’s name over forbidden acts is itself forbidden but, on the sound view, not unbelief; over disliked acts it is disliked, while intending contempt for God makes it unbelief.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p66/r5.anchor: التسمية على الحرام والمكروه مما لا ينبغي بل هي حرام في الحرام لا كفر

ALUSI-FULL:v1p66/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p66/r6.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p66/r6.claim: Reports vary between beginning with praise, the basmala, or remembrance, and between descriptions such as cut off or amputated; the hadith is textually and transmission-wise unsettled, but leniency applies in merits and semantic corroboration strengthens it.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p66/r6.anchor: وقد أضطرب الحديث هنا فوقع في بعض الروايات لا يبدأ فيه بالحمد لله

ALUSI-FULL:v1p66/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p66/r7.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p66/r7.claim: His preferred reconciliation treats the basmala and praise versions as canceling each other’s specific qualifiers, leaving the broader command to begin with remembrance; another view allows either phrase or another remembrance.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p66/r7.anchor: وأستحسن فيه أن روايتي البسملة والحمد له تعارضتا فسقط قيداهما

ALUSI-FULL:v1p66/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p66/r8.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p66/r8.claim: The hadith concerns matters not recognized as complete in religious law: they may be materially finished yet deficient in meaning, since the basmala completes their meanings.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p66/r8.anchor: المراد من الحديث أن لا يكون معتبرا في الشرع فهو غير تام معنى

ALUSI-FULL:v1p66/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v1p66/r9.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v1p66/r9.claim: The basmala’s light is portrayed mystically as restoring sight and hearing, protecting the poisoned, and healing a demon-afflicted person when its letters are written as an incantation.
ALUSI-FULL:v1p66/r9.anchor: ومن مشكاة بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم تشرق على صفحات الأكوان أنوار البهاء

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p49#3/r1.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p49#3/r1.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p49#3/r1.claim: The prefixed bi- governs what follows; its omitted complement is understood as ‘I begin’ or ‘say’ in God’s name.
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p49#3/r1.anchor: الباء أداة تخفض ما بعدها مثل: من وعن، والمتعلق به الباء محذوف

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p49#3/r2.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p49#3/r2.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p49#3/r2.claim: The alif is omitted from ism for ease and frequent use; al-Qutaybi explains the lengthened ba as an honorific opening, and Umar b. Abd al-Aziz ordered careful lettering.
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p49#3/r2.anchor: قال القتيبي ليكون افتتاح كلام كتاب الله بحرف معظم، كان عمر بن عبد العزيز

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p49#3/r3.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p49#3/r3.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p49#3/r3.claim: Another explanation says the ba was lengthened to mark where the omitted alif had been; the spelling keeps the alif in ‘read in the name of your Lord.’
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p49#3/r3.anchor: وقيل: لما أسقطوا الألف ردوا طول الألف على الباء ليكون دالا على سقوط الألف

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p49#3/r4.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p49#3/r4.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p49#3/r4.claim: Ism can mean the named entity itself, as verses call the person Yahya by that name and call worshiped persons ‘names’; more often it means the naming.
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p49#3/r4.anchor: والاسم هو المسمى وعينه وذاته قال الله تعالى

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p49#3/r5.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p49#3/r5.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p49#3/r5.claim: God’s naming himself in the formula teaches people how to begin recitation.
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p49#3/r5.anchor: قيل هو تعليم للعباد كيف يفتتحون القراءة

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p49#3/r6.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p49#3/r6.speaker: المبرد
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p49#3/r6.claim: Al-Mubarrad derives ism from sumuw, ‘loftiness’: the name rises above and manifests its meaning, which lies beneath it.
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p49#3/r6.anchor: قال المبرد من البصريين: هو مشتق من السمو وهو العلو

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p49#3/r7.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p49#3/r7.speaker: ثعلب
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p49#3/r7.claim: Thaʿlab derives ism from wasm, a mark that indicates its meaning; al-Baghawi prefers the derivation from sumuw because of its diminutive and verb forms.
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p49#3/r7.anchor: قال ثعلب من الكوفيين: هو من الوسم والسمة وهي العلامة

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p49#3/r8.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p49#3/r8.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p49#3/r8.claim: The derivation from sumuw is stronger: ism diminishes as sumayy, and its verb is sammaytu; a wasm derivation would yield wasīm and wasamtu.
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p49#3/r8.anchor: والأول أصح لأنه يصغر على السمي ولو كان من السمة لكان يصغر على الوسيم كما يقال في الوعد وعيد

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p49#3/r9.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p49#3/r9.speaker: الخليل وجماعة
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p49#3/r9.claim: Al-Khalil and a group treat Allah as a proper name unique to God, with no derivation, like human proper names.
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p49#3/r9.anchor: قال الخليل وجماعة: هو اسم علم خاص لله عز وجل لا اشتقاق له

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p49#3/r10.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p49#3/r10.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p49#3/r10.claim: Others derive Allah from ilaha, worship; Ibn Abbas’s reading of ‘your gods’ as ‘your worship’ supports the sense that God alone deserves worship.
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p49#3/r10.anchor: اشتقاقه فقيل: من أله إلاهة أي عبد عبادة

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p49#3/r11.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p49#3/r11.speaker: المبرد
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p49#3/r11.claim: Al-Mubarrad connects ilah with Arabs’ phrase for finding repose in someone; a poetic line illustrates resorting to him amid calamities.
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p49#3/r11.anchor: قال المبرد: هو من قول العرب ألهت إلى فلان أي سكنت إليه

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p50/r1.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p50/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p50/r1.claim: Ibn Abbas calls al-Rahman and al-Rahim two tender names, one more tender than the other.
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p50/r1.anchor: قال ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما: هما اسمان رقيقان أحدهما أرق من الآخر

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p50/r2.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p50/r2.speaker: المبرد
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p50/r2.claim: Some treat the two names as synonyms for merciful; al-Mubarrad describes them as favor upon favor, repeated to encourage hopeful hearts.
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p50/r2.anchor: وقال المبرد: هو إنعام بعد إنعام، وتفضل بعد تفضل

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p50/r3.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p50/r3.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p50/r3.claim: A distinction makes al-Rahman’s mercy universal in this world, like provision for all, while al-Rahim’s mercy is particular to believers in the hereafter.
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p50/r3.anchor: فقال: الرحمن بمعنى العموم والرحيم بمعنى الخصوص

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p50/r4.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p50/r4.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p50/r4.claim: On this distinction, people may be called merciful (rahim) but not al-Rahman; the former is general in wording and particular in meaning, the latter opposite.
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p50/r4.anchor: فالرحمن عام المعنى خاص اللفظ، والرحيم عام اللفظ خاص المعنى

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p50/r5.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p50/r5.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p50/r5.claim: Mercy is either God’s willing good for its recipients, an attribute of essence, or withholding deserved punishment and giving unearned good, an attribute of action.
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p50/r5.anchor: والرحمة إرادة الله تعالى الخير لأهله. وقيل هي ترك عقوبة من يستحقها وإسداء الخير إلى من لا يستحق

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p50/r6.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p50/r6.speaker: قرّاء المدينة والبصرة وفقهاء الكوفة
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p50/r6.claim: Medinan and Basran readers and Kufan jurists hold that the basmala is not part of the Fatiha or other surahs, but opens them for blessing.
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p50/r6.anchor: فذهب قراء المدينة والبصرة وفقهاء الكوفة إلى أنها ليست من فاتحة الكتاب، ولا من غيرها من السور

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p50/r7.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p50/r7.speaker: قرّاء مكة والكوفة وأكثر فقهاء الحجاز
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p50/r7.claim: Meccan and Kufan readers and most Hijazi jurists count the basmala as part of the Fatiha only; it is written to separate surahs.
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p50/r7.anchor: وذهب قراء مكة والكوفة وأكثر فقهاء الحجاز إلى أنها من الفاتحة وليست من سائر السور وأنها كتبت للفصل

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p50/r8.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p50/r8.speaker: الثوري وابن المبارك والشافعي
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p50/r8.claim: Al-Thawri, Ibn al-Mubarak, and al-Shafiʿi count the basmala in every surah except al-Tawba, since it is written in the codex in Quranic script.
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p50/r8.anchor: وذهب جماعة إلى أنها من الفاتحة ومن كل سورة إلا سورة التوبة وهو قول الثوري وابن المبارك والشافعي لأنها كتبت في المصحف بخط سائر القرآن

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p50/r9.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p50/r9.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p50/r9.claim: Other derivations connect the divine name with refuge and bewildered longing: creatures flee to God in hardship and need as a child turns to its mother.
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p50/r9.anchor: وقيل أصل الإله "ولاه" فأبدلت الواو بالهمزة مثل وشاح وإشاح

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p51/r1.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p51/r1.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p51/r1.claim: All agree the Fatiha has seven verses, but those counting the basmala begin the final verse at ‘those You favored’; others begin it at ‘not those under wrath.’
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p51/r1.anchor: واتفقوا على أن الفاتحة سبع آيات فالآية الأولى عند من يعدها من الفاتحة

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p51/r2.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p51/r2.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p51/r2.claim: Those counting the basmala cite its Quranic-script placement and a report from Ibn Abbas through Saʿid b. Jubayr: it is the seventh of the seven oft-repeated verses.
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p51/r2.anchor: هي أم القرآن قال أبي وقرأها علي سعيد بن جبير

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p51/r3.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p51/r3.speaker: ابن عباس
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p51/r3.claim: In the same report, Ibn Abbas says the basmala was reserved for this community and not disclosed to anyone before it.
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p51/r3.anchor: قال ابن عباس: فذخرها لكم فما أخرجها لأحد قبلكم

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p51/r4.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p51/r4.speaker: أنس بن مالك
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p51/r4.claim: Anas reports that Abu Bakr, Umar, and Uthman did not recite the basmala when beginning the prayer; this is evidence for excluding it from the Fatiha.
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p51/r4.anchor: عن أنس بن مالك رضي الله عنه أنه قال

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p51/r5.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p51/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p51/r5.claim: Ibn Abbas says the Prophet knew a surah had ended when the basmala descended.
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p51/r5.anchor: قال سعيد بن جبير عن ابن عباس كان رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p51/r6.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p51/r6.speaker: ابن مسعود
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p51/r6.claim: Ibn Masud says the community learned where one surah ended and another began when the basmala was revealed.
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p51/r6.anchor: وعن ابن مسعود قال: كنا لا نعلم فصل ما بين السورتين حتى ينزل بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم

BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p51/r7.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p51/r7.speaker: الشعبي
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p51/r7.claim: Al-Shaʿbi traces changing opening formulas in the Prophet’s writing from ‘in your name, God’ to the complete basmala as the corresponding verses were revealed.
BAGHAWI-FULL:v1p51/r7.anchor: وقال الشعبي: كان رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم يكتب في بدء الأمر على رسم قريش

BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1/r1.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1/r1.speaker: قراء مكة والكوفة وفقهاؤهما وابن المبارك والشافعي
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1/r1.claim: They count the basmala as part of al-Fātiḥa and every sura.
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1/r1.anchor: من الفاتحة، ومن كل سورة، وعليه قراء مكة والكوفة وفقهاؤهما وابن المبارك

BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1/r2.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1/r2.speaker: قراء المدينة والبصرة والشام ومالك والأوزاعي
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1/r2.claim: They disagree that the basmala is part of every sura.
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1/r2.anchor: وخالفهم قراء المدينة والبصرة والشام وفقهاؤها ومالك والأوزاعي

BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1/r3.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1/r3.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1/r3.claim: Abū Ḥanīfa stated no position here, so al-Bayḍāwī infers he did not regard it as part of the sura; Muḥammad al-Ḥasan says all text between the covers is God's speech.
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1/r3.anchor: ولم ينص أبو حنيفة رحمه الله تعالى فيه بشيء فظن أنها ليست من السورة عنده

BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1/r4.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1/r4.speaker: أبو هريرة
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1/r4.claim: The Prophet reportedly called the basmala the first of al-Fātiḥa's seven verses.
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1/r4.anchor: ما روى أبو هريرة رضي الله تعالى عنه، أنه عليه الصلاة والسلام قال

BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1/r5.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1/r5.speaker: أم سلمة
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1/r5.claim: Umm Salama reports that the Prophet counted the basmala as a verse when reciting al-Fātiḥa.
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1/r5.anchor: وقول أم سلمة رضي الله عنها «قرأ رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم الفاتحة وعد

BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1/r6.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1/r6.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1/r6.claim: The disagreement concerns whether the basmala is an independent verse or counted with what follows; Muslims agree it is Qur'an and is written in the codices, which were carefully kept free of additions such as آمين.
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1/r6.anchor: والإجماع على أن ما بين الدفتين كلام الله سبحانه وتعالى، والوفاق على إثباتها في المصاحف

BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1/r7.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1/r7.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1/r7.claim: The prefixed ب is attached to an omitted verb meaning “I read,” since what follows is read; each actor supplies the verb suited to what the naming begins.
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1/r7.anchor: والباء متعلقة بمحذوف تقديره: بسم الله أقرأ لأن الذي يتلوه مقروء

BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1/r8.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1/r8.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1/r8.claim: “I begin” is less suitable because nothing in the wording matches or indicates it, while “my beginning” requires an extra ellipsis.
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1/r8.anchor: وذلك أولى من أن يضمر أبدأ لعدم ما يطابقه ويدل عليه

BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1/r9.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1/r9.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1/r9.claim: Putting the governed phrase first gives emphasis, exclusivity, and reverence; the name precedes recitation and makes an act religiously complete, as in the cited verses.
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1/r9.anchor: وتقديم المعمول ههنا أوقع كما في قوله

BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1/r10.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1/r10.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1/r10.claim: A report says that any significant matter begun without the basmala is cut off or incomplete.
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1/r10.anchor: كل أمر ذي بال لا يبدأ فيه ببسم الله فهو أبتر

BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1/r11.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1/r11.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1/r11.claim: An alternative takes ب as accompaniment: read while seeking blessing through God's name.
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1/r11.anchor: وقيل الباء للمصاحبة، والمعنى متبركا باسم الله تعالى اقرأ

BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1/r12.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1/r12.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1/r12.claim: The basmala and following words through the sura are placed on the servants' tongues to teach invocation, praise, and asking for grace.
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1/r12.anchor: وهذه وما بعده إلى آخر السورة مقول على ألسنة العباد ليعلموا

BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1/r13.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1/r13.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1/r13.claim: The bāʾ is kasra because these particles are obligatorily prepositional, like the kasra of the imperative lām and the genitive lām before nouns.
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1/r13.anchor: وإنما كسرت ومن حق الحروف المفردة أن تفتح، لاختصاصها باللزوم الحرفية والجر

BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1/r14.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1/r14.speaker: أصحابنا البصريين
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1/r14.claim: The Basrans derive اسم from a shortened form whose ending was dropped through frequent use; its beginning was made still and hamzat al-waṣl added to start it with a vowel.
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1/r14.anchor: والاسم عند أصحابنا البصريين من الأسماء التي حذفت أعجازها لكثرة الاستعمال

BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#2/r1.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#2/r1.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#2/r1.claim: Al-Bayḍāwī calls the metathesis proposal remote and irregular, and derives اسم from elevation because it raises the named thing and marks it.
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#2/r1.anchor: والقلب بعيد غير مطرد، واشتقاقه من السمو لأنه رفعة للمسمى

BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#2/r2.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#2/r2.speaker: الكوفيون
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#2/r2.claim: The Kufans derive اسم from السمة, originally وسم, with initial wāw deleted and hamzat al-waṣl compensating for it.
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#2/r2.anchor: وقيل أصله لاه مصدر لاه يليه ليها ولاها، إذا احتجب وارتفع

BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#2/r3.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#2/r3.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#2/r3.claim: He rejects the Kufan etymology because Arabic does not use an initial hamza this way after deleting a word's first letter.
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#2/r3.anchor: ورد بأن الهمزة لم تعهد داخلة على ما حذف صدره في كلامهم

BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#2/r4.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#2/r4.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#2/r4.claim: Shortened forms سم and سم occur, as a poetic line attests.

BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#2/r5.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#2/r5.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#2/r5.claim: If اسم means the spoken expression, it differs from its referent: sounds are discontinuous and vary across peoples and times, whereas the thing named does not.
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#2/r5.anchor: والاسم إن أريد به اللفظ فغير المسمى، لأنه يتألف من أصوات متقطعة غير قارة

BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#2/r6.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#2/r6.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#2/r6.claim: If اسم means the entity itself, it is the referent, but that usage is not well established.
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#2/r6.anchor: وإن أريد به ذات الشيء فهو المسمى لكنه لم يشتهر بهذا المعنى

BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#2/r7.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#2/r7.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#2/r7.claim: In the commands to bless and glorify God's name, اسم can mean the spoken name, whose wording must be kept free of obscenity and discourtesy just as God and His attributes are free of defects.
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#2/r7.anchor: المراد به اللفظ لأنه كما يجب تنزيه ذاته سبحانه وتعالى وصفاته عن النقائص

BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#2/r8.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#2/r8.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#2/r8.claim: Another analysis treats اسم as pleonastic, as in the cited poetic expression.
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#2/r8.anchor: أو الاسم فيه مقحم كما في قول الشاعر

BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#2/r9.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#2/r9.speaker: الشيخ أبو الحسن الأشعري
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#2/r9.claim: Al-Ashʿarī treats the name as an attribute and divides attributes into what is identical with the named essence, other than it, or neither it nor other than it.
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#2/r9.anchor: وإن أريد به الصفة، كما هو رأي الشيخ أبي الحسن الأشعري، انقسم انقسام الصفة عنده

BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#2/r10.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#2/r10.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#2/r10.claim: The formula says “in the name of God” rather than “by God” because blessing and seeking help are through remembrance of His name, or to distinguish oath-taking from seeking blessing.
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#2/r10.anchor: وإنما قال بسم الله ولم يقل بالله، لأن التبرك والاستعانة بذكر اسمه

BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#2/r11.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#2/r11.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#2/r11.claim: The written alif is omitted from بسم through frequent use, with the bāʾ lengthened in its place.
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#2/r11.anchor: ولم تكتب الألف على ما هو وضع الخط لكثرة الاستعمال وطولت الباء عوضا عنها

BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#2/r12.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#2/r12.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#2/r12.claim: الله derives from إله by deleting the hamza and compensating with alif-lām; it is now exclusive to the true deity, though إله originally named any object of worship.
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#2/r12.anchor: والله أصله إله، فحذفت الهمزة وعوض عنها الألف واللام ولذلك قيل

BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#2/r13.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#2/r13.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#2/r13.claim: One etymology derives إله from worship; further proposals connect it with bewilderment, finding rest in God, seeking refuge in fear, or a young animal's attachment to its mother.
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#2/r13.anchor: واشتقاقه من أله ألهة وألوهة وألوهية بمعنى عبد، ومنه تأله واستأله، وقيل

BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#2/r14.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#2/r14.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#2/r14.claim: A proposal derives it from وله, “to be bewildered,” with original wāw changing to hamza; the plural آلهة rather than أولهة argues against it.
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#2/r14.anchor: وكان أصله ولاه فقلبت الواو همزة لاستثقال الكسرة عليها

BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#3/r1.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#3/r1.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#3/r1.claim: The cited poem attests the use of لاه as God's name among tribal elders.
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#3/r1.anchor:
كحلفة من أبي رباح
يشهدها لاهه الكبار

BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#3/r2.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#3/r2.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#3/r2.claim: Some regard الله as the proper name of God's unique essence because it alone accepts His attributes and cannot imply a partner in the confession of divine unity.
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#3/r2.anchor: وقيل علم لذاته المخصوصة لأنه يوصف ولا يوصف به

BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#3/r3.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#3/r3.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#3/r3.claim: The stronger view is that الله was originally descriptive, as derivation and the sense of “God in the heavens” indicate, but exclusive usage made it function like a proper name.
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#3/r3.anchor: والأظهر أنه وصف في أصله لكنه لما غلب عليه بحيث لا يستعمل في غيره

BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#3/r4.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#3/r4.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#3/r4.claim: Another proposal takes the word from Syriac لاه, adapted by dropping its final alif and adding lām.
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#3/r4.anchor: وقيل أصله لاها بالسريانية فعرب بحذف الألف الأخيرة، وإدخال اللام عليه

BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#3/r5.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#3/r5.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#3/r5.claim: God's lām is emphatic when preceded by fatḥa or ḍamma; omitting the alif in pronunciation is an error that invalidates prayer and does not form an explicit oath, though poetry may force it.
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#3/r5.anchor: وتفخيم لامه إذا انفتح ما قبله أو انضم سنة، وقيل مطلقا

BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#3/r6.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#3/r6.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#3/r6.claim: الرحمن and الرحيم are intensive forms of mercy; human mercy is tenderness, but divine names refer to the resulting beneficence rather than an emotional state.
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#3/r6.anchor: اسمان بنيا للمبالغة من رحم، كالغضبان من غضب

BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#3/r7.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#3/r7.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#3/r7.claim: الرحمن is stronger than الرحيم because the added form indicates added meaning; this difference can concern quantity or quality.
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#3/r7.anchor: لأن زيادة البناء تدل على زيادة المعنى كما في قطع وقطع وكبار وكبار

BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#3/r8.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#3/r8.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#3/r8.claim: On a quantitative reading, God is “Merciful of this world” to believers and unbelievers alike, and “Compassionate in the next” specifically to believers.
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#3/r8.anchor: يا رحمن الدنيا لأنه يعم المؤمن والكافر، ورحيم الآخرة لأنه يخص المؤمن

BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#3/r9.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#3/r9.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#3/r9.claim: On a qualitative reading, الرحمن covers both worlds while الرحيم covers this world, since all afterlife blessings are immense but worldly blessings range from great to small.
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#3/r9.anchor: لأن النعم الأخروية كلها جسام، وأما النعم الدنيوية فجليلة وحقيرة

BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#3/r10.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#3/r10.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#3/r10.claim: Although one might expect the less to precede the greater, الرحمن comes first because worldly mercy precedes the afterlife and because the name has become exclusive to God.
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#3/r10.anchor: وإنما قدم والقياس يقتضي الترقي من الأدنى إلى الأعلى، لتقدم رحمة الدنيا

BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#3/r11.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#3/r11.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#3/r11.claim: الرحمن points to the great blessings; الرحيم then includes the blessings left out and may also preserve the verse endings.
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#3/r11.anchor: أو لأن الرحمن لما دل على جلائل النعم وأوصلها ذكر الرحيم ليتناول ما خرج منها

BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#4/r1.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#4/r1.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#4/r1.claim: Al-Bayḍāwī's stronger grammatical view is that الرحمن is indeclinable, despite its exclusive association with God and the usual feminine patterns of its class.
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#4/r1.anchor: والأظهر أنه غير مصروف وإن حظر اختصاصه بالله تعالى أن يكون له مؤنث

BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#4/r2.author: al-Bayḍāwī
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#4/r2.speaker: author
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#4/r2.claim: These particular names teach that only the true God deserves to be invoked for every need: He owns all blessings, immediate and future, great and small, and alone enables their delivery and use.
BAYDAWI-FULL:1:1#4/r2.anchor: وإنما خص التسمية بهذه الأسماء ليعلم العارف أن المستحق لأن يستعان به في مجامع الأمور

BIQAI-FULL:v1p11#2/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p11#2/r1.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p11#2/r1.claim: God is the ever-living witness whose knowledge misses nothing and whose permission governs all things; His universal mercy reaches creation and His special mercy favors His devoted servants.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p11#2/r1.anchor: لا يعزب شيء عن علمه ، ولا يكون شيء إلا بإذنه ، الرحمن الرحيم الذي عمت رحمته الموجودات

BIQAI-FULL:v1p11#2/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p11#2/r2.speaker: أبو الفضل محمد المشدالي المغربي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p11#2/r2.claim: Al-Mashdali's method for Qur'anic coherence is to identify a surah's purpose, its prerequisites and their distance from the goal, then answer expectations raised as the discourse unfolds.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p11#2/r2.anchor: قال شيخنا الإمام المحقق أبو الفضل محمد بن العلامة القدوة أبي عبد الله محمد ابن العلامة القدوة أبي القاسم محمد المشدالي المغربي

BIQAI-FULL:v1p11#2/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p11#2/r3.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p11#2/r3.claim: A surah's name summarizes its purpose, as a title signals the details within; Adam demonstrated this naming principle when he named things before the angels.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p11#2/r3.anchor: أن اسم كل سورة مترجم عن مقصودها هلأن أسم كل شيء تظهر المناسبة بينه وبين مسماه عنوانه

BIQAI-FULL:v1p11#2/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p11#2/r4.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p11#2/r4.claim: The Fatiha's many titles converge on مراقبة: it is the Mother of the Book, foundation, oft-repeated, treasure, healing, sufficing, complete, protecting, incantation, praise, thanks, supplication and prayer.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p11#2/r4.anchor: فمدار هذه الأسماء كما ترى على أمر خفي كاف لكل مراد وهو المراقبة التي سأقول إنها مقصودها

BIQAI-FULL:v1p11#2/r5.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p11#2/r5.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p11#2/r5.claim: The Fatiha is a treasure, cure, sufficiency, fulfillment, protection and incantation; it gathers praise, gratitude and supplication, with prayer as their greatest assembly.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p11#2/r5.anchor: فكل شيء لا يفتتح بها لا اعتداد به ، وهي كنز لكل شيء شافية لكل داء

BIQAI-FULL:v1p12/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p12/r1.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p12/r1.claim: The Fatiha's purpose is to establish God's exclusive right to all praise and perfection, sovereignty over both worlds, worship and aid, and to ask for the path of the successful rather than the doomed; its center is مراقبة.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p12/r1.anchor: الغرض الذي سبقت له الفاتحة وه إثبات استحقاق الله تعالى لجميع المحامد وصفا الكمال ، واختصاصه بملك الدنيا والآخرة

BIQAI-FULL:v1p12/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p12/r2.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p12/r2.claim: Prophets, scriptures and laws ultimately gather people to truth so they may know their sovereign and what pleases Him; knowledge and practice together serve the Qur'an's purpose.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p12/r2.anchor: لأن المقصود منت إرسال الرسل وإنزال الكتب نصب الشرائع ، والمقصود من نصب الشرائع جمع الخلق على الحق

BIQAI-FULL:v1p12/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p12/r3.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p12/r3.claim: God's name should accompany every movement and stillness because it leads to مراقبة, fear and recognition that affairs begin and end with Him, so the Fatiha opens with the basmala.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p12/r3.anchor: وكان اتزام اسمه تعالى في كل حركة وسكون قائدا إلى مراقبته وداعيا إلى مخافته واعتقاد أن مصادر الأمور ومواردها منه وإليه

BIQAI-FULL:v1p12/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p12/r4.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p12/r4.claim: The prior refuge seeks to clear the reciter's inner life and focus scattered concerns; the basmala's opening and closing letters symbolize return in worldly governance, death in the intermediate realm and resurrection.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p12/r4.anchor: جعلت البسملة كلها للمعاد لأبتدائها بحرف شفوي ، وختام أول كلماتها ومآخرها بآخر إشارة

BIQAI-FULL:v1p12/r5.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p12/r5.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p12/r5.claim: Al-Harali glosses the basmala: باء manifests causal wisdom; ism reveals what is hidden to hearts through hearing; Allah names the one hearts seek beyond reason; Rahman is universally merciful and Rahim grants mercy approved by divinity.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p12/r5.anchor: وقال الأستاذ أبو الحسن الحرالي في تفسيره في غريب ألفاظ البسملة : الباء معناها أظهره الله سبحانه من حكمة التسبيب

BIQAI-FULL:v1p13/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p13/r1.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p13/r1.claim: Al-Harali says the basmala shows that all things proceed through God's name alone, folding apparent causes back to Him; it should therefore begin people's words and deeds.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p13/r1.anchor: وقال في غريب معناها : لما أظهر الله سبحانه حكمة التسبيب وأرى الخلق استفادة بعض الأشياء من أشياء أخر متقدمة عليها

BIQAI-FULL:v1p13/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p13/r2.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p13/r2.claim: The basmala relates to the Fatiha as the Fatiha relates to the Qur'an: each is a compact synthesis of what the larger whole details.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p13/r2.anchor: وأشد منه أنه لما كانت نسبة البسملة من الفاتحة نسبة الفاتحة من القرآن صدرت بها الفاتحة

BIQAI-FULL:v1p13/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p13/r3.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p13/r3.claim: Allah is a proper name encompassing all beautiful names; Rahman precedes Rahim because it is exclusive and more emphatic, following the order of existence, general mercy, then worship-specific mercy.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p13/r3.anchor: ولما كان اسم الجلالة علما وكان جامعا لجميع معاني الأسماء الحسنى أولية الرحمن من حيث أنه كالعلم

BIQAI-FULL:v1p13/r5.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p13/r5.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p13/r5.claim: The basmala has nineteen written and eighteen spoken letters, alluding to the nineteen guardians of Hell and to mercy drawn by the five prayers and witr.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p13/r5.anchor: وكونها تسعة عشر حرفا خطية وثمانية عشر لفظية إشارة إلى أنها دوافع النقمة من النار التي أصحابها تسعة عشر

BIQAI-FULL:v1p13/r6.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p13/r6.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p13/r6.claim: Since the basmala is a kind of praise, it naturally leads to comprehensive al-hamd: begin affairs by praising God as the one deserving every praise, with hope and awe guiding the way.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p13/r6.anchor: ولما كانت البسملة نوعا من الحمد ناسب كل المناسبة تعقيبها باسم الحمد ةالكلي الجامع لجميع أفراده

BIQAI-FULL:v1p16/r5.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p16/r5.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p16/r5.claim: Al-Harali says all Qur'an is God's speech, but some verses voice what creatures at different levels ought to say yet cannot express; God teaches them words that fulfill their duty.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p16/r5.anchor: قال الحرالي : وهذه الآيات أى هذه وما بهدها مما جاء كلام الله فيه جارياعلى لسان خلقه فإن القرآن كله كلام الله

BIQAI-FULL:v1p16/r6.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p16/r6.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p16/r6.claim: Al-Harali explains the sound report that God divided prayer between Himself and His servant: the first three verses are God's praise, which He accepts from the reciting servant as praise and glorification.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p16/r6.anchor: وتلك هي صلاتهم المقسمة التى عبر عنها فيما صح عنه علية الصلاة والسلام من قوله تعالى : ( قسمت الصلاة بيني وبين عبدي نصفين )

BIQAI-FULL:v1p18#2/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p18#2/r3.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p18#2/r3.claim: The Qur'an's arrangement is miraculous, so the Fatiha must retain its required order in prayer; rearrangement or insertion of foreign material invalidates it. Al-Isfahani locates its clearest inimitability in order.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p18#2/r3.anchor: قال الأصبهاني : فإن القرآن معجز والركن الأبين الإعجاز يتعلق بالنظم والترتيب

BIQAI-FULL:v1p18#2/r7.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p18#2/r7.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p18#2/r7.claim: Al-Harali says the seven repeated verses are the Qur'an's gathered essence and its contents will be disclosed at creation's completion; earlier scriptures progress from changeable scrolls and lasting books to the Qur'an, which completes religion.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p18#2/r7.anchor: قال الأستاذ أبو الحسن الحرالي في مفتاح الباب القفل لفهم القرآن المنزل في أخر الباب التاسع منه : ولننه هذه الأبواب

BIQAI-FULL:v1p21/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p21/r1.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p21/r1.claim: Al-Harali contrasts the Qur'an's detailed, dispersed sequence with the Fatiha's seven complete universals, and makes the Fatiha a mirror of the servant's move from misguidance to guidance.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p21/r1.anchor: ووجه فوت أم القرآن مقصود تنزيله التفصيل والجوامع , فيه نجوم مبثوثة غير منتظمة , وحداة إثر واحدة

BIQAI-FULL:v1p21/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p21/r2.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
BIQAI-FULL:v1p21/r2.claim: A Prophetic report says he was sent to complete noble character; the author links this completion with the Fatiha's comprehensive opening and the Qur'an's culmination.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p21/r2.anchor: بعثت لأتمم مكارم الأخلاق . أن إلى ربك المنتهى .

BIQAI-FULL:v1p21/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p21/r3.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p21/r3.claim: Al-Harali describes the Qur'an's majesty through rulings spanning immediate and deferred realities, witnessed experience, and reports of the past and patterns that recur in time.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p21/r3.anchor: ومن مجيده وهو ما حربت أحكامه من بين عاجل ما شهد وآجل ما علم

BIQAI-FULL:v1p21/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p21/r4.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p21/r4.claim: Al-Harali distinguishes gradual descent that moves understanding between states and rulings from descent from high to low, which may occur with or without intermediaries.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p21/r4.anchor: وما كان منه بتدريج وتقريب للأفهام ففاءت من حال إلى حال

BIQAI-FULL:v1p21/r5.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p21/r5.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p21/r5.claim: The passage names al-Baqara 2:281 as the last revealed verse and says its recitation position between the debt verse and the verse before it shows revelation and recitation order can differ.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p21/r5.anchor: وجعلوها بين آية الدين والآية قبلها

BIQAI-FULL:v1p22/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p22/r1.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p22/r1.claim: Al-Harali says the Qur'an's sevenfold gathering in Muhammad's heart relates to the Mother of Qur'an's universals as the Qur'an's gathering in his heart relates to the Mother.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p22/r1.anchor: وأما الجمع ففي قلبه نسبة جوامعه السبع في أم القرآن إلى القرآن بمنزلة نسبة جمعه

BIQAI-FULL:v1p22/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p22/r2.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p22/r2.claim: Al-Harali says the Qur'an reached the Prophet on his tongue over the span of the prophetic mission, after its descent to the lowest heaven.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p22/r2.anchor: وعلى لسانه في أمد أيام النبوة

BIQAI-FULL:v1p22/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p22/r3.speaker: عائشة
BIQAI-FULL:v1p22/r3.claim: Aisha reports that Muhammad's character was the Qur'an, making his conduct the visible form of its inner reality.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p22/r3.anchor: قالت عائشة رضى الله عنها : كان خلقه القرآن

BIQAI-FULL:v1p22/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p22/r4.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p22/r4.claim: Al-Harali says the Fatiha is the Qur'an's mother: its first three verses encompass the divine names and attributes, while its last three cover the creature's way to God, mercy or failure.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p22/r4.anchor: فالآيات الثلاث الول قال شاملة لكل معنى تضمنته الأسماء الحسنى والصفات العلى

BIQAI-FULL:v1p22/r5.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p22/r5.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p22/r5.claim: Recitation order can differ from revelation chronology; the verse allowing the Prophet to marry certain women was placed before a later restriction.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p22/r5.anchor: فقد يتطابق قرآن الأمر وتطور الخلق وقد لا يتابق والله يتولى إقامتها

BIQAI-FULL:v1p22/r6.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p22/r6.speaker: أبو هريرة
BIQAI-FULL:v1p22/r6.claim: In the authentic report in Muslim and the four Sunan, God says the Fatiha is divided between Himself and His servant: He answers praise, glorification and worship, and grants the servant's final requests.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p22/r6.anchor: عن أبي هريرة رضى الله عنه قال : سمعت زسول الله صلى اله عليه وسلم يقول

BIQAI-FULL:v1p24/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p24/r1.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p24/r1.claim: Al-Baqara aims to prove the Book is guidance to follow; belief in the unseen, especially resurrection and the afterlife, is its greatest guidance and organizing theme.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p24/r1.anchor: مقصودها إقامة الدليل على أن الكتاب هدى ليتبع يفي كل ما قال ، وأعظم ما يهدي إليه الإيمالن بالغيب

BIQAI-FULL:v1p24/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p24/r2.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p24/r2.claim: The cow story makes the surah's title apt because resurrection occurs through an apparently slight human cause; it is a clearer sign of divine power than Abraham's story or earlier Israelite resurrections.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p24/r2.anchor: فلذلك سميت بها السورة وكانت بذلك أحق من قصة إبراهيم عليه الصلاة والسلام لأنها في نوع البشر

BIQAI-FULL:v1p24/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p24/r3.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p24/r3.claim: The following comparison of hearts and stones shows the guided and astray: hearts become hard and wretched, while stones display fear and yield benefit that reaches God's servants.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p24/r3.anchor: ولا سيما وقد اتبعت بوصف القلوب والحجارة بما عم اللمهتدين بالكتاب والضالين فوصفها بالقسوة الموجبة للشقوة

BIQAI-FULL:v1p24/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p24/r4.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p24/r4.claim: The Book functions like a caliph from the resolute messengers, guiding every matter to the right exit: rejecting it fails, hesitation nearly perishes, and accepting it brings piety and excellence.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p24/r4.anchor: وفيها إشارة إلى أن هذا الكتاب فينا كما لو كان فينا خليفة من أولي العزم من الرسل يرشدنا في كل أمر

BIQAI-FULL:v1p24/r5.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p24/r5.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p24/r5.claim: Al-Baqara is also called the Radiant and the Hump: it illuminates guidance and sufficiency, brightens believers' faces at judgment, and exalts belief in the afterlife above every other good after monotheism.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p24/r5.anchor: وسميت الزهراء لإنارتها طريق الهداية والكفاية في الدنيا والآخرة ، ولأيجابها إسفار الوجوه يفي يوم الجزاء

BIQAI-FULL:v1p24/r6.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p24/r6.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p24/r6.claim: Al-Harali transmits a report attributed to the Prophet from Ibn Masud: earlier books came through one gate and letter, whereas the Qur'an came through seven gates and seven letters encompassing commands, prohibitions, rulings, ambiguities and parables.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p24/r6.anchor: قال العلامة أبو الحسن الحرالي في كتاب العروة لمفتاح الباب المقفل في معنى ما رواه عن ابن وهب من حديث ابن مسعود رضي الله عنه عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم

BIQAI-FULL:v1p25/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p25/r1.speaker: أبو عمر بن عبد البر
BIQAI-FULL:v1p25/r1.claim: Ibn Abd al-Barr says the seven-letter report is unestablished: Abu Salama did not meet Ibn Masud, his son Salama is not authoritative, and its chain is agreed to be weak; Ahmad ibn Abi Imran also rejected it.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p25/r1.anchor: قال أبو عمر بن عبد البر : هذا الحديث عند أهل الحديث لم يثبت ، وأبو سلمة لم يلق ابن مسعود ، وابنه سلمة

BIQAI-FULL:v1p25/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p25/r2.speaker: البيهقي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p25/r2.claim: Al-Bayhaqi transmits an alternative mursal route through al-Layth, Uqayl, Ibn Shihab, Umm Salama and Abu Salama; he calls the mursal report good because Abu Salama did not meet Ibn Masud.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p25/r2.anchor: قال أبو شامة : وهكذا رواه البيهقي في كتاب المدخل وقال : هذا مرسل جيد ، أبو سلمة لم يدرك ابن مسعود

BIQAI-FULL:v1p25/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p25/r3.speaker: أبو شامة
BIQAI-FULL:v1p25/r3.claim: Abu Shama says that if sound, seven letters means seven forms or categories of Qur'anic content, not the dialects in which recitation was permitted.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p25/r3.anchor: قال أبو شامة : وهكذا رواه البيهقي في كتاب المدخل وقال : هذا مرسل جيد

BIQAI-FULL:v1p25/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p25/r4.speaker: ابن الجزري
BIQAI-FULL:v1p25/r4.claim: Ibn al-Jazari cites the Prophet's report to Ibn Masud from al-Tabarani: the Qur'an's seven categories include lawful, forbidden, clear, ambiguous, parables, commands and warnings, each with its proper response.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p25/r4.anchor: محمد ابن الجزري الدمشقي الشافعي في أوائل كتابه ' النشر في القراءات العشر ' إلى الطبراني

BIQAI-FULL:v1p25/r5.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p25/r5.speaker: أبو هريرة
BIQAI-FULL:v1p25/r5.claim: Al-Bayhaqi also reports from Abu Huraira a version that describes five Qur'anic forms: lawful, forbidden, clear, ambiguous and parables.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p25/r5.anchor: ورواه البيهقي في فضل القرآن من الشعب عن أبي هريرة رضي الله عنه بلفظ

BIQAI-FULL:v1p25/r6.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p25/r6.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p25/r6.claim: Al-Harali reads the seven letters as a completion of creation and religious, worldly and afterlife well-being: Muhammad is the comprehensive final prophet and his book seals the scriptures; he cites the report I was sent to complete noble character.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p25/r6.anchor: قال الحرالي : زفي حديث آخر من طريق ابن عمر رضي الله عنهما : إن الكتب كانت تنزل من باب واحد

BIQAI-FULL:v1p27/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p27/r1.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v1p27/r1.claim: The quoted supplication asks God to set right religion as the safeguard of one's affairs, worldly livelihood and the afterlife to which one returns.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p27/r1.anchor: اللهم أصلح لي ديني الذي هو عصمة أمري

BIQAI-FULL:v1p27/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p27/r2.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p27/r2.claim: Al-Harali divides the three domains of well-being into action and restraint, yielding six letters; God then grants Muhammad a seventh, inclusive letter, so the Qur'an descends in seven letters.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p27/r2.anchor: فلما استوفى الستة وهبه ربه حرفا جامعا سابعا فردا لا زوج له ن فتم إنزاله على سبعة أحرف .

BIQAI-FULL:v1p27/r3.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p27/r3.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p27/r3.claim: The worldly pair is halal and haram: lawful things cultivate body and soul, forbidden things must be purified away; the pair originates in the Torah and is completed in the Qur'an.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p27/r3.anchor: فأدنى تلك الحروف هو حرف إصلاح الدنيا ، فلها حرفان ، أحدهما : حرف الحرام

BIQAI-FULL:v1p27/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p27/r4.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p27/r4.claim: The afterlife pair is warning and command; avoiding prohibitions purifies and obeying commands advances the next life, even when it sacrifices temporary worldly benefits for enduring whole good.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p27/r4.anchor: ثم يلي هذين حرفا صلاح المعاد : أحدهما حرف الزجر والنهي التي لا تصلح الآخرة إلا بالتطهير منه

BIQAI-FULL:v1p27/r5.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p27/r5.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p27/r5.claim: The religious pair is clear guidance about heart, character and bodily duties, and ambiguous matters beyond limited reason that require declaring God incomparable; five letters are for practice and the sixth for restraint.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p27/r5.anchor: ثم يلي هذين حرفا صلاح الدين : أحدهما حرف المحكم الذي بان للعبد فيه خطاب ربه

BIQAI-FULL:v1p27/r6.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p27/r6.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p27/r6.claim: The six letters are shared with prior scriptures but perfected in the Qur'an; its unique seventh is the inclusive letter of praise, gifted directly to Muhammad and embodied in his heart, recitation and character.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p27/r6.anchor: فهذه الحروف الستة يشترك فيها القرآن مع سائر الكتب ويزيد عليها تمامها وبركة جمعها ، ويختص القرآن بالحرف السابع الجامع

BIQAI-FULL:v1p28/r1.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p28/r1.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p28/r1.claim: Because praise is the seventh inclusive letter, the Fatiha begins with it and gathers the seven universals diffused through the Qur'an, as the Qur'an gathers earlier scriptures.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p28/r1.anchor: ولما كان حرف الحمد هو سابعها الجامع افتتح الله به سبحانه وتعالى الفاتحة أم القرآن وأم الكتاب

BIQAI-FULL:v1p28/r2.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p28/r2.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p28/r2.claim: The first verse contains praise's seventh letter; the second contains the lawful and forbidden letters that Rahmaniyyah establishes for worldly life, allowing enjoyment and removing either prohibition's burden or sin.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p28/r2.anchor: فالآية الأولى تشتمل على حرف الحمد السابع ، والثانية تشتمل على حرفي الحلال والحرام

BIQAI-FULL:v1p28/r7.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p28/r7.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p28/r7.claim: The Qur'an begins with the sixth, ambiguous letter so confessing ignorance and believing without grasping it invites divine gift; this trains compliance with the rest without claiming mastery.
BIQAI-FULL:v1p28/r7.anchor: ولما ابتئت الفاتحة أم القرآن بالسابع الجامع الموهوب ابتدئ القرآن بالحرف السادس المعجوز عنه

BIQAI-FULL:v1p28/r8.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v1p28/r8.speaker: الحرالي
BIQAI-FULL:v1p28/r8.claim: After the ambiguous opening, the Qur'an presents the clear letter in the traits of believers; observance from faith is clear guidance, while external compliance without faith remains mere command.
