ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r2.anchor: وقال أبو هريرة ،   وعطاء بن يسار ،   ومجاهد ،   وسواد بن زياد

ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r3.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r3.speaker: قيل
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r3.claim: A further view calls al-Fātiḥa both Meccan and Medinan.
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r3.anchor: هي مدنية ،   وقيل إنها مكية مدنية

ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r4.speaker: أبي
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r4.claim: A report from Ubay identifies al-Fātiḥa as the seven oft-repeated verses and one of the seven long sūras, revealed some time after al-Ḥijr.
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r4.anchor: وفي حديث أبي : إنها السبع المثاني والسبع الطوال

ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r5.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r5.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r5.claim: Prayer was prescribed in Mecca, and no prayer in Islam is known to have been performed without al-Fātiḥa.
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r5.anchor: ولا خلاف أن فرض الصلاة كان بمكة ،   وما حفظ أنه كانت في الإسلام

ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r6.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r6.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r6.claim: The bāʾ has uses for attachment, instrument, oath, cause, circumstance, location, and transfer; Abū Ḥayyān illustrates each with Arabic examples.
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r6.anchor: باء الجر تأتي لمعان : للإلصاق ،   والاستعانة ،   والقسم

ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r7.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r7.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r7.claim: Other uses of bāʾ include emphasis, substitution, exchange, separation, and superiority, each supported with an example.
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r7.anchor: وتأتي زائدة للتوكيد : شربن بماء البحر

ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r8.speaker: بعضهم
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r8.claim: Some grammarians call circumstantial bāʾ accompaniment, add a causal sense, subsume instrument under cause, and explain circumstantial bāʾ as “with.”
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r8.anchor: وكنى بعضهم عن الحال بالمصاحبة ،   وزاد فيها كونها للتعليل

ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r9.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r9.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r9.claim: Ism is reported with several forms, while the Basrans derive it from s-m-w and the Kufans from w-s-m; Abū Ḥayyān prefers the Basran derivation.
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r9.anchor: والبصري يقول : مادته سين وميم وواو

ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r10.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r10.speaker: الكوفي
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r10.claim: The Kufan derivation makes the root of ism w-s-m, whereas Abū Ḥayyān prefers the Basran s-m-w analysis.
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r10.anchor: والكوفي يقول : واو وسين وميم ،   والأرجح الأول

ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r11.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r11.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r11.claim: Grammarians assign al- uses including particular or generic reference, presence, evocation of a quality, predominance, relative meaning, and fixed or nonfixed augmentation.
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r11.anchor: الاستدلال في كتب النحو : أل للعهد في شخص أو جنس ،   وللحضور

ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r12.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r12.speaker: الأكثرون
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r12.claim: Most authorities consider Allāh a proper name for the true deity only, originally un-derived.
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r12.anchor: علم لا يطلق إلا على المعبود بحق مرتجل غير مشتق عند الأكثرين

ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r13.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r13.speaker: ابن إسحاق وأبو عمر والنضر والمبرد
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r13.claim: Competing derivations connect Allāh to rising, concealment, fear, bewilderment, worship, or rest; Abū Ḥayyān reports these without choosing among them.
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r13.anchor: من أله أي فزع ،   قاله ابن إسحاق

ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r14.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r14.speaker: الخليل والقناد
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r14.claim: Al-Khalīl and al-Qannād derive Allāh from w-l-h, “to be transported with delight,” with hamza substituted for wāw; Abū Ḥayyān calls the proposal weak.
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r14.anchor: من وله ،   أي طرب ،   وأبدلت الهمزة فيه من الواو نحو أشاح

ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r15.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r15.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r15.claim: The plural āliha can be parsed as faʿāl with a passive meaning, like kitāb meaning “written.”
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r15.anchor: وقولهم في الجمع آلهة ،   وتكون فعالا بمعنى مفعول

ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r16.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r16.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r16.claim: If Allāh derives from al-ilāh, al- marks predominance: ilāh can name true or false deities, while Allāh names only the true deity; the comparison to al-Najm is challenged.
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r16.anchor: وأل في الله إذا قلنا أصله الإله ،   قالوا للغلبة

ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r17.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r17.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r17.claim: On the other proposed derivations, al- is an inseparable extra article; omitting it in lāh abūka is anomalous.
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r17.anchor: فأل فيه زائدة لازمة ،   وشذ حذفها في قولهم لاه أبوك

ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r18.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r18.speaker: أبو بكر بن العربي والسهيلي
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r18.claim: They say al- is part of Allāh and the hamza became connective through frequent use; Abū Ḥayyān rejects this because the resulting form would be fʿāl and would not explain the lack of tanwīn.
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r18.anchor: وزعم بعضهم أن أل في الله من نفس الكلمة ،   ووصلت الهمزة لكثرة الاستعمال

ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r19.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r19.speaker: أبو يزيد البلخي
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r19.claim: Abū Yazīd al-Balkhī calls Allāh a foreign word, citing Jewish and Christian lāhā and saying Arabs adopted and changed it.
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r19.anchor: قال أبو يزيد البلخي : هو أعجمي ،   فإن اليهود والنصارى يقولون لاها

ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r20.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r20.speaker: قيل
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r20.claim: A reported view treats Allāh as an attribute rather than a personal name because God is not sensed or immediately apprehended and is known through His attributes; Abū Ḥayyān calls this unusual.
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r20.anchor: ومن غريب ما قيل في الله أنه صفة وليس اسم ذات

ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r21.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r21.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r21.claim: The final alif in Allāh is variously said to be omitted to distinguish its spelling from lāhū, to lighten it, or because of a spelling convention.
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r21.anchor: وحذفت الألف الأخيرة من الله لئلا يشكل بخط اللاه اسم الفاعل

ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r22.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r22.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r22.claim: Raḥmān is an intensive faʿlān form from mercy, with al- marking predominance; it is used only of God, like His proper name.
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r22.anchor: { الرحمن } : فعلان من الرحمة ،   وأصل بنائه من اللازم

ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r23.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r23.speaker: ثعلب
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r23.claim: Thaʿlab reports the unusual claim that raḥmān is foreign, with its khāʾ adapted to Arabic ḥāʾ.
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r23.anchor: أعجمي بالخاء المعجمة فعرب بالحاء ،   قاله ثعلب

ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r24.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r24.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r24.claim: Raḥīm is an intensive faʿīl form; faʿīl is one of the five standard intensive patterns, with some grammarians adding another faʿīl pattern.
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r24.anchor: { الرحيم } : فعيل محول من فاعل للمبالغة ،   وهو أحد الأمثلة الخمسة

ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r25.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r25.speaker: العملس بن عقيل
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r25.claim: The poet al-ʿAmalas ibn ʿUqayl uses raḥīm to mean marḥūm, “one shown mercy.”
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r25.anchor: وقيل : وجاء رحيم بمعنى مرحوم ،   قال العملس بن عقيل

ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r26.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r26.speaker: الكوفيون
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r26.claim: The Kufans parse the bāʾ as instrumental and the phrase as accusative with an implied “I begin”; they posit that implied verb for acts begun with the formula.
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r26.anchor: الباء في بسم الله للاستعانة ،   نحو كتبت بالقلم ،   وموضعها نصب

ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r27.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r27.speaker: الزمخشري
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r27.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī supplies a delayed verb such as “I read” or “I recite,” and claims fronting yields exclusivity; Abū Ḥayyān disputes the latter claim.
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r27.anchor: وقدره الزمخشري فعلا غير بدأت وجعله متأخرا

ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r28.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r28.speaker: سيبويه
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r28.claim: Sībawayh says fronting an object is good Arabic just as ordinary order is; Abū Ḥayyān cites this against the claim that fronting necessarily entails exclusivity.
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r28.anchor: قال سيبويه : وقد تكلم على ضربت زيدا ما نصه

ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r29.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r29.speaker: البصريون
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r29.claim: The Basrans parse ism as nominative in an implied nominal sentence, approximately “my beginning is fixed/stable in the name of God”; Abū Ḥayyān weighs this against the verbal parse.
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r29.anchor: وقيل موضع اسم رفع التقدير ابتدائي ثابت ،   أو مستقر باسم الله

ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r30.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r30.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r30.claim: Ism is a conventional word denoting an existent, perceptible or intelligible, without marking time; its referent is the named thing, while naming makes the word a sign for that meaning.
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r30.anchor: والاسم هو اللفظ الدال بالوضع على موجود في العيان ،   إن كان محسوسا

ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r31.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r31.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r31.claim: Abū Ḥayyān distinguishes the word, its referent, and the act of naming; a judgment attributed literally to a name can instead use “name” metaphorically for its referent.
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r31.anchor: فقد اتضحت المباينة بين الاسم والمسمى والتسمية

ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r32.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r32.speaker: السهيلي
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r32.claim: Al-Suhaylī reads “glorify the name of your Lord” as an insertion directing people to glorify the Lord and ensuring remembrance includes spoken utterance as well as inward recollection.
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r32.anchor: وقد تأول السهيلي ،   رحمه الله ،   قوله تعالى

ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r33.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r33.speaker: السهيلي
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r33.claim: Al-Suhaylī explains “you worship only names” as a metaphor for idols with false, unreal names, so their worship is effectively worship of invented names.
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r33.anchor: بأنها أسماء كاذبة غير واقعة على حقيقة

ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r34.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r34.speaker: الكسائي والأخفش
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r34.claim: Al-Kisāʾī and al-Akhfash allow dropping the alif in bi-sm with other divine names; al-Farrāʾ restricts deletion to the full basmala.

ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r35.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r35.speaker: الأعلم
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r35.claim: Al-Aʿlam treats raḥmān as a proper name and therefore appositional rather than adjectival, citing its independent use in other verses.
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r35.anchor: وذهب الأعلم وغيره إلى أنه بدل ،   وزعم أن الرحمن علم

ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r36.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r36.speaker: السهيلي
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r36.claim: Al-Suhaylī rejects apposition and explanatory apposition because Allāh needs no clarification; raḥmān is an epithet of praise, though it can function like a proper name.
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r36.anchor: قال أبو زيد السهيلي : البدل فيه عندي ممتنع

ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r37.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r37.speaker: قيل
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r37.claim: One view says the two names are synonymous; another distinguishes them, making raḥmān more emphatic and encompassing major blessings while raḥīm completes it with subtle blessings.
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r37.anchor: قيل دلالتهما واحد نحو ندمان ونديم ،   وقيل معناهما مختلف

ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r38.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r38.speaker: الزمخشري
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r38.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī favors raḥmān for foundational blessings and raḥīm as a complement for finer, subtler blessings.
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r38.anchor: ليكون كالتتمة والرديف ليتناول ما دق منها ولطف ،   واختاره الزمخشري

ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r39.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r39.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r39.claim: Abū Ḥayyān holds that the names intensify mercy in different ways, so their combination is not mere repetition: faʿlān suggests fullness or dominance, while faʿīl suggests repeated occurrence at objects of mercy.
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r39.anchor: والذي يظهر أن جهة المبالغة مختلفة ،   فلذلك جمع بينهما ،   فلا يكون

ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r40.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r40.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r40.claim: The intensive forms differ in transitivity: faʿlān does not take an object, whereas faʿīl does, like an active participle.
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r40.anchor: ولذلك لا يتعدى فعلان ،   ويتعدى فعيل

ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r41.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r41.speaker: مجاهد
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r41.claim: Mujāhid distinguishes the names as mercy for this world and mercy for the next.
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r41.anchor: فقال مجاهد : رحمن الدنيا ورحيم الآخرة

ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r42.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r42.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r42.claim: A report through Ibn Masʿūd and Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī attributes to the Prophet the same distinction; Abū Ḥayyān says it must be accepted if sound.
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r42.anchor: أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم قال : « الرحمن رحمن الدنيا

ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r43.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r43.speaker: القرطبي
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r43.claim: Al-Qurṭubī gives the reverse allocation: raḥmān for the next life and raḥīm for this life.
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r43.anchor: وقال القرطبي : رحمن الآخرة ورحيم الدنيا

ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r44.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r44.speaker: الضحاك
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r44.claim: Al-Ḍaḥḥāk says the two names concern the inhabitants of heaven and earth.

ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r45.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r45.speaker: عكرمة
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r45.claim: ʿIkrima distinguishes one mercy from one hundred mercies.
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r45.anchor: وقال عكرمة : برحمة واحدة وبمائة رحمة

ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r46.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r46.speaker: المزني
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r46.claim: Al-Muzanī distinguishes blessings of worldly life from blessings of religion.

ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r47.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r47.speaker: العزيزي
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r47.claim: Al-ʿAzīzī assigns raḥmān to universal gifts such as rain and the senses, and raḥīm to believers through guidance and divine care.

ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r48.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r48.speaker: المحاسبي
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r48.claim: Al-Muḥāsibī distinguishes mercy toward souls from mercy toward hearts.
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r48.anchor: وقال المحاسبي : برحمة النفوس ورحمة القلوب

ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r49.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r49.speaker: يحيى بن معاذ
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r49.claim: Yaḥyā ibn Muʿādh relates the names to needs of the afterlife and worldly life.
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r49.anchor: وقال يحيى بن معاذ : لمصالح المعاد والمعاش

ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r50.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r50.speaker: الصادق
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r50.claim: Al-Ṣādiq says the generally framed name concerns provision broadly, while the specially framed name concerns forgiveness for believers.
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r50.anchor: وقال الصادق : خاص اللفظ بصيغة عامة في الرزق

ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r51.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r51.speaker: ثعلب
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r51.claim: Thaʿlab says raḥmān is more emphatic in praise and raḥīm is gentler.
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r51.anchor: وقال ثعلب : الرحمن أمدح ،   والرحيم ألطف

ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r52.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r52.speaker: قيل
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r52.claim: Another view says raḥmān gives blessings of kinds humans cannot provide, while raḥīm gives blessings of kinds humans can provide.
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r52.anchor: وقيل : الرحمن المنعم بما لا يتصور جنسه من العباد

ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r53.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r53.speaker: أبو علي الفارسي
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r53.claim: Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī says raḥmān covers every kind of mercy and belongs uniquely to God, while raḥīm concerns believers, as in 33:43.
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r53.anchor: قال أبو علي الفارسي : الرحمن اسم عام في جميع أنواع الرحمة

ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r54.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r54.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r54.claim: Divine mercy may figuratively mean beneficence, an attribute of action; another view defines it as willing good, an attribute of essence, raising the dispute over whether attributes of action are originated or eternal.
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r54.anchor: ووصف الله تعالى بالرحمة مجاز عن إنعامه على عباده

ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r55.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r55.speaker: قوم
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r55.claim: Some theologians define divine mercy as God's will to bring good to whomever He wills, making it an attribute of essence.
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r55.anchor: وقال قوم : هي إرادة الخير لمن أراد الله تعالى به ذلك

ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r56.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r56.speaker: قيل
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r56.claim: Human mercy is defined either as tenderness in the heart or as intending good or averting harm, since one can help another without feeling tenderness.
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r56.anchor: وأما الرحمة التي من العباد فقيل هي رقة تحدث في القلب

ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r57.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r57.speaker: السهيلي
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r57.claim: Al-Suhaylī rejects the idea that omitting the verb merely lightens speech: omission keeps God's name first and matches utterance to the heart's intention to remember only God.
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r57.anchor: قال أبو القاسم السهيلي : وليس كما زعموا ،   إذ لو كان

ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r58.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r58.speaker: السهيلي
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r58.claim: Al-Suhaylī compares this ellipsis with “God is greatest,” whose unstated completion lets the wording match the heart's intended exclusivity.
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r58.anchor: كما تقول في الصلاة الله أكبر ،   ومعناه من كل شيء ،

ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r59.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r59.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r59.claim: The alif is omitted in writing in bi-sm Allāh and in raḥmān because of frequent use.
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r59.anchor: ومن الحذف أيضا حذف الألف في بسم الله وفي الرحمن في الخط

ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r60.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r60.speaker: author
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r60.claim: Repeating descriptive epithets can magnify the one described or reinforce the meaning until it settles in the mind.
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r60.anchor: النوع الثاني : التكرار في الوصف ،   ويكون إما لتعظيم الموصوف

ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r61.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r61.speaker: قوم من الكوفيين
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r61.claim: Some Kufans pause after raḥīm with its mīm quiescent, then begin al-ḥamdu with a cut hamza.
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r61.anchor: قرأ قوم من الكوفيين بسكون الميم ،   ويقفون عليها

ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r62.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r62.speaker: الجمهور
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r62.claim: The majority connect raḥīm to al-ḥamdu, retaining the genitive ending and joining the following hamza.
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r62.anchor: والجمهور على جر الميم ووصل الألف من الحمد

ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r63.author: Abū Ḥayyān
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r63.speaker: الكسائي
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r63.claim: Al-Kisāʾī reports a Bedouin reading with an opened mīm and connected hamza, explained as transferring the hamza's vowel to the mīm before elision.
ABUHAYYAN:1:1/r63.anchor: وحكى الكسائي عن بعض العرب أنه يقرأ الرحيم الحمد بفتح الميم

ALUSI:1:1/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r1.claim: Al-Ālūsī says most authorities classify al-Fātiḥa as Meccan, even counting it among the earliest revealed passages.

ALUSI:1:1/r2.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r2.speaker: علي وابن عباس وقتادة وأكثر الصحابة
ALUSI:1:1/r2.claim: Reports from ʿAlī, Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatāda, and most Companions support its Meccan origin.
ALUSI:1:1/r2.anchor: وهو المروي عن علي وابن عباس وقتادة وأكثر الصحابة

ALUSI:1:1/r3.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r3.speaker: مجاهد
ALUSI:1:1/r3.claim: Mujāhid calls the sūra Medinan; al-Ālūsī treats this solitary view as an error, noting it would mean years of prayer without al-Fātiḥa.
ALUSI:1:1/r3.anchor: وعن مجاهد أنها مدنية( {[2]} ) ،  وقد تفرد بذلك حتى عد هفوة منه

ALUSI:1:1/r4.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r4.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r4.claim: Other accounts say it descended both when prayer became obligatory in Mecca and when the qibla changed in Medina, or that parts are Meccan and Medinan; he calls the latter weak.
ALUSI:1:1/r4.anchor: وقيل نزلت بمكة حين فرضت الصلاة وبالمدينة لما حولت القبلة

ALUSI:1:1/r5.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r5.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r5.claim: The Meccan setting of 15:87 is often used to date al-Fātiḥa, but the argument depends on identifying the seven mathānī with it and on denying prior divine endowment.
ALUSI:1:1/r5.anchor: والأقوى الاستدلال بالنقل عن الصحابة الذين شاهدوا الوحي التنزيل

ALUSI:1:1/r6.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r6.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r6.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and others also explained the seven mathānī as the seven long sūras, weakening the dating argument from 15:87.
ALUSI:1:1/r6.anchor: إلا أنه قد صح أيضا عن ابن عباس وغيره تفسيرها بالسبع الطوال

ALUSI:1:1/r7.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r7.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r7.claim: Al-Ālūsī notes that prior mention does not prove an event already occurred: 48:1 describes a future conquest in the past tense to assure its fulfillment.
ALUSI:1:1/r7.anchor: فهو قبل الفتح بسنين والتعبير بالماضي تحقيق للوقوع

ALUSI:1:1/r8.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r8.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r8.claim: He rejects repeated descent as an explanation reconciling reports: reports can validate an occurrence without causing it, and the alleged repeat lacks a sound rationale.
ALUSI:1:1/r8.anchor: وما قالوا في الجواب عن الاعتراض بأن النزول ظهور من عالم الغيب

ALUSI:1:1/r9.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r9.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r9.claim: Sūra may derive, with hamza, from the remnant of something, or without hamza from a building tier, an enclosing city wall, or elevation.

ALUSI:1:1/r10.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r10.speaker: النابغة
ALUSI:1:1/r10.claim: Al-Nābigha’s verse uses sūra for an elevated rank or station, supporting the sense of height.
ALUSI:1:1/r10.anchor: كما في قول النابغة : ألم تر أن الله أعطاك سورة

ALUSI:1:1/r11.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r11.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r11.claim: He defines a sūra as Qurʾān containing an opening and a conclusion; another definition, an independent portion, distinguishes named units such as Āyat al-Kursī.
ALUSI:1:1/r11.anchor: قرآن يشتمل على ذي فاتحة وخاتمة

ALUSI:1:1/r12.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r12.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r12.claim: Al-Fātiḥa was originally an adjective for the first part because it opens the whole; alternatively it is a verbal noun used for the object, as with al-Khātima.
ALUSI:1:1/r12.anchor: صفة جعلت إما لأول الشيء لكونه واسطة في فتح الكل

ALUSI:1:1/r13.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r13.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r13.claim: He finds an instrumental reading of fātiḥa unsuitable: the instrument need not share the action, and it could wrongly imply that the opening part is incidental.
ALUSI:1:1/r13.anchor: وليس هذا كالأول لقلة فاعلة في المصادر إلا أنه أولى

ALUSI:1:1/r14.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r14.speaker: أبو السعود
ALUSI:1:1/r14.claim: Abū al-Suʿūd explains the title’s first addition as the name of the named sūra and its second as possessive, meaning the opening of the Book.

ALUSI:1:1/r15.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r15.speaker: ابن كيسان والسيرافي وجمع
ALUSI:1:1/r15.claim: Ibn Kaysān, al-Sīrāfī, and others treat the part-to-whole addition as partitive, with some grammarians extending that analysis to all such constructions.

ALUSI:1:1/r16.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r16.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r16.claim: Fātiḥat al-Kitāb means the opening of the Qurʾān in its received order, not the first lesson taught or the first sūra revealed.
ALUSI:1:1/r16.anchor: لا لأنها يفتتح بها في التعليم وفي القراءة في الصلاة كما زعمه

ALUSI:1:1/r17.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r17.speaker: المرسي
ALUSI:1:1/r17.claim: Al-Mursī says it was named because it was the first sūra written on the Preserved Tablet; al-Ālūsī says this needs transmission and sequence of writing is uncertain.
ALUSI:1:1/r17.anchor: لأنها أول سورة كتبت في اللوح

ALUSI:1:1/r18.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r18.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r18.claim: Umm al-Kitāb and Umm al-Qurʾān reflect its priority, like a mother preceding what follows, a banner leading an army, or its encompassing the Qurʾān’s aims.
ALUSI:1:1/r18.anchor: وسميت بذلك لأن الابتداء كتابة أو تلاوة أو نزولا على قول

ALUSI:1:1/r19.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r19.speaker: الحسن البصري
ALUSI:1:1/r19.claim: The alleged prophetic prohibition on calling it Umm al-Kitāb has no basis; sound reports establish that title, and al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī also used it.

ALUSI:1:1/r20.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r20.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r20.claim: Al-Ālūsī says al-Fātiḥa gathers praise, worship, and promise or warning; these summarize the guidance sent through messengers and revealed books for worldly and final welfare.
ALUSI:1:1/r20.anchor: لأن بعثة الرسل وإنزال الكتب رحمة للعباد وإرشادا إلى ما يصلحهم

ALUSI:1:1/r21.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r21.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r21.claim: Praise appears in al-ḥamdu lillāh; worship is taught by its implied command, guidance-seeking, or the declaration of worship, while command entails prohibition.
ALUSI:1:1/r21.anchor: وأما التعبد فإما من الحمد لله لأنه للتعليم فيقدر أمر يفيده

ALUSI:1:1/r22.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r22.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r22.claim: He answers the Muʿtazilī objection that worship has no prior command: monotheism is worship’s foundation, and Muhammad’s prior charge to proclaim it suffices.
ALUSI:1:1/r22.anchor: بأن رأس العبادة التوحيد وفي الصدر

ALUSI:1:1/r23.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r23.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r23.claim: Promise and warning appear in the favored and the angered or astray, and in the Day of Recompense understood as reward and punishment.
ALUSI:1:1/r23.anchor: وأما الوعد والوعيد فمن قوله تعالى

ALUSI:1:1/r24.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r24.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r24.claim: Al-Ālūsī offers a second map: theoretical knowledge is covered through the Day of Judgment, practical conduct by worship and guidance, and human outcomes by the final verse.
ALUSI:1:1/r24.anchor: والأول مستفاد من أول السورة إلى قوله

ALUSI:1:1/r25.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r25.speaker: البيضاوي
ALUSI:1:1/r25.claim: Al-Bayḍāwī’s threefold scheme may hint, in line with Muʿtazilī doctrine, that rational gratitude to the benefactor is obligatory; al-Ālūsī notes this implication.
ALUSI:1:1/r25.anchor: تلميحا إلى أن شكر المنعم واجب عقلا مراعاة لمذهب الاعتزال

ALUSI:1:1/r26.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r26.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r26.claim: A four-discipline scheme maps theology to Lordship and mercy, prophecy to those favored, and the afterlife to the Day of Judgment.
ALUSI:1:1/r26.anchor: علم الأصول ومعاقده معرفة الله تعالى وصفاته

ALUSI:1:1/r27.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r27.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r27.claim: The same scheme maps worship to practical law, reliance and guidance to ethics and spiritual progress, and the final verse to narratives, outcomes, and warning.
ALUSI:1:1/r27.anchor: علم الأخلاق وأجله الوصول إلى الحضرة الصمدانية

ALUSI:1:1/r28.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r28.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r28.claim: A report says al-Fātiḥa equals two-thirds of the Qurʾān; al-Ālūsī disputes al-Shihāb’s reward-based explanation that the summary’s concision supplies a third.
ALUSI:1:1/r28.anchor: ومن العجب ما قيل هنا من أن ذلك

ALUSI:1:1/r29.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r29.speaker: أبو الدرداء
ALUSI:1:1/r29.claim: Al-Dailamī’s report from Abū al-Dardāʾ says al-Fātiḥa outweighs the Qurʾān sevenfold on the scale; al-Ālūsī says its apparent reward claim challenges that explanation.
ALUSI:1:1/r29.anchor: الديلمي في الفردوس عن أبي الدرداء

ALUSI:1:1/r30.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r30.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r30.claim: He suggests reconciling the virtue reports through increased later reward, differing circumstances, an inclusive use of equals, or Qurʾān meaning prayer as in 17:78.
ALUSI:1:1/r30.anchor: ويمكن التوفيق بين الخبرين وبه يزول الإشكال بأن الأول كان أولا

ALUSI:1:1/r31.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r31.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r31.claim: Other proposed explanations for the title Umm al-Qurʾān include being the best sūra, having the sanctity of the whole Qurʾān, or being the believers’ refuge; he leaves these unendorsed.
ALUSI:1:1/r31.anchor: لأنها أفضل السور أو لأن حرمتها كحرمة القرآن

ALUSI:1:1/r32.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r32.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r32.claim: Other titles include al-Kanz, al-Wāfiya, al-Kāfiya, and al-Asās, associated with its gathered treasures, sufficiency, indivisibility in prayer, and status as Qurʾānic foundation.
ALUSI:1:1/r32.anchor: لما مر من اشتمالها على الجواهر المكنوزة

ALUSI:1:1/r33.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r33.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r33.claim: Names such as al-Ḥamd, al-Shukr, al-Duʿāʾ, Taʿlīm al-Masʾala, and al-Suʾāl describe its praise, gratitude, supplication, and instruction in asking.
ALUSI:1:1/r33.anchor: سورة الحمد وسورة الشكر وسورة الدعاء وسورة تعليم المسألة وسورة السؤال

ALUSI:1:1/r34.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r34.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r34.claim: Al-Munājāt and al-Tafwīḍ name its intimate address to God and the servant’s entrusting matters to Him.
ALUSI:1:1/r34.anchor: سورة المناجاة وسورة التفويض لأن العبد يناجي ربه بقوله إياك نعبد

ALUSI:1:1/r35.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r35.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r35.claim: Sound hadiths support its names al-Ruqya, al-Shifāʾ, and al-Shāfiya; it is also called al-Ṣalāh because it is required or recommended in prayer.
ALUSI:1:1/r35.anchor: الأحاديث الصحيحة مشعرة بذلك والتاسع عشر

ALUSI:1:1/r36.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r36.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r36.claim: Calling the sūra al-Ṣalāh is supported by the report “I divided the prayer”; prayer may stand for the sūra by whole-part relation or convention.
ALUSI:1:1/r36.anchor: قسمت الصلاة بيني وبين عبدي نصفين

ALUSI:1:1/r37.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r37.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r37.claim: Al-Nūr refers to its prominence, its illumination of hearts, or its embodiment of Qurʾānic meaning; al-Qurʾān al-ʿAẓīm is another title.
ALUSI:1:1/r37.anchor: النور لظهورها بكثرة استعمالها أو لتنويرها القلوب لجلالة قدرها

ALUSI:1:1/r38.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r38.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r38.claim: It is the seven mathānī by agreement on seven verses; disputes over counting the basmala or “those You favored” are governed by transmitted reports.
ALUSI:1:1/r38.anchor: باتفاق وما رأينا مشاركا لها سوى

ALUSI:1:1/r39.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r39.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r39.claim: Mathānī may refer to repeated recitation, repetition with another sūra, two revelation occasions, its combination of praise and prayer, or God’s response to each verse.
ALUSI:1:1/r39.anchor: أو المراد المتعارف الأغلب من الصلاة فلا ترد الركعة الواحدة

ALUSI:1:1/r40.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r40.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r40.claim: Other derivations connect mathānī to praise of God or its reciter, or to God’s special bestowal of it on this community.
ALUSI:1:1/r40.anchor: ويحتمل أن تكون من الثناء لما فيها من الثناء على الله تعالى

ALUSI:1:1/r41.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r41.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r41.claim: Dividing the Qurʾān into sūras energizes readers, makes each memorized unit feel complete, and establishes each sūra as an independent sign and miracle.
ALUSI:1:1/r41.anchor: أن يكون أنشط للقارئ وأبعث على التحصيل كالمسافر إذا قطع ميلا

ALUSI:1:1/r42.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r42.speaker: أبو بكر التونسي
ALUSI:1:1/r42.claim: Abū Bakr al-Tūnisī transmits a consensus that God opened every revealed book with the basmala; another report calls it the opening of every book.
ALUSI:1:1/r42.anchor: إجماع علماء كل ملة على أن الله تعالى افتتح كل كتاب بها

ALUSI:1:1/r43.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r43.speaker: السيوطي عن السرميني
ALUSI:1:1/r43.claim: Al-Suyūṭī, citing al-Sarmīnī, reports “the basmala is the opening of every book”; al-Ālūsī cautions that the transmission is the reporter’s responsibility.
ALUSI:1:1/r43.anchor: والعهدة عليه : بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم فاتحة كل كتاب

ALUSI:1:1/r44.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r44.speaker: السرميني
ALUSI:1:1/r44.claim: Al-Sarmīnī argues the Qurʾānic basmala is unique, citing the staged change from “in Your name” to “in God’s name,” then “the Merciful,” then the full formula.
ALUSI:1:1/r44.anchor: فأمر بكتابة بسم الله حتى نزل

ALUSI:1:1/r45.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r45.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r45.claim: Al-Ālūsī replies that lack of an earlier command does not prove earlier absence, and only the Qurʾān’s Arabic wording and arrangement may be distinctive.
ALUSI:1:1/r45.anchor: وأن المختص بالقرآن اللفظ العربي بهذا الترتيب والكتب السماوية بأسرها

ALUSI:1:1/r46.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r46.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r46.claim: Outside the sūra context of 27:30, scholars held ten positions: from nowhere a Qurʾānic verse to a verse or verse-part in all or selected sūras.
ALUSI:1:1/r46.anchor: اختلف الناس في البسملة في غير النمل إذ هي فيها بعض آية بالاتفاق

ALUSI:1:1/r47.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r47.speaker: ابن عباس وابن المبارك وأهل مكة وأهل الكوفة وغالب أصحاب الشافعي والإمامية
ALUSI:1:1/r47.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn al-Mubārak, Meccan and most Kufan readers, most Shāfiʿīs, and Imāmīs hold it is a verse in every sūra except al-Tawba.
ALUSI:1:1/r47.anchor: فابن عباس وابن المبارك وأهل مكة

ALUSI:1:1/r48.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r48.speaker: بعض الشافعية وحمزة
ALUSI:1:1/r48.claim: Some Shāfiʿīs and Ḥamza, with a view attributed to Aḥmad, count the basmala as a verse of al-Fātiḥa alone.
ALUSI:1:1/r48.anchor: وقال بعض الشافعية وحمزة ونسب للإمام أحمد بالثالث

ALUSI:1:1/r49.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r49.speaker: أهل المدينة ومالك والأوزاعي وأبو عمرو ويعقوب
ALUSI:1:1/r49.claim: The Medinese, Mālik, al-Awzāʿī, Abū ʿAmr, and Yaʿqūb hold it is a separate verse revealed to mark sūra openings; al-Ālūsī calls this the common Hanafi doctrine.
ALUSI:1:1/r49.anchor: وأهل المدينة ومنهم مالك والشام ومنهم الأوزاعي والبصرة ومنهم أبو عمرو

ALUSI:1:1/r50.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r50.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r50.claim: Al-Ālūsī says the Hanafi position treats the basmala as an independent Qurʾānic verse, not part of al-Fātiḥa, while many Hanafis require its recitation in prayer.
ALUSI:1:1/r50.anchor: الصحيح من مذهبنا أن بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم آية مستقلة وهي من القرآن

ALUSI:1:1/r51.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r51.speaker: الزيلعي والزهيدي وابن وهبان
ALUSI:1:1/r51.claim: Al-Zaylaʿī and al-Zāhidī report the sound Hanafi view as obligation, including each rakʿa with obligatory recitation; Ibn Wahbān prescribes prostration for forgetful omission.
ALUSI:1:1/r51.anchor: أن الأصح أنها واجبة ، وذكر الزاهدي

ALUSI:1:1/r52.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r52.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r52.claim: Al-Ālūsī endorses the cautious view that omitting the basmala warrants the forgetfulness prostration, against Qāḍīkhān and the author of al-Khulāṣa.
ALUSI:1:1/r52.anchor: وهو الأحوط وبه أقول خلافا لقاضيخان

ALUSI:1:1/r53.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r53.speaker: أم سلمة
ALUSI:1:1/r53.claim: A report attributed to Umm Salama has the Prophet count the basmala as al-Fātiḥa’s first verse; al-Ālūsī questions the chain because Abū Mulayka’s hearing from her is unestablished.
ALUSI:1:1/r53.anchor: روى الشافعي عن ابن جريج عن أبي مليكة عن أم سلمة أنها قالت

ALUSI:1:1/r54.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r54.speaker: أبو عبيد وأحمد وأبو داود
ALUSI:1:1/r54.claim: They transmit Umm Salama’s report that the Prophet paused verse by verse, beginning with the basmala; al-Ālūsī says this proves its Qurʾānic status, not its membership in al-Fātiḥa.
ALUSI:1:1/r54.anchor: كان رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم يقطع قراءته آية آية بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم

ALUSI:1:1/r55.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r55.speaker: ابن خزيمة والحاكم
ALUSI:1:1/r55.claim: Their version has the Prophet count the basmala as a verse while reciting in prayer; al-Ālūsī reads it as the first Qurʾānic verse, not necessarily al-Fātiḥa’s.
ALUSI:1:1/r55.anchor: أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم قرأ في الصلاة بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم فعدها آية

ALUSI:1:1/r56.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r56.speaker: الدارقطني
ALUSI:1:1/r56.claim: Al-Dāraquṭnī’s version says the Prophet counted the basmala but did not pause after “those You favored”; al-Ālūsī says it is not explicit that it belongs to al-Fātiḥa.
ALUSI:1:1/r56.anchor: والدارقطني بلفظ : «كان يقرأ بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم الحمد لله

ALUSI:1:1/r57.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r57.speaker: أبو هريرة
ALUSI:1:1/r57.claim: A report from Abū Hurayra says the seven verses of al-Fātiḥa begin with the basmala; al-Ālūsī reads the wording as counting seven al-Ḥamd verses and separately affirming the basmala as Qurʾān.
ALUSI:1:1/r57.anchor: فاتحة الكتاب سبع آيات أولاهن بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم

ALUSI:1:1/r58.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r58.speaker: أبو هريرة
ALUSI:1:1/r58.claim: Al-Dāraquṭnī’s report urges reciting the basmala before al-Ḥamd and calls it one of its verses; al-Ālūsī offers a figurative reading that preserves seven verses without it.
ALUSI:1:1/r58.anchor: إذا قرأتم الحمد فاقرءوا بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم إنها أم القرآن

ALUSI:1:1/r59.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r59.speaker: أبو هريرة
ALUSI:1:1/r59.claim: In the sound Muslim report, God divides prayer between Himself and the servant; the three verses before the central pair and three after total seven without the basmala.
ALUSI:1:1/r59.anchor: عن أبي هريرة عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم قال

ALUSI:1:1/r60.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r60.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r60.claim: Al-Ālūsī prefers the Muslim version over al-Thaʿlabī’s and rejects readings that make the division merely semantic or mean half the prayer; it does not deny the basmala is Qurʾān.
ALUSI:1:1/r60.anchor: ولا شك أن هذه الرواية أصح من رواية الثعلبي ولا أقدم ثعلبياً على مسلم

ALUSI:1:1/r61.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r61.speaker: أبو ميسرة
ALUSI:1:1/r61.claim: An author-cited report from Abū Maysara says the Prophet first heard the call in Mecca, then recited al-Fātiḥa; al-Ālūsī says it would strongly prove Meccan origin if sound.
ALUSI:1:1/r61.anchor: عن أبي ميسرة أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم كان إذا برز سمع مناديا

ALUSI:1:1/r62.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r62.speaker: أبي بن كعب
ALUSI:1:1/r62.claim: Abū Hurayra reports that the Prophet asked Ubayy the Qurʾān’s greatest verse; Ubayy answered the basmala and the Prophet affirmed it, proving a verse but not its place in al-Fātiḥa.
ALUSI:1:1/r62.anchor: ما أعظم آية في القرآن ؟ قال : بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم

ALUSI:1:1/r63.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r63.speaker: جابر بن عبد الله
ALUSI:1:1/r63.claim: Al-Thaʿlabī transmits Jābir’s report that the Prophet instructed him to say the basmala when beginning prayer; al-Ālūsī says it does not establish sūra-part status.
ALUSI:1:1/r63.anchor: جعفر بن محمد عن أبيه عن جابر بن عبد الله

ALUSI:1:1/r64.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r64.speaker: علي
ALUSI:1:1/r64.claim: Al-Thaʿlabī attributes to ʿAlī the practice of beginning each sūra in prayer with the basmala and saying omission diminishes the prayer; al-Ālūsī does not accept this as proof of inclusion.
ALUSI:1:1/r64.anchor: عن علي كرم الله تعالى وجهه

ALUSI:1:1/r65.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r65.speaker: طلحة بن عبيد الله
ALUSI:1:1/r65.claim: A report attributed to Ṭalḥa says whoever leaves the basmala has left a verse of God’s Book; al-Ālūsī says such reports establish its Qurʾānic status only.
ALUSI:1:1/r65.anchor: عن طلحة بن عبيد الله قال

ALUSI:1:1/r66.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r66.speaker: أبو هريرة
ALUSI:1:1/r66.claim: A report says the Prophet rebuked a worshipper for beginning al-Ḥamd without the basmala and called omission a broken prayer; al-Ālūsī questions its wording and evidentiary force.
ALUSI:1:1/r66.anchor: يا رجل قطعت على نفسك الصلاة أما علمت أن بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم

ALUSI:1:1/r67.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r67.speaker: معاوية
ALUSI:1:1/r67.claim: Reports say Medinese objected when Muʿāwiya omitted the basmala and he repeated the prayer; al-Ālūsī says this could concern a missed obligatory act and does not prove inclusion.
ALUSI:1:1/r67.anchor: فقرأ أم القرآن ولم يقرأ البسملة فلما قضى صلاته ناداه المهاجرون

ALUSI:1:1/r68.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r68.speaker: أنس
ALUSI:1:1/r68.claim: Al-Shāfiʿī’s report says Muʿāwiya omitted both the basmala and transition takbīrs, then repeated prayer after objections; al-Ālūsī says this poses no difficulty for his view.
ALUSI:1:1/r68.anchor: لم يكبر عند الخفض إلى الركوع والسجود

ALUSI:1:1/r69.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r69.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r69.claim: Al-Ālūsī’s central reply to al-Rāzī is that obligation, Qurʾānic writing, and being an independent verse do not entail that the basmala is part of al-Fātiḥa.
ALUSI:1:1/r69.anchor: الصحيح من مذهبنا أن بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم آية مستقلة وهي من القرآن

ALUSI:1:1/r70.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r70.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r70.claim: The command “read in your Lord’s name” does not prove the basmala is part of al-Fātiḥa; the verse’s context concerns reading itself, and obligation does not entail inclusion.

ALUSI:1:1/r71.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r71.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r71.claim: Its appearance in Qurʾānic script is al-Rāzī’s strongest evidence that it is Qurʾān, but it still does not show that it is part of al-Fātiḥa.
ALUSI:1:1/r71.anchor: فهو أقوى ما يستدل به على كون البسملة من القرآن وأما على أنها من الفاتحة فلا

ALUSI:1:1/r72.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r72.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r72.claim: The argument from seven verses assumes that Abū Ḥanīfa’s count is wrong; al-Ālūsī says that premise is difficult to establish.
ALUSI:1:1/r72.anchor: كلام مولانا أبي حنيفة رحمه الله تعالى

ALUSI:1:1/r73.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r73.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r73.claim: Al-Ālūsī rejects the claim that a prayer without the basmala is incomplete under the “every important matter” report: prayer begins with its required opening takbīr.
ALUSI:1:1/r73.anchor: لأن الفاتحة جزء من الصلاة المفتتحة بالتكبير المقارن للنية

ALUSI:1:1/r74.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r74.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r74.claim: The verse about following earlier prophets does not establish a binding basmala formula for Muhammad or prove that formula’s membership in al-Fātiḥa.
ALUSI:1:1/r74.anchor: لا أدري ما أقول فيه سوى أنه جهل بالتفسير وعدم اطلاع

ALUSI:1:1/r75.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r75.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r75.claim: Repeated Qurʾānic phrases in other sūras do not prove the basmala is a constituent verse there; the comparison with repeated refrains is invalid.

ALUSI:1:1/r76.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r76.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r76.claim: The report that the Prophet wrote “in Your name, O God” before the full basmala helps show Qurʾānic status, but not al-Fātiḥa membership.
ALUSI:1:1/r76.anchor: روى أنه عليه السلام كان يكتب

ALUSI:1:1/r77.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r77.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r77.claim: Al-Ālūsī says the independent Qurʾānic basmala should be recited in prayer; Hanafis may require it, and caution favors the ruling.
ALUSI:1:1/r77.anchor: ولا ينبغي لمن وقف على الأحاديث أن يتوقف في قرآنيتها أو ينكر وجوب قراءتها

ALUSI:1:1/r78.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r78.speaker: أنس
ALUSI:1:1/r78.claim: Anas reports that he heard no basmala from the Prophet, Abū Bakr, ʿUmar, or ʿUthmān; al-Ālūsī takes this as silent recitation, not omission.
ALUSI:1:1/r78.anchor: صليت خلف النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم وأبي بكر وعمر وعثمان فلم أسمع

ALUSI:1:1/r79.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r79.speaker: ابن عباس
ALUSI:1:1/r79.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās reports that the Prophet did not recite the basmala aloud; al-Ālūsī reconciles this with occasional audible recitation for instruction.
ALUSI:1:1/r79.anchor: فعن ابن عباس لم يجهر النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم بالبسملة حتى مات

ALUSI:1:1/r80.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r80.speaker: عبد الله بن المغفل
ALUSI:1:1/r80.claim: Ibn al-Mughafal recounts his father’s objection to audible basmala, saying the Prophet and first caliphs began aloud with al-Ḥamd; al-Ālūsī infers they concealed the basmala.
ALUSI:1:1/r80.anchor: إياك والحدث في الإسلام فقد صليت

ALUSI:1:1/r81.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r81.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r81.claim: Al-Ālūsī lists many authorities for silent basmala recitation, including Sufyān, Ibn al-Mubārak, Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn al-Zubayr, Mujāhid, and Aḥmad.
ALUSI:1:1/r81.anchor: وهو مذهب الثوري وابن المبارك وابن مسعود وابن الزبير وعمار بن ياسر

ALUSI:1:1/r82.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r82.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r82.claim: Al-Ālūsī says the explicit sound evidence for audible recitation is limited; reports of occasional loud recitation can demonstrate that it is read without making it habitual.
ALUSI:1:1/r82.anchor: وأحاديث الجهر لم يصح منها سوى حديث ابن عباس الذي أخرجه الشافعي

ALUSI:1:1/r83.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r83.speaker: الدارقطني
ALUSI:1:1/r83.claim: Al-Dāraquṭnī reportedly concluded, when pressed to identify sound evidence for audible basmala, that no report on the matter is sound.

ALUSI:1:1/r84.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r84.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r84.claim: Conflicting Anas reports should be weighed by their chains; al-Ālūsī rejects accusing Anas of lying to protect an allegation about Umayyad pressure.
ALUSI:1:1/r84.anchor: ما يوافقنا إذ هو على شرط الشيخين

ALUSI:1:1/r85.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r85.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r85.claim: Al-Rāzī’s six arguments for loud recitation fail: membership would not require identical volume, praise may be quiet, and reports and inferred commands are inconclusive.
ALUSI:1:1/r85.anchor: ذكر ست حجج لإثبات الجهر هي أخفى من العدم

ALUSI:1:1/r86.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r86.speaker: الزمخشري
ALUSI:1:1/r86.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī favors the bāʾ of accompaniment: blessing and reverence are readily understood, and accompaniment suggests God’s name pervades the whole act.
ALUSI:1:1/r86.anchor: وما يدل عليه كلام الزمخشري أرجحية الثاني

ALUSI:1:1/r87.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r87.speaker: البيضاوي
ALUSI:1:1/r87.claim: Al-Bayḍāwī’s reading makes the bāʾ instrumental or one of seeking help; al-Ālūsī ultimately prefers this interpretation.
ALUSI:1:1/r87.anchor: فالذي يشعر به كلام البيضاوي أرجحية الأول

ALUSI:1:1/r88.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r88.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r88.claim: Attachment, superiority, redundancy, and oath are also proposed for the bāʾ, but al-Ālūsī rejects these readings.
ALUSI:1:1/r88.anchor: والأربعة الأخيرة ليست بشيء وإن استؤنس لبعض ببعض الآيات

ALUSI:1:1/r89.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r89.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r89.claim: He prefers seeking divine aid because it expresses humility, denies independent human power, and anticipates “You alone we worship and You alone we ask for help.”
ALUSI:1:1/r89.anchor: بل يكاد أن تكون متعينة إذ فيها من الأدب

ALUSI:1:1/r90.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r90.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r90.claim: The instrumental sense also fits 96:1 as a response to the Prophet’s “I am not a reader,” and echoes the command to seek God’s help.

ALUSI:1:1/r91.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r91.speaker: ابن جرير
ALUSI:1:1/r91.claim: Ibn Jarīr supplies an implied “I recite,” the specific act of the person uttering the basmala; al-Ālūsī finds this broad and contextually apt.

ALUSI:1:1/r92.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r92.speaker: الفراء وابن عباس
ALUSI:1:1/r92.claim: Al-Farrāʾ, with a view attributed to Ibn ʿAbbās, supplies an imperative addressed to people, urging them to begin in God’s name.
ALUSI:1:1/r92.anchor: عن ابن عباس لأنه تعالى قدم التسمية

ALUSI:1:1/r93.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r93.speaker: النحويون
ALUSI:1:1/r93.claim: Grammarians supply a general “I begin”; they argue it suits every basmala, but al-Ālūsī says it fails to convey that the entire recitation is aided by God’s name.
ALUSI:1:1/r93.anchor: وذهب النحويون إلى تقديره عاما نحو أبتدئ وأيد بوجوه

ALUSI:1:1/r94.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r94.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r94.claim: Al-Ālūsī prefers Ibn Jarīr’s specific verb because it makes the whole recitation occur with divine aid; the implied generic beginning adds little.
ALUSI:1:1/r94.anchor: وما ذهب إليه الإمام أمس وأخص بالمقصود وأتم شمولا

ALUSI:1:1/r95.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r95.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r95.claim: An implied verbal noun such as “my beginning” adds an extra omitted predicate and loses the ongoing force of a finite verb.
ALUSI:1:1/r95.anchor: وذهب البعض إلى تقدير ابتدائي مثلا وفيه زيادة إضمار

ALUSI:1:1/r96.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r96.speaker: ابن عربي
ALUSI:1:1/r96.claim: Ibn ʿArabī reads the phrase’s implied predicate as the beginning and emergence of the cosmos through the divine names, an allusive reading beyond ordinary syntax.
ALUSI:1:1/r96.anchor: وجعل الشيخ الأكبر قدس سره هذا الجار خبر مبتدأ مضمر هو ابتداء العالم

ALUSI:1:1/r97.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r97.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r97.claim: Al-Ālūsī favors placing the implied act before the basmala: God’s name precedes it in rank, and the order suggests beginning through divine aid.
ALUSI:1:1/r97.anchor: أن تقدير المتعلق هنا مؤخرا أحرى

ALUSI:1:1/r98.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r98.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r98.claim: He rejects a delayed implied verb because its placement fragments the construction or makes mercy seem to cause a reading that already occurred.
ALUSI:1:1/r98.anchor: وأما بعد التمام فيظهر نقص دقيق لأن في الجملة تعليق الحكم

ALUSI:1:1/r99.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r99.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r99.claim: The prepositional phrase is “stable” under one terminology because its governing word is omitted; definitions of stable and non-stable adverbials vary by convention.
ALUSI:1:1/r99.anchor: وحيث لا مشاحة فيه اختار الأول فيكون الظرف هنا مستقرا

ALUSI:1:1/r100.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r100.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r100.claim: The bāʾ is kasra-marked despite the preference for light vowels on isolated particles: its prepositional function and genitive effect distinguish it.

ALUSI:1:1/r101.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r101.speaker: ابن الفارض
ALUSI:1:1/r101.claim: Ibn al-Fāriḍ’s verse makes the bāʾ’s kasra a sign of servile humility that is raised by divine generosity, not by human contrivance.
ALUSI:1:1/r101.anchor: سيدي عمر بن الفارض قدس الله تعالى سره

ALUSI:1:1/r102.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r102.speaker: الشبلي وابن عربي
ALUSI:1:1/r102.claim: Al-Shiblī identifies himself with the dot under bāʾ, and Ibn ʿArabī makes that dot a reminder of the heart and the secret of servanthood.
ALUSI:1:1/r102.anchor: وقال سيدي الشيخ الأكبر قدس سره

ALUSI:1:1/r103.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r103.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r103.claim: Al-Ālūsī’s allusion makes alif signify the divine essence and bāʾ its manifested attributes; its genitive kasra signifies lowered humility and mercy’s priority.
ALUSI:1:1/r103.anchor: والباء إما إشارة إلى صفاته التي أظهرتها نقطة الكون

ALUSI:1:1/r104.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r104.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r104.claim: He links the basmala’s bāʾ to Muḥammad’s merciful reality and cites 21:107 and 9:128; the basmala’s opening then signals the Prophet’s mercy and mission.
ALUSI:1:1/r104.anchor: ولكون الغالب عليه الصلاة والسلام صفة الرحمة لا سيما على مؤمني الأمة

ALUSI:1:1/r105.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r105.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r105.claim: He associates the missing basmala in al-Tawba with that sūra’s manifest severity, while claiming a concealed allusion to the Prophetic reality remains.
ALUSI:1:1/r105.anchor: ولما كان الجلال في سورة براءة ظاهرا ترك الإشارة بالبسملة

ALUSI:1:1/r106.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r106.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r106.claim: The Basrans derive ism from sumūw, “height,” with a deleted wāw; its function is to raise what is named from obscurity into recognition.
ALUSI:1:1/r106.anchor: وأصله سمو حذفت الواو تخفيفا لكثرة الاستعمال

ALUSI:1:1/r107.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r107.speaker: الكوفيون
ALUSI:1:1/r107.claim: The Kufans derive ism from wasm, “mark,” and posit a compensatory hamza; al-Ālūsī rejects this as unsupported and prefers the Basran derivation.

ALUSI:1:1/r108.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r108.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r108.claim: Al-Ālūsī records eighteen dialect forms for ism, including sim, sumā, and samāʾ, using inflected forms such as asāmī and summiyy to support the Basran root.

ALUSI:1:1/r109.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r109.speaker: الأشاعرة والمعتزلة
ALUSI:1:1/r109.claim: Ashʿarīs say the name is the named, whereas Muʿtazilīs say it is other than the named; al-Ālūsī argues the dispute confuses essence with verbal designation.
ALUSI:1:1/r109.anchor: طال التشاجر في أن الاسم هل هو عين المسمى

ALUSI:1:1/r110.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r110.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r110.claim: He argues that “glorify the name of your Lord” and “names you invented” can use name for the divine essence or idols, not merely their words.
ALUSI:1:1/r110.anchor: في المعروف إنما يتوجه إلى الذات الأقدس

ALUSI:1:1/r111.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r111.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r111.claim: He distinguishes God’s eternal names in eternal speech from later names used of Him; the former follow the dispute about divine speech, while created designations are other than God.
ALUSI:1:1/r111.anchor: قديم وهو ما سمى الله تعالى به نفسه في كلامه القديم

ALUSI:1:1/r112.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r112.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r112.claim: Al-Ālūsī says objections that identity would multiply or change the named apply only to names as created expressions, not names used for the essence.
ALUSI:1:1/r112.anchor: والكل غير وارد إلا على تقدير القول بالعينية بناء على القسم الثاني

ALUSI:1:1/r113.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r113.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r113.claim: Some take ism here as God’s essence because help cannot be sought through a bare word and none of the ninety-nine names is literally “name”; al-Ālūsī distinguishes constructions with bi-
ALUSI:1:1/r113.anchor: لأن الاستعانة بالألفاظ مجردها مما لا معنى لها وليس في التسعة والتسعين

ALUSI:1:1/r114.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r114.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r114.claim: Others say seeking blessing applies to a name even if seeking help applies to the named essence; they cite the distinction between swearing and auspicious invocation.
ALUSI:1:1/r114.anchor: وقال غير واحد سلمنا أن الاستعانة لا تكون إلا بالذات إلا أن التبرك

ALUSI:1:1/r115.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r115.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r115.claim: The written basmala omits the alif of ism; explanations include frequent usage, the bāʾ replacing the initial hamza, and whether the governing word is stated.
ALUSI:1:1/r115.anchor: ولم تكتب همزة الوصل مع أن الأصل في كل كلمة أن ترسم

ALUSI:1:1/r116.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r116.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r116.claim: Al-Ālūsī treats the Uthmānic spelling’s hidden alif as an allusion to the fullness of the bāʾ-sīn-mīm connection and universal mercy.
ALUSI:1:1/r116.anchor: والقريب من الفهم أن الهمزة إنما حذفت في الخط ليكون اتصال السين بالباء

ALUSI:1:1/r117.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r117.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
ALUSI:1:1/r117.claim: A report says the Prophet instructed Muʿāwiya in calligraphy, including elongating the bāʾ, separating the sīns, and shaping the mīm; ʿUmar b. ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz gave similar advice.
ALUSI:1:1/r117.anchor: ألق الدواة وحرف القلم وانصب الباء وفرق السين ولا تعور الميم

ALUSI:1:1/r118.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r118.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r118.claim: Authorities derive Allāh either from al-ilāh or ilāh with hamza loss and compensatory alif-lām; Ibn Mālik instead argues for a distinct root and original proper name.
ALUSI:1:1/r118.anchor: على الأظهر وعوض عنها الألف واللام

ALUSI:1:1/r119.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r119.speaker: السيد السند والسعد والرضي
ALUSI:1:1/r119.claim: Al-Sayyid, al-Saʿd, and al-Raḍī differ on whether al-ilāh is generic or already exclusive, and whether Allāh became a proper name through deletion or assimilation.

ALUSI:1:1/r120.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r120.speaker: ابن مالك
ALUSI:1:1/r120.claim: Ibn Mālik denies that Allāh derives from al-ilāh, arguing their forms and meanings differ and that deletion or hamza transfer lacks a sound morphological parallel.
ALUSI:1:1/r120.anchor: وادعى ابن مالك أن الله من الأعلام التي قارن وضعها أل

ALUSI:1:1/r121.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r121.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r121.claim: Proposed roots for Allāh include worship, bewilderment, finding refuge, seeking, and a calf’s attachment to its mother; al-Ālūsī weighs these as conjectural alternatives.
ALUSI:1:1/r121.anchor: واشتقاقه من أله كعبد إلاهة كعبادة وألوهة كعبودة

ALUSI:1:1/r122.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r122.speaker: الأعشى
ALUSI:1:1/r122.claim: Al-Aʿshā’s verse uses lāh as a divine designation, supporting the proposal that Allāh comes from a root meaning to be exalted or veiled.

ALUSI:1:1/r123.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r123.speaker: البلخي
ALUSI:1:1/r123.claim: Al-Balkhī says Allāh is an Arabized Hebrew or Syriac word meaning powerful; al-Ālūsī rejects this without evidence and notes that Arabic morphology weighs against it.

ALUSI:1:1/r124.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r124.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r124.claim: Al-Ālūsī favors Allāh as an Arabic proper name for the essence encompassing every attribute, following major theologians and the Naqshbandī tradition.
ALUSI:1:1/r124.anchor: فالذي أرتضيه لا عن تقليد أن هذا الاسم الأعظم موضوع للذات الجامعة

ALUSI:1:1/r125.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r125.speaker: البيضاوي
ALUSI:1:1/r125.claim: Al-Bayḍāwī says Allāh began as an adjective but became proper through exclusive use; al-Ālūsī rejects his arguments from description, the heavenly predicate, and derivation.
ALUSI:1:1/r125.anchor: فاختار أنه وصف في أصله لكنه لما غلب عليه بحيث لا يستعمل

ALUSI:1:1/r126.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r126.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r126.claim: The exclusive declaration “no god but God” supports a proper name: an adjective or generic noun would not itself prevent sharing, even if conventionally reserved.
ALUSI:1:1/r126.anchor: لو كان وصفا لم تكن الكلمة توحيدا مثل لا إله إلا الرحمن

ALUSI:1:1/r127.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r127.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r127.claim: The lām is emphatic after fatḥa or ḍamma according to common recitation practice; deletion of the alif is reported in pause, but retention is more eloquent.
ALUSI:1:1/r127.anchor: وتفخيم اللام من هذا الاسم الكريم إذا انفتح ما قبله أو انضم

ALUSI:1:1/r128.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r128.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r128.claim: Ibn al-Ṣalāḥ reports dropping Allāh’s alif; al-Taysīr confines it to pause, and some jurists call it erroneous enough to invalidate prayer or an explicit oath.

ALUSI:1:1/r129.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r129.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r129.claim: Al-Ālūsī points readers to Ibn ʿArabī’s extensive mystical treatment of the word’s letters, hidden and audible alif, and opening and ending structure.
ALUSI:1:1/r129.anchor: وأتى بالعجب العجاب ، وفي ظهور الألف تارة

ALUSI:1:1/r130.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r130.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r130.claim: The conventional analysis makes al-Raḥmān and al-Raḥīm intensive adjectives from rahima, sometimes positing transfer to intransitive rahuma; al-Ālūsī disputes this derivation.
ALUSI:1:1/r130.anchor: المشهور أنهما صفتان مشبهتان بنيتا لإفادة المبالغة

ALUSI:1:1/r131.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r131.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r131.claim: Interpreters explain divine mercy as its effect, the will to do good, a king’s compassion by analogy, or a metaphorical attribute; some call it a revealed technical sense.
ALUSI:1:1/r131.anchor: إما على طريقة المجاز المرسل بذكر لفظ السبب وإرادة المسبب

ALUSI:1:1/r132.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r132.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r132.claim: Al-Ālūsī rejects metaphorical reduction: mercy is truly God’s attribute in a manner befitting Him, without likening it to created emotion or specifying its modality.
ALUSI:1:1/r132.anchor: أو بتركه كذلك وإثباتها له حقيقة بالمعنى اللائق

ALUSI:1:1/r133.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r133.speaker: السكوني والأشعري
ALUSI:1:1/r133.claim: Al-Sakūnī condemns interpreting mercy metaphorically as an Muʿtazilī tendency; al-Ālūsī says al-Ashʿarī’s final position follows affirmation without asking how.
ALUSI:1:1/r133.anchor: قد نطق الإمام السكوني في كتابه

ALUSI:1:1/r134.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r134.speaker: الأشعري
ALUSI:1:1/r134.claim: Al-Ālūsī says reports that al-Ashʿarī interpreted mercy are either unestablished or superseded by the creed in his later al-Ibāna.
ALUSI:1:1/r134.anchor: إذا سئل أعطى والرحيم إذا لم يسئل غضب

ALUSI:1:1/r135.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r135.speaker: الراغب وابن المبارك
ALUSI:1:1/r135.claim: Al-Rāghib says raḥīm marks frequent action and raḥmān frequent, repeated action; Ibn al-Mubārak says the Merciful gives when asked, while the Compassionate is angered if not asked.
ALUSI:1:1/r135.anchor: ابن المبارك الرحمن : إذا سئل أعطى

ALUSI:1:1/r136.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r136.speaker: الجويني
ALUSI:1:1/r136.claim: Al-Juwaynī treats the two names as equal in force, distinguishing repeated abundance in raḥmān from enduring action in raḥīm.
ALUSI:1:1/r136.anchor: وفرق بعضهم بينهما بأن الرحمة دال على الصفة القائمة

ALUSI:1:1/r137.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r137.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r137.claim: Some distinguish raḥmān as the attribute of mercy and raḥīm as its relation to recipients, citing human use of raḥīm in 9:117 and 33:43 but not raḥmān.
ALUSI:1:1/r137.anchor: وفرق بعضهم بينهما بأن الرحمة دال على الصفة القائمة

ALUSI:1:1/r138.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r138.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r138.claim: Al-Ālūsī challenges the rule that greater form means greater intensity and disputes whether raḥmān is more abundant, more enduring, or simply equal to raḥīm.
ALUSI:1:1/r138.anchor: وأما سادسا فلأن كون الرحمن أبلغ من الرحيم غير مسلم

ALUSI:1:1/r139.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r139.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r139.claim: One distinction makes raḥmān’s worldly mercy encompass believers and unbelievers and raḥīm’s afterlife mercy favor believers; al-Ālūsī questions the allocation and its assumptions.
ALUSI:1:1/r139.anchor: فعلى الأول قيل يا رحمن الدنيا لأنه يعم المؤمن والكفار

ALUSI:1:1/r140.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r140.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r140.claim: The Prophet’s intercession for all people at the gathering and reports of punishment relief complicate claims that afterlife mercy reaches only believers.
ALUSI:1:1/r140.anchor: لما كان المقصود تعليم وجه التيمن بأسمائه الحسنى

ALUSI:1:1/r141.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r141.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r141.claim: Proposed reasons for placing al-Raḥmān first include its encompassing major blessings, al-Raḥīm completing lesser ones, or preserving verse-end rhyme; al-Ālūsī rejects rhyme alone.

ALUSI:1:1/r142.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r142.speaker: البيضاوي
ALUSI:1:1/r142.claim: Al-Bayḍāwī’s ordering moves from God’s universal outpouring of existence to each creature’s particular share and perfection; al-Ālūsī questions the distinction.
ALUSI:1:1/r142.anchor: وللعلماء في هذا الترتيب كلام كثير

ALUSI:1:1/r143.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r143.speaker: ابن هشام وابن خروف
ALUSI:1:1/r143.claim: Ibn Hishām treats al-Raḥmān as a substitute, not adjective, with al-Raḥīm modifying it; Ibn Khurūf calls it a dominant adjective.
ALUSI:1:1/r143.anchor: وأن استفاضة إضافته نحو رحمن الدنيا تنافيه فتأمل

ALUSI:1:1/r144.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r144.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r144.claim: Al-Ālūsī’s allusive reading makes al-Raḥīm an epithet of Muḥammad from 9:128: Adam bears the names, while Muḥammad bears their meanings and completes creation.
ALUSI:1:1/r144.anchor: وعندي من باب الإشارة أن تأخير الرحيم لأنه صفة محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم

ALUSI:1:1/r145.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r145.speaker: ابن الحاجب والزمخشري والرضي وابن مالك والبيضاوي والسعد
ALUSI:1:1/r145.claim: Grammarians dispute whether raḥmān declines: most prefer diptote treatment by analogy with the predominant faʿlā feminine pattern, while al-Saʿd allows both.
ALUSI:1:1/r145.anchor: واختلف فيما لزم تذكيره كلحيان بمعنى كبير اللحية

ALUSI:1:1/r146.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r146.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r146.claim: Banū Ḥanīfa called Musaylima “the Merciful of Yamāma”; al-Ālūsī treats this as blasphemous excess, not evidence that the sacred name is ordinarily shared.
ALUSI:1:1/r146.anchor: وأنت غيث الورى لا زلت رحمانا

ALUSI:1:1/r147.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r147.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r147.claim: The basmala opens God’s discourse because it summarizes what follows and is a profound blessing; analyzing even its brief wording draws on many disciplines.
ALUSI:1:1/r147.anchor: لأنها إجمال ما بعدها وهي آية عظيمة ونعمة للعارف جسيمة

ALUSI:1:1/r148.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r148.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r148.claim: Its study ranges from syntax, morphology, rhetoric, language, and script to logic, theology, jurisprudence, hadith method, ethics, and esoteric knowledge.
ALUSI:1:1/r148.anchor: إذا أراد أن يبحث عن الباء من حيث إنها حرف جر

ALUSI:1:1/r149.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r149.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r149.claim: Al-Ālūsī finds layered triads in its articulation, omitted letters, written and spoken forms, word classes, genitives, divine names, grammatical roles, and connections.
ALUSI:1:1/r149.anchor: وانظر لم اشتملت حروفها على الطبائع الأربع

ALUSI:1:1/r150.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r150.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r150.claim: A second reason for opening with the basmala is to teach people how to begin: invoking God declares dependence on His power in every undertaking.
ALUSI:1:1/r150.anchor: لتعليم العباد إذا بدءوا بأمر كيف يبدءون

ALUSI:1:1/r151.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r151.speaker: أبو هريرة
ALUSI:1:1/r151.claim: Abū Hurayra transmits the Prophet’s maxim that an important matter begun without God’s name is incomplete; al-Ālūsī interprets it broadly to include trivial matters.
ALUSI:1:1/r151.anchor: كل أمر ذي بال لا يبدأ فيه ببسم الله فهو أبتر

ALUSI:1:1/r152.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r152.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r152.claim: Al-Ālūsī takes dhū bāl as comprehensive—anything that enters the mind—rather than restricting it to dignified matters, since God’s aid matters in small acts too.
ALUSI:1:1/r152.anchor: أي كل أمر يخطر بالبال جليلا كان أو حقيرا

ALUSI:1:1/r153.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r153.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r153.claim: Reports urge asking God even for a sandal strap, and God tells Moses to ask for salt and a shoe strap; these support invocation in minor needs.
ALUSI:1:1/r153.anchor: يا موسى سلني حتى ملح قدرك وشراك نعلك

ALUSI:1:1/r154.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r154.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r154.claim: Reciting the basmala over forbidden acts is itself forbidden without being disbelief according to the sound view; over disliked acts it is disliked, unless contempt makes it disbelief.
ALUSI:1:1/r154.anchor: التسمية على الحرام والمكروه مما لا ينبغي بل هي حرام في الحرام

ALUSI:1:1/r155.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r155.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r155.claim: The maxim’s variants include beginning with praise, “praise of God,” or another remembrance, and incomplete versus severed; al-Ālūsī calls it unstable in wording and chain but strengthened in meaning.
ALUSI:1:1/r155.anchor: وقد اضطرب الحديث هنا فوقع في بعض الروايات

ALUSI:1:1/r156.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r156.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r156.claim: Al-Ālūsī reconciles variants by taking the intended opening as remembrance that manifests divine perfection; matters may be outwardly complete yet deficient in meaning without it.
ALUSI:1:1/r156.anchor: واستحسن فيه أن روايتي البسملة والحمدلة تعارضتا

ALUSI:1:1/r157.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI:1:1/r157.speaker: author
ALUSI:1:1/r157.claim: Since the basmala is a kind of praise, it fittingly precedes the comprehensive praise that follows.
ALUSI:1:1/r157.anchor: ولما افتتح سبحانه وتعالى كتابة البسملة وهي نوع من الحمد ناسب

BAGHAWI:1:1/r1.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI:1:1/r1.speaker: author
BAGHAWI:1:1/r1.claim: Al-Fatiha is known by three names: Fatiḥat al-Kitāb, Umm al-Qurʾān, and al-Sabʿ al-Mathānī.
BAGHAWI:1:1/r1.anchor: ولها ثلاثة أسماء معروفة : فاتحة الكتاب ، وأم القرآن ، والسبع المثاني .

BAGHAWI:1:1/r2.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI:1:1/r2.speaker: author
BAGHAWI:1:1/r2.claim: It is called Fatiḥat al-Kitāb because God began the Qur'an with it.
BAGHAWI:1:1/r2.anchor: سميت فاتحة الكتاب : لأنه تعالى بها افتتح القرآن .

BAGHAWI:1:1/r3.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI:1:1/r3.speaker: author
BAGHAWI:1:1/r3.claim: It is Umm al-Kitāb because it is the Qur'an's origin; umm means origin, as Mecca is Umm al-Qura, where the land was spread out from beneath it.
BAGHAWI:1:1/r3.anchor: وأم الكتاب : لأنها أصل القرآن منها بدئ القرآن ، وأم الشيء : أصله ،

BAGHAWI:1:1/r4.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI:1:1/r4.speaker: author
BAGHAWI:1:1/r4.claim: Another explanation of Umm al-Kitāb is that it precedes and leads the following surahs, being first written in codices and read in prayer.
BAGHAWI:1:1/r4.anchor: وقيل : لأنها مقدمة وإمام لما يتلوها من السور يبدأ بكتابتها في الصحف ، وبقراءتها في الصلاة .

BAGHAWI:1:1/r5.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI:1:1/r5.speaker: author
BAGHAWI:1:1/r5.claim: It is the seven oft-repeated because scholars agree that it consists of seven verses.
BAGHAWI:1:1/r5.anchor: والسبع المثاني لأنها سبع آيات باتفاق العلماء .

BAGHAWI:1:1/r6.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI:1:1/r6.speaker: author
BAGHAWI:1:1/r6.claim: It is called oft-repeated because it is recited in every prayer cycle.
BAGHAWI:1:1/r6.anchor: وسميت مثاني لأنها تثنى في الصلاة ، فتقرأ في كل ركعة .

BAGHAWI:1:1/r7.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI:1:1/r7.speaker: مجاهد
BAGHAWI:1:1/r7.claim: Mujahid says God reserved the seven oft-repeated for this community and stored it for them.
BAGHAWI:1:1/r7.anchor: وقال مجاهد : سميت مثاني لأن الله تعالى استثناها لهذه الأمة فذخرها لهم .

BAGHAWI:1:1/r8.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI:1:1/r8.speaker: author
BAGHAWI:1:1/r8.claim: Most scholars call the surah Meccan, and Baghawi prefers this because al-Hijr is Meccan, so its seven oft-repeated could not have been promised before its revelation.
BAGHAWI:1:1/r8.anchor: والأول أصح ، أنها مكية ، لأن الله تعالى من على الرسول صلى الله عليه وسلم بقوله : " ولقد آتيناك سبعاً من المثاني "

BAGHAWI:1:1/r10.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI:1:1/r10.speaker: author
BAGHAWI:1:1/r10.claim: Another view says it was revealed twice, once in Mecca and once in Medina, which explains the name al-Mathānī.
BAGHAWI:1:1/r10.anchor: وقيل : نزلت مرتين ، مرة بمكة ومرة بالمدينة ؛ ولذلك سميت مثاني .

BAGHAWI:1:1/r11.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI:1:1/r11.speaker: author
BAGHAWI:1:1/r11.claim: The prefixed bāʾ is extra and makes the following noun genitive, like min and ʿan.
BAGHAWI:1:1/r11.anchor: الباء زائدة يخفض ما بعدها مثل : من وعن ،

BAGHAWI:1:1/r12.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI:1:1/r12.speaker: author
BAGHAWI:1:1/r12.claim: The governing verb is omitted and inferred as either “I begin in God's name” or “Say in God's name.”
BAGHAWI:1:1/r12.anchor: والمتعلق به محذوف لدلالة الكلام عليه ، تقديره أبدأ بسم الله ، أو قل بسم الله ،

BAGHAWI:1:1/r13.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI:1:1/r13.speaker: author
BAGHAWI:1:1/r13.claim: The alif in ism is omitted for lightness because the expression is used very frequently.
BAGHAWI:1:1/r13.anchor: وأسقطت الألف من الاسم طلباً للخفة ، لكثرة استعمالها ،

BAGHAWI:1:1/r14.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI:1:1/r14.speaker: القطيبي
BAGHAWI:1:1/r14.claim: Al-Qutaybi says the bāʾ is elongated so God's Book begins with a majestic letter; ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz instructed scribes to shape the letters reverently.
BAGHAWI:1:1/r14.anchor: قال القطيبي : ليكون افتتاح كلام كتاب الله بحرف معظم ، كان عمر بن عبد العزيز رحمه الله ، يقول لكتابه : طولوا الباء ،

BAGHAWI:1:1/r15.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI:1:1/r15.speaker: author
BAGHAWI:1:1/r15.claim: Another explanation says the elongated bāʾ compensates for the omitted alif; in “Read in your Lord's name” the alif remains, and it is not omitted outside this construction with God's name.
BAGHAWI:1:1/r15.anchor: وقيل لما أسقطوا الألف ردوا طول الألف على الباء ليكون دالاً على سقوط الألف ، ألا ترى أنه لما كتب الألف في ( اقرأ باسم ربك )

BAGHAWI:1:1/r16.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI:1:1/r16.speaker: author
BAGHAWI:1:1/r16.claim: Ism can denote the named entity itself, as Qur'anic examples call Yahya by his name and use “names” for the worshipped persons.
BAGHAWI:1:1/r16.anchor: والاسم هو المسمى ، وعينه وذاته قال تعالى ( إنا نبشرك بغلام اسمه يحيى )

BAGHAWI:1:1/r17.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI:1:1/r17.speaker: author
BAGHAWI:1:1/r17.claim: Ism also means the act of naming, and this usage is more common than its use for the named thing.
BAGHAWI:1:1/r17.anchor: ثم يقال للتسمية أيضاً اسم ، فاستعماله في التسمية أكثر من المسمى .

BAGHAWI:1:1/r18.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI:1:1/r18.speaker: author
BAGHAWI:1:1/r18.claim: God's naming Himself in the basmala teaches servants how to begin recitation.
BAGHAWI:1:1/r18.anchor: فإن قيل : ما معنى التسمية من الله لنفسه ؟ قيل : هو تعليم العباد كيف يستفتحون القراءة

BAGHAWI:1:1/r19.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI:1:1/r19.speaker: المبرد
BAGHAWI:1:1/r19.claim: Al-Mubarrad and the Basrans derive ism from sumuww, loftiness: the name rises over and makes its meaning apparent.
BAGHAWI:1:1/r19.anchor: قال المبرد في البصريين ، هو مشتق من السمو ، وهو العلو ، فكأنه علا على معناه

BAGHAWI:1:1/r20.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI:1:1/r20.speaker: ثعلب
BAGHAWI:1:1/r20.claim: Thaʿlab and the Kufans derive ism from wasm or sima, a mark that signifies the meaning and the named thing.
BAGHAWI:1:1/r20.anchor: وقال ثعلب في الكوفيين : هو من الوسم والسمة وهي العلامة ،

BAGHAWI:1:1/r21.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI:1:1/r21.speaker: author
BAGHAWI:1:1/r21.claim: Baghawi prefers sumuww: ism diminishes as sumayy and its verb is samiitu; a wasm derivation would yield wasīm and wasamtu.
BAGHAWI:1:1/r21.anchor: والأول أصح لأنه يصغر على سمي ، ولو كان من السمت لكان يصغر على الوسيم ،

BAGHAWI:1:1/r22.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI:1:1/r22.speaker: الخليل
BAGHAWI:1:1/r22.claim: Al-Khalil and others treat Allah as a proper name specific to God, not derived, like human names Zayd and ʿAmr.
BAGHAWI:1:1/r22.anchor: قال الخليل وجماعة : هو اسم علم خاص لله عز وجل لا اشتقاق له كأسماء الأعلام للعباد

BAGHAWI:1:1/r23.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI:1:1/r23.speaker: author
BAGHAWI:1:1/r23.claim: Others derive Allah from aliha, worship; Ibn ʿAbbas reads “your gods” in 7:127 as “your worship,” showing that God alone deserves worship.
BAGHAWI:1:1/r23.anchor: من أله إلاهة أي عبد عبادة ، وقرأ ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما

BAGHAWI:1:1/r24.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI:1:1/r24.speaker: author
BAGHAWI:1:1/r24.claim: Another view takes Allah from the original ilāh, supported by the statement that if another god were with God each god would take its creation.
BAGHAWI:1:1/r24.anchor: وقيل أصله إله ، قال الله عز وجل : ( وما كان معه من إله إذاً لذهب كل إله بما خلق )

BAGHAWI:1:1/r25.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI:1:1/r25.speaker: المبرد
BAGHAWI:1:1/r25.claim: Al-Mubarrad links ilāh to Arabic alihtu ilayhi, finding calm with someone; creatures find repose in God and are comforted by remembering Him, as the cited line illustrates.
BAGHAWI:1:1/r25.anchor: قال المبرد : هو من قول العرب ، ألهت إلى فلان أي سكنت إليه قال الشاعر : ألهت إليها والحوادث جمة

BAGHAWI:1:1/r26.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI:1:1/r26.speaker: المبرد
BAGHAWI:1:1/r26.claim: Al-Mubarrad also cites a poetic use of alihtu ilayhi for fleeing or seeking refuge in someone.
BAGHAWI:1:1/r26.anchor: ويقال ألهت إليه أي فزعت إليه قال الشاعر : ألهت إليها والركائب وقف

BAGHAWI:1:1/r27.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI:1:1/r27.speaker: author
BAGHAWI:1:1/r27.claim: Another etymology derives Allah from walah, with initial wāw changed to hamza like wishāḥ/ishāḥ: people flee to God in hardship and need as a child clings to its mother.
BAGHAWI:1:1/r27.anchor: وقيل أصل الإله ولاه ، فأبدلت الواو بالهمزة ، مثل وشاح وإشاح ، اشتقاقه من الوله ،

BAGHAWI:1:1/r28.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI:1:1/r28.speaker: author
BAGHAWI:1:1/r28.claim: A further explanation derives it from walah as loss of reason at losing someone dear.
BAGHAWI:1:1/r28.anchor: وقيل هو من الوله وهو ذهاب العقل لفقد من يعز عليك .

BAGHAWI:1:1/r29.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI:1:1/r29.speaker: ابن عباس
BAGHAWI:1:1/r29.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas calls Rahman and Rahim two tender names, one more tender than the other.
BAGHAWI:1:1/r29.anchor: قال ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما ، هما اسمان رقيقان أحدهما أرق من الآخر ،

BAGHAWI:1:1/r30.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI:1:1/r30.speaker: author
BAGHAWI:1:1/r30.claim: Some regard the names as synonyms meaning “possessor of mercy”; their repetition encourages hope among those who seek God.
BAGHAWI:1:1/r30.anchor: منهم من قال : هما بمعنى واحد مثل ندمان ونديم ومعناهما ذو الرحمة ، وذكر أحدهما بعد الآخر تطميعاً لقلوب الراغبين ،

BAGHAWI:1:1/r31.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI:1:1/r31.speaker: المبرد
BAGHAWI:1:1/r31.claim: Al-Mubarrad reads the sequence as bounty upon bounty and favor upon favor.
BAGHAWI:1:1/r31.anchor: وقال المبرد : هو إنعام بعد إنعام ، وتفضل بعد تفضل ،

BAGHAWI:1:1/r32.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI:1:1/r32.speaker: author
BAGHAWI:1:1/r32.claim: Those who distinguish them say Rahman is universal mercy, providing for all creatures in this world, while Rahim is particular mercy and forgiveness for believers in the hereafter.
BAGHAWI:1:1/r32.anchor: فالرحمن بمعنى الرزاق في الدنيا ، وهو على العموم لكافة الخلق . والرحيم بمعنى المعافي في الآخرة ،

BAGHAWI:1:1/r33.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI:1:1/r33.speaker: author
BAGHAWI:1:1/r33.claim: The invocation “Rahman of this world, Rahim of the hereafter” reflects universal Rahman but particular Rahim; people may call another merciful but not Rahman.
BAGHAWI:1:1/r33.anchor: ولذلك قيل في الدعاء " يا رحمن الدنيا ، ورحيم الآخرة " فالرحمن : من يصل رحمته إلى الخلق على العموم

BAGHAWI:1:1/r34.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI:1:1/r34.speaker: author
BAGHAWI:1:1/r34.claim: Mercy may mean God's willing good for its recipients, which makes it an attribute of essence.
BAGHAWI:1:1/r34.anchor: والرحمة إرادة الله تعالى الخير لأهله ، وقيل :هي ترك عقوبة من يستحقها

BAGHAWI:1:1/r35.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI:1:1/r35.speaker: author
BAGHAWI:1:1/r35.claim: Alternatively, mercy is withholding deserved punishment and giving good to the undeserving, which makes it an attribute of action.
BAGHAWI:1:1/r35.anchor: وقيل :هي ترك عقوبة من يستحقها ، وإسداء الخير إلى من لا يستحق .

BAGHAWI:1:1/r36.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI:1:1/r36.speaker: author
BAGHAWI:1:1/r36.claim: The Medinan and Basran readers and Kufan jurists say the basmala is not part of any surah; it opens them for blessing.
BAGHAWI:1:1/r36.anchor: فذهب قراء المدينة ، والبصرة ، وفقهاء الكوفة ، إلى أنها ليست من فاتحة الكتاب ، ولا من غيرها من السور ،

BAGHAWI:1:1/r37.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI:1:1/r37.speaker: author
BAGHAWI:1:1/r37.claim: Meccan and Kufan readers and most Hijazi jurists count it as part of al-Fatiha only, written to separate surahs.
BAGHAWI:1:1/r37.anchor: وذهب قراء مكة ، والكوفة ، وأكثر فقهاء الحجاز ، إلى أنها من الفاتحة ، وليست من سائر السور .

BAGHAWI:1:1/r38.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI:1:1/r38.speaker: author
BAGHAWI:1:1/r38.claim: Another position, held by al-Thawri, Ibn al-Mubarak, and al-Shafiʿi in one view, counts it in al-Fatiha and every surah except al-Tawba because it is written like the Qur'an in the codex.
BAGHAWI:1:1/r38.anchor: وهو قول الثوري ، و ابن المبارك ، و الشافعي - في قول لأنها كتبت في المصحف بخط سائر القرآن .

BAGHAWI:1:1/r39.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI:1:1/r39.speaker: author
BAGHAWI:1:1/r39.claim: All agree al-Fatiha has seven verses: those counting the basmala begin the final verse at “the path of those”; those excluding it begin the first at “praise be to God” and the last at “not those angered.”
BAGHAWI:1:1/r39.anchor: واتفقوا على أن الفاتحة سبع آيات ، والآية الأولى عند من يعدها من الفاتحة ( بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم )

BAGHAWI:1:1/r40.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI:1:1/r40.speaker: author
BAGHAWI:1:1/r40.claim: Those who count the basmala as part of al-Fatiha and the surahs cite its writing in the codex in the same script as Qur'anic text.
BAGHAWI:1:1/r40.anchor: واحتج من جعلها من الفاتحة ، ومن السور ، بأنها كتبت في المصحف بخط القرآن .

BAGHAWI:1:1/r41.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI:1:1/r41.speaker: ابن عباس
BAGHAWI:1:1/r41.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas, through Saʿid ibn Jubayr, identifies the basmala as the seventh verse of the seven oft-repeated, saying God reserved it for this community; it supports counting it in al-Fatiha.
BAGHAWI:1:1/r41.anchor: قال أبي وقرأها علي سعيد بن جبير حتى ختمها ثم قال : " بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم " الآية السابعة . قال سعيد : قرأها علي ابن عباس

BAGHAWI:1:1/r42.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI:1:1/r42.speaker: أنس بن مالك
BAGHAWI:1:1/r42.claim: Anas reports that Abu Bakr, ʿUmar, and ʿUthman did not recite the basmala when beginning prayer, evidence for excluding it from al-Fatiha.
BAGHAWI:1:1/r42.anchor: عن أنس بن مالك رضي الله عنه أنه قال " قمت وراء أبي بكر الصديق ، وعمر بن الخطاب ، وعثمان بن عفان

BAGHAWI:1:1/r43.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI:1:1/r43.speaker: ابن عباس
BAGHAWI:1:1/r43.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas says the Prophet recognized the end of a surah only when “In the name of God, the Compassionate, the Merciful” was revealed.
