IBNASHUR:1:1/r15.claim: Umm means the origin or source of a thing, which explains the title Umm al-Qurʾān.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r15.anchor: ووجه تسميتها أم القرآن أن الأم يطلق على أصل الشيء ومنشئه

IBNASHUR:1:1/r16.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r16.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:1/r16.claim: One explanation of Umm al-Qurʾān is that Fātiha begins the Qur’an and is therefore like a mother as origin and source of what follows.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r16.anchor: أنها مبدؤه ومفتتحه فكأنها أصله ومنشؤه

IBNASHUR:1:1/r17.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r17.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:1/r17.claim: A second explanation is that Fātiha gathers the Qur’an’s three central aims: praise, commands and prohibitions, and promise and warning; the rest elaborates them.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r17.anchor: أنها تشتمل محتوياتها على أنواع مقاصد القرآن وهي ثلاثة أنواع

IBNASHUR:1:1/r18.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r18.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:1/r18.claim: Commands and prohibitions guide people toward well-being in both abodes; knowing the divine Commander and hoping for reward while fearing punishment complete the rationale for the Qur’an’s central aims.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r18.anchor: ولما توقفت الأوامر والنواهي على معرفة الآمر وأنه الله الواجب وجوده خالق الخلق

IBNASHUR:1:1/r19.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r19.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:1/r19.claim: A third explanation is that Fātiha compresses all Qur’anic theoretical knowledge and practical rulings, including creed, prophecy, admonition, stories, worship, transactions, ethics, and legal manners.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r19.anchor: أنها تشتمل معانيها على جملة معاني القرآن من الحكم النظرية والأحكام العملية

IBNASHUR:1:1/r20.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r20.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:1/r20.claim: Its phrases map onto those aims: praise covers divine perfection, Lord of the worlds divine acts, the merciful names legislation, Master of Judgment the Hereafter, worship and aid religion, and guidance human conduct and past peoples.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r20.anchor: يشمل أصول التشريع الراجعة للرحمة بالمكلفين

IBNASHUR:1:1/r21.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r21.speaker: عز الدين بن عبد السلام
IBNASHUR:1:1/r21.claim: Ibn ʿAbd al-Salām distinguishes outward bodily practice as Sharia from inward heart practice as reality; worship expresses Sharia and seeking help expresses reality, together establishing servitude.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r21.anchor: { فإياك نعبد } شريعة { وإياك نستعين } حقيقة

IBNASHUR:1:1/r22.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r22.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:1/r22.claim: The path of those favored points to the exemplary past of communities and individuals; the final phrase evokes stories and details of misguided nations recounted in the Qur’an.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r22.anchor: يشير إلى أحوال الأمم والأفراد الماضية الفاضلة

IBNASHUR:1:1/r23.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r23.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:1/r23.claim: Fātiha gives the reciter a general grasp of the Qur’an and invites fuller study according to capacity; this is why it is recited in every prayer rakʿa.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r23.anchor: ولأجل هذا فرضت قراءة الفاتحة في كل ركعة من الصلاة حرصا على التذكر لما في مطاويها

IBNASHUR:1:1/r24.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r24.speaker: أبو سعيد ابن المعلى
IBNASHUR:1:1/r24.claim: In al-Bukhari, the Prophet identifies al-Ḥamdu lillāh as the seven oft-repeated verses and the mighty Qur’an given to him.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r24.anchor: أن رسول الله قال الحمد لله رب العالمين هي السبع المثاني والقرآن العظيم الذي أوتيته

IBNASHUR:1:1/r25.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r25.speaker: الحسن البصري
IBNASHUR:1:1/r25.claim: Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī dissents from the seven-verse count and says Fātiha has eight verses.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r25.anchor: إلا الحسن البصري فقال هي ثمان آيات

IBNASHUR:1:1/r26.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r26.speaker: الحسين الجعفي
IBNASHUR:1:1/r26.claim: Al-Ḥusayn al-Juʿfī is reported to count six verses in Fātiha.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r26.anchor: الحسين{[2]} الجعفي فقال هي ست آيات

IBNASHUR:1:1/r27.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r27.speaker: بعض الناس
IBNASHUR:1:1/r27.claim: An unspecified group is reported to count nine verses; that count requires excluding the basmala and combining two other verse units.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r27.anchor: وقال بعض الناس تسع آيات ويتعين حينئذ كون البسملة ليست من الفاتحة

IBNASHUR:1:1/r28.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r28.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:1/r28.claim: Mathānī has several possible morphological analyses; all derive from pairing a second with a first, and the verse is called repeated because it is recited in every rakʿa.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r28.anchor: ووجه الوصف به أن تلك الآيات تثنى في كل ركعة كذا في الكشاف

IBNASHUR:1:1/r29.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r29.speaker: عمر بن الخطاب
IBNASHUR:1:1/r29.claim: A view attributed to ʿUmar says the verses are repeated because another sura is joined to them in each rakʿa; Ibn ʿĀshūr considers this sound.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r29.anchor: وهو مأثور عن عمر بن الخطاب

IBNASHUR:1:1/r30.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r30.speaker: عائشة
IBNASHUR:1:1/r30.claim: A sound hadith from ʿĀʾisha says prayers were first prescribed as two rakʿas, then travel prayer remained so while resident prayer was lengthened; Ibn ʿĀshūr uses this to explain the title.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r30.anchor: فإن الصلوات فرضت ركعتين ثم أقرت صلاة السفر وأطيلت صلاة الحضر

IBNASHUR:1:1/r31.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r31.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:1/r31.claim: Another view takes mathānī as repetition in prayer generally, supported by Arabic use of dual forms for repeated action and by the Qur’an’s recurrent stories and themes.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r31.anchor: وقيل لأنها تثنى في الصلاة أي تكرر فتكون التثنية بمعنى التكرير

IBNASHUR:1:1/r32.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r32.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:1/r32.claim: The claim that Fātiha is called mathānī because it descended twice, in Mecca and Medina, is very remote: the sura is agreed to be Meccan, making a second descent pointless.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r32.anchor: وقيل سميت المثاني لأنها ثنيت في النزول فنزلت بمكة ثم نزلت في المدينة وهذا قول بعيد جدا

IBNASHUR:1:1/r33.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r33.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:1/r33.claim: Fātiha opens the suras as a preface to a speech or book, while its summary of Qur’anic aims makes it a rhetorically apt introduction.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r33.anchor: وهذه السورة وضعت في أول السور لأنها تنزل منها منزل ديباجة الخطبة أو الكتاب

IBNASHUR:1:1/r34.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r34.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:1/r34.claim: The majority agree Fātiha is Meccan; the author’s preferred chronology is al-ʿAlaq, then al-Muddaththir, then Fātiha.

IBNASHUR:1:1/r35.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r35.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:1/r35.claim: Other accounts place Sūrat Nūn wa-l-Qalam and al-Muzzammil before Fātiha.

IBNASHUR:1:1/r36.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r36.speaker: بعضهم
IBNASHUR:1:1/r36.claim: Some say Fātiha was the first complete sura revealed, in contrast to al-Qalam, which they regard as having come in fragments.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r36.anchor: وقال بعضهم هي أول سورة نزلت كاملة

IBNASHUR:1:1/r37.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r37.speaker: بعض العلماء
IBNASHUR:1:1/r37.claim: Some scholars conclude Fātiha descended when prayer became obligatory, so Muslims recited it in prayer from the outset.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r37.anchor: وقد حقق بعض العلماء أنها نزلت عند فرض الصلاة فقرأ المسلمون بها في الصلاة عند فرضها

IBNASHUR:1:1/r38.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r38.speaker: جابر بن زيد
IBNASHUR:1:1/r38.claim: A report attributed to Jābir ibn Zayd places Fātiha fifth in the order of sura revelation.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r38.anchor: وقد عدت في رواية عن جابر بن زيد السورة الخامسة في ترتيب نزول السور

IBNASHUR:1:1/r39.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r39.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:1/r39.claim: Its later revelation does not conflict with its first position: once enough Qur’an existed to form a Book, Fātiha was revealed as its preface.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r39.anchor: ولا يناكد ذلك نزولها بعد سور أخرى لمصلحة اقتضت سبقها قبل أن يتجمع من القرآن مقدار

IBNASHUR:1:1/r40.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r40.speaker: أبو هريرة
IBNASHUR:1:1/r40.claim: The Ṣaḥīḥayn report has God divide the prayer between Himself and the servant, answering each recited passage from praise through the request for guidance.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r40.anchor: قسمت الصلاة نصفين بيني وبين عبدي فنصفها لي ونصفها لعبدي ولعبدي ما سأل

IBNASHUR:1:1/r41.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r41.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:1/r41.claim: This report confirms seven verses arranged as three, one, and three.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r41.anchor: فهن ثلاث ثم واحدة ثم ثلاث

IBNASHUR:1:1/r42.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r42.speaker: أهل المدينة
IBNASHUR:1:1/r42.claim: Medinan verse-counting does not count the basmala and treats anʿamta ʿalayhim as a separate verse.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r42.anchor: فعند أهل المدينة لا تعد البسملة آية

IBNASHUR:1:1/r43.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r43.speaker: أهل مكة وأهل الكوفة
IBNASHUR:1:1/r43.claim: Meccan and Kufan counting treats the basmala as a verse and anʿamta ʿalayhim as part of the following verse.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r43.anchor: وعند أهل مكة وأهل الكوفة تعد البسملة آية

IBNASHUR:1:1/r44.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r44.speaker: الحسن البصري
IBNASHUR:1:1/r44.claim: Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī counts both the basmala and anʿamta ʿalayhim as separate verses.

IBNASHUR:1:1/r45.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r45.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:1/r45.claim: Basmala is a coined noun formed by blending letters from bismi and Allāh; naḥt creates a compact expression from a frequently spoken phrase.

IBNASHUR:1:1/r46.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r46.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:1/r46.claim: Arabic used blending for ambiguous affiliations, such as ʿabshamī from ʿAbd Shams; later speakers extended the method to shorten common phrases.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r46.anchor: كما قالوا في النسبة إلى عبد شمس عبشمي خشية الالتباس بالنسب إلى عبد أو إلى شمس

IBNASHUR:1:1/r47.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r47.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:1/r47.claim: Poets al-Rāʿī and ʿUmar ibn Abī Rabīʿa attest basmala as a verb for saying bismillah; common usage extended it to the full phrase despite omitted letters.

IBNASHUR:1:1/r48.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r48.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:1/r48.claim: Arabic forms the regular verbal noun basmala and the active participle from basmala; no passive participle is attested.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r48.anchor: فشاع قولهم بسمل في معنى قال بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم

IBNASHUR:1:1/r49.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r49.speaker: المطرز
IBNASHUR:1:1/r49.claim: Al-Muṭarriz lists coined verbs for formulae including basmala, sabḥala, ḥayʿala, ḥawqala, ḥamdala, halala, jaʿala, ṭayqala, and damʿaza.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r49.anchor: الأفعالُ التي نحتت من أسمائها سبعة

IBNASHUR:1:1/r50.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r50.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:1/r50.claim: Muslims agree the basmala is Qur’anic because it occurs in Solomon’s letter; beginning important acts with it is also established, though the cited hadith is described as ḥasan and is not in the Sunan or Mustadrak.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r50.anchor: هو لفظ قرآني لأنه جزء آية

IBNASHUR:1:1/r51.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r51.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:1/r51.claim: The report that any important matter begun without the basmala is cut off is described as ḥasan, though major Sunan and Mustadrak compilers did not include it.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r51.anchor: كل أمر ذي بال لا يبدأ فيه بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم فهو أقطع

IBNASHUR:1:1/r52.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r52.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:1/r52.claim: Most scholars say early muṣḥaf scribes wrote the basmala at every sura except Barāʾa; its presence at Fātiha’s beginning is undisputed but is not itself a sura divider.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r52.anchor: وقال الجمهور إن البسملة رسمها الذين كتبوا المصاحف في أوائل السور ما عدا سورة براءة

IBNASHUR:1:1/r53.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r53.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:1/r53.claim: The dispute concerns whether Qur’anic status recurs at sura openings, not whether the basmala is Qur’an at all; Ibn Rushd al-Ḥafīd makes this distinction.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r53.anchor: كما أشار إليه ابن رشد الحفيد

IBNASHUR:1:1/r54.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r54.speaker: مالك والأوزاعي وفقهاء المدينة والشام والبصرة
IBNASHUR:1:1/r54.claim: Mālik, al-Awzāʿī, and jurists of Medina, Syria, and Basra hold that the basmala is not a verse at sura openings, though it is part of the verse in Sūrat al-Naml.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r54.anchor: إلى أنها ليست بآية من أوائل السور لكنها جزء آية من سورة النمل

IBNASHUR:1:1/r55.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r55.speaker: الشافعي وأحمد وإسحاق وأبو ثور
IBNASHUR:1:1/r55.claim: One view of al-Shāfiʿī, Aḥmad, Isḥāq, Abū Thawr, and most Meccan and Kufan jurists counts it as a verse at the start of Fātiha only.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r55.anchor: إلى أنها آية في أول سورة الفاتحة خاصة

IBNASHUR:1:1/r56.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r56.speaker: عبد الله بن المبارك والشافعي
IBNASHUR:1:1/r56.claim: Ibn al-Mubārak and al-Shāfiʿī’s view judged more authentic by Ibn ʿĀshūr count it as a verse at the beginning of every sura.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r56.anchor: إلى أنها آية من كل سورة

IBNASHUR:1:1/r57.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r57.speaker: أبو حنيفة
IBNASHUR:1:1/r57.claim: No direct statement is transmitted from Abū Ḥanīfa; al-Zamakhsharī inferred that he did not regard it as part of the suras, an inference Ibn ʿĀshūr accepts.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r57.anchor: عن أبي حنيفة من فقهاء الكوفة فيها شيء

IBNASHUR:1:1/r58.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r58.speaker: الباقلاني
IBNASHUR:1:1/r58.claim: Al-Bāqillānī argues proof of Qur’anic status would require mass transmission, which would preclude disagreement, or solitary reports, which would make the Qur’an probabilistic and invite claims of textual alteration.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r58.anchor: لو كانت التسمية من القرآن لكان طريق إثباتها إما التواتر أو الآحاد

IBNASHUR:1:1/r59.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r59.speaker: ابن العربي
IBNASHUR:1:1/r59.claim: Ibn al-ʿArabī adds that disagreement itself shows it is not Qur’an, since the Qur’an is not disputed.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r59.anchor: يكفيك أنها ليست من القرآن الاختلاف فيها

IBNASHUR:1:1/r60.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r60.speaker: عبد الوهاب
IBNASHUR:1:1/r60.claim: ʿAbd al-Wahhāb argues the Prophet conveyed Qur’an uniformly and publicly; had the basmala belonged to Fātiha he would have made that clear, excluding secret or missing Qur’an.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r60.anchor: فلو كانت البسملة من الحمد لبيّنها رسول الله بيانا شافيا

IBNASHUR:1:1/r61.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r61.speaker: الغزالي
IBNASHUR:1:1/r61.claim: Al-Ghazālī replies that denying the basmala’s Qur’anic status faces the same transmission dilemma; its written Qur’anic script weakens the presumption of non-Qur’anic status, so proof is needed.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r61.anchor: إن كون التسمية مكتوبة بخط القرآن يوهن كونها ليست من القرآن

IBNASHUR:1:1/r62.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r62.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:1/r62.claim: Ibn ʿĀshūr rejects al-Ghazālī and al-Rāzī’s reply as question-begging: it ultimately relies on the basmala’s written placement, which requires separate examination.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r62.anchor: إذ قد صار مرجع استدلال الغزالي وفخر الدين إلى رسم البسملة في المصاحف

IBNASHUR:1:1/r63.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r63.speaker: أبو هريرة
IBNASHUR:1:1/r63.claim: In the Muwattaʾ report of God dividing prayer, the response begins after the servant says al-ḥamdu lillāh; Mālik uses the omission of the basmala as evidence.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r63.anchor: ووجه الدليل منه أنه لم يذكر بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم

IBNASHUR:1:1/r64.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r64.speaker: أبي بن كعب
IBNASHUR:1:1/r64.claim: In a Muwattaʾ and Ṣaḥīḥayn report, the Prophet asks Ubayy how he opens prayer; Ubayy recites from al-ḥamdu lillāh through the end without the basmala.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r64.anchor: فقرأت { الحمد لله رب العالمين } حتى أتيت

IBNASHUR:1:1/r65.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r65.speaker: أنس بن مالك
IBNASHUR:1:1/r65.claim: Anas reports that the Prophet, Abū Bakr, and ʿUmar began recitation with al-ḥamdu lillāh and did not mention the basmala at the beginning or end.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r65.anchor: فكانوا يستفتحون بالحمد لله رب العالمين لا يذكرون

IBNASHUR:1:1/r66.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r66.speaker: عائشة
IBNASHUR:1:1/r66.claim: ʿĀʾisha reports that the Prophet began prayer with the takbīr and began recitation with al-ḥamdu lillāh.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r66.anchor: كان رسول الله يستفتح الصلاة بالتكبير والقراءة بالحمد الله رب العالمين

IBNASHUR:1:1/r67.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r67.speaker: عبد الله بن مغفل
IBNASHUR:1:1/r67.claim: Ibn Mughaffal reports that he heard none of the Prophet, Abū Bakr, ʿUmar, or ʿUthmān say the basmala, and advises beginning with al-ḥamdu lillāh.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r67.anchor: عن عبد الله بن مغفل قال

IBNASHUR:1:1/r68.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r68.speaker: أهل المدينة
IBNASHUR:1:1/r68.claim: The author calls continuous Medinan mosque practice decisive: the Prophet, caliphs, Companions, and scholars did not recite the basmala aloud in public prayers, a practice he considers mass-transmitted.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r68.anchor: فإن المسجد النبوي من وقت نزول الوحي إلى زمن مالك صلى فيه رسول الله والخلفاء الراشدون

IBNASHUR:1:1/r69.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r69.speaker: عائشة
IBNASHUR:1:1/r69.claim: Ibn ʿĀshūr adds a reliable marfūʿ report from ʿĀʾisha on the first revelation: the angel said Read, then recited al-ʿAlaq without first saying the basmala.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r69.anchor: فلم يقل فقال لي بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم

IBNASHUR:1:1/r70.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r70.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:1/r70.claim: An Arabic-style argument against making the basmala a Fātiha verse is the close repetition of al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm in a short passage, which weakens eloquence.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r70.anchor: وذلك يوجب أن يتكرر لفظان وهما

IBNASHUR:1:1/r71.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r71.speaker: الرازي
IBNASHUR:1:1/r71.claim: Al-Rāzī answers that Qur’anic repetition can emphasize meaning and that affirming God’s mercy is especially important.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r71.anchor: إن التكرار لأجل التأكيد كثير في القرآن وإن تأكيد كونه تعالى رحمانا رحيما من أعظم المهمات

IBNASHUR:1:1/r72.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r72.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:1/r72.claim: Ibn ʿĀshūr rejects the emphasis reply: the context has no reason for repetition, certainty of mercy is not denied, and close repetition is disfavored in eloquent speech.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r72.anchor: ولأن شأن التوكيد اللفظي أن يقترن فيه اللفظان بلا فصل

IBNASHUR:1:1/r73.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r73.speaker: البيضاوي
IBNASHUR:1:1/r73.claim: Al-Bayḍāwī says repeating the two attributes explains why God deserves praise; al-Salkūtī presents this as a reply to the Hanafi repetition objection.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r73.anchor: وأجاب البيضاوي بأن نكتة التكرير هنا

IBNASHUR:1:1/r74.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r74.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:1/r74.claim: Ibn ʿĀshūr finds al-Bayḍāwī’s answer inadequate: if the repeated attributes are needed to explain praise, removing them from the basmala would avoid repetition more directly.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r74.anchor: فدفع التكرير يقتضي تجريد البسملة التي في أول الفاتحة من هاتين الصفتين

IBNASHUR:1:1/r75.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r75.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:1/r75.claim: For the view that the basmala opens every sura as a verse, Ibn ʿĀshūr prefers the argument that identical openings everywhere violate the rhetorical art of varying openings.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r75.anchor: أن تكون فواتح سور القرآن كلها متماثلة وذلك مما لا يحمد في كلام البلغاء

IBNASHUR:1:1/r76.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r76.speaker: أبو هريرة
IBNASHUR:1:1/r76.claim: A report that Fātiha has seven verses, the first being the basmala, is cited for the Shāfiʿī position; it appears in al-Ṭabarānī, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqī, below Ṣaḥīḥ status.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r76.anchor: ما روى أبو هريرة أن النبيء عليه الصلاة والسلام قال

IBNASHUR:1:1/r77.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r77.speaker: أم سلمة
IBNASHUR:1:1/r77.claim: A report says the Prophet recited Fātiha and counted the basmala with al-ḥamdu lillāh as a verse; al-Ṭaḥāwī objects that Ibn Abī Mulayka did not hear Umm Salama, and another report from him conflicts.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r77.anchor: وقول أم سلمة قرأ رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم الفاتحة

IBNASHUR:1:1/r78.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r78.speaker: زكرياء شيخ الإسلام
IBNASHUR:1:1/r78.claim: Zakariyyāʾ notes the cited wording is not the transmitted wording; other versions only show that the basmala is a verse by itself, not that it belongs to Fātiha.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r78.anchor: على أن شيخ الإسلام زكرياء قد صرح

IBNASHUR:1:1/r79.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r79.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:1/r79.claim: Agreement that everything between the muṣḥaf’s covers is Qur’an proves the basmala is Qur’anic, which is uncontested; it does not prove it must be recited at each written opening.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r79.anchor: فالجواب أنه لا يقتضي إلا أن البسملة قرآن وهذا لا نزاع فيه

IBNASHUR:1:1/r80.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r80.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:1/r80.claim: If early Muslims also wrote sura names and Meccan or Medinan labels, writing is no proof that the basmala belongs at each opening; the single-color ink evidence defeats a colored-ink theory.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r80.anchor: المشاهد في مصاحف السلف أن حبرها بلون واحد

IBNASHUR:1:1/r81.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r81.speaker: أنس بن مالك
IBNASHUR:1:1/r81.claim: Anas’s report in al-Bukhārī that the Prophet elongated the basmala does not establish verse status: the reciting and elongating pronouns refer to Anas, who gives it as a familiar example.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r81.anchor: وإنما جاء بالبسملة على وجه التمثيل لكيفية القراءة لشهرة البسملة

IBNASHUR:1:1/r82.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r82.speaker: أنس بن مالك
IBNASHUR:1:1/r82.claim: Ibn al-Mubārak and al-Shāfiʿī cite Muslim’s report that the Prophet recited the basmala before Sūrat al-Kawthar after God revealed it.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r82.anchor: فقرأ بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم { إنا أعطيناك الكوثر }

IBNASHUR:1:1/r83.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r83.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:1/r83.claim: Ibn ʿĀshūr argues this report does not say the basmala is part of the sura: it can be the opening formula, understood as an omitted request for refuge in God’s name.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r83.anchor: بل افتتح بها عند إرادة القراءة لأنها تغني عن الاستعاذة

IBNASHUR:1:1/r84.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r84.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:1/r84.claim: If this interpretation is refused, Anas contradicts his other report that he never heard the Prophet say the basmala in prayer, so the reports would conflict fatally.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r84.anchor: لزم اضطراب أنس في روايته اضطرابا يوجب سقوطها

IBNASHUR:1:1/r85.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r85.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:1/r85.claim: Ibn ʿĀshūr’s preferred account is that the basmala was written to separate suras, make the muṣḥaf’s transitions fitting, and avoid a separator made of non-Qur’anic wording.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r85.anchor: أنها كتبت للفصل بين السور ليكون الفصل مناسبا لابتداء المصحف

IBNASHUR:1:1/r86.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r86.speaker: عثمان بن عفان
IBNASHUR:1:1/r86.claim: In a report authenticated by al-Tirmidhī, Ibn ʿAbbās asks ʿUthmān why al-Anfāl and Barāʾa were joined without a basmala; ʿUthmān says their similar subject and the Prophet’s silence led him to join them.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r86.anchor: وكانت براءة من آخر ما أنزل من القرآن وكانت قصتها شبيهة بقصتها

IBNASHUR:1:1/r87.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r87.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:1/r87.claim: Ibn ʿĀshūr infers that the basmala was added between suras only when the Qur’an was assembled in ʿUthmān’s single muṣḥaf, not in Zayd’s separate sheets under Abū Bakr.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r87.anchor: إلا حين جمع القرآن في مصحف واحد زمن عثمان

IBNASHUR:1:1/r88.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r88.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:1/r88.claim: Readers agree to say the basmala when beginning any sura except Barāʾa, regardless of whether their juristic school counts it as a verse.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r88.anchor: فإن القراء اتفقوا على قراءة البسملة عند الشروع في قراءة سورة من أولها غير براءة

IBNASHUR:1:1/r89.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r89.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:1/r89.claim: Readers who do not count it as a verse may recite it at a sura opening as a recommended act of blessing that imitates the muṣḥaf scribes; this practice does not prove their legal position.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r89.anchor: فتكون قراءتهم البسملة أمرا مستحبا للتأسي في القراءة بما فعله الصحابة الكاتبون للمصحف

IBNASHUR:1:1/r90.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r90.speaker: ورش وابن عامر وأبو عمرو وحمزة ويعقوب وخلف
IBNASHUR:1:1/r90.claim: Warsh in his best-known transmission, Ibn ʿĀmir, Abū ʿAmr, Ḥamza, Yaʿqūb, and Khalaf omit the basmala between suras; they treat its script as marking the beginning, not separation.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r90.anchor: لا يبسملون بين السورتين وذلك يعلل بأن التشبه بفعل كتاب المصحف خاص بالابتداء

IBNASHUR:1:1/r91.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r91.speaker: قالون وابن كثير وعاصم والكسائي وأبو جعفر
IBNASHUR:1:1/r91.claim: Qālūn, Ibn Kathīr, ʿĀṣim, al-Kisāʾī, and Abū Jaʿfar recite the basmala between suras except between al-Anfāl and Barāʾa, following inherited recitation practice.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r91.anchor: يبسملون بين السورتين سوى ما بين الأنفال وبراءة

IBNASHUR:1:1/r92.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r92.speaker: مؤرج السدوسي
IBNASHUR:1:1/r92.claim: Al-Jāḥiẓ tells of al-Muʾarrij al-Sadūsī restoring the basmala before Barāʾa after hearing a phrase about the Commander returning rights; if true, Ibn ʿĀshūr treats it as a joke.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r92.anchor: فرجع مؤرج إلى مصحفه فرد على براءة بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم

IBNASHUR:1:1/r93.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r93.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:1/r93.claim: Recitation traditions do not settle juristic rulings: readers transmit how teachers read, while prayer practice follows legal reasoning; regional alignment between readers and jurists reflects shared local learning.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r93.anchor: وليست مذاهب القراء بمعدودة من أدلة الفقه

IBNASHUR:1:1/r94.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r94.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:1/r94.claim: Although Ibn ʿĀshūr follows Mālik’s view that the basmala is not a verse at the start of al-Baqara, he explains it here because earlier commentators made this customary.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r94.anchor: كان حقا علينا أن لا نتعرض لتفسيرها هنا وأن نرجئه إلى الكلام على قوله تعالى في سورة النمل

IBNASHUR:1:1/r95.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r95.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:1/r95.claim: The governed element after bi is omitted, here understood as I read; omission is conventional because the basmala accompanies the beginning of good deeds and the intended action supplies the cue.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r95.anchor: متعلق المجرور في { بسم الله } محذوف تقديره هنا

IBNASHUR:1:1/r96.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r96.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:1/r96.claim: The phrase is a mobile adverbial dependent on an omitted verb, not a stable predicative adverb; the specific action, rather than a generic begin, is understood.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r96.anchor: فالمجرور ظرف لغو معمول للفعل المحذوف ومتعلق به وليس ظرفا مستقرا

IBNASHUR:1:1/r97.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r97.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:1/r97.claim: The omitted verb should name the action being begun, so all of that action is associated with God’s blessing; a generic begin would cover only its first instant.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r97.anchor: هي الفعل المشروع فيه المبدوء بالبسملة

IBNASHUR:1:1/r98.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r98.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:1/r98.claim: Qur’anic and Arabic examples show context supplies omitted actions: Pharaoh’s magicians act by his might, while wedding greetings and travel formulas omit their intended verbs.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r98.anchor: قول سحرة فرعون عند شروعهم في السحر

IBNASHUR:1:1/r99.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r99.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:1/r99.claim: The omitted verb precedes the basmala as in normal word order; al-Zamakhsharī’s postposed estimate, which could suggest restriction, is unjustified because no exclusivity is intended.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r99.anchor: وإذ قد كان المتعلق محذوفا تعين أن يقدر في موضعه متقدما على المتعلق به

IBNASHUR:1:1/r100.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r100.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:1/r100.claim: Omitting the action makes the formula concise and reusable before any deed without altering Qur’anic wording; omitted elements differ from stable adverbs whose governors are never expressed.

IBNASHUR:1:1/r101.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r101.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:1/r101.claim: The bāʾ means association or accompaniment, also including attachment; this is its commonest sense and offers a fuller blessing than construing it as an instrument.

IBNASHUR:1:1/r102.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r102.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:1/r102.claim: The noun ism denotes a word assigned to a particular concrete or abstract entity, whether an individual or a kind.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r102.anchor: والاسم لفظ جعل دالا على ذات حسية أو معنوية بشخصها أو نوعها

IBNASHUR:1:1/r103.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r103.speaker: أئمة البصرة
IBNASHUR:1:1/r103.claim: Basran grammarians derive ism from sumūw, elevation, since names often denote things esteemed; its original form had a final weak wāw deleted for ease or frequent use.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r103.anchor: وجعله أئمة البصرة مشتقا من السمو وهو الرفعة

IBNASHUR:1:1/r104.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r104.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:1/r104.claim: The forms asmāʾ, asāmī, sumayy, and sammaytu support a weak final wāw; Ibn ʿĀshūr says these inflections make the Basran morphology stronger.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r104.anchor: وأن الفعل منه سمَّيْت ، وهي حجج

IBNASHUR:1:1/r105.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r105.speaker: أبو خالد القناني
IBNASHUR:1:1/r105.claim: A rajaz line by Abū Khālid al-Qanānī uses suman for name; Ibn Yaʿīsh doubts it proves the form, while ʿAbd al-Ḥakīm appeals to its written ya.

IBNASHUR:1:1/r106.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r106.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:1/r106.claim: Ibn ʿĀshūr favors the Basran derivation on morphological evidence; spelling does not establish pronunciation, while the Kufan account has stronger semantic motivation.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r106.anchor: ورأي البصريين أرجح من ناحية تصاريف هذا اللفظ

IBNASHUR:1:1/r107.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r107.speaker: الكوفيون
IBNASHUR:1:1/r107.claim: Kufan grammarians derive ism from wasm, mark, because a name is a sign; they say initial wāw was dropped and hamzat al-waṣl preserves the form.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r107.anchor: وذهب الكوفيون إلى أن أصله وسم بكسر الواو لأنه من السمة وهي العلامة

IBNASHUR:1:1/r108.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r108.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:1/r108.claim: The Kufan counterargument that Basran forms arose through metathesis is unlikely: it violates the default and would not persist across inflections; morphology reveals original and altered letters.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r108.anchor: وأجيب عن ذلك بأن هذا بعيد لأنه خلاف الأصل وبأن القلب لا يلزم الكلمة في سائر تصاريفها

IBNASHUR:1:1/r109.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r109.speaker: ابن حزم
IBNASHUR:1:1/r109.claim: Ibn Ḥazm calls both derivations false inventions and ism a non-derived word; Ibn ʿĀshūr condemns this as reckless and cites the instruction to ask learned people.

IBNASHUR:1:1/r110.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r110.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:1/r110.claim: Bismillah says in the name of God, not by God, because it marks the deed as monotheistic practice and associates it with God’s name rather than invoking His essence.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r110.anchor: وإنما أقحم لفظ اسم مضافا إلى علم الجلالة

IBNASHUR:1:1/r111.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r111.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:1/r111.claim: In sacrifices and actions seeking blessing or aid, scripture uses the name of God and in the name of your Lord; the name accompanies the deed, while by God would imply appeal to divine power.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r111.anchor: وكالأفعال التي يقصد بها التيمن والتبرك وحصول المعونة

IBNASHUR:1:1/r112.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r112.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:1/r112.claim: Commands to glorify God’s name mean to say Glory be to God, whereas commands to glorify Him mean declaring His essence and attributes free of imperfection.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r112.anchor: أَمْرٌ بتنزيه ذاته وصفاته عن النقائص

IBNASHUR:1:1/r113.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r113.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:1/r113.claim: God’s name functions like a tribe’s identifying brand or an army’s recognized slogan, signaling affiliation with the one Lord.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r113.anchor: فاستعمال لفظ الاسم في هذا بمنزلة استعمال سمات الإبل عند القبائل

IBNASHUR:1:1/r114.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r114.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:1/r114.claim: The full basmala means: I read in a way accompanied by the blessing of this blessed name.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r114.anchor: أقرأ قراءة ملابسة لبركة هذا الاسم المبارك

IBNASHUR:1:1/r115.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r115.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:1/r115.claim: Arabic may use ism for the named thing itself, insert it redundantly to mean peace, or use it as a metonym for proving a referent exists. None explains the basmala.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r115.anchor: فهذه اطلاقات أخرى ليس ذكر اسم الله في البسملة من قبيلها

IBNASHUR:1:1/r116.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r116.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:1/r116.claim: Ibn ʿĀshūr conjectures that the elongated bāʾ was first written in Solomon’s letter to mark its opening, then copied as a sign of a new discourse at sura beginnings.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r116.anchor: والذي يظهر لي أن الصحابة لما كتبوا المصحف طولوها في سورة النمل

IBNASHUR:1:1/r117.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r117.speaker: البيضاوي
IBNASHUR:1:1/r117.claim: Al-Bayḍāwī says the supplicant names God’s essence to show aid is sought from Him, then invokes al-Raḥmān for His favors and al-Raḥīm for further reasons discussed later.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r117.anchor: يذكر علم الذات إشارة إلى استحقاقه

IBNASHUR:1:1/r118.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r118.speaker: محمد عبده
IBNASHUR:1:1/r118.claim: Muḥammad ʿAbduh proposes that the Islamic opening counters Christian formulas invoking Father, Son, and Holy Spirit: one God’s multiple names are attributes, not multiple beings; Ibn ʿĀshūr calls it subtle if the premise is true.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r118.anchor: فجاءت فاتحة كتاب الإسلام بالرد عليهم موقظة لهم بأن الإله الواحد وإن تعددت أسماؤه

IBNASHUR:1:1/r119.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR:1:1/r119.speaker: author
IBNASHUR:1:1/r119.claim: Ibn ʿĀshūr suspects the formula continues Abrahamic monotheist practice: Abraham invokes the Merciful and the compassionate, and Solomon opens his letter with the basmala, likely inheriting that prophetic tradition.
IBNASHUR:1:1/r119.anchor: والمظنون أن سليمان اقتدى في افتتاح كتابه بالبسملة بسنة موروثة من عهد إبراهيم

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p24/r11.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p24/r11.speaker: هارون العتكي
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p24/r11.claim: Harun al-Ataki's accusative reading of al-hamdu lillahi is cited as evidence that al-hamdu is an absolute object.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p24/r11.anchor: كما احتجوا على أن أصل ) الحمد لله ( أنه منصوب على المفعول المطلق بقراءة هارون العتكي

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p77/r10.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p77/r10.speaker: المازري
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p77/r10.claim: Al-Mazari, citing Makki ibn Abi Talib, says the regional counters did not count the opening basmala as a verse in each surah; they differed only for al-Fatiha.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p77/r10.anchor: قال المازري في شرح البرهان : قال مكي بن أبي طالب قد أجمع أهل العدد من أهل الكوفة والبصرة والمدينة والشام على ترك عد البسملة آية في أول كل سورة

IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p77/r11.author: Ibn ʿĀshūr
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p77/r11.speaker: author
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p77/r11.claim: For al-Fatiha, the Kufan and Meccan counters counted the basmala as a verse, while the Basran, Syrian, and Medinan counters did not.
IBNASHUR-FULL:v1p77/r11.anchor: فعدها آية الكوفي والمكي ولم يعدها آية البصري ولا الشامي ولا المدني

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r1.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r1.speaker: ابن عباس، وموسى بن جعفر عن أبيه، وعلي بن الحسين، وقتادة، وأبو العالية، ومحمد بن يحيى بن حبان
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r1.claim: Ibn Abbas, Musa b. Ja'far from his father, Ali b. al-Husayn, Qatada, Abu al-Aliya and Muhammad b. Yahya b. Habban hold that al-Fatiha is Meccan; 15:87 supports this because al-Hijr is unanimously Meccan.
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r1.anchor: قال ابن عباس ، وموسى بن جعفر عن أبيه ، وعلي بن الحسين ، وقتادة ، وأبو العالية

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r2.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r2.speaker: أبي بن كعب
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r2.claim: Ubayy's report identifies al-Fatiha as the seven oft-repeated; the seven long surahs were revealed some time after al-Hijr, supporting a Meccan dating.
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r2.anchor: وفي حديث أُبَيّ بن كعب أنها السبع المثاني

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r3.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r3.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r3.claim: Prayer became obligatory in Mecca, and no report preserves a Muslim prayer without reciting al-Fatiha; this supports its Meccan origin.
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r3.anchor: ولا خلاف أن فرض الصلاة كان بمكة ، وما حفظ أنها كانت قط

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r4.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r4.speaker: عطاء بن يسار، وسوادة بن زياد، والزهري محمد بن مسلم، وعبد الله بن عبيد بن عمير
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r4.claim: Ata b. Yasar, Sawada b. Ziyad, al-Zuhri and Abd Allah b. Ubayd b. Umayr instead regard al-Fatiha as Medinan.

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r5.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r5.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r5.claim: There is no disagreement that the surah is called Fatihat al-Kitab because its position makes it the opening of the Book.
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r5.anchor: وأما أسماؤها فلا خلاف أنها يقال لها فاتحة الكتاب ، لأن موضعها يعطي ذلك

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r6.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r6.speaker: الحسن بن أبي الحسن
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r6.claim: Hasan b. Abi al-Hasan objects to the title Umm al-Kitab, reserving that name for the lawful and unlawful, as in 3:7.
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r6.anchor: فكره الحسن بن أبي الحسن ذلك وقال

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r7.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r7.speaker: ابن عباس وغيره
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r7.claim: Ibn Abbas and others accept Umm al-Kitab as a name for al-Fatiha.

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r8.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r8.speaker: البخاري
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r8.claim: Al-Bukhari explains the title Umm al-Kitab by al-Fatiha being written first in the codex and recited first in prayer.
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r8.anchor: وقال البخاري : سميت أم الكتاب لأنها يبدأ بكتابتها في المصحف وبقراءتها في الصلاة

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r9.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r9.speaker: ابن سيرين
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r9.claim: Ibn Sirin disliked calling al-Fatiha Umm al-Quran.
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r9.anchor: فكره ذلك ابن سيرين وجوزه جمهور العلماء

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r10.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r10.speaker: جمهور العلماء
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r10.claim: The majority of scholars permit the title Umm al-Quran, contrary to Ibn Sirin's dislike.
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r10.anchor: فكره ذلك ابن سيرين وجوزه جمهور العلماء

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r11.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r11.speaker: يحيى بن يعمر
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r11.claim: Yahya b. Ya'mar analogizes Umm al-Quran to Umm al-Qura for Mecca and Umm Khurasan for Merv.

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r12.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r12.speaker: الحسن بن أبي الحسن
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r12.claim: Hasan b. Abi al-Hasan also gives al-Fatiha the name Umm al-Quran.
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r12.anchor: وقال الحسن بن أبي الحسن : اسمها أم القرآن

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r13.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r13.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r13.claim: One explanation of al-Mathani is that the surah is repeated in every prayer cycle.
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r13.anchor: فقيل سميت بذلك لأنها تثنى في كل ركعة

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r14.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r14.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r14.claim: Another explanation is that al-Fatiha was reserved as a treasure for this community and had not been revealed to anyone before it.
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r14.anchor: وقيل سميت بذلك لأنها استثنيت لهذه الأمة فلم تنزل على أحد قبلها ذخرا لها

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r15.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r15.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم عن أبي بن كعب
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r15.claim: The Prophet told Ubayy that no comparable surah had been revealed in the Torah, Gospel or Qur'an.
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r15.anchor: في حديث أُبَيّ بن كعب «إنها لم ينزل في التوراة ولا في الإنجيل

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r16.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r16.speaker: غير مسمى
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r16.claim: An unnamed report says al-Fatiha is equivalent to two-thirds of the Qur'an.

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r17.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r17.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r17.claim: The reported equivalence may reflect the surah's meanings or be a divine preference not rationally explained; similar equivalences are reported for al-Ikhlas and al-Zalzala.
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r17.anchor: وهذا العدل إما أن يكون في المعاني ، وإما أن يكون تفضيلا من الله تعالى لا يعلل

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r18.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r18.speaker: أنس بن مالك عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r18.claim: Anas reports that the Prophet assigned al-Fatiha thirty more merits than other speech.
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r18.anchor: وروى أنس بن مالك أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم قال

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r19.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r19.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r19.claim: A further Prophetic report assigns twenty merits to saying la ilaha illa Allah and thirty to saying al-hamdu lillahi rabb al-alamin.
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r19.anchor: وورد حديث آخر أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم قال

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r20.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r20.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r20.claim: The merit comparison concerns believers seeking reward: al-hamdu combines praise with the monotheism contained in la ilaha illa Allah, while the latter contains monotheism alone.
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r20.anchor: لأن قوله : { الحمد لله } في ضمنها التوحيد الذي هو معنى لا إله إلا الله ، ففي قوله توحيد وحمد

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r21.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r21.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r21.claim: In their role of warding off unbelief and association, la ilaha illa Allah is superior; the Prophet called it the best statement he and earlier prophets had uttered.
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r21.anchor: أفضل ما قلته أنا والنبيون من قبلي

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r22.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r22.speaker: جعفر بن محمد الصادق
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r22.claim: Ja'far al-Sadiq calls the basmala the crowns of the surahs.
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r22.anchor: روي عن جعفر بن محمد الصادق رضي الله عنه أنه قال : البسملة تيجان السور

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r23.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r23.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r23.claim: When a man cursed Satan in the Prophet's presence, the Prophet said this magnified Satan and instructed him to say the basmala, which makes Satan shrink smaller than a fly.
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r23.anchor: فقال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم «لا تقل ذلك فإنه يتعاظم عنده ولكن قل بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم فإنه يصغر حتى يصير أقل

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r24.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r24.speaker: علي بن الحسين
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r24.claim: Ali b. al-Husayn interprets the turning away in 17:46 when the Lord is mentioned alone as occurring when one says the basmala.
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r24.anchor: وقال علي بن الحسين رضي الله عنه في تفسير قوله تعالى { وإذا ذكرت ربك في القرآن وحده ولوا على أدبارهم نفورا } قال معناه إذا قلت بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r25.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r25.speaker: جابر بن عبد الله عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r25.claim: Jabir says that when he told the Prophet he opened prayer with al-hamdu lillahi rabb al-alamin, the Prophet told him to say the basmala.
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r25.anchor: وروي عن جابر بن عبد الله

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r26.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r26.speaker: أبو هريرة عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r26.claim: Abu Hurayra reports that Gabriel taught the Prophet prayer and recited the basmala aloud.
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r26.anchor: وروى أبو هريرة أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم قال

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r27.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r27.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r27.claim: Ibn Atiyya says that, on their face, the Jabir and Abu Hurayra reports imply the basmala is an ayah of al-Fatiha.
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r27.anchor: وهذان الحديثان يقتضيان أنها آية من الحمد

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r28.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r28.speaker: أبي بن كعب عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r28.claim: An authentic report has the Prophet ask Ubayy to recite the surah; Ubayy begins with al-hamdu lillahi rabb al-alamin and continues to its end, without the basmala.
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r28.anchor: حديث أبي بن كعب الصحيح إذ قال له النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r29.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r29.speaker: الله تعالى في الحديث القدسي
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r29.claim: The sound hadith qudsi describing prayer as divided between God and the servant quotes the servant beginning with al-hamdu lillahi rabb al-alamin, not the basmala.
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r29.anchor: ويرده الحديث الصحيح بقوله عز وجل { قسمت الصلاة بيني وبين عبدي ، يقول العبد الحمد لله رب العالمين

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r30.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r30.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r30.claim: No record says the Prophet or Abu Bakr, Umar or Uthman recited the basmala in prayer.
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r30.anchor: ويرده أنه لم يحفظ عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم ولا عن أبي بكر ولا عن عمر ولا عثمان رضي الله عنهم أنهم قرؤوا في صلاتهم

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r31.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r31.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r31.claim: The surah is counted as seven verses by consensus, apart from the anomalous report that al-Husayn al-Ju'fi counted six.
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r31.anchor: الإجماع أنها سبع آيات إلا ما روي عن حسين الجعفي أنها ست آيات وهذا شاذ لا يعول عليه

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r32.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r32.speaker: حسين الجعفي
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r32.claim: Al-Husayn al-Ju'fi reportedly counts six verses in al-Fatiha; Ibn Atiyya calls this anomalous and unreliable.
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r32.anchor: إلا ما روي عن حسين الجعفي أنها ست آيات وهذا شاذ لا يعول عليه

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r33.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r33.speaker: عمرو بن عبيد
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r33.claim: Amr b. Ubayd makes iyyaka na'budu a separate verse, yielding eight; Ibn Atiyya also calls this anomalous.
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r33.anchor: روي عن عمرو بن عبيد أنه جعل { إياك نعبد } آية ، فهي على عده ثماني آيات ، وهذا أيضا شاذ

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r34.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r34.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r34.claim: The statement that God gave the Prophet seven oft-repeated verses in 15:87 settles the verse-count question.
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r34.anchor: وقول الله تعالى { ولقد آتيناك سبعا من المثاني } هو الفصل في ذلك

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r35.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r35.speaker: الشافعي
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r35.claim: Al-Shafi'i counts the basmala as a verse of al-Fatiha.
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r35.anchor: والشافعي رحمه الله يعد بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم آية من الحمد

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r36.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r36.speaker: قراء مكة والكوفة
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r36.claim: Many Meccan and Kufan reciters do not count an'amta alayhim as a verse.
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r36.anchor: وكثير من قراء مكة والكوفة لا يعدون { أنعمت عليهم }

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r37.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r37.speaker: مالك، وأبو حنيفة، وجمهور الفقهاء والقراء
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r37.claim: Malik, Abu Hanifa and the majority of jurists and reciters do not count the basmala as a verse.
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r37.anchor: ومالك رحمه الله وأبو حنيفة وجمهور الفقهاء والقراء لا يعدون البسملة آية

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r38.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r38.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r38.claim: If sound, the Jabir and Abu Hurayra reports can be understood as lessons: the Prophet saw them rehearsing prayer outside prayer and taught the basmala for that reason, not because it was a verse.
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r38.anchor: والذي يحتمله عندي حديث جابر وأبي هريرة إذا صحا أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم رأى قراءة جابر وحكايته أمر الصلاة قراءة في غير صلاة

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r39.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r39.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r39.claim: The Prophet did not include the basmala in his exchange with Ubayy because he was identifying the special surah and its virtue, whereas that purpose was absent in the instructional exchanges with Jabir and Abu Hurayra.
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r39.anchor: ولم يفعل ذلك مع أبي لأنه قصد تخصيص السورة ووسمها من الفضل بما لها ، فلم يدخل معها ما ليس منها

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r40.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r40.speaker: ابن المبارك
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r40.claim: Ibn al-Mubarak holds that the basmala is a verse in every surah; Ibn Atiyya calls this an anomalous view rejected by others.
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r40.anchor: وقال ابن المبارك : إن البسملة آية في كل سورة وهذا قول شاذ رد الناس عليه

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r41.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r41.speaker: الشعبي والأعمش
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r41.claim: Al-Sha'bi and al-A'mash report a progression in the Prophet's written basmala: first Bismika Allahumma, then Bismillah, then Bismillah al-Rahman, and after 27:30 the full formula.
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r41.anchor: وروى الشعبي والأعمش أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم كان يكتب

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r42.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r42.speaker: عمرو بن شرحبيل
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r42.claim: Amr b. Shurahbil reports that Gabriel first came to the Prophet saying, “Say: In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Compassionate.”
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r42.anchor: وروى عمرو بن شرحبيل أن جبريل أول ما جاء النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم قال له قل بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r43.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r43.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r43.claim: Ibn Abbas reports that the first thing Gabriel brought down was the basmala.
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r43.anchor: وروي عن ابن عباس أن أول ما نزل به جبريل بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r44.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r44.speaker: خديجة عن ورقة
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r44.claim: In some versions of Khadija's taking the Prophet to Waraqa, Gabriel first tells the Prophet to say the basmala; the Prophet says it, then Gabriel commands him to read, and he replies that he cannot read.
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r44.anchor: وفي بعض طرق حديث خديجة وحملها رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم إلى ورقة

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r45.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r45.speaker: بعض الناس
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r45.claim: Some say the nineteen letters of the basmala correspond one by one to the nineteen keepers of Hell in 74:30, whose repeated basmala gives them strength.

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r46.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r46.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r46.claim: Ibn Atiyya calls the letter-count explanation a playful exegetical conceit, not sound scholarship.
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r46.anchor: وهذه من ملح التفسير وليست من متين العلم

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r47.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r47.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r47.claim: He compares that numerology with claims that the Night of Decree is the twenty-seventh night because of a word in its surah, and that thirty-some angels rushed to record a thirty-some-letter praise formula.
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r47.anchor: وهي نظير قولهم في ليلة القدر :

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r48.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r48.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r48.claim: A similar letter-count claim says thirty-some angels competed to record “Our Lord, to You belongs praise, abundant, good and blessed praise”; Ibn Atiyya presents it as the same sort of numerology.
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r48.anchor: ونظير قولهم في عدد الملائكة الذين ابتدروا قول القائل

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r49.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r49.speaker: نحاة البصرة
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r49.claim: Basran grammarians attach the preposition bi- to an implied noun such as ibtida'i, mustaqirr or thabit, making the whole basmala nominative in their analysis.
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r49.anchor: والباء في بسم الله متعلقة عند نحاة البصرة

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r50.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r50.speaker: نحاة الكوفة
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r50.claim: Kufan grammarians attach bi- to an implied verb, “I begin,” and parse the basmala as accusative.
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r50.anchor: وعند نحاة الكوفة بفعل تقديره : ابتدأت

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r51.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r51.speaker: سيبويه
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r51.claim: Ibn Atiyya says Sibawayh apparently attaches bi- to a noun, yet treats the phrase as accusative through attachment to thabit or mustaqirr, like Zayd is in the house.
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r51.anchor: والظاهر من مذهب سيبويه أن الباء متعلقة باسم كما تقدم . وبسم الله في موضع نصب تعلقا بثابت أو مستقر

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r52.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r52.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r52.claim: The kasra on bi- is explained as matching its grammatical action, because it governs nouns, or to distinguish it from particles that can also be nouns.
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r52.anchor: وكسرت باء الجر ليناسب لفظها عملها

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r53.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r53.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r53.claim: Al-A'sha's use of kaf is cited as an example of a particle that can function as a noun, motivating a distinctive genitive mark for bi-.
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r53.anchor: أو ليفرق بينها وبين ما قد يكون من الحروف اسما نحو الكاف في قول الأعشى

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r54.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r54.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r54.claim: The alif is omitted from the written basmala for brevity and ease because the phrase is so frequently used.
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r54.anchor: وحذفت الألف من بسم الله في الخط اختصارا وتخفيفا لكثرة الاستعمال

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r55.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r55.speaker: الكسائي وسعيد الأخفش، ويحيى بن زياد
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r55.claim: Al-Kisa'i and Sa'id al-Akhfash omit the alif in bism al-Rahman and bism al-Qahir; Yahya b. Ziyad says omission applies only with Allah because that phrase is especially frequent. Ibn Atiyya says the alif remains with other names.
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r55.anchor: فقال الكسائي وسعيد الأخفش يحذف الألف

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r56.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r56.speaker: نحاة البصرة
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r56.claim: Basran grammarians derive ism from sumuww, elevation, from sama yasmu; the form is associated with either damma or kasra in the initial consonant.
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r56.anchor: وهو عند البصريين مشتق من السمو ، يقال سما يسمو

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r57.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r57.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r57.claim: The diminutive sumayy, plural asma', and plural-of-plural asami support the Basran etymology; a poetic form simahu is also cited.
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r57.anchor: وإنما استدل على هذا الأصل الذي ذكرناه

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r58.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r58.speaker: نحاة الكوفة
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r58.claim: Kufans derive ism from wasm, a mark, since a name marks its bearer; Ibn Atiyya says this sense is apt but morphology counters it, since the forms should be wasim and awsām.

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r59.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r59.speaker: الطبري
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r59.claim: Al-Tabari says the name-and-named question is not appropriate here and criticizes theologians for debating it and similar questions.
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r59.anchor: فقال الطبري رحمه الله : إنه ليس بموضع

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r60.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r60.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r60.claim: A name such as Zayd or lion can mean its referent, as in Zayd stands, or the word itself, as in lion has three letters; only in the first use does the name mean the named.
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r60.anchor: الاسم كزيد وأسد وفرس قد يرد في الكلام

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r61.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r61.speaker: أكثر أهل العلم
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r61.claim: Many scholars take name to mean the named essence in 87:1, 55:78 and 53:23; they cite Labid's line about the name of peace as a greeting.
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r61.anchor: وعلى هذا حمل أكثر أهل العلم

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r62.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r62.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r62.claim: More commonly, ism denotes the verbal name itself: examples include Adam being taught the names, the hadith of God's ninety-nine names, and grammarians' technical usage.
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r62.anchor: وقد يجري اسم في اللغة مجرى ذات العبارة وهو الأكثر من استعمالها فمنه قوله تعالى { وعلم آدم الأسماء كلها }

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r63.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r63.speaker: مالك
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r63.claim: When asked whether the name is the named, Malik answered that it is neither it nor other than it, meaning this is not true in every context.
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r63.anchor: ومر بي أن مالكا رحمه الله سئل عن الاسم أهو المسمى فقال ليس به ولا هو غيره

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r64.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r64.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r64.claim: Allah is the most striking and frequently used of God's names, usually preceding the others, which generally function as attributes.
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r64.anchor: أبهر أسماء الله تعالى وأكثرها استعمالا

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r65.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r65.speaker: فرقة من أهل العلم
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r65.claim: One group of scholars treats Allah as an un-derived proper name, with alif-lam integral to the name rather than a marker of definiteness.
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r65.anchor: فقالت فرقة من أهل العلم هو اسم مرتجل لا اشتقاق له من فعل وإنما هو اسم موضوع له تبارك وتعالى

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r66.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r66.speaker: كثير من أهل العلم
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r66.claim: Many scholars derive Allah from alaha, worship, or ta'allaha, devotion; Ibn Abbas and others gloss the Qur'anic wa-alihatak in 7:127 as your worship.
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r66.anchor: وذهب كثير من أهل العلم إلى أنه مشتق من أله الرجل إذا عبد وتأله إذا تنسك

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r67.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r67.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r67.claim: Three accounts explain the change from ilah to Allah: irregular loss of hamza before alif-lam, alif-lam added to ilah with hamza-vowel transfer and lam assimilation, or an original lah; Ibn Atiyya favors the first.
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r67.anchor: فقيل حذفت الهمزة حذفا على غير قياس

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r68.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r68.speaker: الخليل
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r68.claim: Al-Khalil says the original was ilah or walah, with hamza substituted for waw as in ishaḥ/wishaḥ and isadah/wisadah.
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r68.anchor: وروي عن الخليل أن أصل إله ولاه وأن الهمزة مبدلة من واو

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r69.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r69.speaker: قيل
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r69.claim: Another account derives the word from walah, bewilderment: intellects are bewildered by the realities of God's attributes and by thought about knowing Him.

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r70.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r70.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r70.claim: The final alif of Allah is said to be omitted to distinguish its script from al-Lat, for ease, or as a dialect form; Ibn al-A'rabi's verse is cited for the latter.
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r70.anchor: وحذفت الألف الأخيرة من الله لئلا يشكل بخط اللات ، وقيل طرحت تخفيفا

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r71.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r71.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r71.claim: Al-Rahman is an intensive form from mercy, reaching its utmost limit and belonging specifically to God; rahim exceeds rahim as a description of one who showed mercy once, while al-Rahman marks the utmost degree.
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r71.anchor: والرحمن صفة مبالغة من الرحمة ومعناها أنه انتهى إلى غاية الرحمة

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r72.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r72.speaker: بعض الناس
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r72.claim: Some say al-Rahman and al-Rahim share the same meaning and root, like nadman and nadim, with one form more emphatic.
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r72.anchor: وقال بعض الناس : الرحمن الرحيم بمعنى واحد

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r73.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r73.speaker: العرزمي
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r73.claim: Al-Arzami explains al-Rahman as mercy to all creation through rain, senses and general blessings, and al-Rahim as mercy to believers through guidance and kindness.

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r74.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r74.speaker: أبو سعيد الخدري وابن مسعود عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r74.claim: Abu Sa'id al-Khudri and Ibn Mas'ud report the Prophet explaining al-Rahman as merciful in this world and the next, al-Rahim as merciful in the next world.
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r74.anchor: أن أبا سعيد الخدري وابن مسعود رويا

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r75.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r75.speaker: أبو علي الفارسي
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r75.claim: Abu Ali al-Farisi says al-Rahman names God's mercy in all its kinds and is exclusive to Him, while al-Rahim is for believers, as 33:43 says; Ibn Atiyya says the readings reinforce one another.
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r75.anchor: وقال أبو علي الفارسي : الرحمن اسم عام

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r76.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r76.speaker: عطاء الخراساني
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r76.claim: Ata al-Khurasani says God paired al-Rahman with al-Rahim after Musaylima adopted the name al-Rahman, making the combination exclusive to God.

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r77.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r77.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r77.claim: Ibn Atiyya rejects Ata's account as weak: the basmala preceded Musaylima's rise, and Musaylima's use of the name did not become established.
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r77.anchor: وهذا قول ضعيف لأن بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم كان قبل أن ينجم أمر مسيلمة

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r78.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r78.speaker: قوم
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r78.claim: Some say Arabs did not know or use al-Rahman, citing their question in 25:60 about what al-Rahman is.
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r78.anchor: وقال قوم : إن العرب كانت لا تعرف لفظة الرحمن

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r79.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r79.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r79.claim: Ibn Atiyya rejects that lexical claim: the Arabs objected to identifying the deity they were ordered to worship, not to the word al-Rahman itself.
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r79.anchor: وإنما وقفت العرب على تعيين الإله الذي أمروا بالسجود له لا على نفس اللفظة

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r80.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r80.speaker: أم سلمة عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r80.claim: A report from Umm Salama says the Prophet paused on the sukun of rahim, stopped there, and began al-hamd with a hamzat al-qat'; some Kufans recited this way.
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r80.anchor: فروي عن أم سلمة عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r81.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r81.speaker: جمهور الناس
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r81.claim: Most reciters read al-rahimi l-hamdu with the genitive ending and connect the alif of al-hamd.

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r82.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r82.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r82.claim: The connected reading can be explained by positing a pause on a silent mim, then voicing it to avoid adjacent sukun letters without treating the hamza of al as cut; Ibn Atiyya finds the simpler account more concise.
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r82.anchor: ومن شاء أن يقدر أنه أسكن الميم ثم لما وصل حركها للالتقاء ولم يعتد بألف الوصل فذلك سائغ والأول أخصر

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r83.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r83.speaker: الكسائي
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r83.claim: Al-Kisa'i reports an Arab reading al-rahima al-hamdu with a fatḥa on mim and a connected alif, explained by transferring the hamza's vowel to the mim after elision.

IBNATIYYA:1:1/r84.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r84.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r84.claim: Ibn Atiyya knows no one who transmitted al-Kisa'i's form as a recognized reading; it matches Yahya b. Ziyad's grammatical analysis of Alif Lam Mim Allah.
IBNATIYYA:1:1/r84.anchor: ولم ترو هذه قراءةً عن أحد فيما علمت

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r1.speaker: ابن عمر
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r1.claim: Ibn ʿUmar says the basmala was revealed in every sūra.
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r1.anchor: قال ابن عمر نزلت في كل سورة

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r2.speaker: العلماء
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r2.claim: Scholars disagree whether the basmala is a complete verse; Aḥmad has two transmitted positions.
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r2.anchor: وقد اختلف العلماء هل هي آية كاملة أم لا وفيه عن أحمد روايتان

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r3.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r3.speaker: العلماء
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r3.claim: Scholars also disagree whether it is part of al-Fātiḥa; two positions are transmitted from Aḥmad.
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r3.anchor: واختلفوا هل هي من الفاتحة أم لا فيه عن أحمد روايتان أيضا

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r4.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r4.speaker: القائلون إنها من الفاتحة
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r4.claim: Those who count it as part of al-Fātiḥa require its recitation in prayer because al-Fātiḥa itself is obligatory.
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r4.anchor: فأما من قال إنها من الفاتحة فانه يوجب قرائتها في الصلاة إذا قال فوجوب الفاتحة

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r5.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r5.speaker: القائلون إنها ليست من الفاتحة
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r5.claim: Those who do not count it as part of al-Fātiḥa regard reciting it in prayer as sunnah, while Mālik does not recommend its recitation.
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r5.anchor: وأما من لم يرها من الفاتحة فإنه يقول قراءتها في الصلاة سنة ما عدا مالكا فانه لا يستحب قراءتها

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r6.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r6.speaker: أحمد ومن وافقه
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r6.claim: Aḥmad and the listed Companions and early authorities do not regard reciting the basmala aloud in audible prayers as recommended.
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r6.anchor: فنقل جماعة عن أحمد أنه لا يسن الجهر بها وهو قول أبي بكر وعمر وعثمان وعلي وابن مسعود

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r7.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r7.speaker: الشافعي
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r7.claim: Al-Shāfiʿī recommends reciting the basmala aloud; this view is also reported from Muʿāwiya, ʿAṭāʾ, Ṭāwūs, and Mujāhid.
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r7.anchor: وذهب الشافعي إلى أن الجهر مسنون وهو مروي عن معاوية بن أبي سفيان وعطاء وطاووس ومجاهد

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r8.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r8.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r8.claim: Bismillāh is elliptical for I begin or I began in God's name.
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r8.anchor: قوله بسم الله اختصار كانه قال أبدأ بسم الله أو بدأت باسم الله

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r9.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r9.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r9.claim: The word ism has five reported forms, including ism, asm, sim, sum, and samā; the cited poetry witnesses these forms.
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r9.anchor: وفي الإسم خمس لغات إسم بكسر الألف وأسم بضم الألف إذا ابتدات بها وسم بكسر السين وسم بضمها وسما

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r10.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r10.speaker: الفراء
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r10.claim: Al-Farrāʾ records forms with smah among some Qays speakers and some Quḍāʿa speakers, citing a line that uses the form.
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r10.anchor: قال الفراء بعض قيس يقولون سمه يريدون اسمه وبعض قضاعة يقولون سمه

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r11.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r11.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r11.claim: Qarḍāb means a cutter, and a sword can be called qarḍāb.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r12.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r12.speaker: العلماء
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r12.claim: Scholars disagree whether the divine name Allāh is derived or an underived proper name.
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r12.anchor: واختلف العلماء في اسم الله الذي هو الله فقال قوم مشتق وقال آخرون إنه علم ليس بمشتق

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r13.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r13.speaker: الخليل
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r13.claim: One view attributed to al-Khalīl says Allāh is not derived and its alif-lām cannot be dropped as it can from al-Raḥmān.
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r13.anchor: إحداهما أنه ليس بمشتق ولا يجوز حذف الألف واللام منه كما يجوز من الرحمن

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r14.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r14.speaker: الخليل عن سيبويه
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r14.claim: A second report from al-Khalīl, transmitted by Sībawayh, holds that Allāh is derived.
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r14.anchor: والثانية رواها عنه سيبويه انه مشتق

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r15.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r15.speaker: أبو سليمان الخطابي
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r15.claim: Al-Khaṭṭābī transmits an etymology from a-l-h, meaning to seek refuge; God is so named as the one who protects and grants safety.
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r15.anchor: ذكر أبو سليمان الخطابي عن بعض العلماء أن أصله في الكلام مشتق من أله الرجل يأله إذا فزع إليه

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r16.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r16.speaker: غيره
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r16.claim: Another etymology derives Allāh from wālah, with initial wāw changed into hamza, as in wisāda and wishāḥ becoming ishāḥ.
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p7/r16.anchor: وقال غيره أصله ولاه فأبدلت الواو همزة فقيل إله كما قالوا وسادة ووشاح وإشاح

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p9/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p9/r1.speaker: بعضهم
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p9/r1.claim: Some derive the divine name from bewilderment: hearts are bewildered when contemplating God's greatness.
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p9/r1.anchor: وقال بعضهم أصله من أله الرجل يأله إذا تحير لأن القلوب تتحير عند التفكر في عظمته

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p9/r2.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p9/r2.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p9/r2.claim: The derivation from hearts' longing is linked to 16:53, where people call upon God in distress.
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p9/r2.anchor: واشتق من الوله لأن قلوب العباد توله نحوه كقوله تعالى ﴿ ثم إذا مسكم الضر فإليه تجأرون ﴾ النحل 53

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p9/r3.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p9/r3.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p9/r3.claim: On the derivation from longing, the expected form would be maʾlūh like maʿbūd, but it diverges from that pattern to become a proper name, as kitāb and ḥisāb do.
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p9/r3.anchor: وكان القياس أن يقال مألوه كما قيل معبود إلا أنهم خالفوا به البناء ليكون علما كما قالوا للمكتوب كتاب

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p9/r4.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p9/r4.speaker: بعض اللغويين
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p9/r4.claim: Some linguists derive the word from alaha yaʾlah, meaning to worship.
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p9/r4.anchor: وحكي عن بعض اللغويين أله الرجل يأله إلاه بمعنى عبد يعبد عبادة

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p9/r5.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p9/r5.speaker: ابن عباس
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p9/r5.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās glosses Pharaoh's reference to his gods at 7:127 as your worship; taʾalluh means worship, and the deity is the worshiped one.
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p9/r5.anchor: وروي عن ابن عباس انه قال ﴿ ويذرك وآلهتك ﴾ الأعراف 127 أي عبادتك قال والتأله التعبد

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p9/r6.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p9/r6.speaker: رؤبة
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p9/r6.claim: A line by Ruʾba uses taʾalluh as evidence for the worship-related derivation.
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p9/r6.anchor: قال رؤبة لله در الغانيات المده سبحن واسترجعن من تألهي

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p9/r7.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p9/r7.speaker: الجمهور
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p9/r7.claim: Most scholars derive al-Raḥmān from mercy as an intensive form, meaning the possessor of unmatched mercy; faʿlān marks intensity.
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p9/r7.anchor: فذهب الجمهور إلى أنه مشتق من الرحمة مبني على المبالغة ومعناه ذو الرحمة التي لا نظير له فيها

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p9/r8.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p9/r8.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p9/r8.claim: The intensive pattern faʿlān is illustrated by words for someone very full or very satiated.
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p9/r8.anchor: وبناء فعلان في كلامهم للمبالغة فانهم يقولون للشديد الامتلاء ملآن وللشديد الشبع شبعان

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p9/r9.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p9/r9.speaker: الخطابي
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p9/r9.claim: Al-Khaṭṭābī says al-Raḥmān's encompassing mercy covers creatures' provisions and interests and includes believers and unbelievers.
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p9/r9.anchor: قال الخطابي في الرحمن ذو الرحمة الشاملة التي وسعت الخلق في أرزاقهم ومصالحهم وعمت المؤمن والكافر

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p9/r11.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p9/r11.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p9/r11.claim: Abū Hurayra reports that the Prophet said no comparable sūra was revealed in the Torah, Gospel, Psalms, or Qur'an; al-Fātiḥa is the seven oft-repeated verses and the great Qur'an given to him.
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p9/r11.anchor: روى أبو هريرة أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم قال وقرأ عليه أبي بن كعب أم القرأن فقال والذي نفسي بيده ما أنزل في التوراة ولا في الانجيل

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p9/r12.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p9/r12.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p9/r12.claim: Al-Fātiḥa is so named because the book begins with it in recitation and writing; Umm al-Qur'an and Umm al-Kitāb because it leads the book; al-sabʿ al-mathānī is explained later in 15:87.
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p9/r12.anchor: فمن أسمائها الفاتحة لأنه يستفتح الكتاب بها تلاوة وكتابة ومن أسمائها أم القرأن وأم الكتاب لأنها أمت الكتاب بالتقدم

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p9/r13.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p9/r13.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب والحسن وأبو العالية وقتادة وأبو ميسرة
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p9/r13.claim: One view holds that al-Fātiḥa was revealed in Mecca.
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p9/r13.anchor: أحدهما أنها مكية وهو مروي عن علي بن أبي طالب والحسن وأبي القالية وقتادة وأبي ميسرة

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p9/r14.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p9/r14.speaker: أبو هريرة ومجاهد وعبيد بن عمير وعطاء الخراساني
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p9/r14.claim: A second view holds that al-Fātiḥa was revealed in Medina; Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to have held both views.
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p9/r14.anchor: والثاني أنها مدنية وهو مروي عن أبي هريرة ومجاهد وعبيد بن عمير وعطاء الخراساني وعن ابن عباس كالقولين

KASHSHAF:1:1/r1.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:1:1/r1.speaker: قراء المدينة والبصرة والشام وفقهاؤها
KASHSHAF:1:1/r1.claim: Medina, Basra, and Syrian readers and jurists hold that the basmala is not a verse of al-Fatiha or any surah.
KASHSHAF:1:1/r1.anchor: قرّاء المدينة والبصرة والشام وفقهاؤها على أنّ التسمية ليست بآية من الفاتحة ولا من غيرها من السور

KASHSHAF:1:1/r2.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:1:1/r2.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:1:1/r2.claim: It was written to separate surahs and seek blessing by beginning with it, as people begin important acts with it.
KASHSHAF:1:1/r2.anchor: وإنما كتبت للفصل والتبرك بالابتداء بها ، كما بدىء بذكرها في كل أمر ذي بال

KASHSHAF:1:1/r3.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:1:1/r3.speaker: أبو حنيفة ومن تابعه
KASHSHAF:1:1/r3.claim: Abu Hanifa and his followers share that position and therefore do not recite it aloud in prayer.
KASHSHAF:1:1/r3.anchor: وهو مذهب أبي حنيفة - رحمه الله - ومن تابعه ، ولذلك لا يجهر بها عندهم في الصلاة

KASHSHAF:1:1/r4.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:1:1/r4.speaker: قراء مكة والكوفة وفقهاؤهما
KASHSHAF:1:1/r4.claim: Meccan and Kufan readers and jurists, with al-Shafii and followers, count it as a verse of al-Fatiha and every surah.
KASHSHAF:1:1/r4.anchor: وقرّاء مكة والكوفة وفقهاؤهما على أنها آية من الفاتحة ومن كل سورة ، وعليه الشافعي وأصحابه

KASHSHAF:1:1/r5.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:1:1/r5.speaker: قراء مكة والكوفة وفقهاؤهما
KASHSHAF:1:1/r5.claim: Because they count it as a verse, this group recites it aloud in prayer.
KASHSHAF:1:1/r5.anchor: وعليه الشافعي وأصحابه رحمهم الله ، ولذلك يجهرون بها

KASHSHAF:1:1/r6.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:1:1/r6.speaker: قراء مكة والكوفة وفقهاؤهما
KASHSHAF:1:1/r6.claim: Their proof is that early Muslims included it in the codex while requiring the Quran be stripped of additions, but omitted Amin.
KASHSHAF:1:1/r6.anchor: وقالوا : قد أثبتها السلف في المصحف مع توصيتهم بتجريد القرآن

KASHSHAF:1:1/r7.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:1:1/r7.speaker: ابن عباس
KASHSHAF:1:1/r7.claim: Ibn Abbas says whoever omits the basmala has omitted 114 verses of God's Book.
KASHSHAF:1:1/r7.anchor: وعن ابن عباس : «من تركها فقد ترك مائة وأربع عشرة آية من كتاب الله تعالى »

KASHSHAF:1:1/r8.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:1:1/r8.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:1:1/r8.claim: The prefixed bā attaches to an omitted verb, understood as I read or recite in God's name.
KASHSHAF:1:1/r8.anchor: بمحذوف تقديره : بسم الله اقرأ أو أتلو ؛ لأن الذي يتلو التسمية مقروء

KASHSHAF:1:1/r9.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:1:1/r9.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:1:1/r9.claim: Travel formulas, slaughter, and acts begun in God's name similarly omit the verb that states the introduced act.
KASHSHAF:1:1/r9.anchor: وكذلك الذابح وكل فاعل يبدأ في فعله ؛ ب «بسم الله » كان مضمرا ما جعل التسمية مبدأ له

KASHSHAF:1:1/r10.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:1:1/r10.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:1:1/r10.claim: The omitted governor in 27:12 is understood as go with nine signs to Pharaoh and his people.
KASHSHAF:1:1/r10.anchor: ونظيره في حذف متعلق الجار قوله عز وجل : { في تسع آيات إلى فرعون وقومه } [ النمل : 12 ]

KASHSHAF:1:1/r11.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:1:1/r11.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:1:1/r11.claim: Wedding and blessing formulas omit a verb meaning you wed; the cited verse about going to food is another ellipsis example.
KASHSHAF:1:1/r11.anchor: وكذلك قول العرب في الدعاء للمعرس : بالرفاء والبنين ، وقول الأعرابي : باليمن والبركة

KASHSHAF:1:1/r12.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:1:1/r12.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:1:1/r12.claim: The omitted verb follows the basmala because God's name is the focus: fronting it gives exclusive force against beginning in idol names.
KASHSHAF:1:1/r12.anchor: لأنهم كانوا يبدءون بأسماء آلهتهم فيقولون : باسم اللات ، باسم العزى

KASHSHAF:1:1/r13.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:1:1/r13.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:1:1/r13.claim: This exclusivity resembles the fronted object in 1:5 and is supported by 11:41.
KASHSHAF:1:1/r13.anchor: وذلك بتقديمه وتأخير الفعل كما فعل في قوله : { إياك نعبد } ، حيث صرح بتقديم الاسم

KASHSHAF:1:1/r14.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:1:1/r14.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:1:1/r14.claim: Though 96:1 puts the verb first, there the command to read took precedence because it opened the first surah revealed.
KASHSHAF:1:1/r14.anchor: فإن قلت : فقد قال : { اقرأ باسم ربك } [ العلق : 1 ] ، فقدّم الفعل

KASHSHAF:1:1/r15.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:1:1/r15.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:1:1/r15.claim: One analysis makes bā instrumental: a believer's act is not legally sound or in keeping with Sunna unless begun in God's name.

KASHSHAF:1:1/r16.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:1:1/r16.speaker: النبي
KASHSHAF:1:1/r16.claim: The instrumental analysis invokes the Prophetic saying that an important matter begun without God's name is incomplete.
KASHSHAF:1:1/r16.anchor: كل أمر ذي بال لم يبدأ فيه باسم الله فهو أبتر

KASHSHAF:1:1/r17.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:1:1/r17.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:1:1/r17.claim: The other analysis makes bā mean accompaniment and blessing, as in a plant growing with oil; al-Zamakhshari calls this clearer and better.
KASHSHAF:1:1/r17.anchor: والثاني أن يتعلق بها تعلق الدهن بالإنبات في قوله : { تنبت بالدهن } [ المؤمنون : 20 ]

KASHSHAF:1:1/r18.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:1:1/r18.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:1:1/r18.claim: The words are spoken on servants' tongues, as when one recites poetry for another; the Quran teaches blessing and praise.
KASHSHAF:1:1/r18.anchor: هذا مقول على ألسنة العباد ، كما يقول الرجل الشعر على لسان غيره

KASHSHAF:1:1/r19.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:1:1/r19.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:1:1/r19.claim: The genitive lām is kasra to distinguish it from the emphatic lām; bā is kasra because it is inherently a particle governing the genitive.
KASHSHAF:1:1/r19.anchor: أما اللام فللفصل بينها وبين لام الابتداء ، وأما الباء فلكونها لازمة للحرفية والجر

KASHSHAF:1:1/r20.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:1:1/r20.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:1:1/r20.claim: Ism begins with a helping hamza initially because its first consonant is quiescent; in connected speech no addition is needed.
KASHSHAF:1:1/r20.anchor: والاسم أحد الأسماء العشرة التي بنوا أوائلها على السكون ، فإذا نطقوا بها مبتدئين زادوا همزة

KASHSHAF:1:1/r21.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:1:1/r21.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:1:1/r21.claim: Some omit the helping hamza and instead move the quiescent consonant, saying sim or sum.
KASHSHAF:1:1/r21.anchor: ومنهم من لم يزدها واستغنى عنها بتحريك الساكن ، فقال : سم وسم

KASHSHAF:1:1/r22.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:1:1/r22.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:1:1/r22.claim: Ism has a deleted ending like yad and dam; asma and sammaytu show its original sumu and derivation from elevation.
KASHSHAF:1:1/r22.anchor: وهو من الأسماء المحذوفة الأعجاز : كيد ودم ، وأصله : سمو ، بدليل تصريفه : كأسماء

KASHSHAF:1:1/r23.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:1:1/r23.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:1:1/r23.claim: Naming raises the named one's standing; nabz derives from a word meaning raised voice and also means upper palm bark.
KASHSHAF:1:1/r23.anchor: لأن التسمية تنويه بالمسمى وإشادة بذكره ، ومنه قيل للقب النبز : من النبز بمعنى النبر

KASHSHAF:1:1/r24.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:1:1/r24.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:1:1/r24.claim: The written alif is dropped by analogy with connected pronunciation; the bā is lengthened to compensate for the omission.
KASHSHAF:1:1/r24.anchor: قد اتبعوا في حذفها حكم الدرج دون الابتداء الذي عليه وضع الخط لكثرة الاستعمال

KASHSHAF:1:1/r25.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:1:1/r25.speaker: عمر بن عبد العزيز
KASHSHAF:1:1/r25.claim: Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz told his scribe to lengthen bā, show tooth-like strokes, and round mīm.
KASHSHAF:1:1/r25.anchor: وعن عمر بن عبد العزيز أنه قال لكاتبه : طوّل الباء وأظهر السنات ودوّر الميم

KASHSHAF:1:1/r26.author: al-Zamakhsharī
KASHSHAF:1:1/r26.speaker: author
KASHSHAF:1:1/r26.claim: Allah derives from al-ilah, with hamza removed; al-nas likewise derives from al-unas, with the hamza replaced by the article.
KASHSHAF:1:1/r26.anchor: قال : معاذ الإله أن تكون كظبيةٍ
